question: A company hosts more than 300 global websites and applications. The company requires a platform to analyze more than 30 TB of clickstream data each day. What should a solutions architect do to transmit and process the clickstream data?
options: Design an AWS Data Pipeline to archive the data to an Amazon S3 bucket and run an Amazon EMR cluster with the data to generate analytics.
Create an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 instances to process the data and send it to an Amazon S3 data lake for Amazon Redshift to use for analysis.
Cache the data to Amazon CloudFront. Store the data in an Amazon S3 bucket. When an object is added to the S3 bucket. run an AWS Lambda function to process the data for analysis.
Collect the data from Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to transmit the data to an Amazon S3 data lake. Load the data in Amazon Redshift for analysis.
explanation: The correct answer is D. Option A (INCORRECT): AWS Data Pipeline is designed for batch-oriented ETL workflows rather than high-throughput, real-time streaming ingestion. Managing and scheduling EMR jobs daily to process 30 TB of clickstream data adds significant operational overhead and latency. Option B (INCORRECT): Auto Scaling EC2 instances for custom data processing requires you to build, manage, and scale your own streaming pipeline. This approach increases operational complexity and is not as elastic or fault-tolerant as managed streaming services. Option C (INCORRECT): Amazon CloudFront is a CDN for content delivery, not a data ingestion service for clickstream analytics. Invoking AWS Lambda per S3 object add would face concurrency limits and high overhead when processing tens of terabytes daily. Option D (CORRECT): Amazon Kinesis Data Streams provides a scalable, fault-tolerant stream for ingesting clickstream events in real time. Kinesis Data Firehose can buffer and automatically deliver the data into an S3 data lake with minimal management overhead. Using Redshift’s COPY command from S3 enables fast, cost-efficient analytics on large volumes of clickstream data. In summary, using Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with Kinesis Data Firehose and Amazon Redshift provides a fully managed, highly scalable, and performant solution for ingesting, storing, and analyzing over 30 TB of clickstream data per day. This question belongs to Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company is building a new dynamic ordering website. The company wants to minimize server maintenance and patching. The website must be highly available and must scale read and write capacity as quickly as possible to meet changes in user demand.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Host static content in Amazon S3. Host dynamic content by using Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda. Use Amazon DynamoDB with on-demand capacity for the database. Configure Amazon CloudFront to deliver the website content.

Host static content in Amazon S3. Host dynamic content by using Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda. Use Amazon Aurora with Aurora Auto Scaling for the database. Configure Amazon CloudFront to deliver the website content.

Host all the website content on Amazon EC2 instances. Create an Auto Scaling group to scale the EC2 instances. Use an Application Load Balancer to distribute traffic. Use Amazon DynamoDB with provisioned write capacity for the database.

Host all the website content on Amazon EC2 instances. Create an Auto Scaling group to scale the EC2 instances. Use an Application Load Balancer to distribute traffic. Use Amazon Aurora with Aurora Auto Scaling for the database.
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): Although Amazon Aurora with Auto Scaling is a managed relational database, it still requires patching windows and doesn’t scale write capacity as instantly as DynamoDB on-demand. Relational engines introduce additional maintenance overhead (engine upgrades, parameter tuning) compared to a fully serverless NoSQL solution. Option C (INCORRECT): Hosting dynamic content on EC2 instances means you must manage, patch, and scale servers yourself. Using DynamoDB with provisioned capacity can lead to throttling or over-provisioning; it doesn’t automatically adjust to sudden demand spikes. Option D (INCORRECT): EC2 instances introduce server maintenance and patching responsibilities. Aurora Auto Scaling doesn’t match the instantaneous, push-button scaling of DynamoDB on-demand for both reads and writes. Option A (CORRECT): Static assets in S3 + CloudFront provide a highly available, globally distributed cache with zero server maintenance. API Gateway + Lambda delivers dynamic content with a fully managed, serverless compute layer—no patching or provisioning. DynamoDB on-demand scales read/write capacity instantly to handle unpredictable traffic patterns without throttling or planning. In summary, the serverless stack in Option A eliminates server maintenance, provides instantaneous scaling for both application and database layers, and ensures high availability. This question tests Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company runs a critical data analysis job each week before the first day of the work week. The job requires at least 1 hour to complete the analysis. The job is stateful and cannot tolerate interruptions. The company needs a solution to run the job on AWS. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Create a container for the job. Schedule the job to run as an AWS Fargate task on an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster by using Amazon EventBridge Scheduler.
Configure the job to run in an AWS Lambda function. Create a scheduled rule in Amazon EventBridge to invoke the Lambda function.
Configure an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 Spot Instances that run Amazon Linux. Configure a crontab entry on the instances to run the analysis.
Configure an AWS DataSync task to run the job. Configure a cron expression to run the task on a schedule.
explanation: The correct answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): “Configure the job to run in an AWS Lambda function. Create a scheduled rule in Amazon EventBridge to invoke the Lambda function.” • Lambda functions have a maximum execution time of 15 minutes, which is far less than the required 1 hour. • The job is stateful and cannot tolerate restarts or timeouts—Lambda’s short-lived nature and forced cold starts make it unsuitable. Option C (INCORRECT): “Configure an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 Spot Instances that run Amazon Linux. Configure a crontab entry on the instances to run the analysis.” • Spot Instances can be interrupted by AWS with a two-minute warning, risking job failure. • The job cannot tolerate interruptions or restarts, so relying on Spot capacity is not dependable. Option D (INCORRECT): “Configure an AWS DataSync task to run the job. Configure a cron expression to run the task on a schedule.” • AWS DataSync is designed for data transfer tasks, not arbitrary data analysis workloads. • It cannot execute custom stateful analysis logic or handle job-specific dependencies. Option A (CORRECT): “Create a container for the job. Schedule the job to run as an AWS Fargate task on an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster by using Amazon EventBridge Scheduler.” Fargate runs containers without managing servers and does not impose a 15-minute execution limit. Tasks run until completion, so a 1-hour stateful job can execute without interruptions. EventBridge Scheduler provides a reliable cron-style trigger each week before business starts. You only pay for the seconds of vCPU and memory usage during the task runtime, simplifying cost management. In this discussion, we learned how to choose the right AWS compute service for a long-running, stateful job that must not be interrupted. AWS Fargate with ECS and EventBridge Scheduler ensures reliability and meets duration requirements without the complexity or interruption risks of Lambda or Spot Instances. This question falls under Domain 2 - Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A gaming company wants to launch a new internet-facing application in multiple AWS Regions. The application will use the TCP and UDP protocols for communication. The company needs to provide high availability and minimum latency for global users.Which combination of actions should a solutions architect take to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
options: Create internal Network Load Balancers in front of the application in each Region.
Create external Application Load Balancers in front of the application in each Region.
Create an AWS Global Accelerator accelerator to route traffic to the load balancers in each Region.
Configure Amazon Route 53 to use a geolocation routing policy to distribute the traffic.
Configure Amazon CloudFront to handle the traffic and route requests to the application in each Region
explanation: The correct answer is A and C. Option B (INCORRECT): Create external Application Load Balancers in front of the application in each Region. Application Load Balancers only support HTTP and HTTPS (Layer 7). They do not handle arbitrary TCP or UDP protocols. The requirement is to support both TCP and UDP traffic, so ALBs cannot meet this need. Option D (INCORRECT): Configure Amazon Route 53 to use a geolocation routing policy to distribute the traffic. Geolocation routing sends users to endpoints based on their declared location, not necessarily the nearest healthy endpoint. It does not provide built-in health checks or latency-based failover across Regions, so minimum latency and high availability are not guaranteed. Option E (INCORRECT): Configure Amazon CloudFront to handle the traffic and route requests to the application in each Region. CloudFront is designed for HTTP/HTTPS content delivery (Layer 7) and does not proxy or route arbitrary TCP/UDP traffic. It cannot front non-HTTP/HTTPS gaming protocols, so it fails the protocol requirement. Option A (CORRECT): Create internal Network Load Balancers in front of the application in each Region. Network Load Balancers operate at Layer 4 and support both TCP and UDP traffic. When paired with AWS Global Accelerator, an internal NLB can be exposed via static Accelerator IP addresses, making it accessible publicly. This design ensures high throughput, low latency, and automatic scaling across Availability Zones. Option C (CORRECT): Create an AWS Global Accelerator accelerator to route traffic to the load balancers in each Region. Global Accelerator provides two static anycast IP addresses that route user traffic to the optimal AWS Region based on health, geography, and routing policies. It supports both TCP and UDP protocols and continuously monitors endpoint health to fail over rapidly if needed. By using Global Accelerator, you minimize latency for global users and ensure high availability across Regions. Summary: We learned that for a multi-Region, TCP/UDP gaming application requiring high availability and minimal latency, the optimal solution is to deploy Network Load Balancers in each Region and front them with AWS Global Accelerator. This question belongs to Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company is developing a microservices application that will provide a search catalog for customers. The company must use REST APIs to present the frontend of the application to users. The REST APIs must access the backend services that the company hosts in containers in private VPC subnets.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Design a WebSocket API by using Amazon API Gateway. Host the application in Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) in a private subnet. Create a private VPC link for API Gateway to access Amazon ECS.

Design a REST API by using Amazon API Gateway. Host the application in Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) in a private subnet. Create a private VPC link for API Gateway to access Amazon ECS.

Design a WebSocket API by using Amazon API Gateway. Host the application in Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) in a private subnet. Create a security group for API Gateway to access Amazon ECS.
Design a REST API by using Amazon API Gateway. Host the application in Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) in a private subnet. Create a security group for API Gateway to access Amazon ECS.
explanation: The correct answer is Option B. Option A (INCORRECT): “Design a WebSocket API by using Amazon API Gateway. Host the application in Amazon ECS in a private subnet. Create a private VPC link for API Gateway to access Amazon ECS.” The requirement specifies REST APIs, not WebSocket APIs. While VPC Link is needed for private integrations, choosing WebSocket breaks the REST API requirement. Option C (INCORRECT): “Design a WebSocket API by using Amazon API Gateway. Host the application in Amazon ECS in a private subnet. Create a security group for API Gateway to access Amazon ECS.” Again, this uses WebSocket instead of REST. API Gateway private integrations require a VPC Link resource; you cannot simply assign a security group directly to API Gateway. Option D (INCORRECT): “Design a REST API by using Amazon API Gateway. Host the application in Amazon ECS in a private subnet. Create a security group for API Gateway to access Amazon ECS.” Although this uses REST as required, API Gateway in a private VPC must use a VPC Link to reach private resources. Security groups apply to the ENIs managed by the VPC Link, not directly on API Gateway; you can’t skip the VPC Link. Option B (CORRECT): “Design a REST API by using Amazon API Gateway. Host the application in Amazon ECS in a private subnet. Create a private VPC link for API Gateway to access Amazon ECS.” This meets the REST API requirement for the frontend. By deploying ECS tasks in private subnets and creating a Private VPC Link, API Gateway can securely call the containerized services without exposing them publicly. API Gateway’s VPC Link resource creates elastic network interfaces (ENIs) in your VPC, which you secure via security groups on the ENIs. In summary, we learned how to expose private backend services in ECS through API Gateway using a VPC Link for secure REST API integration. This question belongs to Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company wants to use artificial intelligence (AI) to determine the quality of its customer service calls. The company currently manages calls in four different languages, including English. The company will offer new languages in the future. The company does not have the resources to regularly maintain machine learning (ML) models. The company needs to create written sentiment analysis reports from the customer service call recordings. The customer service call recording text must be translated into English.Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose three.)
options: Use Amazon Comprehend to translate the audio recordings into English.
Use Amazon Lex to create the written sentiment analysis reports.
Use Amazon Polly to convert the audio recordings into text.
Use Amazon Transcribe to convert the audio recordings in any language into text.
Use Amazon Translate to translate text in any language to English.
Use Amazon Comprehend to create the sentiment analysis reports.
explanation: The correct answer is D, E, F. Option A (INCORRECT): Amazon Comprehend is used for natural language processing tasks such as sentiment analysis, entity recognition, and key phrase extraction on text. It does not perform audio or language translation. Option B (INCORRECT): Amazon Lex is a service for building conversational interfaces (chatbots) and not intended for sentiment analysis reporting or batch text processing. Option C (INCORRECT): Amazon Polly converts text into lifelike speech (text-to-speech). It cannot transcribe audio into text. Option D (CORRECT): Use Amazon Transcribe to convert speech in any supported language into text. It handles multiple languages and produces accurate transcripts without you having to build or maintain ML models. Option E (CORRECT): Use Amazon Translate to translate the transcript text from its original language into English. This fully managed service supports many languages and can scale automatically as you add more languages. Option F (CORRECT): Use Amazon Comprehend to perform sentiment analysis on the English-translated text and generate the written sentiment reports. In summary, we learned how to chain AWS managed AI services—Transcribe, Translate, and Comprehend—to build a multilingual sentiment-analysis pipeline without maintaining custom ML models. This question falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: An ecommerce company is migrating its on-premises workload to the AWS Cloud. The workload currently consists of a web application and a backend Microsoft SQL database for storage. The company expects a high volume of customers during a promotional event. The new infrastructure in the AWS Cloud must be highly available and scalable. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST administrative overhead?
options: Migrate the web application to two Amazon EC2 instances across two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer. Migrate the database to Amazon RDS for Microsoft SQL Server with read replicas in both Availability Zones.

Migrate the web application to an Amazon EC2 instance that runs in an Auto Scaling group across two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer. Migrate the database to two EC2 instances across separate AWS Regions with database replication.

Migrate the web application to Amazon EC2 instances that run in an Auto Scaling group across two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer. Migrate the database to Amazon RDS with Multi-AZ deployment.

Migrate the web application to three Amazon EC2 instances across three Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer. Migrate the database to three EC2 instances across three Availability Zones.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): Migrate the web application to two EC2 instances across two AZs behind an ALB and use RDS for SQL Server with read replicas in both AZs. Read replicas are intended for read-scaling and are not promoted automatically on primary failure—manual promotion adds administrative overhead. This setup does not provide automated failover for writes; you’d still have a single primary instance that could become a single point of failure. Maintaining read replicas across AZs increases complexity compared to a managed Multi-AZ deployment. Option B (INCORRECT): Use an Auto Scaling group across two AZs for the web app and run two EC2 instances in separate AWS Regions with database replication. Cross-region replication increases network latency and costs, and adds complexity to failover processes. Managing SQL Server on EC2 instances requires patching, backups, monitoring and failover orchestration—high administrative overhead. This does not leverage RDS managed failover or scaling capabilities. Option D (INCORRECT): Deploy three EC2 instances across three AZs for the app and three EC2 instances across three AZs for the database. Running SQL Server on EC2 means you must handle OS and database maintenance, backups, replication and failure recovery yourself. Provisioning and managing three database servers is complex and deviates from the “least administrative overhead” requirement. This approach ignores managed services like RDS that streamline HA and failover. Option C (CORRECT): Migrate the web application to EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across two AZs behind an Application Load Balancer, and migrate the database to Amazon RDS with Multi-AZ deployment. Auto Scaling plus ALB provides automatic scaling and distribution of traffic for the web tier without manual intervention. RDS Multi-AZ ensures synchronous data replication, automatic failover, and managed backups—minimizing administrative tasks. This design meets high availability and scalability requirements while leveraging AWS managed services for the least overhead. Summary: We evaluated four architectures and determined that only Option C leverages AWS managed services (Auto Scaling, ALB, RDS Multi-AZ) to provide high availability, scalability, and minimal administrative overhead. This question belongs to Domain 2 - Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company has 700 TB of backup data stored in network attached storage (NAS) in its data center. This backup data need to be accessible for infrequent regulatory requests and must be retained 7 years. The company has decided to migrate this backup data from its data center to AWS. The migration must be complete within 1 month. The company has 500 Mbps of dedicated bandwidth on its public internet connection available for data transfer. What should a solutions architect do to migrate and store the data at the LOWEST cost?
options: Order AWS Snowball devices to transfer the data. Use a lifecycle policy to transition the files to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
Deploy a VPN connection between the data center and Amazon VPC. Use the AWS CLI to copy the data from on premises to Amazon S3 Glacier.
Provision a 500 Mbps AWS Direct Connect connection and transfer the data to Amazon S3. Use a lifecycle policy to transition the files to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
Use AWS DataSync to transfer the data and deploy a DataSync agent on premises. Use the DataSync task to copy files from the on-premises NAS storage to Amazon S3 Glacier.
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): Deploying a VPN and using the AWS CLI to copy 700 TB over a 500 Mbps link would take far longer than one month. At 500 Mbps you can transfer roughly 160 TB in 30 days—well below the 700 TB requirement. Directly writing to S3 Glacier via the CLI isn’t supported; you must upload to S3 first then transition via lifecycle policies. Maintaining a long-lived VPN for such a bulk transfer is impractical and still bandwidth-limited. Option C (INCORRECT): Provisioning a 500 Mbps Direct Connect link also cannot move 700 TB in one month (max ~160 TB), and Direct Connect typically takes weeks to provision. Bandwidth constraint remains the same as regular internet (500 Mbps). Procuring a new Direct Connect line involves ordering, installation, and testing delays. Even after transfer, data must be stored in S3 then moved to Glacier Deep Archive via lifecycle. Option D (INCORRECT): AWS DataSync accelerates transfers over the network but cannot overcome the 500 Mbps cap—only ~160 TB in 30 days. DataSync still uses your available bandwidth; you cannot reach 700 TB in the window. DataSync writes to S3 Standard first, requiring an extra lifecycle step for deep archiving. Cost of DataSync and prolonged transfer time makes this option more expensive and slower. Option A (CORRECT): Order AWS Snowball devices to import 700 TB on-premises into AWS quickly, then use an S3 lifecycle policy to transition objects to Glacier Deep Archive. AWS Snowball can move large datasets in days rather than weeks/months over the network. Multiple Snowball devices can be ordered in parallel to complete 700 TB import within one month. Storing in S3 with a lifecycle rule to Glacier Deep Archive yields the lowest long-term storage cost. In this scenario we learned that for very large, infrequently accessed datasets—and a tight migration window—physical data transport (AWS Snowball) plus automated lifecycle to Glacier Deep Archive is the most cost-effective, timely solution. This question belongs to Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company is deploying a new public web application to AWS. The application will run behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The application needs to be encrypted at the edge with an SSL/TLS certificate that is issued by an external certificate authority (CA). The certificate must be rotated each year before the certificate expires. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
options: Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to issue an SSL/TLS certificate. Apply the certificate to the ALB. Use the managed renewal feature to automatically rotate the certificate.

Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to issue an SSL/TLS certificate. Import the key material from the certificate. Apply the certificate to the ALUse the managed renewal feature to automatically rotate the certificate.

Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) Private Certificate Authority to issue an SSL/TLS certificate from the root CA. Apply the certificate to the ALB. Use the managed renewal feature to automatically rotate the certificate.

Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to import an SSL/TLS certificate. Apply the certificate to the ALB. Use Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) to send a notification when the certificate is nearing expiration. Rotate the certificate manually.
explanation: The correct answer is D Option A (INCORRECT): “Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to issue an SSL/TLS certificate. Apply the certificate to the ALB. Use the managed renewal feature to automatically rotate the certificate.” This issues a certificate from Amazon’s public CA, not from your external CA. The requirement clearly states the certificate must be issued by an external CA. Option B (INCORRECT): “Use ACM to issue an SSL/TLS certificate. Import the key material from the certificate. Apply the certificate to the ALB. Use the managed renewal feature to automatically rotate the certificate.” You cannot import key material for a certificate that ACM issues—it manages the private key internally. Even if you could, ACM’s managed renewal only works for certificates issued by Amazon’s public CA, not for imported or external ones. Option C (INCORRECT): “Use AWS Certificate Manager Private Certificate Authority to issue an SSL/TLS certificate from the root CA. Apply the certificate to the ALB. Use the managed renewal feature to automatically rotate the certificate.” ACM Private CA issues certificates from a private (internal) CA hierarchy, not from a publicly trusted CA. Browsers will not trust a private CA root without manual trust configuration, so it cannot secure a public web application at the edge. Option D (CORRECT): “Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to import an SSL/TLS certificate. Apply the certificate to the ALB. Use Amazon EventBridge (CloudWatch Events) to send a notification when the certificate is nearing expiration. Rotate the certificate manually.” This allows you to bring in a certificate issued by your external CA, satisfying the “external CA” requirement. Imported certificates cannot be automatically renewed by ACM, so you set up EventBridge to alert you ahead of the annual expiration. You then manually upload the renewed certificate each year, ensuring continuous edge encryption without service interruption. From this discussion, we’ve learned how to meet a public-edge TLS requirement with an external CA by importing certificates into ACM and using EventBridge for renewal alerts. This scenario falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company collects data from thousands of remote devices by using a RESTful web services application that runs on an Amazon EC2 instance. The EC2 instance receives the raw data, transforms the raw data, and stores all the data in an Amazon S3 bucket. The number of remote devices will increase into the millions soon. The company needs a highly scalable solution that minimizes operational overhead. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
options: Use AWS Glue to process the raw data in Amazon S3.
Use Amazon Route 53 to route traffic to different EC2 instances.
Add more EC2 instances to accommodate the increasing amount of incoming data.
Send the raw data to Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS). Use EC2 instances to process the data.
Use Amazon API Gateway to send the raw data to an Amazon Kinesis data stream. Configure Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to use the data stream as a source to deliver the data to Amazon S3.
explanation: The correct answer is A, E Option B (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon Route 53 to route traffic to different EC2 instances.” Route 53 is a DNS service, not an application-level load balancer or streaming ingestion mechanism. It cannot buffer or queue millions of device requests nor handle data transformations. There’s no direct integration with Amazon S3 for data delivery. Option C (INCORRECT): “Add more EC2 instances to accommodate the increasing amount of incoming data.” Manual EC2 scaling increases operational overhead (patching, monitoring, capacity planning). It’s less resilient and scalable compared to fully managed services like Kinesis and Firehose. Does not provide automatic buffering or decoupling for burst traffic from millions of devices. Option D (INCORRECT): “Send the raw data to Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS). Use EC2 instances to process the data.” SQS decouples ingestion but still relies on EC2 for processing, retaining operational overhead. Pull-based SQS can introduce higher latency and complexity in scaling workers. Does not natively integrate with S3—additional code is required to batch and deliver data. Option A (CORRECT): “Use AWS Glue to process the raw data in Amazon S3.” AWS Glue is a fully managed, serverless ETL service that scales automatically—no EC2 to manage. It can crawl and catalog raw data in S3, then transform it into analytics-ready formats. Glue jobs can be triggered on S3 events or on a schedule for near real-time or batch processing. Option E (CORRECT): “Use Amazon API Gateway to send the raw data to an Amazon Kinesis data stream. Configure Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to use the data stream as a source to deliver the data to Amazon S3.” API Gateway provides a fully managed, auto-scaling REST endpoint that handles millions of device requests. Kinesis Data Streams buffers and orders incoming data, decoupling producers from consumers. Kinesis Data Firehose ingests from the stream and continuously delivers data to S3 (with optional Lambda transforms), all without EC2 management. In summary, shifting to a serverless streaming architecture (API Gateway → Kinesis Data Streams → Kinesis Data Firehose → S3) combined with serverless ETL (AWS Glue) provides a highly scalable, resilient, and low-overhead solution for ingesting, transforming, and storing data from millions of devices. This scenario belongs to Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures, as it focuses on maximizing throughput, scalability, and managed services.

question: A company recently migrated its entire IT environment to the AWS Cloud. The company discovers that users are provisioning oversized Amazon EC2 instances and modifying security group rules without using the appropriate change control process. A solutions architect must devise a strategy to track and audit these inventory and configuration changes. Which actions should the solutions architect take to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
options: Enable AWS CloudTrail and use it for auditing.
Use data lifecycle policies for the Amazon EC2 instances.
Enable AWS Trusted Advisor and reference the security dashboard.
Enable AWS Config and create rules for auditing and compliance purposes.
Restore previous resource configurations with an AWS CloudFormation template.
explanation: The correct answer is A, D Option B (INCORRECT): “Use data lifecycle policies for the Amazon EC2 instances.” Data lifecycle policies (e.g., for snapshots or Amazon S3) manage retention and deletion of data, not auditing of API calls or configuration changes. They do not provide visibility into who changed instance sizes or security group rules. Option C (INCORRECT): “Enable AWS Trusted Advisor and reference the security dashboard.” Trusted Advisor offers best-practice recommendations (cost optimization, security, fault tolerance) but does not audit every API call or track configuration drift over time. It cannot produce an audit trail of changes to instance types or security group rules. Option E (INCORRECT): “Restore previous resource configurations with an AWS CloudFormation template.” CloudFormation can deploy or roll back stacks, but it doesn’t automatically track all ad-hoc changes made outside the stack. It doesn’t provide continuous auditing or monitoring of manual configuration changes. Option A (CORRECT): “Enable AWS CloudTrail and use it for auditing.” CloudTrail records all API calls (including RunInstances, ModifyInstanceAttribute, AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress, etc.) with details on who made the call, when, and what parameters were used. You get a complete, queryable audit trail to track oversized instance provisioning and security-group modifications. Option D (CORRECT): “Enable AWS Config and create rules for auditing and compliance purposes.” AWS Config continuously records the configuration state of EC2 instances, security groups, and other resources. Custom and managed Config Rules can alert or even auto-remediate when resources drift from approved configurations (e.g., instance types, open ports). In summary, by enabling AWS CloudTrail and AWS Config, you gain both an API-level audit trail and continuous configuration monitoring to enforce your change control process. This question belongs to Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company is building an ecommerce application and needs to store sensitive customer information. The company needs to give customers the ability to complete purchase transactions on the website. The company also needs to ensure that sensitive customer data is protected, even from database administrators.Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Store sensitive data in an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. Use EBS encryption to encrypt the data. Use an IAM instance role to restrict access.
Store sensitive data in Amazon RDS for MySQL. Use AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) client-side encryption to encrypt the data.
Store sensitive data in Amazon S3. Use AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) server-side encryption to encrypt the data. Use S3 bucket policies to restrict access.
Store sensitive data in Amazon FSx for Windows Server. Mount the file share on application servers. Use Windows file permissions to restrict access.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): “Store sensitive data in an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. Use EBS encryption to encrypt the data. Use an IAM instance role to restrict access.” • EBS encryption is transparent at the block device level. Once attached to an EC2 instance, data is mounted and available in plaintext to OS administrators (including DBAs). • IAM instance role controls API actions, but does not prevent someone with OS or database privileges from reading decrypted data on the volume. Option C (INCORRECT): “Store sensitive data in Amazon S3. Use AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) server-side encryption to encrypt the data. Use S3 bucket policies to restrict access.” • Server-side encryption with SSE-KMS decrypts data when a valid GET request is made; administrators or roles with S3/KMS permissions can retrieve plaintext. • Bucket policies restrict API access, but once access is granted the data is transparently decrypted by AWS for the client, so DBAs or admins with permissions can read it. Option D (INCORRECT): “Store sensitive data in Amazon FSx for Windows Server. Mount the file share on application servers. Use Windows file permissions to restrict access.” • FSx for Windows Server uses SMB shares with Windows ACLs, but data at rest is decrypted on the server. • Any user or administrator on the underlying file server (or database) could access files if they have OS-level privileges; no strong encryption barrier protects against DBA access. Option B (CORRECT): “Store sensitive data in Amazon RDS for MySQL. Use AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) client-side encryption to encrypt the data.” • Client-side encryption ensures data is encrypted before it is sent to the database; only the application possessing KMS decrypt permissions can access plaintext. • Database administrators see only ciphertext in the database and cannot decrypt without explicit KMS decrypt permissions, satisfying the requirement to protect data even from DBAs. In this discussion we learned how client-side encryption with AWS KMS can protect sensitive data from privileged database administrators by ensuring decryption happens only in the application layer. This question falls under Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company is developing software that uses a PostgreSQL database schema. The company needs to configure multiple development environments and databases for the company's developers. On average, each development environment is used for half of the 8-hour workday.Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Configure each development environment with its own Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL database
Configure each development environment with its own Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL Single-AZ DB instances
Configure each development environment with its own Amazon Aurora On-Demand PostgreSQL-Compatible database
Configure each development environment with its own Amazon S3 bucket by using Amazon S3 Object Select
explanation: The correct answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): Configure each development environment with its own Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL database. Standard Aurora clusters incur instance-hour charges even when the database is idle. They do not auto-pause if unused, so you pay for 24×7 capacity. Not optimized for development environments that are only active half a day. Option B (INCORRECT): Configure each development environment with its own Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL Single-AZ DB instances. Single-AZ RDS instances also incur continuous hourly charges, regardless of usage. They cannot automatically pause when idle, leading to wasted cost in the unused half-day. More expensive over time compared to an on-demand or serverless option for infrequently used DEV environments. Option D (INCORRECT): Configure each development environment with its own Amazon S3 bucket by using Amazon S3 Object Select. S3 Object Select is for querying objects stored in S3, not a relational database engine. Does not provide PostgreSQL compatibility, schema enforcement, or SQL transactional capabilities. Cannot replace a managed PostgreSQL database for application development. Option C (CORRECT): Configure each development environment with its own Amazon Aurora On-Demand PostgreSQL-Compatible database. Refers to Aurora Serverless (on-demand) which scales capacity automatically and can pause when idle. You pay only for the database capacity you consume, and billing pauses when unused (development off-hours). Allows each developer to have an isolated PostgreSQL-compatible endpoint while minimizing costs. In summary, the most cost-effective solution for multiple development environments that are used only half the day is to leverage Amazon Aurora’s on-demand (serverless) capability so you pay per use and auto-pause during idle periods. This question falls under Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company that uses AWS is building an application to transfer data to a product manufacturer. The company has its own identity provider (IdP). The company wants the IdP to authenticate application users while the users use the application to transfer data. The company must use Applicability Statement 2 (AS2) protocol.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Use AWS DataSync to transfer the data. Create an AWS Lambda function for IdP authentication.
Use Amazon AppFlow flows to transfer the data. Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task for IdP authentication.
Use AWS Transfer Family to transfer the data. Create an AWS Lambda function for IdP authentication.
Use AWS Storage Gateway to transfer the data. Create an Amazon Cognito identity pool for IdP authentication.
explanation: The correct answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): “Use AWS DataSync to transfer the data. Create an AWS Lambda function for IdP authentication.” AWS DataSync does not support the AS2 protocol—it’s designed for online data transfer over NFS, SMB, or object storage endpoints, not AS2. DataSync has no built-in AS2 capabilities, so it cannot satisfy the requirement to use AS2 for data exchange with the manufacturer. Option B (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon AppFlow flows to transfer the data. Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task for IdP authentication.” Amazon AppFlow is for SaaS-to-AWS and AWS-to-AWS data integration, but it does not support the AS2 protocol. Implementing custom ECS tasks still does not overcome the lack of AS2 support in AppFlow. Option D (INCORRECT): “Use AWS Storage Gateway to transfer the data. Create an Amazon Cognito identity pool for IdP authentication.” AWS Storage Gateway provides hybrid storage services (volume, tape, file gateways) and does not support AS2 protocol transfers. Amazon Cognito identity pools are not designed to directly integrate a corporate IdP for AS2 user authentication in this scenario. Option C (CORRECT): “Use AWS Transfer Family to transfer the data. Create an AWS Lambda function for IdP authentication.” AWS Transfer Family natively supports the AS2 protocol for secure, managed file transfers with trading partners. Transfer Family allows you to integrate your own identity provider through API Gateway and AWS Lambda to authenticate users—meeting the requirement to use the company’s IdP. This solution fully satisfies both the protocol requirement (AS2) and the custom authentication requirement. In summary, AWS Transfer Family with a Lambda-based IdP integration is the only option that supports AS2 and custom user authentication. This question falls under Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures, as it addresses secure data transfer protocols and identity management.

question: A company is building a web-based application running on Amazon EC2 instances in multiple Availability Zones. The web application will provide access to a repository of text documents totaling about 900 TB in size. The company anticipates that the web application will experience periods of high demand. A solutions architect must ensure that the storage component for the text documents can scale to meet the demand of the application at all times. The company is concerned about the overall cost of the solution. Which storage solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS)
Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS)
Amazon OpenSearch Service (Amazon Elasticsearch Service)
Amazon S3
explanation: The correct answer is D Option A (INCORRECT): Amazon EBS is a block‐storage service designed for single EC2‐instance attachment. While EBS can deliver high I/O performance, it cannot natively scale across multiple Availability Zones or hundreds of terabytes without complex volume management. The 900 TB of data would require dozens of volumes, complicating management and increasing costs far beyond what S3 offers. Option B (INCORRECT): Amazon EFS provides a managed NFS file system that scales to petabytes, but its throughput‐based billing model and higher per‐GB cost make it significantly more expensive for a 900 TB repository. EFS is optimized for shared file access patterns, not for cost‐efficient, large‐volume cold or warm text storage at this scale. Option C (INCORRECT): Amazon OpenSearch Service is a search and analytics engine, not a primary storage layer for massive raw document repositories. While you could index metadata or full text for search, you would still need a durable object store for the 900 TB of documents, incurring extra costs and architectural complexity. Option D (CORRECT): Amazon S3 is an object storage service that automatically scales to exabytes of data, offers 99.999999999% durability, and provides a low per‐GB storage cost. It natively distributes data across multiple AZs, supports high concurrency during traffic spikes, and offers lifecycle policies, Intelligent-Tiering, and Glacier for further cost optimization. This makes S3 the most cost‐effective, scalable solution for a 900 TB text repository. Summary: We’ve ruled out EBS (limited to single‐instance block storage), EFS (higher cost for large, cold storage), and OpenSearch (not a primary storage layer). Amazon S3 meets all requirements—unlimited scale, high availability, pay‐as‐you‐go pricing. This scenario falls under Domain 4 – Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company’s data platform uses an Amazon Aurora MySQL database. The database has multiple read replicas and multiple DB instances across different Availability Zones. Users have recently reported errors from the database that indicate that there are too many connections. The company wants to reduce the failover time by 20% when a read replica is promoted to primary writer.Which solution will meet this requirement?
options: Switch from Aurora to Amazon RDS with Multi-AZ cluster deployment.
Use Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the Aurora database.
Switch to Amazon DynamoDB with DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) for read connections.
Switch to Amazon Redshift with relocation capability.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): “Switch from Aurora to Amazon RDS with Multi-AZ cluster deployment.” Amazon RDS Multi-AZ deployments involve synchronous replication with a standby, but failover times (~60–120 seconds) are typically longer than Aurora’s built-in failover. Switching away from Aurora forfeits features like read-replica auto-promotion and fast crash recovery that already minimize downtime. This change would not necessarily achieve a 20% reduction in failover time and requires a major migration effort. Option C (INCORRECT): “Switch to Amazon DynamoDB with DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) for read connections.” DynamoDB is a NoSQL key-value store, not a drop-in replacement for Aurora MySQL relational workloads. Migrating schema, SQL queries, transactions and existing applications would be a large-scale rework. Although DAX speeds up reads, it does not address relational connections or writer failover scenarios. Option D (INCORRECT): “Switch to Amazon Redshift with relocation capability.” Amazon Redshift is a data warehouse service intended for analytics, not an OLTP relational database. Relocation capability moves clusters between AZs, but it’s optimized for administrative activities, not reducing primary-writer promotion time. This approach does not solve connection-pool exhaustion on an operational MySQL workload. Option B (CORRECT): “Use Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the Aurora database.” RDS Proxy pools and shares database connections, reducing the total number of open connections and avoiding “too many connections” errors. During failover or replica promotion, clients remain connected to the proxy endpoint; the proxy swiftly redirects traffic to the new writer, cutting failover time by over 20%. No major application or database migration is required—just configure the proxy and update the connection string. Summary: By introducing Amazon RDS Proxy, we both solve the “too many connections” issue and speed up primary-writer promotion by over 20%, without rearchitecting the database tier. This question falls under Domain 2 – Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company uses an Amazon EC2 instance to run a script to poll for and process messages in an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. The company wants to reduce operational costs while maintaining its ability to process a growing number of messages that are added to the queue.What should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?
options: Increase the size of the EC2 instance to process messages faster.
Use Amazon EventBridge to turn off the EC2 instance when the instance is underutilized.
Migrate the script on the EC2 instance to an AWS Lambda function with the appropriate runtime.
Use AWS Systems Manager Run Command to run the script on demand.
explanation: The correct answer is C_x000D_ _x000D_ Option A (INCORRECT): Increasing the size of the EC2 instance only boosts processing speed at a higher cost. It does not address automated scaling or reduce operational overhead as the message volume grows._x000D_ _x000D_ _x000D_ Option B (INCORRECT): Using EventBridge to turn off the EC2 instance when underutilized still requires you to manage EC2 lifecycles, patching, and polling logic. It does not dynamically scale out to handle spikes in queue messages, nor minimizes operational burden._x000D_ _x000D_ _x000D_ Option D (INCORRECT): Running the script on demand via Systems Manager Run Command simply shifts invocation control but still relies on EC2 instance management and a polling model. It does not inherently scale with queue depth or reduce the need to manage servers._x000D_ _x000D_ _x000D_ Option C (CORRECT): Migrating the polling and processing logic to an AWS Lambda function with the appropriate runtime: _x000D_ _x000D_ Eliminates EC2 operational overhead—no servers to provision, patch, or monitor._x000D_ Automatically scales out in response to the number of SQS messages (when using Lambda event source mapping for SQS)._x000D_ Charges only for actual execution time and request count, reducing cost when message volume is low and seamlessly handling growth._x000D_ _x000D_ _x000D_ _x000D_ _x000D_ In summary, by moving from a constantly running EC2 polling script to an AWS Lambda function, you achieve automatic scaling, lower operational overhead, and pay-per-use pricing. question: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The application uses a database that runs on an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. The application performs slowly when traffic increases. The database experiences a heavy read load during periods of high traffic. Which actions should a solutions architect take to resolve these performance issues? (Choose two.)
options: Turn on auto scaling for the DB instance.
Create a read replica for the DB instance. Configure the application to send read traffic to the read replica.
Convert the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment. Configure the application to send read traffic to the standby DB instance.
Create an Amazon ElastiCache cluster. Configure the application to cache query results in the ElastiCache cluster.
Configure the Auto Scaling group subnets to ensure that the EC2 instances are provisioned in the same Availability Zone as the DB instance.
explanation: The correct answer is B, D Option A (INCORRECT): “Turn on auto scaling for the DB instance.” RDS storage autoscaling only adjusts storage size, not compute capacity. There is no built-in auto scaling for CPU/Memory on a standalone RDS for PostgreSQL instance. To scale compute, you’d need to manually change the instance class or use Aurora Serverless, which is not the scenario here. Option C (INCORRECT): “Convert the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment. Configure the application to send read traffic to the standby DB instance.” Multi-AZ provides high availability and failover support, but the standby is not accessible for read operations under normal operations. You cannot direct read traffic to the standby—reads still go to the primary, so this does not alleviate read load. Option E (INCORRECT): “Configure the Auto Scaling group subnets to ensure that the EC2 instances are provisioned in the same Availability Zone as the DB instance.” Latency differences across AZs are minimal in AWS, and placing all EC2 instances in a single AZ reduces fault tolerance. This change would not address the underlying database read-traffic bottleneck. Option B (CORRECT): “Create a read replica for the DB instance. Configure the application to send read traffic to the read replica.” Read replicas offload read-only queries from the primary, reducing CPU and I/O contention on your master database. The application can be modified (or use a proxy) to route SELECTs to the replica and writes to the primary, improving overall throughput. Option D (CORRECT): “Create an Amazon ElastiCache cluster. Configure the application to cache query results in the ElastiCache cluster.” ElastiCache (Redis or Memcached) serves as an in-memory caching layer, dramatically reducing read latency for frequently accessed data. Caching results of expensive queries reduces load on the RDS instance, improving performance during traffic spikes. In summary, to address heavy read-traffic and performance bottlenecks on an RDS for PostgreSQL instance, you should offload reads via read replicas and introduce an in-memory cache with ElastiCache. These changes fall under Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company is migrating its applications and databases to the AWS Cloud. The company will use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), AWS Direct Connect, and Amazon RDS. Which activities will be managed by the company's operational team? (Choose three.)
options: Management of the Amazon RDS infrastructure layer, operating system, and platforms
Creation of an Amazon RDS DB instance and configuring the scheduled maintenance window
Configuration of additional software components on Amazon ECS for monitoring, patch management, log management, and host intrusion detection
Installation of patches for all minor and major database versions for Amazon RDS
Ensure the physical security of the Amazon RDS infrastructure in the data center
Encryption of the data that moves in transit through Direct Connect
explanation: The correct answer is B, C, F Let’s step through why A, D, and E are not correct, and why B, C, and F are the right choices: Option A (INCORRECT): Management of the Amazon RDS infrastructure layer, operating system, and platforms Amazon RDS is a managed service where AWS is responsible for the underlying infrastructure, OS, and database engine platform. The customer does not manage the hardware, hypervisor, or OS patching for RDS instances. Option D (INCORRECT): Installation of patches for all minor and major database versions for Amazon RDS AWS automatically handles minor version patches for you in RDS (as part of the managed service). The user can choose the maintenance window, but AWS applies OS and engine updates. Major version upgrades require user initiation, but patching itself is managed by AWS. Option E (INCORRECT): Ensure the physical security of the Amazon RDS infrastructure in the data center Physical security of AWS data centers is entirely the responsibility of AWS. Customers never have access to the underlying racks, cages, or facilities. Option B (CORRECT): Creation of an Amazon RDS DB instance and configuring the scheduled maintenance window The customer is responsible for provisioning DB instances and choosing maintenance windows. This includes selecting instance types, storage, and when AWS applies minor patches and updates. Option C (CORRECT): Configuration of additional software components on Amazon ECS for monitoring, patch management, log management, and host intrusion detection When using Amazon ECS on EC2, the customer must manage OS-level and agent-based software. This includes installing and configuring monitoring agents, patch management tools, log collectors, and intrusion-detection agents on the container hosts. Option F (CORRECT): Encryption of the data that moves in transit through Direct Connect AWS Direct Connect provides a private network link, but encryption in transit (e.g., IPsec VPN over Direct Connect) is configured and managed by the customer. The customer chooses and manages encryption protocols, certificates, and keys. In summary, the operational team is responsible for provisioning and configuring RDS instances (including maintenance windows), managing software on ECS hosts, and ensuring encryption over Direct Connect. This question relates to Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures, as it touches on shared-responsibility and security controls in AWS services.

question: A company wants to send all AWS Systems Manager Session Manager logs to an Amazon S3 bucket for archival purposes.Which solution will meet this requirement with the MOST operational efficiency?
options: Enable S3 logging in the Systems Manager console. Choose an S3 bucket to send the session data to.
Install the Amazon CloudWatch agent. Push all logs to a CloudWatch log group. Export the logs to an S3 bucket from the group for archival purposes.
Create a Systems Manager document to upload all server logs to a central S3 bucket. Use Amazon EventBridge to run the Systems Manager document against all servers that are in the account daily.

Install an Amazon CloudWatch agent. Push all logs to a CloudWatch log group. Create a CloudWatch logs subscription that pushes any incoming log events to an Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream. Set Amazon S3 as the destination.
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): This approach uses the CloudWatch agent to collect logs, which is intended for operating-system and application logs—not Session Manager session data. It then requires you to manually export from CloudWatch Logs to S3, adding operational overhead and latency. Session Manager already provides a direct integration to S3, making this route unnecessary and less efficient. Option C (INCORRECT): Creating a custom Systems Manager document and scheduling it daily means logs only land in S3 once per day, not in real time. This solution increases operational complexity (you must maintain the document and EventBridge rule) and risks gaps if a run fails. Session Manager has built-in support for continuous archival, making this ad-hoc method suboptimal. Option D (INCORRECT): Deploying the CloudWatch agent, shipping data to CloudWatch Logs, then using a Logs Subscription + Kinesis Data Firehose is over-engineered for simply archiving sessions. It introduces multiple moving parts (agent, log group, Firehose stream) and higher operational maintenance. While it works, it isn’t the “most operationally efficient” path when Session Manager can natively deliver to S3. Option A (CORRECT): Session Manager provides a built-in “Session log” preference where you simply specify an S3 bucket. No agents, custom documents, or extra services are required—AWS handles continuous delivery of all session data to S3. This is the simplest, most maintainable, and most operationally efficient solution for archival. In summary, we learned that AWS Systems Manager Session Manager can directly archive session transcripts to an S3 bucket via its built-in logging preferences. This avoids extra agents or custom automation and fits squarely in Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures, since it addresses secure, auditable session logging with minimal operational burden.

question: A company created a new organization in AWS Organizations. The organization has multiple accounts for the company's development teams. The development team members use AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS Single Sign-On) to access the accounts. For each of the company's applications, the development teams must use a predefined application name to tag resources that are created. A solutions architect needs to design a solution that gives the development team the ability to create resources only if the application name tag has an approved value. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Create an IAM group that has a conditional Allow policy that requires the application name tag to be specified for resources to be created.
Create a cross-account role that has a Deny policy for any resource that has the application name tag.
Create a resource group in AWS Resource Groups to validate that the tags are applied to all resources in all accounts.
Create a tag policy in Organizations that has a list of allowed application names.
explanation: The correct Answer is D Option A (INCORRECT): “Create an IAM group that has a conditional Allow policy that requires the application name tag to be specified for resources to be created.” IAM policies can check for the presence or value of tags via condition keys (aws:RequestTag), but they are scoped per identity or role—not centrally managed across all accounts in an Organization. Managing approved application names in every IAM policy is error-prone and doesn’t prevent someone from creating resources without the tag or with an unapproved tag if they switch to another role or group. Option B (INCORRECT): “Create a cross-account role that has a Deny policy for any resource that has the application name tag.” A Deny policy targeting any resource that has the tag would block all tagged resources—this is the opposite of the requirement. It does not specify allowed values, nor does it permit untagged resources to be created conditionally; it simply denies everything that carries the tag. Option C (INCORRECT): “Create a resource group in AWS Resource Groups to validate that the tags are applied to all resources in all accounts.” Resource Groups can help you discover and organize existing resources based on tags, but they cannot enforce tag policies or prevent non-compliant resource creation. They are purely a management and visibility tool—not a guardrail for enforcing approved tag values at creation time. Option D (CORRECT): “Create a tag policy in Organizations that has a list of allowed application names.” A tag policy at the AWS Organizations level lets you centrally define which tag keys and values are permitted across all member accounts. Once attached to the root or an OU, any attempt to create or update a resource with a non-approved application name tag is automatically rejected. This approach scales across all accounts, eliminates manual IAM policy updates, and enforces a consistent tagging standard. Summary: We’ve learned that to enforce specific tag values across multiple AWS accounts in an Organization, the best practice is to use a centralized tag policy in AWS Organizations (Option D). This ensures that resources can only be created if they use an approved tag value, providing a consistent guardrail for your development teams. This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures, since it involves enforcing security and compliance controls through tagging policies.

question: A company needs to provide its employees with secure access to confidential and sensitive files. The company wants to ensure that the files can be accessed only by authorized users. The files must be downloaded securely to the employees’ devices. The files are stored in an on-premises Windows file server. However, due to an increase in remote usage, the file server is running out of capacity. . Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Migrate the file server to an Amazon EC2 instance in a public subnet. Configure the security group to limit inbound traffic to the employees’ IP addresses.
Migrate the files to an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system. Integrate the Amazon FSx file system with the on-premises Active Directory. Configure AWS Client VPN.
Migrate the files to Amazon S3, and create a private VPC endpoint. Create a signed URL to allow download.
Migrate the files to Amazon S3, and create a public VPC endpoint. Allow employees to sign on with AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS Single Sign-On).
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): “Migrate the file server to an Amazon EC2 instance in a public subnet. Configure the security group to limit inbound traffic to the employees’ IP addresses.” No integration with Active Directory for user authentication and authorization. Public subnet exposes the server to the internet; limiting by IP is brittle (employees’ IPs change). Does not provide an encrypted, managed SMB service or scale-out file storage. Option C (INCORRECT): “Migrate the files to Amazon S3, and create a private VPC endpoint. Create a signed URL to allow download.” Signed URLs are time-limited and shareable; no per-user authentication tied to corporate directory. Requires custom application logic or scripts to generate/manage URLs for each user. No native Windows file-share interface (SMB) or AD integration, making it harder for end users accustomed to mapped drives. Option D (INCORRECT): “Migrate the files to Amazon S3, and create a public VPC endpoint. Allow employees to sign on with AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS Single Sign-On).” AWS IAM Identity Center is for AWS console and SSO to cloud apps, not direct SMB/HTTPS file shares. Public access endpoint contradicts need for fully private, secure file downloads. Again, lacks native Windows file-share support and seamless AD integration. Option B (CORRECT): “Migrate the files to an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system. Integrate the Amazon FSx file system with the on-premises Active Directory. Configure AWS Client VPN.” Amazon FSx for Windows File Server provides a fully managed, highly available SMB file share. Integration with on-premises Active Directory ensures only authorized users can access files using their existing credentials. AWS Client VPN secures remote connections, encrypting data in transit and providing scalable access for remote employees. Clients can map the FSx file share just like an on-premises server, with no changes to workflow. In summary, Amazon FSx for Windows File Server integrated with your on-premises AD and accessed over AWS Client VPN meets all requirements: secure, directory-based authorization, encrypted downloads, familiar SMB interface, and seamless scalability. This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company is running its production and nonproduction environment workloads in multiple AWS accounts. The accounts are in an organization in AWS Organizations. The company needs to design a solution that will prevent the modification of cost usage tags.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Create a custom AWS Config rule to prevent tag modification except by authorized principals.
Create a custom trail in AWS CloudTrail to prevent tag modification.
Create a service control policy (SCP) to prevent tag modification except by authorized principals.
Create custom Amazon CloudWatch logs to prevent tag modification.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): Create a custom AWS Config rule to prevent tag modification except by authorized principals. • AWS Config rules are evaluators—they detect non-compliant resources and can trigger remediation, but they cannot outright block API calls in real time. • You could detect when tags are changed and then remediate or alert, but you cannot “prevent” the modification before it happens with Config alone. Option B (INCORRECT): Create a custom trail in AWS CloudTrail to prevent tag modification. • CloudTrail provides audit logging of API calls—it records events after they occur. • It cannot stop or deny an API call; it only tracks it for auditing and monitoring. Option D (INCORRECT): Create custom Amazon CloudWatch logs to prevent tag modification. • CloudWatch Logs can collect and store logs (including from CloudTrail) and trigger alarms or metrics filters. • Like CloudTrail, it only observes after-the-fact; it cannot enforce or block the API request itself. Option C (CORRECT): Create a service control policy (SCP) to prevent tag modification except by authorized principals. • SCPs in AWS Organizations control what actions IAM principals in member accounts can perform. • You can write an SCP that denies specific tag-related APIs (e.g., TagResource, UntagResource) except when the request is from a designated IAM role or user. • This enforces the restriction at the organization level, preventing unauthorized users in any account from modifying cost allocation tags. In summary, to prevent the modification of cost usage tags across multiple AWS accounts, you need a mechanism that denies API calls in real time—this is precisely what an SCP provides. We learned the distinction between recording/auditing tools (CloudTrail, CloudWatch, Config) versus enforcement tools (SCPs). This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures, since it addresses governance and enforcement controls.

question: A company has two VPCs that are located in the us-west-2 Region within the same AWS account. The company needs to allow network traffic between these VPCs. Approximately 500 GB of data transfer will occur between the VPCs each month. What is the MOST cost-effective solution to connect these VPCs?
options: Implement AWS Transit Gateway to connect the VPCs. Update the route tables of each VPC to use the transit gateway for inter-VPC communication.
Implement an AWS Site-to-Site VPN tunnel between the VPCs. Update the route tables of each VPC to use the VPN tunnel for inter-VPC communication.
Set up a VPC peering connection between the VPCs. Update the route tables of each VPC to use the VPC peering connection for inter-VPC communication.
Set up a 1 GB AWS Direct Connect connection between the VPCs. Update the route tables of each VPC to use the Direct Connect connection for inter-VPC communication.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): Using an AWS Transit Gateway to connect just two VPCs in the same region is overkill. Transit Gateway incurs an hourly attachment charge plus a per-GB processing fee, making it significantly more expensive than simpler solutions for 500 GB/month of data transfer. Option B (INCORRECT): A Site-to-Site VPN between two VPCs carries hourly VPN tunnel charges and a per-GB data transfer fee (about $0.05 /GB). For 500 GB/month this totals more than $25 + tunnel fees, which is costlier than VPC Peering. Option D (INCORRECT): AWS Direct Connect requires a physical connection with a port-hour fee (often several hundred dollars per month for a 1 Gbps port) plus data costs. It’s intended for on-premises to AWS links, not inter-VPC traffic within the same region—and it’s far more expensive for just 500 GB/month. Option C (CORRECT): VPC Peering is a simple, regional, pay-only-for-data-transfer model. Peering data transfer in the same AZ/region is around $0.01/GB, so 500 GB costs only about $5/month. There are no hourly or setup fees, making this the most cost-effective way to enable direct network traffic between two VPCs in the same region. In summary, VPC Peering provides low-latency, high-bandwidth connectivity at minimal cost. We’ve learned how each inter-VPC solution is priced and why peering wins for modest intra-region data needs. This question belongs to Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company is developing a file-sharing application that will use an Amazon S3 bucket for storage. The company wants to serve all the files through an Amazon CloudFront distribution. The company does not want the files to be accessible through direct navigation to the S3 URL. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
options: Write individual policies for each S3 bucket to grant read permission for only CloudFront access.
Create an IAM user. Grant the user read permission to objects in the S3 bucket. Assign the user to CloudFront.
Write an S3 bucket policy that assigns the CloudFront distribution ID as the Principal and assigns the target S3 bucket as the Amazon Resource Name (ARN).
Create an origin access identity (OAI). Assign the OAI to the CloudFront distribution. Configure the S3 bucket permissions so that only the OAI has read permission.
explanation: The correct answer is Option D. Option A (INCORRECT): “Write individual policies for each S3 bucket to grant read permission for only CloudFront access.” This approach is overly complex and error-prone—managing separate policies per bucket for CloudFront is unnecessary. CloudFront does not assume an IAM role or user; it requires an Origin Access Identity (OAI) or Origin Access Control (OAC) to securely fetch from S3. You cannot directly tie CloudFront’s service principal in an IAM policy to restrict reads—it needs an OAI in the bucket policy. Option B (INCORRECT): “Create an IAM user. Grant the user read permission to objects in the S3 bucket. Assign the user to CloudFront.” CloudFront cannot use an IAM user to fetch objects from S3—there is no mechanism to “assign” an IAM user to a distribution. This approach would expose credentials in CloudFront, which is neither supported nor secure. Option C (INCORRECT): “Write an S3 bucket policy that assigns the CloudFront distribution ID as the Principal and assigns the target S3 bucket as the ARN.” You cannot use the CloudFront distribution ID as an IAM principal in a bucket policy—CloudFront is not a recognized AWS principal. The proper principal to restrict CloudFront is the Origin Access Identity (OAI) or Origin Access Control (OAC), not the distribution ID. Option D (CORRECT): “Create an origin access identity (OAI). Assign the OAI to the CloudFront distribution. Configure the S3 bucket permissions so that only the OAI has read permission.” OAI serves as a virtual identity that CloudFront uses to access your S3 bucket. You update the S3 bucket policy to allow read (`s3:GetObject`) only for that OAI, denying all other public or direct S3 access. With this setup, files are delivered only through CloudFront URLs; any direct S3 URL request is blocked by the bucket policy. In summary, by using an Origin Access Identity and restricting the S3 bucket policy to that identity, you ensure that content is served exclusively through CloudFront and cannot be accessed directly via the S3 URL. This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company is developing a new application on AWS. The application consists of an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster, an Amazon S3 bucket that contains assets for the application, and an Amazon RDS for MySQL database that contains the dataset for the application. The dataset contains sensitive information. The company wants to ensure that only the ECS cluster can access the data in the RDS for MySQL database and the data in the S3 bucket. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Create a new AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key to encrypt both the S3 bucket and the RDS for MySQL database. Ensure that the KMS key policy includes encrypt and decrypt permissions for the ECS task execution role.

Create an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) AWS managed key to encrypt both the S3 bucket and the RDS for MySQL database. Ensure that the S3 bucket policy specifies the ECS task execution role as a user.

Create an S3 bucket policy that restricts bucket access to the ECS task execution role. Create a VPC endpoint for Amazon RDS for MySQL. Update the RDS for MySQL security group to allow access from only the subnets that the ECS cluster will generate tasks in.

Create a VPC endpoint for Amazon RDS for MySQL. Update the RDS for MySQL security group to allow access from only the subnets that the ECS cluster will generate tasks in. Create a VPC endpoint for Amazon S3. Update the S3 bucket policy to allow access from only the S3 VPC endpoint.
explanation: The correct answer is D Option A (INCORRECT): • Encrypting both S3 and RDS with a customer-managed KMS key controls data-at-rest encryption but does not prevent other principals from accessing the data if they hold valid credentials. • KMS key policies alone cannot lock down network access to RDS or S3—any IAM user or role with Decrypt permissions could read the data. • There is no enforcement that *only* the ECS cluster can connect; you still need network and resource policies. Option B (INCORRECT): • AWS-managed KMS keys cannot be customized to limit decrypt permissions to just the ECS task role. • Specifying the ECS task execution role in the S3 bucket policy without VPC restrictions still allows other roles (if granted) to access the bucket. • This solution does not lock down database connections at the network layer, nor does it give you strict control over decrypt permissions. Option C (INCORRECT): • While restricting S3 access via bucket policy to the ECS task role is valid, there is *no* VPC Endpoint service for RDS MySQL traffic—RDS sits inside your VPC and you control access via Security Groups and subnet placement. • Attempting to create an RDS VPC endpoint is not supported for database connectivity. • The extra, non-existent endpoint adds confusion without delivering real access control. Option D (CORRECT): • You keep your RDS instance inside a private VPC subnet and lock down its Security Group to accept connections only from the ECS cluster’s subnets. This ensures *network-level* isolation—no other resource can reach the database endpoint. • You create an S3 Gateway VPC endpoint and then update the bucket policy to allow access *only* via that endpoint. This ensures that S3 calls must originate from your VPC, and only from resources that assume your ECS task role. • Combined, these measures guarantee that only ECS tasks running in your specified subnets can reach the RDS database and the S3 bucket. Summary: We’ve learned how to enforce *both* network-level and resource-policy controls to limit RDS and S3 access exclusively to an ECS cluster. This question belongs to Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company is migrating a data center from its on-premises location to AWS. The company has several legacy applications that are hosted on individual virtual servers. Changes to the application designs cannot be made. Each individual virtual server currently runs as its own EC2 instance. A solutions architect needs to ensure that the applications are reliable and fault tolerant after migration to AWS. The applications will run on Amazon EC2 instances.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Create an Auto Scaling group that has a minimum of one and a maximum of one. Create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) of each application instance. Use the AMI to create EC2 instances in the Auto Scaling group Configure an Application Load Balancer in front of the Auto Scaling group.

Use AWS Backup to create an hourly backup of the EC2 instance that hosts each application. Store the backup in Amazon S3 in a separate Availability Zone. Configure a disaster recovery process to restore the EC2 instance for each application from its most recent backup.

Create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) of each application instance. Launch two new EC2 instances from the AMI. Place each EC2 instance in a separate Availability Zone. Configure a Network Load Balancer that has the EC2 instances as targets.

Use AWS Mitigation Hub Refactor Spaces to migrate each application off the EC2 instance. Break down functionality from each application into individual components. Host each application on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with an AWS Fargate launch type.
explanation: The correct answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): “Create an Auto Scaling group with minimum = 1 and maximum = 1, build an AMI, then place it behind an Application Load Balancer.” With min=1 and max=1, the Auto Scaling group maintains only a single instance—no multi-AZ fault tolerance. An ALB can distribute traffic across AZs only if there are healthy targets in each AZ. Here only one instance exists in one AZ, creating a single point of failure. Does not satisfy the requirement for high availability across multiple Availability Zones.
