Snapshots are stored in S3, providing durable backups without additional operational overhead. In summary, AWS Storage Gateway cached volumes best satisfy the requirement for low-latency block storage with minimal on-premises capacity usage, offering the highest operational efficiency. This question falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures, as it focuses on delivering performant, low-latency storage access.

question: An ecommerce company is preparing to deploy a web application on AWS to ensure continuous service for customers. The architecture includes a web application that the company hosts on Amazon EC2 instances, a relational database in Amazon RDS, and static assets that the company stores in Amazon S3. The company wants to design a robust and resilient architecture for the application. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Deploy Amazon EC2 instances in a single Availability Zone. Deploy an RDS DB instance in the same Availability Zone. Use Amazon S3 with versioning enabled to store static assets.
Deploy Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. Deploy a Multi-AZ RDS DB instance. Use Amazon CloudFront to distribute static assets.
Deploy Amazon EC2 instances in a single Availability Zone. Deploy an RDS DB instance in a second Availability Zone for cross-AZ redundancy. Serve static assets directly from the EC2 instances.

Use AWS Lambda functions to serve the web application. Use Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 for the database. Store static assets in Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) One Zone-Infrequent Access (One Zone-IA).
explanation: The correct answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): Deploying EC2 instances and RDS in a single Availability Zone creates a single point of failure. If that AZ goes down, your application and database both become unavailable. While S3 versioning protects against accidental overwrites or deletions, it does not address high availability or performance for static asset delivery. Option B (CORRECT): Auto Scaling across multiple Availability Zones ensures that your EC2 instances remain available even if one AZ fails. Multi-AZ RDS provides automatic synchronous replication to a standby in a different AZ, giving high availability and automated failover. Using Amazon CloudFront to distribute your S3-hosted static assets delivers low-latency, high-throughput performance and built-in edge-cache redundancy. Option C (INCORRECT): Hosting EC2 instances in a single AZ still exposes you to downtime if that zone fails. Although having RDS in a second AZ offers DB redundancy, the web tier remains vulnerable. Serving static assets from EC2 increases operational overhead and does not leverage AWS edge caching for performance or resilience. Option D (INCORRECT): Using AWS Lambda for a full web application can introduce cold-start latency and may complicate session management or file uploads. Aurora Serverless v2 is scalable but may not provide the same instant high-availability guarantees as a Multi-AZ provisioned RDS deployment. Storing static assets in Amazon EFS One Zone-IA places them all in a single AZ, undermining resilience and performance. In summary, Option B is the only design that meets the requirement for a robust, highly available web tier (multi-AZ Auto Scaling), a resilient database (Multi-AZ RDS), and performant, fault-tolerant static content delivery (CloudFront + S3). This question falls under Domain 2 – Design Resilient Architectures, since it focuses on high availability and fault tolerance.

question: A company stores data in PDF format in an Amazon S3 bucket. The company must follow a legal requirement to retain all new and existing data in Amazon S3 for 7 years.Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Turn on the S3 Versioning feature for the S3 bucket. Configure S3 Lifecycle to delete the data after 7 years. Configure multi-factor authentication (MFA) delete for all S3 objects.
Turn on S3 Object Lock with governance retention mode for the S3 bucket. Set the retention period to expire after 7 years. Recopy all existing objects to bring the existing data into compliance.
Turn on S3 Object Lock with compliance retention mode for the S3 bucket. Set the retention period to expire after 7 years. Recopy all existing objects to bring the existing data into compliance.
Turn on S3 Object Lock with compliance retention mode for the S3 bucket. Set the retention period to expire after 7 years. Use S3 Batch Operations to bring the existing data into compliance.
explanation: The correct answer is D Option A (INCORRECT): Using S3 Versioning plus Lifecycle rules does not enforce a WORM (Write Once Read Many) retention period—objects can still be permanently deleted by users with delete permissions before the lifecycle age. MFA Delete adds protection but requires manual MFA tokens for every delete operation, increasing operational overhead. It does not satisfy a true tamper-proof, 7-year retention requirement. Option B (INCORRECT): S3 Object Lock in Governance mode can be overridden by AWS principals with the s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permission—so it’s not strictly enforceable. You still must recopy existing objects manually to apply the lock, adding significant operational overhead. Option C (INCORRECT): S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode provides the required WORM protection, but you must recopy every existing object into a new lock-enabled bucket or prefix. Manual recopying is time-consuming and error-prone for large datasets, increasing operational overhead. Option D (CORRECT): Turns on S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode—true WORM retention that cannot be shortened or overridden. Sets the retention period to 7 years, meeting the legal requirement without manual deletes. Uses S3 Batch Operations to apply the Object Lock retention settings in bulk to existing objects—eliminating manual recopying and minimizing operational overhead. In summary, enabling S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode combined with S3 Batch Operations delivers a fully enforceable 7-year retention policy with minimal manual intervention. This question maps to Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures because it addresses data protection and compliance requirements.

question: A company wants to migrate its three-tier application from on premises to AWS. The web tier and the application tier are running on third-party virtual machines (VMs). The database tier is running on MySQL. The company needs to migrate the application by making the fewest possible changes to the architecture. The company also needs a database solution that can restore data to a specific point in time. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Migrate the web tier and the application tier to Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets. Migrate the database tier to Amazon RDS for MySQL in private subnets.
Migrate the web tier to Amazon EC2 instances in public subnets. Migrate the application tier to EC2 instances in private subnets. Migrate the database tier to Amazon Aurora MySQL in private subnets.
Migrate the web tier to Amazon EC2 instances in public subnets. Migrate the application tier to EC2 instances in private subnets. Migrate the database tier to Amazon RDS for MySQL in private subnets.
Migrate the web tier and the application tier to Amazon EC2 instances in public subnets. Migrate the database tier to Amazon Aurora MySQL in public subnets.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): “Migrate both web and application tiers to EC2 in private subnets, and the database to Amazon RDS for MySQL in private subnets.” Hosting the web tier in a private subnet prevents direct internet access, requiring additional NAT gateways or load-balancer configurations to serve user traffic. This adds extra networking complexity and operational overhead, which conflicts with the requirement to make the fewest possible architectural changes. Option C (INCORRECT): “Migrate web tier to EC2 in public subnets, application tier to EC2 in private subnets, and database to Amazon RDS for MySQL in private subnets.” While RDS for MySQL supports automated backups and point-in-time recovery, it still requires instance sizing, storage management, patching windows, and manual read replica setups for high availability. Amazon Aurora MySQL offers auto-scaling storage, continuous backups, and built-in fault tolerance, which reduce administrative tasks compared to RDS for MySQL. Option D (INCORRECT): “Migrate both web and application tiers to EC2 in public subnets, and database to Amazon Aurora MySQL in public subnets.” Exposing the database tier in a public subnet poses a significant security risk by allowing direct internet access to your data store. Best practices dictate placing databases in private subnets behind security groups and network ACLs to protect sensitive data. Option B (CORRECT): “Migrate the web tier to EC2 instances in public subnets, the application tier to EC2 instances in private subnets, and the database tier to Amazon Aurora MySQL in private subnets.” Amazon EC2 for web and app tiers preserves your existing VM-based architecture with minimal changes and uses standard public/private subnet design for secure internet-facing and backend components. Amazon Aurora MySQL is a highly managed, MySQL-compatible service that provides continuous backups to Amazon S3 and supports point-in-time recovery with minimal configuration. Aurora’s auto-scaling storage, automated patching, and multi-AZ fault tolerance minimize operational overhead compared to self-managed MySQL or standard RDS instances. In summary, by choosing EC2 for your web and application tiers and Aurora MySQL for your database tier—placed in the appropriate public and private subnets—you meet the migration requirement with the fewest architectural changes and the least operational overhead. This question falls under Domain 2 - Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company has a production web application in which users upload documents through a web interface or a mobile app. According to a new regulatory requirement. new documents cannot be modified or deleted after they are stored.What should a solutions architect do to meet this requirement?
options: Store the uploaded documents in an Amazon S3 bucket with S3 Versioning and S3 Object Lock enabled.
Store the uploaded documents in an Amazon S3 bucket. Configure an S3 Lifecycle policy to archive the documents periodically.
Store the uploaded documents in an Amazon S3 bucket with S3 Versioning enabled. Configure an ACL to restrict all access to read-only.
Store the uploaded documents on an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) volume. Access the data by mounting the volume in read-only mode.
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): • Storing documents in an S3 bucket and using a Lifecycle policy to archive them does not prevent deletion or modification. Lifecycle actions can permanently delete or transition objects, which violates the “immutable” requirement. Option C (INCORRECT): • Enabling S3 Versioning alone retains prior object versions, but users with proper permissions can still delete object versions or change the bucket’s versioning settings. • ACLs set to read-only may impede casual writes but do not enforce true immutability or WORM compliance. Option D (INCORRECT): • Mounting an EFS volume as read-only can be bypassed by remounting or by privileged users. • EFS does not provide built-in immutability or legal-hold capabilities required by the new regulation. Option A (CORRECT): • Amazon S3 Object Lock in compliance mode enforces a WORM (Write-Once-Read-Many) model, preventing any object version from being overwritten or deleted until its retention period expires. • Versioning ensures that if a new version is accidentally uploaded, the previous version remains intact. • This combination fully meets the regulatory requirement for immutability and non-repudiation. In summary, we’ve seen that S3 Object Lock with Versioning is the only solution that enforces true immutability. This scenario belongs to Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures, as it addresses data protection and compliance requirements.

question: A company is using a content management system that runs on a single Amazon EC2 instance. The EC2 instance contains both the web server and the database software. The company must make its website platform highly available and must enable the website to scale to meet user demand.What should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?
options: Move the database to Amazon RDS, and enable automatic backups. Manually launch another EC2 instance in the same Availability Zone. Configure an Application Load Balancer in the Availability Zone, and set the two instances as targets.

Migrate the database to an Amazon Aurora instance with a read replica in the same Availability Zone as the existing EC2 instance. Manually launch another EC2 instance in the same Availability Zone. Configure an Application Load Balancer, and set the two EC2 instances as targets.

Move the database to Amazon Aurora with a read replica in another Availability Zone. Create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) from the EC2 instance. Configure an Application Load Balancer in two Availability Zones. Attach an Auto Scaling group that uses the AMI across two Availability Zones.

Move the database to a separate EC2 instance, and schedule backups to Amazon S3. Create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) from the original EC2 instance. Configure an Application Load Balancer in two Availability Zones. Attach an Auto Scaling group that uses the AMI across two Availability Zones.
explanation: The correct Answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): • Moves the database to Amazon RDS but does not specify Multi-AZ deployment—leaving the database as a single point of failure. • Both EC2 web servers are launched in the same Availability Zone, so an AZ outage would take down the entire site. • Manually launching instances offers no automated scaling to meet variable user demand. Option B (INCORRECT): • Creates an Aurora read replica but places it in the same Availability Zone—failing to provide true AZ-level high availability for the database. • Still manually spins up a second EC2 in the same AZ—no AZ redundancy for the web tier. • Does not leverage Auto Scaling, so the solution cannot automatically adjust capacity under load. Option D (INCORRECT): • Keeps the database on a standalone EC2 instance—no managed high-availability or automated failover for the database. • Although the web tier is scaled across AZs via an Auto Scaling group and ALB, the single-node database remains a critical single point of failure. • Backups to S3 do not provide immediate failover or database continuity in case of an AZ outage. Option C (CORRECT): • Moves the database to Amazon Aurora with a cross-AZ read replica—enabling automated failover and high availability for the database tier. • Creates an AMI of the existing EC2 (web server) and deploys it in an Auto Scaling group across two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer—ensuring both fault tolerance and the ability to scale out under heavy load. • Fully addresses both requirements: high availability (multi-AZ DB + multi-AZ web tier) and automatic scaling to meet user demand. In summary, the recommended architecture decouples and scales each tier independently—using Amazon Aurora’s multi-AZ capabilities for resilience and an Auto Scaling group plus ALB across AZs for a high-performing, highly available web layer. This question falls under Domain 2 - Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company has deployed a multiplayer game for mobile devices. The game requires live location tracking of players based on latitude and longitude. The data store for the game must support rapid updates and retrieval of locations. The game uses an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance with read replicas to store the location data. During peak usage periods, the database is unable to maintain the performance that is needed for reading and writing updates. The game's user base is increasing rapidly. What should a solutions architect do to improve the performance of the data tier?
options: Take a snapshot of the existing DB instance. Restore the snapshot with Multi-AZ enabled.
Migrate from Amazon RDS to Amazon OpenSearch Service with OpenSearch Dashboards.
Deploy Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) in front of the existing DB instance. Modify the game to use DAX.
Deploy an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster in front of the existing DB instance. Modify the game to use Redis.
explanation: The correct answer is D. Option A (INCORRECT): Restoring the snapshot with Multi-AZ enabled only improves availability and failover, not the read/write performance required for rapid location updates. Multi-AZ deployments maintain synchronous standby replicas, but they are not used to offload read traffic. Option B (INCORRECT): Amazon OpenSearch Service is optimized for full-text search and analytics, not high-velocity read/write workloads with extremely low latency for point-based location lookups. Migrating to OpenSearch would add complexity without solving the performance bottleneck for rapid location updates. Option C (INCORRECT): DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is a caching layer exclusively for Amazon DynamoDB. It cannot be placed in front of an RDS for PostgreSQL instance. You would need to migrate your data to DynamoDB first, which is beyond the scope of simply improving performance on the existing RDS DB. Option D (CORRECT): Deploying an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster in front of your RDS for PostgreSQL instance and modifying the game to use Redis for live location data provides: Sub-millisecond latency for both reads and writes, ideal for real-time location updates. High throughput to handle peak usage and rapid scaling as the user base grows. An in-memory data store that offloads the primary database, reducing pressure on RDS and improving overall performance. In summary, adding a Redis cache layer with Amazon ElastiCache addresses the need for extremely fast, frequent updates and lookups of player locations, which RDS alone cannot sustain at scale. This question falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company wants to move its application to a serverless solution. The serverless solution needs to analyze existing data and new data by using SQL. The company stores the data in an Amazon S3 bucket. The data must be encrypted at rest and replicated to a different AWS Region. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Create a new S3 bucket that uses server-side encryption with AWS KMS multi-Region keys (SSE-KMS). Configure Cross-Region Replication (CRR). Load the data into the new S3 bucket. Use Amazon Athena to query the data.

Create a new S3 bucket that uses server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3). Configure Cross-Region Replication (CRR). Load the data into the new S3 bucket. Use Amazon RDS to query the data.
Configure Cross-Region Replication (CRR) on the existing S3 bucket. Use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3). Use Amazon Athena to query the data.
Configure S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) on the existing S3 bucket. Use server-side encryption with AWS KMS multi-Region keys (SSE-KMS). Use Amazon RDS to query the data.
explanation: The correct answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): “Create a new S3 bucket that uses server-side encryption with AWS KMS multi-Region keys (SSE-KMS). Configure Cross-Region Replication (CRR). Load the data into the new S3 bucket. Use Amazon Athena to query the data.” You’re introducing extra operational overhead by creating and managing a second bucket and a multi-Region KMS key. Multi-Region KMS keys require careful replication and key policy maintenance across regions. SSE-KMS isn’t necessary when SSE-S3 already meets the at-rest encryption requirement with zero key management. Option B (INCORRECT): “Create a new S3 bucket that uses server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3). Configure Cross-Region Replication (CRR). Load the data into the new S3 bucket. Use Amazon RDS to query the data.” Loading data from S3 into RDS adds ETL/ingestion work and ongoing operational overhead. RDS isn’t a serverless analytics engine for ad-hoc SQL over S3 data. Amazon Athena is the native, serverless, SQL-on-S3 solution—no need for RDS. Option D (INCORRECT): “Configure S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) on the existing S3 bucket. Use server-side encryption with AWS KMS multi-Region keys (SSE-KMS). Use Amazon RDS to query the data.” This combines two unnecessary pieces of complexity: multi-Region KMS key management and RDS ETL. You don’t need KMS keys when SSE-S3 satisfies encryption-at-rest without additional management. RDS again adds operational overhead for ingestion, backups, scaling—contrary to serverless goals. Option C (CORRECT): “Configure Cross-Region Replication (CRR) on the existing S3 bucket. Use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3). Use Amazon Athena to query the data.” Leverages built-in SSE-S3 for at-rest encryption with zero key management. Uses CRR on the existing bucket—no need to create or maintain extra buckets or KMS keys. Amazon Athena provides serverless, SQL-on-S3 analytics with no infrastructure to manage. This setup meets encryption, replication, and serverless analytics with the least operational overhead. In summary, we learned how to meet encryption-at-rest, cross-Region replication, and serverless SQL querying with the least operational overhead by using SSE-S3, S3 CRR, and Athena. This question falls under Domain 2 – Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company runs a web application on multiple Amazon EC2 instances in a VPC. The application needs to write sensitive data to an Amazon S3 bucket. The data cannot be sent over the public internet. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3. Create a route in the VPC route table to the endpoint.
Create an internal Network Load Balancer that has the S3 bucket as the target.
Deploy the S3 bucket inside the VPCreate a route in the VPC route table to the bucket.
Create an AWS Direct Connect connection between the VPC and an S3 regional endpoint.
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): “Create an internal Network Load Balancer that has the S3 bucket as the target.” S3 buckets cannot be registered as targets behind a Network Load Balancer. Load balancers route to EC2 instances, IPs, or Lambda functions—not to AWS-managed services like S3. Option C (INCORRECT): “Deploy the S3 bucket inside the VPC. Create a route in the VPC route table to the bucket.” AWS S3 is a regional service and cannot be “deployed” inside your VPC. There is no direct VPC route to an S3 bucket without using a VPC endpoint. Option D (INCORRECT): “Create an AWS Direct Connect connection between the VPC and an S3 regional endpoint.” Direct Connect is an on-premises to AWS dedicated link; it’s overkill for intra-AWS traffic. Even with Direct Connect, you’d need a Gateway endpoint or public interface—this does not automatically route S3 traffic privately within your VPC. Option A (CORRECT): “Create a Gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3. Create a route in the VPC route table to the endpoint.” A Gateway VPC Endpoint for S3 provides private, scalable connectivity between your VPC and S3 without using the internet. Traffic to the bucket stays within the AWS network and is not exposed to public internet. No additional bandwidth charges or Direct Connect circuits are required—just simple routing via the endpoint. Summary: We learned that to securely connect EC2 instances to S3 without traversing the public internet, a Gateway VPC Endpoint is the simplest and most cost-effective solution. This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company runs several Amazon RDS for Oracle On-Demand DB instances that have high utilization. The RDS DB instances run in member accounts that are in an organization in AWS Organizations. The company's finance team has access to the organization's management account and member accounts. The finance team wants to find ways to optimize costs by using AWS Trusted Advisor. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
options: Use the Trusted Advisor recommendations in the management account.
Use the Trusted Advisor recommendations in the member accounts where the RDS DB instances are running.
Review the Trusted Advisor checks for Amazon RDS Reserved Instance Optimization.
Review the Trusted Advisor checks for Amazon RDS Idle DB Instances.
Review the Trusted Advisor checks for compute optimization. Crosscheck the results by using AWS Compute Optimizer.
explanation: The correct answer is B, C Option A (INCORRECT): “Use the Trusted Advisor recommendations in the management account.” Trusted Advisor reports are scoped per AWS account; the management account does not automatically aggregate all cost-optimization checks for member accounts. The finance team needs to view RDS cost recommendations where the DB instances actually run—that is, in each member account. Option D (INCORRECT): “Review the Trusted Advisor checks for Amazon RDS Idle DB Instances.” This check flags under-utilized or idle RDS instances, but the question states the DB instances have high utilization. It won’t surface opportunities for Reserved Instances, which are the right path for heavily used databases. Option E (INCORRECT): “Review the Trusted Advisor checks for compute optimization. Cross-check the results by using AWS Compute Optimizer.” Compute optimization checks focus on EC2, Lambda, and related services—not on Amazon RDS. AWS Compute Optimizer does not analyze RDS instances for reservation or sizing recommendations. Option B (CORRECT): “Use the Trusted Advisor recommendations in the member accounts where the RDS DB instances are running.” Trusted Advisor cost-optimization checks must be viewed in the account that owns the resources. This ensures you see the specific RDS recommendations (e.g., RI purchase advice) for each account. Option C (CORRECT): “Review the Trusted Advisor checks for Amazon RDS Reserved Instance Optimization.” This check analyzes RDS usage patterns and recommends appropriate Reserved Instances to reduce on-demand costs. For highly utilized Oracle DB instances, purchasing RIs can deliver significant savings versus on-demand pricing. In summary, we learned that cost-optimization recommendations for RDS—especially Reserved Instance advice—are surfaced via Trusted Advisor per member account. To address high utilization workloads, the finance team should review the RDS Reserved Instance Optimization check (Option C) in each member account (Option B). This question falls under Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: QUESTION: A data analytics company wants to migrate its batch processing system to AWS. The company receives thousands of small data files periodically during the day through FTP. An on-premises batch job processes the data files overnight. However, the batch job takes hours to finish running. The company wants the AWS solution to process incoming data files as soon as possible with minimal changes to the FTP clients that send the files. The solution must delete the incoming data files after the files have been processed successfully. Processing for each file needs to take 3-8 minutes.Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way?
options: Use an Amazon EC2 instance that runs an FTP server to store incoming files as objects in Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval. Configure a job queue in AWS Batch. Use Amazon EventBridge rules to invoke the job to process the objects nightly from S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval. Delete the objects after the job has processed the objects.

Use an Amazon EC2 instance that runs an FTP server to store incoming files on an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. Configure a job queue in AWS Batch. Use Amazon EventBridge rules to invoke the job to process the files nightly from the EBS volume. Delete the files after the job has processed the files.

Use AWS Transfer Family to create an FTP server to store incoming files on an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. Configure a job queue in AWS Batch. Use an Amazon S3 event notification when each file arrives to invoke the job in AWS Batch. Delete the files after the job has processed the files.

Use AWS Transfer Family to create an FTP server to store incoming files in Amazon S3 Standard. Create an AWS Lambda function to process the files and to delete the files after they are processed. Use an S3 event notification to invoke the Lambda function when the files arrive.
explanation: The correct answer is D Option A (INCORRECT): • Storing files in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval introduces retrieval delays (minutes to hours), which violates the requirement to process files as soon as they arrive. • Using AWS Batch nightly means you still process in a batch window overnight rather than in near real-time. • Glacier is meant for long-term archival, not for high-throughput, low-latency file processing. Option B (INCORRECT): • Running your own FTP server on EC2 with EBS is an operational burden and not fully managed. • Invoking AWS Batch via EventBridge nightly again defers processing until the end of the day, rather than processing each file within minutes of arrival. • You still need to manage EC2 patching, scaling, and FTP software. Option C (INCORRECT): • AWS Transfer Family supports S3 or EFS as the storage backend, not EBS volumes, so this architecture is not valid. • Even if EBS were supported, you’d still rely on AWS Batch, which is more suited to large-scale batch jobs, not lightweight per-file processing within minutes. Option D (CORRECT): • AWS Transfer Family provides a fully managed FTP endpoint that writes directly to S3 Standard—no EC2 to manage and minimal changes for FTP clients. • S3 Event Notifications can trigger a Lambda function for each incoming file, ensuring files are processed within minutes of arrival. • Lambda’s 15-minute timeout comfortably covers the 3–8 minute processing window, and the function can delete each file upon successful processing. • This solution is fully serverless, highly scalable, and operationally efficient. In summary, by using AWS Transfer Family, S3 event notifications, and AWS Lambda, we achieve near real-time file processing with minimal operational overhead. This design question belongs to Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company wants to create an Amazon EMR cluster that multiple teams will use. The company wants to ensure that each team’s big data workloads can access only the AWS services that each team needs to interact with. The company does not want the workloads to have access to Instance Metadata Service Version 2 (IMDSv2) on the cluster’s underlying EC2 instances.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Configure interface VPC endpoints for each AWS service that the teams need. Use the required interface VPC endpoints to submit the big data workloads.
Create EMR runtime roles. Configure the cluster to use the runtime roles. Use the runtime roles to submit the big data workloads.
Create an EC2 IAM instance profile that has the required permissions for each team. Use the instance profile to submit the big data workloads.
Create an EMR security configuration that has the EnableApplicationScopedIAMRole option set to false. Use the security configuration to submit the big data workloads.
explanation: The correct answer is D. Option A (INCORRECT): “Configure interface VPC endpoints for each AWS service that the teams need. Use the required interface VPC endpoints to submit the big data workloads.” This approach restricts network-level access to AWS services, but it does not enforce IAM-level permissions per team. Workloads would still rely on the Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) for credentials and could potentially access any service allowed by the instance profile. It does not disable or restrict IMDSv2 on the EC2 instances, so credentials remain retrievable via metadata. Option B (INCORRECT): “Create EMR runtime roles. Configure the cluster to use the runtime roles. Use the runtime roles to submit the big data workloads.” EMR runtime roles are associated with EMR on EKS virtual clusters—not a standard EMR cluster on EC2. This option does not address disabling the Instance Metadata Service, so IMDSv2 would still be available. It does not leverage EMR’s per-application IAM role feature for EC2-based clusters. Option C (INCORRECT): “Create an EC2 IAM instance profile that has the required permissions for each team. Use the instance profile to submit the big data workloads.” This gives each cluster instance an IAM profile via IMDS, so the metadata service remains in use (IMDSv2 accessible). Permissions are tied to the instance profile and cannot be scoped per individual team job or application. Does not disable IMDSv2 or restrict access to only the required AWS services at the application level. Option D (CORRECT): “Create an EMR security configuration that has the EnableApplicationScopedIAMRole option set to true. Use the security configuration to submit the big data workloads.” Enabling application-scoped IAM roles ensures each team’s workload runs with its own IAM role, scoped only to the AWS services that role permits. EMR replaces use of EC2 instance metadata by issuing tokens to applications via a secure local proxy, effectively disabling IMDSv2 for those jobs. This meets both requirements: per-team service access control and no direct access to the Instance Metadata Service. In summary, we learned that EMR security configurations can enforce per-application IAM roles and eliminate reliance on the Instance Metadata Service, addressing both least-privilege access and IMDSv2 restrictions. This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company has an organization in AWS Organizations. The company runs Amazon EC2 instances across four AWS accounts in the root organizational unit (OU). There are three nonproduction accounts and one production account. The company wants to prohibit users from launching EC2 instances of a certain size in the nonproduction accounts. The company has created a service control policy (SCP) to deny access to launch instances that use the prohibited types.Which solutions to deploy the SCP will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
options: Attach the SCP to the root OU for the organization.
Attach the SCP to the three nonproduction Organizations member accounts.
Attach the SCP to the Organizations management account.
Create an OU for the production account. Attach the SCP to the OU. Move the production member account into the new OU.
Create an OU for the required accounts. Attach the SCP to the OU. Move the nonproduction member accounts into the new OU.
explanation: The correct answer is: B and E Option A (INCORRECT): Attaching the SCP to the root OU would apply the deny policy to all member accounts (including the production account). The requirement is to prohibit instance launches only in nonproduction accounts, so this is too broad. Option C (INCORRECT): Attaching the SCP to the AWS Organizations management (formerly “master”) account has no effect, because SCPs must be attached to OUs or member accounts, not to the management account itself. Option D (INCORRECT): Creating a new OU for the production account, attaching the SCP there, and moving production into it would apply the deny to production (the opposite of what’s needed). We want to restrict nonproduction, not production. Option B (CORRECT): You can attach the SCP directly to each of the three nonproduction member accounts. That ensures the prohibited instance types are denied only in those nonproduction accounts, leaving production unaffected. Option E (CORRECT): A cleaner approach is to create a dedicated OU for the nonproduction accounts, attach the deny SCP to that OU, and move the three nonproduction accounts into it. This meets the requirement with fewer attachments and clearer organization. In summary, attaching the SCP only to the nonproduction accounts (either directly or via a dedicated OU) enforces the launch restrictions precisely where needed. This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures, as it focuses on applying security controls across AWS accounts using AWS Organizations.

question: A company has an API that receives real-time data from a fleet of monitoring devices. The API stores this data in an Amazon RDS DB instance for later analysis. The amount of data that the monitoring devices send to the API fluctuates. During periods of heavy traffic, the API often returns timeout errors. After an inspection of the logs, the company determines that the database is not capable of processing the volume of write traffic that comes from the API. A solutions architect must minimize the number of connections to the database and must ensure that data is not lost during periods of heavy traffic. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Increase the size of the DB instance to an instance type that has more available memory.
Modify the DB instance to be a Multi-AZ DB instance. Configure the application to write to all active RDS DB instances.
Modify the API to write incoming data to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Use an AWS Lambda function that Amazon SQS invokes to write data from the queue to the database.
Modify the API to write incoming data to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic. Use an AWS Lambda function that Amazon SNS invokes to write data from the topic to the database.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): Increase the size of the DB instance to an instance type that has more available memory. Scaling up the RDS instance may provide more CPU and memory, but it does not address spikes gracefully—it is a reactive, one‐time action and can be expensive. During sudden bursts of write traffic you still risk exhausting connections and I/O capacity, leading to timeouts. No buffering or decoupling is introduced, so the API will continue to fail if the database can’t keep up. Option B (INCORRECT): Modify the DB instance to be a Multi-AZ DB instance. Configure the application to write to all active RDS DB instances. Multi-AZ is for high availability (failover), not for read/write scaling—only the primary accepts writes. You cannot write to the standby in a Multi-AZ setup; there is no mechanism to distribute write traffic across multiple AZs. This option does not reduce connection count or buffer spikes. Option D (INCORRECT): Modify the API to write incoming data to an Amazon SNS topic. Use an AWS Lambda function that Amazon SNS invokes to write data from the topic to the database. SNS is a pub/sub service—not a queue—so it immediately pushes messages to all subscribers, which can cause a storm of concurrent Lambda invocations. High Lambda concurrency leads to many simultaneous DB connections, not fewer. There is no built-in retry/back-pressure mechanism to smooth out spikes: if Lambda or RDS is overwhelmed, messages could be dropped (SNS does not guarantee individual delivery once Lambda fails). Option C (CORRECT): Modify the API to write incoming data to an Amazon SQS queue. Use an AWS Lambda function that Amazon SQS invokes to write data from the queue to the database. SQS provides durable, ordered buffering of incoming messages, absorbing traffic spikes without dropping data. Lambda’s event-source mapping with SQS controls concurrency and the number of messages per batch, limiting simultaneous DB connections. Failed writes can be retried automatically by Lambda (and messages can move to a dead-letter queue if needed), ensuring no data loss. In summary, we learned that to handle fluctuating write volumes and protect the database, decoupling with Amazon SQS and Lambda is the best pattern: it buffers bursts, controls concurrency, and guarantees delivery. This question falls under Domain 2 - Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company needs a backup strategy for its three-tier stateless web application. The web application runs on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group with a dynamic scaling policy that is configured to respond to scaling events. The database tier runs on Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. The web application does not require temporary local storage on the EC2 instances. The company’s recovery point objective (RPO) is 2 hours. The backup strategy must maximize scalability and optimize resource utilization for this environment. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Take snapshots of Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes of the EC2 instances and database every 2 hours to meet the RPO.
Configure a snapshot lifecycle policy to take Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) snapshots. Enable automated backups in Amazon RDS to meet the RPO.
Retain the latest Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) of the web and application tiers. Enable automated backups in Amazon RDS and use point-in-time recovery to meet the RPO.
Take snapshots of Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes of the EC2 instances every 2 hours. Enable automated backups in Amazon RDS and use point-in-time recovery to meet the RPO.
explanation: The correct answer is: Option C Option A (INCORRECT): Take snapshots of Amazon EBS volumes of the EC2 instances and database every 2 hours to meet the RPO. Snapshots of stateless web-tier instances are unnecessary—instances are immutable and auto-scaled, so no persistent data lives on their root volumes. Manual DB snapshots every 2 hours duplicate what RDS automated backups and continuous transaction logs already provide; it’s less efficient and doesn’t optimize resource use. Option B (INCORRECT): Configure a snapshot lifecycle policy to take Amazon EBS snapshots. Enable automated backups in Amazon RDS to meet the RPO. Automating EBS snapshots still wastes resources on ephemeral root volumes for stateless instances—it doesn’t add value to a three-tier stateless design. While RDS automated backups can meet the 2-hour RPO with point-in-time recovery, this option overlooks the more scalable approach for the web/app tier. Option D (INCORRECT): Take snapshots of Amazon EBS volumes of the EC2 instances every 2 hours. Enable automated backups in Amazon RDS and use point-in-time recovery to meet the RPO. This still requires periodic EBS snapshots of stateless instances, which is operationally complex and wasteful. The RDS portion is valid, but the unnecessary EC2 snapshots fail to maximize scalability or resource optimization. Option C (CORRECT): Retain the latest Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) of the web and application tiers. Enable automated backups in Amazon RDS and use point-in-time recovery to meet the RPO. Stateless EC2 instances require no local data backups—keeping a golden AMI lets Auto Scaling launch identical instances on demand, maximizing scalability. RDS automated backups with point-in-time recovery easily satisfy a 2-hour RPO by replaying transaction logs to any second within the retention window. This approach optimizes resource use by avoiding redundant EBS snapshots and leverages AWS managed features for resilience. In summary, we’ve learned that stateless, auto-scaled EC2 tiers are best protected by maintaining up-to-date AMIs rather than frequent EBS snapshots, while RDS’s automated backups and PITR fulfill stringent RPOs efficiently. This question falls under Domain 2 - Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company uses Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) to run a container application. The EKS cluster stores sensitive information in the Kubernetes secrets object. The company wants to ensure that the information is encrypted. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Use the container application to encrypt the information by using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS).
Enable secrets encryption in the EKS cluster by using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS).
Implement an AWS Lambda function to encrypt the information by using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS).
Use AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store to encrypt the information by using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS).
explanation: The correct Answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): “Use the container application to encrypt the information by using AWS KMS.” This would require custom code changes in every container and adds operational overhead for encryption/decryption logic. It does not leverage native Kubernetes/EKS capabilities for securing secrets at rest. Option C (INCORRECT): “Implement an AWS Lambda function to encrypt the information by using AWS KMS.” Introducing Lambda adds an extra integration point and increases operational complexity. Secrets would still be stored in Kubernetes objects, requiring manual wiring between Lambda and the application. Option D (INCORRECT): “Use AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store to encrypt the information by using AWS KMS.” Shifting to Parameter Store changes the storage mechanism out of Kubernetes Secrets, requiring application modifications. It adds operational overhead to manage permissions and API calls to Parameter Store instead of using built-in EKS features. Option B (CORRECT): “Enable secrets encryption in the EKS cluster by using AWS KMS.” EKS offers envelope encryption for Kubernetes Secrets at rest by integrating with AWS KMS with a single cluster configuration change. This requires minimal operational effort—no code changes or additional services—leveraging the native EKS control plane support. You simply specify a KMS key in the EKS encryption configuration and Kubernetes will automatically encrypt/decrypt Secrets using that key. In summary, we’ve learned that Amazon EKS can natively encrypt Kubernetes Secrets at rest by integrating with AWS KMS, offering a secure and low-overhead solution. This question falls under Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A media company stores movies in Amazon S3. Each movie is stored in a single video file that ranges from 1 GB to 10 GB in size. The company must be able to provide the streaming content of a movie within 5 minutes of a user purchase. There is higher demand for movies that are less than 20 years old than for movies that are more than 20 years old. The company wants to minimize hosting service costs based on demand. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Store all media content in Amazon S3. Use S3 Lifecycle policies to move media data into the Infrequent Access tier when the demand for a movie decreases.

Store newer movie video files in S3 Standard. Store older movie video files in S3 Standard-infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA). When a user orders an older movie, retrieve the video file by using standard retrieval.

Store newer movie video files in S3 Intelligent-Tiering. Store older movie video files in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval. When a user orders an older movie, retrieve the video file by using expedited retrieval.
Store newer movie video files in S3 Standard. Store older movie video files in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval. When a user orders an older movie, retrieve the video file by using bulk retrieval.
explanation: The correct answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): “Store all media content in Amazon S3. Use S3 Lifecycle policies to move media data into the Infrequent Access tier when the demand for a movie decreases.” You cannot automatically infer “demand decreases” in real time with Lifecycle rules—they trigger based solely on object age, not on dynamic access patterns. S3 Standard-IA storage has a 30-day minimum charge; movies could sit longer than intended, reducing flexibility. Although retrieval is immediate, you miss deeper cost savings available in Glacier for very infrequently accessed objects. Option B (INCORRECT): “Store newer movie video files in S3 Standard. Store older movie video files in S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA). When a user orders an older movie, retrieve the video file by using standard retrieval.” S3 Standard-IA retrieval cost (~$0.01/GB) and storage cost (~$0.0125/GB-month) are higher than Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage cost (~$0.0036/GB-month). To minimize overall hosting costs, we want the lowest storage tier for rarely accessed objects—Glacier is a better fit. This option does not leverage Glacier’s lowest-cost storage with expedited retrieval for rare but time-sensitive access. Option D (INCORRECT): “Store newer movie video files in S3 Standard. Store older movie video files in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval. When a user orders an older movie, retrieve the video file by using bulk retrieval.” Glacier Bulk retrieval takes 5–12 hours, which fails the requirement to start streaming within 5 minutes of purchase. Bulk retrieval is cost-optimized for extremely infrequent access, not when sub-5-minute access is needed. Option C (CORRECT): “Store newer movie video files in S3 Intelligent-Tiering. Store older movie video files in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval. When a user orders an older movie, retrieve the video file by using expedited retrieval.” S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves newer, frequently accessed movies between frequent and infrequent tiers without operational overhead or retrieval fees. Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage is the lowest cost for older, rarely accessed movies (≈$0.0036/GB-month). Expedited retrieval from Glacier completes in 1–5 minutes, satisfying the “start streaming within 5 minutes” requirement. This design balances cost optimization for old movies with performance SLA for on-demand access. In summary, we learned how to match AWS storage classes to access patterns and cost/performance SLAs—leveraging Intelligent-Tiering for dynamic demand and Glacier with expedited retrieval for time-sensitive, low-frequency access. This question falls under Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company needs a solution to prevent AWS CloudFormation stacks from deploying AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) resources that include an inline policy or “*” in the statement. The solution must also prohibit deployment of Amazon EC2 instances with public IP addresses. The company has AWS Control Tower enabled in its organization in AWS Organizations.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Use AWS Control Tower proactive controls to block deployment of EC2 instances with public IP addresses and inline policies with elevated access or “*”.
Use AWS Control Tower detective controls to block deployment of EC2 instances with public IP addresses and inline policies with elevated access or “*”.
Use AWS Config to create rules for EC2 and IAM compliance. Configure the rules to run an AWS Systems Manager Session Manager automation to delete a resource when it is not compliant.
Use a service control policy (SCP) to block actions for the EC2 instances and IAM resources if the actions lead to noncompliance.
explanation: The correct answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): Use AWS Control Tower detective controls to block deployment of EC2 instances with public IP addresses and inline policies with elevated access or “*”. Detective controls only detect and report non-compliance after resources are provisioned—they cannot prevent creation. The requirement is to stop deployments upfront, not merely to alert or remediate afterward. Option C (INCORRECT): Use AWS Config to create rules for EC2 and IAM compliance, then run an SSM automation to delete non-compliant resources. AWS Config is a post-deployment compliance checker; it cannot block resource creation. Deleting resources after they’re created does not satisfy the requirement to prohibit their deployment in the first place. Option D (INCORRECT): Use a service control policy (SCP) to block actions for EC2 instances and IAM resources if the actions lead to noncompliance. SCPs can restrict API actions but cannot inspect inline policy documents or wildcard statements (“*”) for prevention. While you can deny public-IP assignment via SCP conditions, it’s complex and duplicate to the managed guardrails provided by Control Tower. Option A (CORRECT): Use AWS Control Tower proactive controls to block deployment of EC2 instances with public IP addresses and inline policies with elevated access or “*”. Proactive controls are preventive guardrails that enforce compliance at provisioning time, stopping non-compliant resources from being created. AWS Control Tower offers managed proactive controls for both disallowing wildcard IAM permissions and preventing public IP assignments on EC2. This approach directly meets the requirement to prevent deployments rather than detect or remediate after the fact. In summary, the best solution is to leverage AWS Control Tower proactive controls because they enforce preventive guardrails for both IAM policies and EC2 configurations at provisioning time. This question belongs to Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company's production environment consists of Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances that run constantly between Monday and Saturday. The instances must run for only 12 hours on Sunday and cannot tolerate interruptions. The company wants to cost-optimize the production environment.Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Purchase Scheduled Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that run for only 12 hours on Sunday. Purchase Standard Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that run constantly between Monday and Saturday.

Purchase Convertible Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that run for only 12 hours on Sunday. Purchase Standard Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that run constantly between Monday and Saturday.
Use Spot Instances for the EC2 instances that run for only 12 hours on Sunday. Purchase Standard Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that run constantly between Monday and Saturday.
Use Spot Instances for the EC2 instances that run for only 12 hours on Sunday. Purchase Convertible Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that run constantly between Monday and Saturday.
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): Purchase Convertible Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that run only 12 hours on Sunday. Purchase Standard Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that run constantly between Monday and Saturday. Convertible RIs are more expensive than Standard RIs and offer flexibility you don't need for a fixed, predictable schedule. Scheduled Reserved Instances exist specifically to cover predictable time slots (like a 12-hour window every Sunday) at a lower rate. Option C (INCORRECT): Use Spot Instances for the EC2 instances that run for only 12 hours on Sunday. Purchase Standard Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that run constantly between Monday and Saturday. Spot Instances can be interrupted by AWS with little notice, violating the requirement that the Sunday run “cannot tolerate interruptions.” Not suitable for critical production workloads that must run reliably. Option D (INCORRECT): Use Spot Instances for the EC2 instances that run for only 12 hours on Sunday. Purchase Convertible Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that run constantly between Monday and Saturday. Spot Instances remain unreliable for non-interruptible workloads. Convertible RIs add unnecessary cost and flexibility when instance attributes are known and fixed—Standard RIs deliver deeper discounts. Option A (CORRECT): Purchase Scheduled Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that run only 12 hours on Sunday. Purchase Standard Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that run constantly between Monday and Saturday. Scheduled RIs provide the lowest rates for predictable, recurring time windows (e.g., a 12-hour slot each Sunday). Standard RIs deliver the highest savings for instances that run continuously from Monday through Saturday. This combination meets the “no interruptions” requirement and minimizes overall costs. Summary: We’ve learned how to leverage Scheduled Reserved Instances alongside Standard Reserved Instances to achieve maximum cost savings for workloads with fixed schedules and strict availability requirements. This question belongs to Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company has an application that runs on several Amazon EC2 instances. Each EC2 instance has multiple Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) data volumes attached to it. The application’s EC2 instance configuration and data need to be backed up nightly. The application also needs to be recoverable in a different AWS Region. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way?
options: Write an AWS Lambda function that schedules nightly snapshots of the application’s EBS volumes and copies the snapshots to a different Region.
Create a backup plan by using AWS Backup to perform nightly backups. Copy the backups to another Region. Add the application’s EC2 instances as resources.
Create a backup plan by using AWS Backup to perform nightly backups. Copy the backups to another Region. Add the application’s EBS volumes as resources.
Write an AWS Lambda function that schedules nightly snapshots of the application's EBS volumes and copies the snapshots to a different Availability Zone.
explanation: The correct answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): Write an AWS Lambda function that schedules nightly snapshots of the application’s EBS volumes and copies the snapshots to a different Region. Custom scripting and maintenance of Lambda code increases operational overhead. Does not capture the EC2 instance configuration; only EBS volumes are snapshotted. Reinventing features that AWS Backup provides natively is less efficient. Option C (INCORRECT): Create a backup plan by using AWS Backup to perform nightly backups. Copy the backups to another Region. Add the application’s EBS volumes as resources. Backs up only the data volumes, not the EC2 instance configuration (AMI metadata, tags, instance settings). Fails to meet the requirement to recover the full EC2 configuration in the target Region. Option D (INCORRECT): Write an AWS Lambda function that schedules nightly snapshots of the application's EBS volumes and copies the snapshots to a different Availability Zone. Copying to another Availability Zone does not satisfy the multi-Region recovery requirement. Custom Lambda code increases complexity and operational burden. Option B (CORRECT): Create a backup plan by using AWS Backup to perform nightly backups. Copy the backups to another Region. Add the application’s EC2 instances as resources. AWS Backup automates both EBS snapshots and captures EC2 instance configuration as part of the EC2 resource backup. Built-in cross-Region copy support ensures backups are replicated nightly without custom code. Operationally efficient: central backup policies, automated retention, and seamless recovery in another Region. In summary, AWS Backup with EC2 instance–level protection (Option B) meets both data and configuration backup requirements, automates cross-Region replication, and minimizes operational overhead. This question belongs to Domain 2 - Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company's image-hosting website gives users around the world the ability to up load, view, and download images from their mobile devices. The company currently hosts the static website in an Amazon S3 bucket. Because of the website's growing popularity, the website's performance has decreased. Users have reported latency issues when they upload and download images. The company must improve the performance of the website. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST implementation effort?
options: Configure an Amazon CloudFront distribution for the S3 bucket to improve the download performance. Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration to improve the upload performance.

Configure Amazon EC2 instances of the right sizes in multiple AWS Regions. Migrate the application to the EC2 instances. Use an Application Load Balancer to distribute the website traffic equally among the EC2 instances. Configure AWS Global Accelerator to address global demand with low latency.

Configure an Amazon CloudFront distribution that uses the S3 bucket as an origin to improve the download performance. Configure the application to use CloudFront to upload images to improve the upload performance. Create S3 buckets in multiple AWS Regions. Configure replication rules for the buckets to replicate users' data based on the users' location. Redirect downloads to the S3 bucket that is closest to each user's location.
Configure AWS Global Accelerator for the S3 bucket to improve network performance. Create an endpoint for the application to use Global Accelerator instead of the S3 bucket.
explanation: The correct Answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): “Configure Amazon EC2 instances of the right sizes in multiple AWS Regions. Migrate the application to the EC2 instances. Use an Application Load Balancer to distribute the website traffic equally among the EC2 instances. Configure AWS Global Accelerator to address global demand with low latency.” This requires rewriting and migrating a static‐site workload to EC2, which is heavy and unnecessary for static content. Managing EC2 fleets across regions adds operational overhead and cost. The question asks for the least implementation effort; this is far too complex. Option C (INCORRECT): “Configure an Amazon CloudFront distribution that uses the S3 bucket as an origin to improve download performance. Configure the application to use CloudFront to upload images to improve the upload performance. Create S3 buckets in multiple AWS Regions. Configure replication rules for the buckets to replicate users' data based on the users' location. Redirect downloads to the S3 bucket that is closest to each user's location.” Introducing multiple S3 buckets and cross‐region replication greatly increases complexity and cost. Redirecting users based on location is custom logic that increases implementation effort. You already can accelerate uploads globally without managing many buckets. Option D (INCORRECT): “Configure AWS Global Accelerator for the S3 bucket to improve network performance. Create an endpoint for the application to use Global Accelerator instead of the S3 bucket.” AWS Global Accelerator does not natively accelerate S3 bucket access. Global Accelerator is designed for static IP fronting of regional endpoints (e.g., ALBs, NLBs), not for S3 static websites. You cannot point a Global Accelerator directly at an S3 website endpoint. Option A (CORRECT): “Configure an Amazon CloudFront distribution for the S3 bucket to improve download performance. Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration to improve the upload performance.” CloudFront caches and serves content from edge locations worldwide, reducing download latency with virtually no changes to your site. S3 Transfer Acceleration leverages the AWS Edge Network to accelerate uploads into the bucket, improving upload speeds globally. This solution involves minimal configuration—no new servers, no custom replication—and meets both upload and download performance requirements. In summary, we learned that for a static S3‐hosted website with global users, combining Amazon CloudFront (for downloads) and S3 Transfer Acceleration (for uploads) delivers the best performance improvement with the least implementation effort. This question belongs to Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company has a mobile chat application with a data store based in Amazon DynamoDB. Users would like new messages to be read with as little latency as possible. A solutions architect needs to design an optimal solution that requires minimal application changes.Which method should the solutions architect select?
options: Configure Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) for the new messages table. Update the code to use the DAX endpoint.
Add DynamoDB read replicas to handle the increased read load. Update the application to point to the read endpoint for the read replicas.
Double the number of read capacity units for the new messages table in DynamoDB. Continue to use the existing DynamoDB endpoint.
Add an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cache to the application stack. Update the application to point to the Redis cache endpoint instead of DynamoDB.
explanation: The correct Answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): “Add DynamoDB read replicas to handle the increased read load. Update the application to point to the read endpoint for the read replicas.” DynamoDB does not offer traditional read replicas within a single region; instead it has Global Tables for multi-Region replication, which adds complexity and latency across regions. Pointing to a “read endpoint” isn’t a supported pattern in a single-region deployment, and this would require significant architectural changes. This option fails to deliver microsecond-level latency improvements and does not meet the minimal-change requirement. Option C (INCORRECT): “Double the number of read capacity units for the new messages table in DynamoDB. Continue to use the existing DynamoDB endpoint.” Increasing Read Capacity Units only scales throughput, not single-request latency. DynamoDB’s typical single-digit millisecond latency remains unchanged; users still experience higher latency than an in-memory cache solution. This approach also increases cost without solving the core requirement of ultra-low latency. Option D (INCORRECT): “Add an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cache to the application stack. Update the application to point to the Redis cache endpoint instead of DynamoDB.” Integrating Redis requires application-level caching logic (cache puts, cache misses, invalidation) and more code changes. Developers must handle TTLs, cache consistency, and fallback strategies—contrary to “minimal application changes.” Although ElastiCache can reduce latency, it introduces operational overhead and complexity. Option A (CORRECT): “Configure Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) for the new messages table. Update the code to use the DAX endpoint.” DAX is a fully managed, in-memory cache for DynamoDB that delivers microsecond read latency. It supports the DynamoDB API natively—only a single endpoint change is required in your application. DAX handles cache management (write-through and invalidation) automatically, minimizing code and operational overhead. This meets the requirement for minimal application changes while providing the lowest possible read latency. In summary, we learned that for a read-heavy, low-latency DynamoDB use case requiring minimal code changes, Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is the optimal solution. This question falls under Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company runs a real-time data ingestion solution on AWS. The solution consists of the most recent version of Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (Amazon MSK). The solution is deployed in a VPC in private subnets across three Availability Zones. A solutions architect needs to redesign the data ingestion solution to be publicly available over the internet. The data in transit must also be encrypted. Which solution will meet these requirements with the MOST operational efficiency?
options: Configure public subnets in the existing VPC. Deploy an MSK cluster in the public subnets. Update the MSK cluster security settings to enable mutual TLS authentication.
Create a new VPC that has public subnets. Deploy an MSK cluster in the public subnets. Update the MSK cluster security settings to enable mutual TLS authentication.
Deploy an Application Load Balancer (ALB) that uses private subnets. Configure an ALB security group inbound rule to allow inbound traffic from the VPC CIDR block for HTTPS protocol.
Deploy a Network Load Balancer (NLB) that uses private subnets. Configure an NLB listener for HTTPS communication over the internet.
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): “Create a new VPC that has public subnets. Deploy an MSK cluster in the public subnets. Update the MSK cluster security settings to enable mutual TLS authentication.” Creating a brand-new VPC adds unnecessary operational overhead when an existing VPC can be extended. Amazon MSK manages broker ENIs and requires private subnets for best practice and security; you cannot simply place managed brokers in public subnets. Option C (INCORRECT): “Deploy an Application Load Balancer (ALB) that uses private subnets. Configure an ALB security group inbound rule to allow inbound traffic from the VPC CIDR block for HTTPS protocol.” ALBs operate at Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) and do not support the Kafka protocol (TCP/TLS passthrough) needed for MSK. Putting the ALB in private subnets prevents public Internet access, defeating the requirement. Option D (INCORRECT): “Deploy a Network Load Balancer (NLB) that uses private subnets. Configure an NLB listener for HTTPS communication over the internet.” To serve Internet traffic, an NLB must be internet-facing and placed in public subnets, not private ones. TLS termination at the NLB is optional, but mutual TLS for Kafka is done at the broker level—simply configuring HTTPS does not satisfy the Kafka protocol encryption requirement. Option A (CORRECT): “Configure public subnets in the existing VPC. Deploy an MSK cluster in the public subnets. Update the MSK cluster security settings to enable mutual TLS authentication.” Reusing the existing VPC and adding public subnets minimizes operational overhead and leverages existing network configuration. Deploying the MSK cluster in public subnets and enabling mutual TLS ensures both Internet accessibility and in-transit encryption at the Kafka protocol level. This approach meets requirements with the least operational complexity. In summary, we learned that to expose an Amazon MSK cluster publicly while ensuring in-transit encryption, you should extend your existing VPC with public subnets and enable mutual TLS on the brokers. This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company runs database workloads on AWS that are the backend for the company's customer portals. The company runs a Multi-AZ database cluster on Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. The company needs to implement a 30-day backup retention policy. The company currently has both automated RDS backups and manual RDS backups. The company wants to maintain both types of existing RDS backups that are less than 30 days old. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Configure the RDS backup retention policy to 30 days for automated backups by using AWS Backup. Manually delete manual backups that are older than 30 days.
Disable RDS automated backups. Delete automated backups and manual backups that are older than 30 days. Configure the RDS backup retention policy to 30 days for automated backups.
Configure the RDS backup retention policy to 30 days for automated backups. Manually delete manual backups that are older than 30 days.

Disable RDS automated backups. Delete automated backups and manual backups that are older than 30 days automatically by using AWS CloudFormation. Configure the RDS backup retention policy to 30 days for automated backups.
explanation: The correct answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): “Configure the RDS backup retention policy to 30 days for automated backups by using AWS Backup. Manually delete manual backups that are older than 30 days.” Using AWS Backup adds extra service costs when RDS’s native retention setting already handles automated backups up to 35 days free of additional service fees. It’s unnecessary to involve AWS Backup for an RDS-managed retention policy; simply setting the retention period on the DB instance is sufficient. Option B (INCORRECT): “Disable RDS automated backups. Delete automated backups and manual backups that are older than 30 days. Configure the RDS backup retention policy to 30 days for automated backups.” Disabling automated backups contradicts the requirement to maintain automated backups for up to 30 days. Re-enabling automated backups only to set the retention policy is redundant and risks data protection features like point-in-time recovery. Option D (INCORRECT): “Disable RDS automated backups. Delete automated backups and manual backups that are older than 30 days automatically by using AWS CloudFormation. Configure the RDS backup retention policy to 30 days for automated backups.” CloudFormation is not designed for scheduled deletion of snapshots—it’s an infrastructure provisioning tool, not a housekeeping service. Again, disabling automated backups removes the built-in safeguard of point-in-time recovery. This approach complicates the solution without any cost benefit over simply using RDS retention settings. Option C (CORRECT): “Configure the RDS backup retention policy to 30 days for automated backups. Manually delete manual backups that are older than 30 days.” RDS automated backups support a retention period up to 35 days—setting it to 30 days meets the requirement at no added service cost. Manual snapshots persist until you delete them. Periodically removing those older than 30 days ensures compliance and minimizes storage charges. No need for extra services or disabling core backup features; this is the simplest and most cost-effective approach. Summary: We learned that Amazon RDS’s native automated backup retention setting can handle up to 35 days of backups at no extra service cost, and manual snapshots must be pruned manually to enforce retention policies. This question falls under Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company has an internal application that runs on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The EC2 instances are compute optimized and use Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes. The company wants to identify cost optimizations across the EC2 instances, the Auto Scaling group, and the EBS volumes. Which solution will meet these requirements with the MOST operational efficiency?
options: Create a new AWS Cost and Usage Report. Search the report for cost recommendations for the EC2 instances the Auto Scaling group, and the EBS volumes.
Create new Amazon CloudWatch billing alerts. Check the alert statuses for cost recommendations for the EC2 instances, the Auto Scaling group, and the EBS volumes.
Configure AWS Compute Optimizer for cost recommendations for the EC2 instances, the Auto Scaling group and the EBS volumes.

Configure AWS Compute Optimizer for cost recommendations for the EC2 instances. Create a new AWS Cost and Usage Report. Search the report for cost recommendations for the Auto Scaling group and the EBS volumes.
explanation: The correct answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): • AWS Cost and Usage Reports provide detailed billing data, but they do NOT generate automated cost-optimization recommendations. • You would have to manually analyze large CSV files, reducing operational efficiency. Option B (INCORRECT): • CloudWatch billing alerts can notify you when spending exceeds thresholds, but they do NOT offer service-specific right-sizing or volume-type recommendations. • This approach lacks the insights needed for EC2 instance, Auto Scaling group, or EBS optimization. Option D (INCORRECT): • Splitting responsibilities between Compute Optimizer (for EC2) and Cost and Usage Reports (for ASG/EBS) adds operational overhead. • You lose the single pane of glass for recommendations and increase manual effort. Option C (CORRECT): • AWS Compute Optimizer analyzes usage patterns and provides automated recommendations for: EC2 instance families and sizes Auto Scaling group target tracking policies and instance types EBS volume types and throughput configurations • This fully managed service delivers actionable guidance in one place, maximizing operational efficiency. Summary: We learned that AWS Compute Optimizer is the optimal choice to gain automated, service-specific cost recommendations for EC2 instances, Auto Scaling groups, and EBS volumes with minimal manual effort. This question belongs to Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: An ecommerce company wants a disaster recovery solution for its Amazon RDS DB instances that run Microsoft SQL Server Enterprise Edition. The company's current recovery point objective (RPO) and recovery time objective (RTO) are 24 hours. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Create a cross-Region read replica and promote the read replica to the primary instance.
Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to create RDS cross-Region replication.
Use cross-Region replication every 24 hours to copy native backups to an Amazon S3 bucket.
Copy automatic snapshots to another Region every 24 hours.
explanation: The correct answer is D Option A (INCORRECT): • Amazon RDS SQL Server does not support cross-Region Read Replicas. Read replicas are available only for MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, Oracle (with Enterprise Edition), and Aurora. • Even if SQL Server supported it, maintaining a continuous replica would be more expensive than a once-daily snapshot for a 24-hour RPO/RTO. Option B (INCORRECT): • AWS Database Migration Service is intended for homogeneous and heterogeneous migrations with ongoing replication, not for scheduled DR backups. • DMS incurs additional compute and licensing costs for replication instances and isn’t the most cost-effective method when you only need a daily recovery point. Option C (INCORRECT): • “Cross-Region replication every 24 hours to copy native backups to an S3 bucket” is not an automated RDS feature. You’d have to build custom scripts or SQL Server jobs to export and transfer backups, adding operational overhead. • This approach is more complex and error-prone than using built-in snapshot copying. Option D (CORRECT): • Amazon RDS allows you to automatically copy snapshots to another Region on a schedule (e.g., every 24 hours) at minimal additional cost. • This meets a 24-hour RPO (you have the last daily snapshot) and a 24-hour RTO (you can restore the snapshot in the target Region within hours). • No extra replication instances or manual processes are required, making it the most cost-optimized solution for the given requirements. In summary, for a 24-hour RPO and RTO on SQL Server Enterprise Edition, using automated cross-Region snapshot copy is the simplest and most cost-effective disaster recovery solution. This question falls under Domain 4 – Design Cost-Optimized Architectures

question: A company runs a website that stores images of historical events. Website users need the ability to search and view images based on the year that the event in the image occurred. On average, users request each image only once or twice a year. The company wants a highly available solution to store and deliver the images to users. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Store images in Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS). Use a web server that runs on Amazon EC2.
Store images in Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS). Use a web server that runs on Amazon EC2.
Store images in Amazon S3 Standard. Use S3 Standard to directly deliver images by using a static website.
