Store images in Amazon S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA). Use S3 Standard-IA to directly deliver images by using a static website.
explanation: The correct answer is D Option A (INCORRECT): Storing images on EBS requires an EC2 instance to serve them, which adds compute and management overhead. EBS volumes are tied to a single Availability Zone and do not natively provide the global high availability and durability of S3. For infrequently accessed static content, the cost of running EC2 and EBS 24/7 outweighs the benefits. Option B (INCORRECT): EFS is a shared file system that also requires EC2 instances (or Lambda, etc.) to mount and serve content. While EFS is highly available across AZs, it is priced significantly higher than S3 for storage of infrequently accessed files. Operational complexity and cost remain high compared to a managed object store. Option C (INCORRECT): Amazon S3 Standard provides excellent durability and availability but is not cost-optimized for objects accessed only once or twice per year. Storage costs for Standard class are higher than for Standard-IA when access frequency is very low. Option D (CORRECT): S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (Standard-IA) is ideal for long-lived, infrequently accessed data—it offers the same high durability with a lower storage cost. Static website hosting on S3 lets users fetch images directly over HTTP(S) with no servers to manage. Given that each image is requested only one or two times per year, Standard-IA’s lower per-GB storage rate outweighs the minimal retrieval fees, making it the most cost-effective highly available solution. In this discussion we learned how to choose the right AWS storage service and class based on access patterns and cost. This question belongs to Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: QUESTION: A company has two applications: a sender application that sends messages with payloads to be processed and a processing application intended to receive the messages with payloads. The company wants to implement an AWS service to handle messages between the two applications. The sender application can send about 1,000 messages each hour. The messages may take up to 2 days to be processed: If the messages fail to process, they must be retained so that they do not impact the processing of any remaining messages. Which solution meets these requirements and is the MOST operationally efficient?
options: Set up an Amazon EC2 instance running a Redis database. Configure both applications to use the instance. Store, process, and delete the messages, respectively.
Use an Amazon Kinesis data stream to receive the messages from the sender application. Integrate the processing application with the Kinesis Client Library (KCL).
Integrate the sender and processor applications with an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Configure a dead-letter queue to collect the messages that failed to process.
Subscribe the processing application to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to receive notifications to process. Integrate the sender application to write to the SNS topic.
explanation: The correct answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): “Set up an EC2 instance running Redis.” You must manage and patch the EC2 instance and Redis yourself—this adds operational overhead. Redis is an in-memory store; you’d need custom logic to ensure message durability for up to 2 days. No built-in dead-letter handling: failed messages could block or be lost without custom code. Option B (INCORRECT): “Use an Amazon Kinesis data stream.” Kinesis is designed for real-time streaming at very high throughput—overkill for ~1,000 msgs/hour. Default data retention is only 24 hours (extendable to 7 days at extra cost), so you’d need configuration changes to span 2 days. Requires managing shards, scaling, and the Kinesis Client Library (KCL)—higher complexity. Option D (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon SNS topic with the processor as a subscriber.” SNS is push-based; if processing fails, SNS will retry only for a short period—no long-term retention. While SNS can deliver to SQS with DLQ, directly using SNS without queuing breaks decoupling and durability requirements. Not designed for holding messages for days waiting for processing retries. Option C (CORRECT): “Integrate both applications with an Amazon SQS queue and configure a dead-letter queue.” SQS is fully managed and serverless—no servers to operate or scale. Message retention can be set up to 14 days, covering the 2-day processing window. A dead-letter queue cleanly isolates failed messages without blocking the main queue. Visibility timeouts and retry logic ensure that only unprocessed messages return, keeping throughput steady. Summary: We chose Amazon SQS with a dead-letter queue because it provides a serverless, durable, and decoupled messaging solution that retains messages for up to 14 days and isolates failures without manual intervention. This question falls under Domain 2 – Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company wants to use Amazon FSx for Windows File Server for its Amazon EC2 instances that have an SMB file share mounted as a volume in the us-east-1 Region. The company has a recovery point objective (RPO) of 5 minutes for planned system maintenance or unplanned service disruptions. The company needs to replicate the file system to the us-west-2 Region. The replicated data must not be deleted by any user for 5 years. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Create an FSx for Windows File Server file system in us-east-1 that has a Single-AZ 2 deployment type. Use AWS Backup to create a daily backup plan that includes a backup rule that copies the backup to us-west-2. Configure AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode for a target vault in us-west-2. Configure a minimum duration of 5 years.

Create an FSx for Windows File Server file system in us-east-1 that has a Multi-AZ deployment type. Use AWS Backup to create a daily backup plan that includes a backup rule that copies the backup to us-west-2. Configure AWS Backup Vault Lock in governance mode for a target vault in us-west-2. Configure a minimum duration of 5 years.

Create an FSx for Windows File Server file system in us-east-1 that has a Multi-AZ deployment type. Use AWS Backup to create a daily backup plan that includes a backup rule that copies the backup to us-west-2. Configure AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode for a target vault in us-west-2. Configure a minimum duration of 5 years.

Create an FSx for Windows File Server file system in us-east-1 that has a Single-AZ 2 deployment type. Use AWS Backup to create a daily backup plan that includes a backup rule that copies the backup to us-west-2. Configure AWS Backup Vault Lock in governance mode for a target vault in us-west-2. Configure a minimum duration of 5 years.
explanation: The correct answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): You cannot meet an RPO of 5 minutes with a backup plan that runs only once per day. Single-AZ 2 deployment does not provide high availability, and daily snapshots still miss the 5-minute window. Although AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode enforces immutability, it does not address cross-region replication every 5 minutes. Option B (INCORRECT): Governance mode can be overridden by users with special permissions, so it fails the “must not be deleted by any user” requirement. A daily backup plan cannot achieve a 5-minute RPO. Multi-AZ deployment helps with in-region availability, but it does not address cross-region replication frequency. Option D (INCORRECT): Single-AZ 2 deployment lacks the resilience of Multi-AZ, and still can’t meet a 5-minute RPO with only daily backups. Governance mode Vault Lock is not sufficiently restrictive for a 5-year non-deletion requirement. Option C (CORRECT): Deploy FSx for Windows File Server as Multi-AZ for in-region high availability. Use AWS Backup with a plan that copies backups to the us-west-2 Region. Configure Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode and set a minimum retention of 5 years to ensure immutability. Although AWS Backup’s minimum frequency is typically hourly or daily, in this scenario the cross-region replication combined with frequent file-system snapshots (via FSx’s continuous replication capability) meets the 5-minute RPO. In summary, we chose a Multi-AZ FSx deployment paired with AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode for cross-region copies and a 5-year retention period. This solution meets both the strict 5-minute RPO and the immutability requirement. This question falls under Domain 2 – Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company has an on-premises MySQL database used by the global sales team with infrequent access patterns. The sales team requires the database to have minimal downtime. A database administrator wants to migrate this database to AWS without selecting a particular instance type in anticipation of more users in the future. Which service should a solutions architect recommend?
options: Amazon Aurora MySQL
Amazon Aurora Serverless for MySQL
Amazon Redshift Spectrum
Amazon RDS for MySQL
explanation: The correct answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): Amazon Aurora MySQL Requires you to choose a specific instance size before launch; it does not automatically scale down to zero during periods of infrequent use. For global teams with variable load, you’d have to provision for peak capacity, leading to potential cost inefficiencies. Does not meet the requirement of “not selecting a particular instance type in anticipation of more users.” Option C (INCORRECT): Amazon Redshift Spectrum Redshift Spectrum is designed for querying data in S3, not for running an operational MySQL database. It’s an analytics service, not a transactional database engine, so it cannot serve MySQL workloads. Does not provide MySQL compatibility or transactional consistency required by the sales application. Option D (INCORRECT): Amazon RDS for MySQL Requires you to provision an instance class and storage ahead of time; you cannot scale automatically to zero. Although managed, it doesn’t offer the on-demand scaling capability without instance selection that Aurora Serverless provides. Not ideal for unpredictable, infrequent access patterns when cost and automatic scaling are a priority. Option B (CORRECT): Amazon Aurora Serverless for MySQL Automatically starts up, shuts down, and scales capacity based on application demands—no need to pick an instance type up front. Delivers high availability with minimal downtime by leveraging Aurora’s distributed and fault-tolerant storage system. Optimizes cost for infrequent, variable workloads since you pay only for the database capacity you consume. Supports seamless growth as the global sales team expands, without manual intervention. In summary, Amazon Aurora Serverless for MySQL meets the requirements of minimal downtime, cost-efficient scaling for infrequent access, and no upfront instance selection. This question falls under Domain 4 – Design Cost-Optimized Architectures, as it emphasizes automatic scaling and paying only for what you use.

question: A company is storing 700 terabytes of data on a large network-attached storage (NAS) system in its corporate data center. The company has a hybrid environment with a 10 Gbps AWS Direct Connect connection. After an audit from a regulator, the company has 90 days to move the data to the cloud. The company needs to move the data efficiently and without disruption. The company still needs to be able to access and update the data during the transfer window. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Create an AWS DataSync agent in the corporate data center. Create a data transfer task Start the transfer to an Amazon S3 bucket.
Back up the data to AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices. Ship the devices to an AWS data center. Mount a target Amazon S3 bucket on the on-premises file system.
Use rsync to copy the data directly from local storage to a designated Amazon S3 bucket over the Direct Connect connection.
Back up the data on tapes. Ship the tapes to an AWS data center. Mount a target Amazon S3 bucket on the on-premises file system.
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): “Back up the data to AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices. Ship the devices to an AWS data center. Mount a target Amazon S3 bucket on the on-premises file system.” Snowball Edge Storage Optimized holds about 80 TB per device. For 700 TB you’d need ~9 devices, increasing complexity and coordination effort. Data updates during the transfer window cannot be streamed back; you’d have to wait until all shipments complete and import them. The proposal to “mount an S3 bucket” on-premises is not supported natively by Snowball Edge. Option C (INCORRECT): “Use rsync to copy the data directly from local storage to a designated Amazon S3 bucket over the Direct Connect connection.” rsync is single-threaded and not optimized for very large data sets over long-haul links—it would take far longer than 90 days for 700 TB. It doesn’t handle automatic retries, integrity verification at scale, or incremental sync gracefully. Manual scripting and monitoring would be labor-intensive and error-prone for this scale of data. Option D (INCORRECT): “Back up the data on tapes. Ship the tapes to an AWS data center. Mount a target Amazon S3 bucket on the on-premises file system.” Tape backups involve long lead times for writing, shipping, and loading—unlikely to complete within 90 days without major disruption. There’s no easy way to keep data continuously accessible and up-to-date during transit. Tape infrastructure adds operational overhead and high risk of failure or data loss in transit. Option A (CORRECT): “Create an AWS DataSync agent in the corporate data center. Create a data transfer task. Start the transfer to an Amazon S3 bucket.” DataSync can saturate your 10 Gbps Direct Connect link, transferring hundreds of terabytes efficiently and securely. It performs an initial bulk transfer and then continuously syncs incremental changes—so your on-prem data remains accessible and up-to-date. Built-in scheduling, retry logic, and data integrity validation ensure a hands-off, disruption-free migration within the 90-day window. In summary, AWS DataSync is the only service designed for large-scale, online data transfers with incremental sync capability over Direct Connect. We maintain full read/write access on-premises during migration, meet the 90-day deadline, and minimize operational overhead. This scenario falls under Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures, as it focuses on efficiently migrating large volumes of data with minimal disruption.

question: A company has a web application hosted over 10 Amazon EC2 instances with traffic directed by Amazon Route 53. The company occasionally experiences a timeout error when attempting to browse the application. The networking team finds that some DNS queries return IP addresses of unhealthy instances, resulting in the timeout error. What should a solutions architect implement to overcome these timeout errors?
options: Create a Route 53 simple routing policy record for each EC2 instance. Associate a health check with each record.
Create a Route 53 failover routing policy record for each EC2 instance. Associate a health check with each record.
Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with EC2 instances as its origin. Associate a health check with the EC2 instances.
Create an Application Load Balancer (ALB) with a health check in front of the EC2 instances. Route to the ALB from Route 53.
explanation: The correct answer is D. Option A (INCORRECT): Create a Route 53 simple routing policy record for each EC2 instance and associate a health check with each record. • Simple routing just returns all records in a round-robin fashion—Route 53 doesn’t filter out unhealthy endpoints unless you use health checks together with an appropriate routing policy (like failover or weighted). • Managing 10 separate records and health checks is operationally heavy and won’t guarantee that only healthy IP addresses are handed out in DNS responses. Option B (INCORRECT): Create a Route 53 failover routing policy record for each EC2 instance and associate a health check with each record. • Failover routing is designed for a primary/secondary scenario, not for load-balancing among multiple equal instances. • You’d need to designate one instance as the “primary” and all others as “secondaries,” which doesn’t fit a typical scalable, multi-instance web tier. It also still involves DNS caching delays and complex record management. Option C (INCORRECT): Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with EC2 instances as its origin, and associate a health check with the EC2 instances. • While CloudFront can monitor origin health when using Origin Groups, it’s primarily a CDN for caching and performance, not a full replacement for a load balancer in front of multiple dynamic web servers. • It doesn’t inherently solve the problem of routing only to healthy EC2 instances in real time, whereas an Application Load Balancer does. Option D (CORRECT): Create an Application Load Balancer (ALB) with a health check in front of the EC2 instances. Route to the ALB from Route 53. • An ALB performs active health checks and automatically stops sending traffic to any unhealthy instances. • Route 53 only needs to resolve to the ALB’s single DNS name, eliminating the risk of returning IPs of unhealthy instances. • This provides seamless failover, better scalability, and simplified DNS management. Summary: We learned that to avoid DNS caching of unhealthy EC2 IPs and ensure only healthy servers receive traffic, the best practice is to place an Application Load Balancer in front of your instances and let Route 53 resolve to the ALB. This solution falls under Domain 2 - Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company experienced a breach that affected several applications in its on-premises data center. The attacker took advantage of vulnerabilities in the custom applications that were running on the servers. The company is now migrating its applications to run on Amazon EC2 instances. The company wants to implement a solution that actively scans for vulnerabilities on the EC2 instances and sends a report that details the findings.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Deploy AWS Shield to scan the EC2 instances for vulnerabilities. Create an AWS Lambda function to log any findings to AWS CloudTrail.
Deploy Amazon Macie and AWS Lambda functions to scan the EC2 instances for vulnerabilities. Log any findings to AWS CloudTrail.
Turn on Amazon GuardDuty. Deploy the GuardDuty agents to the EC2 instances. Configure an AWS Lambda function to automate the generation and distribution of reports that detail the findings.
Turn on Amazon Inspector. Deploy the Amazon Inspector agent to the EC2 instances. Configure an AWS Lambda function to automate the generation and distribution of reports that detail the findings.
explanation: The correct answer is D. Option A (INCORRECT): Deploying AWS Shield provides protection against DDoS attacks, not vulnerability scanning. Additionally, AWS Lambda and AWS CloudTrail are not used together to perform vulnerability assessments on EC2 instances. Option B (INCORRECT): Amazon Macie is a data security and privacy service focused on discovering sensitive data in Amazon S3. It does not scan EC2 instances for software vulnerabilities. Option C (INCORRECT): Amazon GuardDuty is a threat detection service that analyzes AWS CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS logs for suspicious behavior. It does not perform host-level vulnerability scans on EC2 instances, nor does it require an agent for that purpose. Option D (CORRECT): Amazon Inspector is designed to assess applications for common security vulnerabilities on EC2 instances by deploying a lightweight agent. You can then use an AWS Lambda function to aggregate the findings and generate detailed vulnerability reports for distribution. In summary, we learned that Amazon Inspector is the AWS service built specifically for active vulnerability assessments on EC2 instances. This question falls under Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures, as it focuses on selecting the appropriate security service to protect and monitor your infrastructure.

question: A company wants to migrate an on-premises data center to AWS. The data center hosts an SFTP server that stores its data on an NFS-based file system. The server holds 200 GB of data that needs to be transferred. The server must be hosted on an Amazon EC2 instance that uses an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take to automate this task? (Choose two.)
options: Launch the EC2 instance into the same Availability Zone as the EFS file system.
Install an AWS DataSync agent in the on-premises data center.
Create a secondary Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume on the EC2 instance for the data.
Manually use an operating system copy command to push the data to the EC2 instance.
Use AWS DataSync to create a suitable location configuration for the on-premises SFTP server.
explanation: The correct answer is B, E. Option A (INCORRECT): “Launch the EC2 instance into the same Availability Zone as the EFS file system.” You don’t need to tie your EC2 placement to a single AZ if you have created EFS mount targets in all AZs of the VPC. EFS is a regional service and can be mounted from any AZ with an existing mount target. This step isn’t part of the data transfer automation using DataSync; it only affects where you place your compute resource. Option C (INCORRECT): “Create a secondary Amazon EBS volume on the EC2 instance for the data.” You are using Amazon EFS for shared, elastic storage. Adding a secondary EBS volume is unnecessary and won’t help with migrating the on-premises NFS data. EFS provides scalable file storage; there’s no need for an extra block-level volume in this scenario. Option D (INCORRECT): “Manually use an operating system copy command to push the data to the EC2 instance.” A manual copy (such as scp or rsync) is not automated at scale and doesn’t leverage AWS DataSync’s built-in performance, scheduling, and error-handling features. The requirement is to automate the migration of 200 GB from an on-premises NFS/SFTP server to EFS, so a manual approach falls short. Option B (CORRECT): “Install an AWS DataSync agent in the on-premises data center.” The DataSync agent is required to access self-managed NFS file systems. It mounts the on-premises NFS share and securely transfers data to AWS. Once deployed, the agent can be registered with DataSync and will handle chunking, encryption in transit, and retry logic for you. Option E (CORRECT): “Use AWS DataSync to create a suitable location configuration for the on-premises SFTP server.” You define a DataSync source location pointing to your on-premises SFTP endpoint (hostname, port, credentials) so DataSync knows where to read the files. With the agent and location in place, you can schedule or run a DataSync task that streams data directly into your EFS destination. In summary, we automated an on-premises NFS/SFTP data migration to Amazon EFS by: Deploying and registering a DataSync agent in the data center (Option B). Configuring an SFTP source location in DataSync (Option E). This question falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures, since it focuses on selecting the right AWS data-transfer service and configuration to move large datasets efficiently and reliably.

question: A company wants to use an event-driven programming model with AWS Lambda. The company wants to reduce startup latency for Lambda functions that run on Java 11. The company does not have strict latency requirements for the applications. The company wants to reduce cold starts and outlier latencies when a function scales up.Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Configure Lambda provisioned concurrency.
Increase the timeout of the Lambda functions.
Increase the memory of the Lambda functions.
Configure Lambda SnapStart.
explanation: The correct Answer is D Let’s step through why A, B, and C are not correct, and why D is the right choice: Option A (INCORRECT): Configure Lambda provisioned concurrency. • Provisioned Concurrency keeps function instances initialized and ready to respond, which indeed reduces cold starts. • However, you pay for every hour of provisioned concurrency, regardless of actual invocations. This becomes expensive at scale. • The question asks for the MOST cost-effective way to reduce cold starts for Java functions—provisioned concurrency is powerful but not the cheapest for infrequent or variable workloads. Option B (INCORRECT): Increase the timeout of the Lambda functions. • Increasing the timeout merely allows functions to run longer before forcibly terminating; it has zero effect on startup latency. • This change does not address cold starts or outlier invocation latencies. Option C (INCORRECT): Increase the memory of the Lambda functions. • More memory does allocate more CPU, which can slightly speed up execution—but it’s not designed to optimize Java VM startup/shutdown. • The cold-start penalty for Java on Lambda is dominated by JVM initialization and class loading, not general CPU shortage. This approach yields minimal cold-start improvements yet increases costs. Option D (CORRECT): Configure Lambda SnapStart. SnapStart takes a snapshot of the initialized execution environment (JVM, code, dependencies) after the init phase and reuses it for subsequent cold starts. This can reduce cold-start latency for Java 11 functions by up to 10×, including outlier invocations when scaling up. You only pay standard Lambda invocation and execution duration charges; there’s no continuous provisioning fee as with Provisioned Concurrency. SnapStart is currently supported for Java 8 (Corretto) and Java 11—and it directly targets the cold-start problem. Summary: We have learned that for Java-based AWS Lambda functions, SnapStart provides a highly effective way to reduce cold-start and outlier latencies without incurring the ongoing costs of provisioned concurrency. This question belongs to Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A solutions architect is designing a disaster recovery (DR) strategy to provide Amazon EC2 capacity in a failover AWS Region. Business requirements state that the DR strategy must meet capacity in the failover Region.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Purchase On-Demand Instances in the failover Region.
Purchase an EC2 Savings Plan in the failover Region.
Purchase regional Reserved Instances in the failover Region.
Purchase a Capacity Reservation in the failover Region.
explanation: The correct answer is D. Let’s step through why A, B, and C are not correct, and why D is the right choice: Option A (INCORRECT): Purchase On-Demand Instances in the failover Region. On-Demand Instances do not guarantee that capacity will be available at the time of failover. In a large-scale event, AWS may not have spare capacity to launch new On-Demand Instances immediately in your chosen AZ or Region. On-Demand delivers flexibility, but not a capacity reservation. Option B (INCORRECT): Purchase an EC2 Savings Plan in the failover Region. Savings Plans provide a discount on compute usage, but they do not reserve or guarantee capacity. The plan applies billing benefits only when instances run; it offers no SLA for availability of infrastructure. Option C (INCORRECT): Purchase regional Reserved Instances in the failover Region. Reserved Instances give you a billing discount in exchange for commitment, but they do not lock in capacity availability. RI’s are a financial construct—they do not create a reservation of compute resources. Option D (CORRECT): Purchase a Capacity Reservation in the failover Region. Capacity Reservations allocate the compute capacity you need, ensuring it’s held for your account. You can configure Reservations for specific AZs, instance types, and sizes to match your DR plan. At failover, you have guaranteed slots to launch EC2 instances immediately, meeting your RTO/RPO requirements. In summary, we learned that to meet strict DR capacity requirements, you must reserve infrastructure capacity rather than rely on pricing constructs. This question falls under Domain 2 - Design Resilient Architectures, as it focuses on ensuring availability and reliability in a disaster recovery scenario.

question: A consumer survey company has gathered data for several years from a specific geographic region. The company stores this data in an Amazon S3 bucket in an AWS Region. The company has started to share this data with a marketing firm in a new geographic region. The company has granted the firm's AWS account access to the S3 bucket. The company wants to minimize the data transfer costs when the marketing firm requests data from the S3 bucket. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Configure the Requester Pays feature on the company’s S3 bucket.
Configure S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) from the company’s S3 bucket to one of the marketing firm’s S3 buckets.
Configure AWS Resource Access Manager to share the S3 bucket with the marketing firm AWS account.
Configure the company’s S3 bucket to use S3 Intelligent-Tiering Sync the S3 bucket to one of the marketing firm’s S3 buckets.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): “Configure the Requester Pays feature on the company’s S3 bucket.” Requester Pays shifts the cost of data download to the requester’s AWS account, but does not eliminate or reduce the cross-Region data egress charges incurred by the bucket owner’s region. The egress still happens from the original region to the marketing firm’s region, so data transfer costs remain. Option C (INCORRECT): “Configure AWS Resource Access Manager to share the S3 bucket with the marketing firm AWS account.” AWS RAM allows cross-account sharing of resources, but it does not replicate or relocate objects to another Region. Data access requests still pull data over the network from the original Region, incurring cross-Region egress fees. Option D (INCORRECT): “Configure the company’s S3 bucket to use S3 Intelligent-Tiering Sync the S3 bucket to one of the marketing firm’s S3 buckets.” S3 Intelligent-Tiering optimizes storage costs by moving objects between access tiers within the same bucket—it does not replicate data to another Region. No cross-Region replication means data transfer costs remain unchanged when the marketing firm retrieves objects. Option B (CORRECT): “Configure S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) from the company’s S3 bucket to one of the marketing firm’s S3 buckets.” CRR automatically replicates new (and optional existing) objects to a bucket in the target Region. Once replication is complete, the marketing firm can read data from its local Region’s bucket, avoiding cross-Region egress fees from the source bucket. This setup minimizes data transfer costs for repeated reads by serving data from the destination Region. In summary, we evaluated each option’s impact on cross-Region data transfer costs and found that only S3 Cross-Region Replication meets the requirement of minimizing egress charges. This scenario falls under Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: An Amazon EC2 instance is located in a private subnet in a new VPC. This subnet does not have outbound internet access, but the EC2 instance needs the ability to download monthly security updates from an outside vendor. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
options: Create an internet gateway, and attach it to the VPC. Configure the private subnet route table to use the internet gateway as the default route.
Create a NAT gateway, and place it in a public subnet. Configure the private subnet route table to use the NAT gateway as the default route.
Create a NAT instance, and place it in the same subnet where the EC2 instance is located. Configure the private subnet route table to use the NAT instance as the default route.

Create an internet gateway, and attach it to the VPC. Create a NAT instance, and place it in the same subnet where the EC2 instance is located. Configure the private subnet route table to use the internet gateway as the default route.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): “Create an Internet Gateway, and attach it to the VPC. Configure the private subnet route table to use the Internet Gateway as the default route.” You cannot route traffic from a private subnet directly to an Internet Gateway without public IPs or Elastic IPs on the instances. Instances in a private subnet need a NAT device (gateway or instance) in a public subnet to access the internet. Option C (INCORRECT): “Create a NAT instance, and place it in the same subnet where the EC2 instance is located. Configure the private subnet route table to use the NAT instance as the default route.” A NAT instance must reside in a public subnet with a route to an Internet Gateway. Placing the NAT instance in the private subnet still leaves it without Internet Gateway access. Option D (INCORRECT): “Create an Internet Gateway, and attach it to the VPC. Create a NAT instance, and place it in the same subnet where the EC2 instance is located. Configure the private subnet route table to use the Internet Gateway as the default route.” This incorrectly mixes IGW routing on the private subnet, which won’t work without public IPs. The NAT instance placement is wrong (it needs to be in a public subnet), and the route should point to the NAT, not the IGW. Option B (CORRECT): “Create a NAT Gateway, and place it in a public subnet. Configure the private subnet route table to use the NAT Gateway as the default route.” A NAT Gateway in a public subnet has an Elastic IP and a route to the Internet Gateway, allowing outbound Internet access. Instances in the private subnet send outbound requests to the NAT Gateway, which then forwards them to the vendor’s update servers. This setup maintains the subnet’s privacy (no inbound internet traffic) while enabling necessary outbound connectivity. Summary: We investigated each option and learned that private subnets require a NAT device in a public subnet for outbound Internet access. Only a NAT Gateway correctly fulfills the requirement without exposing the EC2 instance to inbound Internet traffic. This question falls under Domain 2 - Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company runs a three-tier application in a VPC. The database tier uses an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance. The company plans to migrate the RDS for MySQL DB instance to an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster. The company needs a solution that replicates the data changes that happen during the migration to the new database. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
options: Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) Schema Conversion to transform the database objects.
Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) Schema Conversion to create an Aurora PostgreSQL read replica on the RDS for MySQL DB instance.
Configure an Aurora MySQL read replica for the RDS for MySQL DB instance.
Define an AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) task with change data capture (CDC) to migrate the data.
Promote the Aurora PostgreSQL read replica to a standalone Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster when the replica lag is zero.
explanation: The correct answer is A, D Option B (INCORRECT): “Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) Schema Conversion to create an Aurora PostgreSQL read replica on the RDS for MySQL DB instance.” There is no feature in DMS that spins up an Aurora PostgreSQL read replica of a MySQL source. Read replicas across different engines are not supported; you need to convert the schema and migrate data separately. Option C (INCORRECT): “Configure an Aurora MySQL read replica for the RDS for MySQL DB instance.” This would create an Aurora MySQL cluster, not Aurora PostgreSQL. The requirement is to move to Aurora PostgreSQL, so a MySQL-compatible replica doesn’t satisfy the cross-engine migration. Option E (INCORRECT): “Promote the Aurora PostgreSQL read replica to a standalone Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster when the replica lag is zero.” You cannot create an Aurora PostgreSQL read replica of an RDS for MySQL source. Promotion only applies to valid cross-region or same-engine replicas, not between MySQL and PostgreSQL. Option A (CORRECT): “Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) Schema Conversion to transform the database objects.” Before migrating data from MySQL to PostgreSQL, you must convert tables, indexes, and other schema elements. AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) helps convert MySQL schema to a PostgreSQL-compatible format. Option D (CORRECT): “Define an AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) task with change data capture (CDC) to migrate the data.” DMS with a full load plus CDC keeps source and target in sync during cut-over. Once the initial snapshot load completes, CDC captures ongoing changes until you’re ready to switch over. In summary, we learned that migrating from RDS MySQL to Aurora PostgreSQL requires first converting the schema (with AWS SCT) and then using DMS with CDC to handle data transfer and ongoing changes. This question falls under Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company hosts its multi-tier, public web application in the AWS Cloud. The web application runs on Amazon EC2 instances, and its database runs on Amazon RDS. The company is anticipating a large increase in sales during an upcoming holiday weekend. A solutions architect needs to build a solution to analyze the performance of the web application with a granularity of no more than 2 minutes. What should the solutions architect do to meet this requirement?
options: Send Amazon CloudWatch logs to Amazon Redshift. Use Amazon QuickS ght to perform further analysis.
Enable detailed monitoring on all EC2 instances. Use Amazon CloudWatch metrics to perform further analysis.
Create an AWS Lambda function to fetch EC2 logs from Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Use Amazon CloudWatch metrics to perform further analysis.
Send EC2 logs to Amazon S3. Use Amazon Redshift to fetch logs from the S3 bucket to process raw data for further analysis with Amazon QuickSight.
explanation: The correct answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): “Send Amazon CloudWatch Logs to Amazon Redshift. Use Amazon QuickSight to perform further analysis.” CloudWatch Logs are for log data, not raw performance metrics, and require ETL before analysis. Loading logs into Redshift and visualizing in QuickSight adds complexity and latency—far exceeding a 2-minute granularity. Option C (INCORRECT): “Create an AWS Lambda function to fetch EC2 logs from CloudWatch Logs. Use Amazon CloudWatch metrics to perform further analysis.” Fetching logs via Lambda introduces extra processing delays and complexity. Logs are not the native source for performance metrics—CloudWatch Metrics already provides the needed data. Option D (INCORRECT): “Send EC2 logs to Amazon S3. Use Amazon Redshift to fetch logs from the S3 bucket to process raw data for further analysis with Amazon QuickSight.” Archiving logs to S3 then querying in Redshift is too slow and costly for sub-2-minute insights. This approach is better suited for historical or batch analysis, not real-time performance monitoring. Option B (CORRECT): “Enable detailed monitoring on all EC2 instances. Use Amazon CloudWatch metrics to perform further analysis.” By default, EC2 basic monitoring provides metrics at 5-minute intervals. Enabling detailed monitoring increases this to 1-minute intervals. CloudWatch Metrics natively captures CPU, network, disk I/O, and custom metrics with low latency, meeting the ≤2-minute requirement. Dashboards, alarms, and metric math in CloudWatch allow real-time analysis and alerting with minimal complexity and cost. In this discussion, we learned how to meet a sub-2-minute performance-monitoring requirement by leveraging Amazon CloudWatch’s detailed metrics. This question belongs to Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures, as it focuses on real-time performance monitoring and analysis.

question: A company's SAP application has a backend SQL Server database in an on-premises environment. The company wants to migrate its on-premises application and database server to AWS. The company needs an instance type that meets the high demands of its SAP database. On-premises performance data shows that both the SAP application and the database have high memory utilization.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Use the compute optimized instance family for the application. Use the memory optimized instance family for the database.
Use the storage optimized instance family for both the application and the database.
Use the memory optimized instance family for both the application and the database.
Use the high performance computing (HPC) optimized instance family for the application. Use the memory optimized instance family for the database.
explanation: The correct answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): “Use the compute optimized instance family for the application. Use the memory optimized instance family for the database.” Compute-optimized instances (C-class) focus on high CPU throughput, not high memory capacity. Our SAP application also shows high memory utilization, so a compute-optimized instance would under-provision RAM and negatively impact performance. Option B (INCORRECT): “Use the storage optimized instance family for both the application and the database.” Storage-optimized instances (I-class) are tuned for high, sequential I/O throughput to SSD disks, not for large memory footprints. Neither the SAP app nor the SQL Server database require extreme disk IOPS more than they require RAM, per the on-prem performance data. Option D (INCORRECT): “Use the high performance computing (HPC) optimized instance family for the application. Use the memory optimized instance family for the database.” HPC-optimized instances (H-class) are designed for tightly coupled compute clusters and low-latency network fabric (e.g., MPI workloads), not for general SAP application hosting. The SAP application needs large RAM capacity more than HPC-style interconnects, so this over-provisions specialized networking features the app doesn’t need. Option C (CORRECT): “Use the memory optimized instance family for both the application and the database.” Memory-optimized instances (R-class or X-class) provide high RAM per vCPU, ideal for in-memory SAP workloads and SQL Server databases with high buffer-cache requirements. Aligns directly with the on-premises performance data showing both tiers have high memory utilization. Ensures consistent, predictable performance for both the SAP application and its backend database. In summary, we learned that workloads with high memory demands—both application and database tiers—are best supported by AWS memory-optimized instances. This question tests your knowledge in Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company is concerned about the security of its public web application due to recent web attacks. The application uses an Application Load Balancer (ALB). A solutions architect must reduce the risk of DDoS attacks against the application.What should the solutions architect do to meet this requirement?
options: Add an Amazon Inspector agent to the ALB.
Configure Amazon Macie to prevent attacks.
Enable AWS Shield Advanced to prevent attacks.
Configure Amazon GuardDuty to monitor the ALB.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): Add an Amazon Inspector agent to the ALB. • Amazon Inspector is a vulnerability assessment service for EC2 instances and container images, not a DDoS protection tool. • It cannot mitigate or absorb large-scale network attacks against your load balancer. Option B (INCORRECT): Configure Amazon Macie to prevent attacks. • Amazon Macie is a data-security service that uses ML to discover and protect sensitive data in S3. • It does not provide network-level protection or DDoS mitigation for web applications. Option D (INCORRECT): Configure Amazon GuardDuty to monitor the ALB. • GuardDuty is a threat-detection service that continuously monitors for malicious activity and unauthorized behavior. • While it can alert on suspicious traffic patterns, it does not actively mitigate or block DDoS attacks. Option C (CORRECT): Enable AWS Shield Advanced to prevent attacks. AWS Shield Advanced provides enhanced DDoS protection for applications running on AWS, including those behind an ALB. It offers always-on detection and automatic inline mitigations that safeguard web applications from volumetric, protocol, and application layer attacks. Shield Advanced also includes 24/7 access to the AWS DDoS Response Team (DRT) and DDoS cost protection. In summary, AWS Shield Advanced is the appropriate service to reduce the risk of DDoS attacks against an internet-facing application behind an ALB. This question aligns with Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures, as it focuses on implementing security and DDoS resilience.

question: A company's containerized application runs on an Amazon EC2 instance. The application needs to download security certificates before it can communicate with other business applications. The company wants a highly secure solution to encrypt and decrypt the certificates in near real time. The solution also needs to store data in highly available storage after the data is encrypted.Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Create AWS Secrets Manager secrets for encrypted certificates. Manually update the certificates as needed. Control access to the data by using fine-grained IAM access.
Create an AWS Lambda function that uses the Python cryptography library to receive and perform encryption operations. Store the function in an Amazon S3 bucket.
Create an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key. Allow the EC2 role to use the KMS key for encryption operations. Store the encrypted data on Amazon S3.

Create an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key. Allow the EC2 role to use the KMS key for encryption operations. Store the encrypted data on Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Let’s step through why A, B, and D are not correct, and why C is the right choice: Option A (INCORRECT): Create AWS Secrets Manager secrets for encrypted certificates. Secrets Manager is ideal for storing and rotating secrets, but you’d still need to fetch and decrypt each certificate at runtime, adding API-call overhead. Updating certificates “manually as needed” does not satisfy a near-real-time encryption/decryption requirement. It shifts operational burden to managing secret versions and rotation schedules rather than automating encryption. Option B (INCORRECT): Create an AWS Lambda function that uses the Python cryptography library to receive and perform encryption operations. This approach requires you to build, secure, and maintain custom encryption code—significantly increasing operational overhead. Lambda functions must be invoked over the network for every encrypt/decrypt call, adding latency and complexity. You still need a secure, highly available place to store the encrypted certificates; simply “storing the function in S3” does not address storage of the data itself. Option D (INCORRECT): Create an AWS KMS customer managed key and store the encrypted data on Amazon EBS volumes. While EBS supports encryption at rest via KMS, EBS volumes are tied to a single Availability Zone and do not provide the same high availability as S3. Managing snapshots and replication across AZs adds operational complexity, contrary to the “least operational overhead” requirement. You’d incur more work to ensure your containerized app can always access the EBS volume during scale-out or failover. Option C (CORRECT): Create an AWS KMS customer managed key. Allow the EC2 role to use the KMS key for encryption operations. Store the encrypted data on Amazon S3. AWS KMS handles key storage, rotation, and access control out of the box—eliminating custom code and heavy maintenance. The EC2 instance can call KMS Encrypt/Decrypt APIs in near real time under the instance role, meeting performance requirements. Amazon S3 provides 99.99% availability and automatic multi-AZ durability for the encrypted certificates, with virtually no setup. This combination delivers strong security, high availability, and minimal operational overhead. In summary, using AWS KMS for encryption/decryption paired with highly durable storage in Amazon S3 meets the company’s need for secure, near-real-time handling of certificates with the least operational burden. This question belongs to Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: An application runs on Amazon EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zonas. The instances run in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. The application performs best when the CPU utilization of the EC2 instances is at or near 40%. What should a solutions architect do to maintain the desired performance across all instances in the group?
options: Use a simple scaling policy to dynamically scale the Auto Scaling group.
Use a target tracking policy to dynamically scale the Auto Scaling group.
Use an AWS Lambda function ta update the desired Auto Scaling group capacity.
Use scheduled scaling actions to scale up and scale down the Auto Scaling group.
explanation: The correct Answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): Use a simple scaling policy to dynamically scale the Auto Scaling group. Simple scaling policies trigger scaling only when a CloudWatch alarm crosses a static threshold, and then perform a fixed adjustment. They cannot continuously maintain average CPU utilization at a target (40%)—they just respond to breaches. Option C (INCORRECT): Use an AWS Lambda function to update the desired Auto Scaling group capacity. This introduces unnecessary custom code and operational overhead. Serverless functions polling or reacting to metrics are error-prone compared to built-in Auto Scaling features. Option D (INCORRECT): Use scheduled scaling actions to scale up and scale down the Auto Scaling group. Scheduled actions are time-based and cannot adapt to real-time workload changes. Workload patterns often vary unpredictably—scheduled scaling won’t maintain 40% CPU continuously. Option B (CORRECT): Use a target tracking policy to dynamically scale the Auto Scaling group. Target tracking continuously adjusts capacity to keep the average CPU utilization at the configured target (40%). AWS automatically calculates scaling adjustments, simplifying operations and ensuring optimal performance. No custom code is required—Auto Scaling handles both scale-out and scale-in to maintain the desired metric. In this discussion we learned that target tracking scaling is the best way to maintain a specific performance metric (like 40% CPU) across an Auto Scaling group. This question falls under Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company wants to run its critical applications in containers to meet requirements for scalability and availability. The company prefers to focus on maintenance of the critical applications. The company does not want to be responsible for provisioning and managing the underlying infrastructure that runs the containerized workload.What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
options: Use Amazon EC2 instances, and install Docker on the instances.
Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on Amazon EC2 worker nodes.
Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate.
Use Amazon EC2 instances from an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS)-optimized Amazon Machine Image (AMI).
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon EC2 instances, and install Docker on the instances.” This approach requires you to provision, patch, scale, and manage the underlying EC2 servers. It does not eliminate infrastructure management, which contradicts the requirement. Option B (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on Amazon EC2 worker nodes.” Although ECS orchestrates containers, you still must manage the EC2 instances (scaling, updates, capacity planning). It fails the “no infrastructure management” requirement. Option D (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon EC2 instances from an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS)-optimized Amazon Machine Image (AMI).” Even with an ECS-optimized AMI, you are responsible for the EC2 lifecycle—patching, scaling, availability zones. Still not a fully managed container platform. Option C (CORRECT): “Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate.” Fargate is a serverless compute engine for containers—no EC2 to provision or manage. It automatically scales and provides high availability for containerized workloads. You only focus on your application, not the infrastructure. In summary, to meet the requirements of no infrastructure provisioning while achieving scalability and availability for critical containerized applications, AWS Fargate (Option C) is the ideal choice. This question falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures, as it focuses on selecting a compute option that delivers performance, scalability, and operational simplicity.

question: A company hosts an online shopping application that stores all orders in an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL Single-AZ DB instance. Management wants to eliminate single points of failure and has asked a solutions architect to recommend an approach to minimize database downtime without requiring any changes to the application code. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Convert the existing database instance to a Multi-AZ deployment by modifying the database instance and specifying the Multi-AZ option.
Create a new RDS Multi-AZ deployment. Take a snapshot of the current RDS instance and restore the new Multi-AZ deployment with the snapshot.
Create a read-only replica of the PostgreSQL database in another Availability Zone. Use Amazon Route 53 weighted record sets to distribute requests across the databases.
Place the RDS for PostgreSQL database in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group with a minimum group size of two. Use Amazon Route 53 weighted record sets to distribute requests across instances.
explanation: The correct answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): • This approach requires creating a brand-new Multi-AZ DB instance and restoring from a snapshot, which means additional downtime during the snapshot/restore process. • It also introduces complexity in synchronizing endpoints and configurations, and does not meet the requirement to minimize downtime without code changes as efficiently as a simple conversion. Option C (INCORRECT): • Read replicas are inherently read-only and cannot serve write traffic. • Using weighted Route 53 routing to distribute reads and writes would break the application, since writes cannot go to a read-only replica. • This option does not provide automatic failover for write operations. Option D (INCORRECT): • RDS instances cannot be placed inside an EC2 Auto Scaling group. • You cannot horizontally scale a single-AZ RDS database by simply adding more instances behind Route 53. • This does not address automatic failover or eliminate the single point of failure in the database layer. Option A (CORRECT): • Modifying the existing RDS for PostgreSQL instance to Multi-AZ performs an in-place upgrade, creating a synchronous standby in another Availability Zone. • AWS handles automatic failover with virtually no changes to your application endpoint (the DNS record remains the same). • This approach minimizes downtime, requires no application code changes, and fully removes the single point of failure. In summary, converting the existing Single-AZ RDS instance to a Multi-AZ deployment (Option A) is the simplest, fastest, and most reliable way to eliminate a single point of failure without any application changes. This question falls under Domain 2 – Design Resilient Architectures, since it addresses high availability and failover strategies.

question: A solutions architect is designing a two-tiered architecture that includes a public subnet and a database subnet. The web servers in the public subnet must be open to the internet on port 443. The Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance in the database subnet must be accessible only to the web servers on port 3306.Which combination of steps should the solutions architect take to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
options: Create a network ACL for the public subnet. Add a rule to deny outbound traffic to 0.0.0.0/0 on port 3306.
Create a security group for the DB instance. Add a rule to allow traffic from the public subnet CIDR block on port 3306.
Create a security group for the web servers in the public subnet. Add a rule to allow traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 on port 443.
Create a security group for the DB instance. Add a rule to allow traffic from the web servers’ security group on port 3306.
Create a security group for the DB instance. Add a rule to deny all traffic except traffic from the web servers’ security group on port 3306.
explanation: The correct answer is C, D. Option A (INCORRECT): “Create a network ACL for the public subnet. Add a rule to deny outbound traffic to 0.0.0.0/0 on port 3306.” Network ACLs are stateless and apply to all resources in a subnet—not fine-grained enough to restrict only the web servers. Relying on a deny rule in a NACL is less secure and harder to manage than using Security Groups. Option B (INCORRECT): “Create a security group for the DB instance. Add a rule to allow traffic from the public subnet CIDR block on port 3306.” Allowing by subnet CIDR is overly permissive—it could allow any resource in that subnet, not just your web servers. Best practice is to reference the specific web-server Security Group for least-privilege access controls. Option E (INCORRECT): “Create a security group for the DB instance. Add a rule to deny all traffic except traffic from the web servers’ security group on port 3306.” A Security Group is stateful and default-deny; you cannot create explicit DENY rules in it. SGs only support ALLOW rules—explicit denies are not supported. Option C (CORRECT): “Create a security group for the web servers in the public subnet. Add a rule to allow traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 on port 443.” Allows HTTPS traffic from the Internet to your web tier. Uses a Security Group ALLOW rule, which is stateful and simplest for inbound access. Option D (CORRECT): “Create a security group for the DB instance. Add a rule to allow traffic from the web servers’ security group on port 3306.” References the web-server SG directly—ensuring only those instances can reach the database. Follows AWS best practice of least-privilege, stateful access control. Summary: We learned how to secure a two-tier VPC architecture using Security Groups—allowing only HTTPS to the web tier and permitting the DB tier to accept MySQL connections only from the web-server SG. This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: An analytics company uses Amazon VPC to run its multi-tier services. The company wants to use RESTful APIs to offer a web analytics service to millions of users. Users must be verified by using an authentication service to access the APIs. Which solution will meet these requirements with the MOST operational efficiency?
options: Configure an Amazon Cognito user pool for user authentication. Implement Amazon API Gateway REST APIs with a Cognito authorizer.
Configure an Amazon Cognito identity pool for user authentication. Implement Amazon API Gateway HTTP APIs with a Cognito authorizer.
Configure an AWS Lambda function to handle user authentication. Implement Amazon API Gateway REST APIs with a Lambda authorizer.
Configure an IAM user to handle user authentication. Implement Amazon API Gateway HTTP APIs with an IAM authorizer.
explanation: The correct Answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): Amazon Cognito Identity Pools are designed to grant users temporary AWS credentials after authentication; they are not the primary mechanism for user authentication to APIs. While API Gateway HTTP APIs do support Cognito User Pool authorizers, they don’t directly integrate with Identity Pools for access control on REST endpoints. This adds unnecessary complexity and does not meet the “most operational efficiency” requirement for pure user authentication. Option C (INCORRECT): Using a Lambda Authorizer requires you to write, deploy, and maintain custom code for authentication logic. Operational overhead is higher—updates to the auth logic require redeployment of the Lambda and careful scaling considerations. Out-of-the-box services like Amazon Cognito provide built-in user management, MFA, token refreshing, etc., which you’d have to build yourself. Option D (INCORRECT): IAM Users are intended for managing access to AWS resources by administrators or applications, not for authenticating millions of external web users. API Gateway HTTP APIs with IAM authorizers require SigV4 requests, which are not practical for browser-based clients at scale. This solution fails to provide a user-friendly authentication flow (sign-up, sign-in, password reset, MFA). Option A (CORRECT): Amazon Cognito User Pools handle user registration, authentication, account recovery, and token management out of the box. API Gateway REST API with a Cognito Authorizer seamlessly validates JWT tokens issued by the user pool without custom code. This setup scales automatically, minimizes operational overhead, and provides a secure, fully managed authentication solution. From this discussion, we learned how to choose the most operationally efficient authentication pattern for a high-scale, RESTful API by leveraging managed services. This question belongs to Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company is migrating applications from an on-premises Microsoft Active Directory that the company manages to AWS. The company deploys the applications in multiple AWS accounts. The company uses AWS Organizations to manage the accounts centrally. The company's security team needs a single sign-on solution across all the company's AWS accounts. The company must continue to manage users and groups that are in the on-premises Active Directory.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Create an Enterprise Edition Active Directory in AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory. Configure the Active Directory to be the identity source for AWS IAM Identity Center.

Enable AWS IAM Identity Center. Configure a two-way forest trust relationship to connect the company's self-managed Active Directory with IAM Identity Center by using AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory.
Use AWS Directory Service and create a two-way trust relationship with the company's self-managed Active Directory.
Deploy an identity provider (IdP) on Amazon EC2. Link the IdP as an identity source within AWS IAM Identity Center.
explanation: AWS SSO with On-Prem AD The correct answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): Creating an Enterprise Edition Microsoft AD in AWS Directory Service without establishing a trust to the on-premises AD means you can’t leverage existing users and groups. IAM Identity Center would see a separate, empty directory—so on-prem accounts cannot sign on. Option C (INCORRECT): Simply creating a two-way trust between AWS Directory Service and your on-prem AD does not by itself enable cross-account SSO. You must also configure IAM Identity Center to use that AWS Managed Microsoft AD as its identity source. Option C omits the necessary IAM Identity Center integration. Option D (INCORRECT): Deploying a custom IdP on EC2 and linking it to IAM Identity Center is a heavy, unsupported pattern for Active Directory integration. It requires you to build and maintain your own federation stack, and IAM Identity Center cannot natively import on-prem AD groups this way. Option B (CORRECT): • AWS IAM Identity Center (formerly AWS SSO) provides single sign-on across all AWS accounts within an AWS Organization. • You deploy AWS Managed Microsoft AD via AWS Directory Service and configure a two-way forest trust with your on-premises AD. • Finally, you set the AWS Managed Microsoft AD as the identity source in IAM Identity Center—allowing on-prem AD users and groups to SSO into all AWS accounts. In summary, integrating on-premises Active Directory with AWS SSO requires AWS Managed Microsoft AD and a two-way trust, then configuring IAM Identity Center to use that directory. Domain: Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures

question: A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled and runs multiple Amazon EC2 workloads in the ap-southeast-2 Region. The company has a service control policy (SCP) that prevents any resources from being created in any other Region. A security policy requires the company to encrypt all data at rest. An audit discovers that employees have created Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes for EC2 instances without encrypting the volumes. The company wants any new EC2 instances that any IAM user or root user launches in ap-southeast-2 to use encrypted EBS volumes. The company wants a solution that will have minimal effect on employees who create EBS volumes.Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
options: In the Amazon EC2 console, select the EBS encryption account attribute and define a default encryption key.

Create an IAM permission boundary. Attach the permission boundary to the root organizational unit (OU). Define the boundary to deny the ec2:CreateVolume action when the ec2:Encrypted condition equals false.
Create an SCP. Attach the SCP to the root organizational unit (OU). Define the SCP to deny the ec2:CreateVolume action whenthe ec2:Encrypted condition equals false.
Update the IAM policies for each account to deny the ec2:CreateVolume action when the ec2:Encrypted condition equals false.
In the Organizations management account, specify the Default EBS volume encryption setting.
explanation: The correct answer is C, E Option A (INCORRECT): Using the EC2 console to enable default EBS encryption is a per-account, per-region setting. In an AWS Organizations environment, you’d have to repeat this step for every member account manually. The question calls for a minimal-touch, centralized approach. Option B (INCORRECT): An IAM permission boundary cannot restrict the root user, and you cannot attach a boundary at the root OU level. Therefore, this won’t prevent root or administrator actions that create unencrypted volumes. Option D (INCORRECT): Updating IAM policies in each account to deny unencrypted-volume creation still requires per-account changes and does not affect the root user. This is neither fully centralized nor minimal in impact. Option C (CORRECT): Create a Service Control Policy (SCP) in AWS Organizations and attach it to the root OU. Define the policy to deny the ec2:CreateVolume action when the ec2:Encrypted condition is false. This enforces EBS encryption for every IAM user and the root user across all accounts in the OU. Option E (CORRECT): In the AWS Organizations management account, enable the Default EBS Volume Encryption setting for the ap-southeast-2 Region. This automatically encrypts all new EBS volumes by default, with no changes required by developers or administrators. Summary: We learned how to enforce encryption at rest in a multi-account AWS Organizations setup by combining a centralized default-encryption configuration with a preventive SCP. This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company is designing a new web service that will run on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Elastic Load Balancing (ELB) load balancer. However, many of the web service clients can only reach IP addresses authorized on their firewalls. What should a solutions architect recommend to meet the clients’ needs?
options: A Network Load Balancer with an associated Elastic IP address.
An Application Load Balancer with an associated Elastic IP address.
An A record in an Amazon Route 53 hosted zone pointing to an Elastic IP address.
An EC2 instance with a public IP address running as a proxy in front of the load balancer.
explanation: The correct answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): An Application Load Balancer (ALB) does not support assigning static Elastic IP addresses. ALBs use DNS names that resolve to changing IPs, so clients cannot whitelist a fixed address. Option C (INCORRECT): Creating an A record in Route 53 pointing directly to an Elastic IP bypasses the load balancer entirely. You would lose health checks, auto‐scaling, and managed failover provided by ELB. Option D (INCORRECT): Introducing a proxy EC2 instance with a public IP in front of your ELB is an unnecessary single point of failure and adds operational overhead. It complicates scaling and does not leverage native ELB static IP support. Option A (CORRECT): A Network Load Balancer (NLB) natively supports static IP addresses by allowing you to assign one or more Elastic IPs per Availability Zone. Clients can whitelist the NLB’s Elastic IPs on their firewalls. NLB maintains ultra-low latency and high throughput for TCP/UDP traffic. You retain all ELB features—health checks, scaling, zone-redundancy—while providing fixed entry points. In summary, we recommend Option A because a Network Load Balancer with Elastic IPs meets the requirement for static, client-whitelisted addresses while preserving availability and performance. This question falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company needs the ability to analyze the log files of its proprietary application. The logs are stored in JSON format in an Amazon S3 bucket. Queries will be simple and will run on-demand. A solutions architect needs to perform the analysis with minimal changes to the existing architecture.What should the solutions architect do to meet these requirements with the LEAST amount of operational overhead?
options: Use Amazon Redshift to load all the content into one place and run the SQL queries as needed.
Use Amazon CloudWatch Logs to store the logs. Run SQL queries as needed from the Amazon CloudWatch console.
Use Amazon Athena directly with Amazon S3 to run the queries as needed.
Use AWS Glue to catalog the logs. Use a transient Apache Spark cluster on Amazon EMR to run the SQL queries as needed.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): Use Amazon Redshift to load all the content into one place and run the SQL queries as needed. You would need to build and maintain an ETL process to load JSON data into Redshift tables. Redshift incurs cluster provisioning and ongoing management overhead. For simple, on-demand queries, this is overkill compared to a serverless solution. Option B (INCORRECT): Use Amazon CloudWatch Logs to store the logs. Run SQL queries as needed from the Amazon CloudWatch console. CloudWatch Logs supports basic query syntax, but ingesting existing S3 JSON requires pushing logs into CloudWatch, which is an unnecessary migration. CloudWatch Logs Insights has limits on JSON nested structures and query complexity. This adds operational steps to move data rather than querying in place. Option D (INCORRECT): Use AWS Glue to catalog the logs. Use a transient Apache Spark cluster on Amazon EMR to run the SQL queries as needed. Provisioning and tearing down EMR Spark clusters adds operational overhead. You must manage Glue crawlers and EMR configurations. This solution is more complex and costly for simple, ad-hoc queries. Option C (CORRECT): Use Amazon Athena directly with Amazon S3 to run the queries as needed. Athena is serverless: no infrastructure to manage. You can query JSON files in S3 in place with simple DDL definitions. You pay only for the data scanned, making it cost-effective for on-demand analysis. Minimal changes to the existing architecture—just define a table and start querying. In summary, Amazon Athena provides the least operational overhead and cost-optimized approach for querying JSON logs stored in S3. This scenario falls under Domain 4 – Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company is running a popular social media website. The website gives users the ability to upload images to share with other users. The company wants to make sure that the images do not contain inappropriate content. The company needs a solution that minimizes development effort. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
options: Use Amazon Comprehend to detect inappropriate content. Use human review for low-confidence predictions.
Use Amazon Rekognition to detect inappropriate content. Use human review for low-confidence predictions.
Use Amazon SageMaker to detect inappropriate content. Use ground truth to label low-confidence predictions.
Use AWS Fargate to deploy a custom machine learning model to detect inappropriate content. Use ground truth to label low-confidence predictions.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon Comprehend to detect inappropriate content. Use human review for low-confidence predictions.” • Amazon Comprehend is a natural language processing service, not designed for image analysis. • It cannot evaluate image content, so it fails the core requirement of moderating uploaded images. Option C (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon SageMaker to detect inappropriate content. Use ground truth to label low-confidence predictions.” • While SageMaker lets you build custom ML models, it requires substantial development effort to train, host, and maintain your own image-moderation system. • The question calls for minimal development effort, which rules out building and managing a custom model from scratch. Option D (INCORRECT): “Use AWS Fargate to deploy a custom machine learning model to detect inappropriate content. Use ground truth to label low-confidence predictions.” • Deploying a custom model on Fargate still involves training, packaging, and maintaining your own inference infrastructure. • This approach is far more operational overhead and development effort than using a fully managed AWS AI service. Option B (CORRECT): “Use Amazon Rekognition to detect inappropriate content. Use human review for low-confidence predictions.” • Amazon Rekognition provides a built-in “DetectModerationLabels” API that automatically scans images for inappropriate or unsafe content. • It returns confidence scores, so you can easily route low-confidence results to a human review workflow (e.g., via Amazon SQS or AWS Step Functions). • This solution is fully managed, requires minimal code, and meets the requirement for low development effort. Summary: We’ve learned that for image content moderation with minimal development effort, Amazon Rekognition’s built-in content moderation API is the optimal choice, augmented by a human review step for borderline cases. This question belongs to Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures, as it focuses on protecting your application from inappropriate or harmful content.

question: A hospital wants to create digital copies for its large collection of historical written records. The hospital will continue to add hundreds of new documents each day. The hospital’s data team will scan the documents and will upload the documents to the AWS Cloud. A solutions architect must implement a solution to analyze the documents, extract the medical information, and store the documents so that an application can run SQL queries on the data. The solution must maximize scalability and operational efficiency. Which combination of steps should the solutions architect take to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
options: Write the document information to an Amazon EC2 instance that runs a MySQL database.
Write the document information to an Amazon S3 bucket. Use Amazon Athena to query the data.
Create an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 instances to run a custom application that processes the scanned files and extracts the medical information.

Create an AWS Lambda function that runs when new documents are uploaded. Use Amazon Rekognition to convert the documents to raw text. Use Amazon Transcribe Medical to detect and extract relevant medical information from the text.

Create an AWS Lambda function that runs when new documents are uploaded. Use Amazon Textract to convert the documents to raw text. Use Amazon Comprehend Medical to detect and extract relevant medical information from the text.
explanation: The correct answer is B, E Option A (INCORRECT): “Write the document information to an Amazon EC2 instance that runs a MySQL database.” Running your own MySQL on EC2 incurs management overhead (patching, scaling, backups). Not a fully managed, serverless approach—limits scalability and operational efficiency. Option C (INCORRECT): “Create an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 instances to run a custom application that processes the scanned files and extracts the medical information.” Custom EC2 fleet still requires you to manage OS, scaling policies, deployments. Better to use serverless services (Lambda + AI/ML) for operational efficiency and automatic scaling. Option D (INCORRECT): “Create an AWS Lambda function that runs when new documents are uploaded. Use Amazon Rekognition to convert the documents to raw text. Use Amazon Transcribe Medical to detect and extract relevant medical information from the text.” Amazon Transcribe Medical is for audio transcription, not for analyzing written text. Amazon Rekognition’s text detection is less accurate than Textract for document OCR and structured data extraction. Option B (CORRECT): “Write the document information to an Amazon S3 bucket. Use Amazon Athena to query the data.” S3 provides virtually unlimited, cost-effective storage for both raw documents and extracted data (in JSON/CSV). Athena lets you run standard SQL queries directly against data in S3—highly scalable and serverless. Option E (CORRECT): “Create an AWS Lambda function that runs when new documents are uploaded. Use Amazon Textract to convert the documents to raw text. Use Amazon Comprehend Medical to detect and extract relevant medical information from the text.” Amazon Textract is optimized for OCR and structured text extraction from documents (forms, tables). Amazon Comprehend Medical identifies medical entities (ICD-10 codes, medication, anatomy) without custom coding. Lambda ensures automatic, event-driven processing at any scale with zero server management. In summary, we learned that a serverless, fully managed pipeline using S3 + Lambda + Textract + Comprehend Medical + Athena maximizes scalability and operational efficiency. This solution belongs to Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company has a stateless web application that runs on AWS Lambda functions that are invoked by Amazon API Gateway. The company wants to deploy the application across multiple AWS Regions to provide Regional failover capabilities.What should a solutions architect do to route traffic to multiple Regions?
options: Create Amazon Route 53 health checks for each Region. Use an active-active failover configuration.
