The MySQL database currently uses a 1 TB Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) EBS volume. The company expects traffic of 1,000 IOPS for both reads and writes at peak traffic. The company wants to minimize any disruptions, stabilize performance, and reduce costs while retaining the capacity for double the IOPS. The company wants to move the database tier to a fully managed solution that is highly available and fault tolerant.Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Use a Multi-AZ deployment of an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance with an io2 Block Express EBS volume.
Use a Multi-AZ deployment of an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance with a General Purpose SSD (gp2) EBS volume.
Use Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering access tiers.
Use two large EC2 instances to host the database in active-passive mode.
explanation: The correct Answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): Use a Multi-AZ deployment of an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance with an io2 Block Express EBS volume. io2 Block Express delivers extremely high IOPS (up to millions) and throughput, designed for the most demanding enterprise workloads. At only 1,000 IOPS (and wanting headroom for 2,000 IOPS), io2 Block Express is overkill and significantly more expensive. The requirement is to reduce cost and still support double the current IOPS; standard io2 or gp2 volumes already meet that need. Option C (INCORRECT): Use Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering access tiers. S3 Intelligent-Tiering is an object storage service for files and objects, not a relational database storage solution. You cannot host a MySQL database on S3 or use S3 tiers to serve transactional database IOPS. Option D (INCORRECT): Use two large EC2 instances to host the database in active-passive mode. This continues a self-managed database approach, increasing operational overhead (patching, backups, failover orchestration). It doesn’t satisfy the requirement for a fully managed, highly available, fault-tolerant solution. Running two EC2 instances with EBS volumes doubles management complexity and doesn’t necessarily lower cost or improve stability versus RDS Multi-AZ. Option B (CORRECT): Use a Multi-AZ deployment of an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance with a General Purpose SSD (gp2) EBS volume. A 1 TB gp2 volume provides 3 IOPS/GiB × 1,000 GiB = 3,000 baseline IOPS, comfortably handling 2,000 IOPS peaks without provisioning extra IOPS. Multi-AZ RDS automates synchronous replication to a standby in another AZ, delivering high availability and automatic failover. gp2 storage is significantly cheaper than io2 and Block Express yet meets performance needs, optimizing cost while delivering stability. Fully managed RDS reduces operational overhead (patching, backups, monitoring) compared to self-managed EC2 databases. In summary, moving to Amazon RDS for MySQL in a Multi-AZ configuration with a gp2 volume meets the performance requirement (3,000 IOPS baseline > 2,000 IOPS needed), provides high availability and fault tolerance, and is the most cost-effective choice. This question belongs to Domain 4 – Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company’s developers want a secure way to gain SSH access on the company's Amazon EC2 instances that run the latest version of Amazon Linux. The developers work remotely and in the corporate office. The company wants to use AWS services as a part of the solution. The EC2 instances are hosted in a VPC private subnet and access the internet through a NAT gateway that is deployed in a public subnet. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Create a bastion host in the same subnet as the EC2 instances. Grant the ec2:CreateVpnConnection IAM permission to the developers. Install EC2 Instance Connect so that the developers can connect to the EC2 instances.

Create an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection between the corporate network and the VPC. Instruct the developers to use the Site-to-Site VPN connection to access the EC2 instances when the developers are on the corporate network. Instruct the developers to set up another VPN connection for access when they work remotely.

Create a bastion host in the public subnet of the VPConfigure the security groups and SSH keys of the bastion host to only allow connections and SSH authentication from the developers’ corporate and remote networks. Instruct the developers to connect through the bastion host by using SSH to reach the EC2 instances.

Attach the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore IAM policy to an IAM role that is associated with the EC2 instances. Instruct the developers to use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager to access the EC2 instances.
explanation: The correct Answer is D. Option A (INCORRECT): This suggests creating a bastion host in the same private subnet and granting developers an IAM permission (ec2:CreateVpnConnection) which is irrelevant to SSH access. EC2 Instance Connect only works for instances with a public IP or through a public SSH endpoint; it does not eliminate the need for a secure access path into a private subnet. The IAM action ec2:CreateVpnConnection does not grant SSH privileges. Option B (INCORRECT): Requiring a separate Site-to-Site VPN for corporate and another for remote developers doubles operational overhead and cost. Site-to-Site VPN is designed for network-to-network connectivity, not for individual developer client access. Not as seamless or cost-effective as using AWS-native services tailored for instance management. Option C (INCORRECT): A public-subnet bastion host still exposes an EC2 instance to the internet and requires patching, scaling, and high availability maintenance. Operating and securing an always-on bastion host incurs extra EC2 costs. Does not leverage AWS managed services for secure, auditable, and keyless SSH access. Option D (CORRECT): By attaching AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore to the EC2 instance role, the instances register with AWS Systems Manager. Developers use Session Manager for SSH-like access over the secure SSM channel—no need for bastion hosts, public IPs, or VPNs. Session Manager logs and audits all sessions in CloudWatch Logs or S3, enhancing security and compliance. Cost-effective: no additional EC2 instances or VPN appliances to manage and pay for. In summary, AWS Systems Manager Session Manager provides a secure, auditable, and cost-optimized solution for SSH access to private EC2 instances. This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company seeks a storage solution for its application. The solution must be highly available and scalable. The solution also must function as a file system be mountable by multiple Linux instances in AWS and on premises through native protocols, and have no minimum size requirements. The company has set up a Site-to-Site VPN for access from its on-premises network to its VPC. Which storage solution meets these requirements?
options: Amazon FSx Multi-AZ deployments
Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) Multi-Attach volumes
Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) with multiple mount targets
Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) with a single mount target and multiple access points
explanation: The correct answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): Amazon FSx Multi-AZ deployments FSx for Windows File Server is designed for Windows-based workloads, not Linux. FSx for Lustre is optimized for high-performance computing, but still doesn’t natively support on-premises Linux mounts over VPN in the same way as NFS. Neither FSx option fulfills the requirement “mountable by multiple Linux instances in AWS and on-premises through native protocols” as simply as EFS. Option B (INCORRECT): Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) Multi-Attach volumes EBS Multi-Attach allows a single volume to be attached to multiple EC2 Nitro-based instances, but only within the same Availability Zone. It is a block storage device, not a network file system, so it cannot be mounted simultaneously by on-premises servers. There is also a minimum size requirement and performance considerations per AZ—does not meet “no minimum size” and cross-AZ availability. Option D (INCORRECT): Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) with a single mount target and multiple access points A single mount target lives in one subnet/AZ—if that AZ goes down, Linux clients lose access. Access Points simplify permission management but do not provide high availability across AZs. The requirement asks for a highly available, multi-AZ solution mountable on-premises via VPN—one mount target cannot satisfy high availability. Option C (CORRECT): Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) with multiple mount targets EFS is a fully managed NFS-v4 file system that can be mounted by multiple Linux instances concurrently. By creating mount targets in each AZ of your VPC, EFS provides multi-AZ redundancy and high availability. Mount targets can be accessed over the Site-to-Site VPN from on-premises servers just like any NFS share. There is no minimum size requirement—storage grows and shrinks automatically as you add or remove files. In summary, Amazon EFS with multiple mount targets meets all requirements—high availability, scalability, Linux-native NFS mounts in AWS and on-premises, and no minimum size. This question tests your knowledge in Domain 2 - Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company wants to move from many standalone AWS accounts to a consolidated, multi-account architecture. The company plans to create many new AWS accounts for different business units. The company needs to authenticate access to these AWS accounts by using a centralized corporate directory service.Which combination of actions should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
options: Create a new organization in AWS Organizations with all features turned on. Create the new AWS accounts in the organization.
Set up an Amazon Cognito identity pool. Configure AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS Single Sign-On) to accept Amazon Cognito authentication.
Configure a service control policy (SCP) to manage the AWS accounts. Add AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS Single Sign-On) to AWS Directory Service.
Create a new organization in AWS Organizations. Configure the organization's authentication mechanism to use AWS Directory Service directly.
Set up AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS Single Sign-On) in the organization. Configure IAM Identity Center, and integrate it with the company's corporate directory service.
explanation: The correct answers are A and E Option B (INCORRECT): “Set up an Amazon Cognito identity pool. Configure AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS Single Sign-On) to accept Amazon Cognito authentication.” Amazon Cognito is designed for mobile and web app user authentication, not enterprise SSO into multiple AWS accounts. AWS IAM Identity Center integrates directly with corporate directories (like Active Directory), not via Cognito identity pools. Option C (INCORRECT): “Configure a service control policy (SCP) to manage the AWS accounts. Add AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS Single Sign-On) to AWS Directory Service.” SCPs govern permissions across accounts but do not handle authentication integration with corporate directories. You cannot “add” IAM Identity Center to AWS Directory Service; instead, you connect IAM Identity Center to a directory. Option D (INCORRECT): “Create a new organization in AWS Organizations. Configure the organization's authentication mechanism to use AWS Directory Service directly.” AWS Organizations itself does not provide a direct authentication integration; you must use AWS IAM Identity Center for SSO. You cannot point Organizations directly at a corporate directory without going through IAM Identity Center. Option A (CORRECT): “Create a new organization in AWS Organizations with all features turned on. Create the new AWS accounts in the organization.” Enabling all features in AWS Organizations allows consolidated billing, centralized management, and SCP enforcement. New accounts for each business unit can be created and managed under the single organization. Option E (CORRECT): “Set up AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS Single Sign-On) in the organization. Configure IAM Identity Center, and integrate it with the company's corporate directory service.” IAM Identity Center provides centralized SSO across all AWS accounts in the organization. You can connect Identity Center to an existing corporate directory (e.g., Active Directory) for authentication. In summary, to build a consolidated, multi-account AWS environment with centralized corporate directory–based authentication, you enable AWS Organizations with all features (Option A) and deploy AWS IAM Identity Center integrated with your corporate directory (Option E). This question fits within Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures, since it focuses on secure account structure and centralized authentication.

question: A company uses AWS Organizations. The company wants to operate some of its AWS accounts with different budgets. The company wants to receive alerts and automatically prevent provisioning of additional resources on AWS accounts when the allocated budget threshold is met during a specific period.Which combination of solutions will meet these requirements? (Choose three.)
options: Use AWS Budgets to create a budget. Set the budget amount under the Cost and Usage Reports section of the required AWS accounts.
Use AWS Budgets to create a budget. Set the budget amount under the Billing dashboards of the required AWS accounts.
Create an IAM user for AWS Budgets to run budget actions with the required permissions.
Create an IAM role for AWS Budgets to run budget actions with the required permissions.

Add an alert to notify the company when each account meets its budget threshold. Add a budget action that selects the IAM identity created with the appropriate config rule to prevent provisioning of additional resources.

Add an alert to notify the company when each account meets its budget threshold. Add a budget action that selects the IAM identity created with the appropriate service control policy (SCP) to prevent provisioning of additional resources.
explanation: The correct answer is B, D, F Option A (INCORRECT): “Use AWS Budgets to create a budget. Set the budget amount under the Cost and Usage Reports section of the required AWS accounts.” The Cost and Usage Reports feature is for detailed data exports, not where you configure budgets. You set budgets in the AWS Budgets console (Billing dashboards), not within Cost & Usage Reports. Option C (INCORRECT): “Create an IAM user for AWS Budgets to run budget actions with the required permissions.” AWS Budgets requires an IAM role (with a trust policy) to assume permissions and execute actions, not an IAM user. Service integrations (like applying an SCP) rely on a role that AWS Budgets can assume. Option E (INCORRECT): “Add an alert to notify the company when each account meets its budget threshold. Add a budget action that selects the IAM identity created with the appropriate config rule to prevent provisioning of additional resources.” AWS Config rules govern resource compliance, not budget enforcement. You cannot use a Config rule as a Budget action; Budget actions support notifications, IAM policy attachments, or Service Control Policies (SCPs). Option B (CORRECT): “Use AWS Budgets to create a budget. Set the budget amount under the Billing dashboards of the required AWS accounts.” The AWS Budgets console in the Billing dashboard is the correct place to define cost or usage budgets per account. Budgets will track cost or usage against the specified threshold over the chosen time period. Option D (CORRECT): “Create an IAM role for AWS Budgets to run budget actions with the required permissions.” AWS Budgets needs an IAM role (e.g., AWSBudgetActionExecutionRole) with a trust policy to assume permissions to perform actions like attaching SCPs or IAM policies. This role is referenced by the budget action so that AWS Budgets can enforce the desired preventive measures. Option F (CORRECT): “Add an alert to notify the company when each account meets its budget threshold. Add a budget action that selects the IAM identity created with the appropriate service control policy (SCP) to prevent provisioning of additional resources.” You can configure a Budget action of type “Apply an AWS Service Control Policy” to the target account or OU when the threshold is breached. The IAM role created (in Option D) and the specified SCP work together to automatically deny new resource provisioning once the budget limit is hit. Summary: We learned that AWS Budgets must be created in the Billing dashboard, and budget actions require an IAM role with permissions to apply SCPs. When thresholds are met, an SCP action can automatically restrict further provisioning. This question belongs to Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company runs its ecommerce application on AWS. Every new order is published as a massage in a RabbitMQ queue that runs on an Amazon EC2 instance in a single Availability Zone. These messages are processed by a different application that runs on a separate EC2 instance. This application stores the details in a PostgreSQL database on another EC2 instance. All the EC2 instances are in the same Availability Zone. The company needs to redesign its architecture to provide the highest availability with the least operational overhead.What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
options: Migrate the queue to a redundant pair (active/standby) of RabbitMQ instances on Amazon MQ. Create a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the application. Create another Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the PostgreSQL database.

Migrate the queue to a redundant pair (active/standby) of RabbitMQ instances on Amazon MQ. Create a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the application. Migrate the database to run on a Multi-AZ deployment of Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL.

Create a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the RabbitMQ queue. Create another Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the application. Migrate the database to run on a Multi-AZ deployment of Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL.

Create a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the RabbitMQ queue. Create another Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the application. Create a third Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the PostgreSQL database
explanation: The correct answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): This suggests migrating RabbitMQ to an active/standby pair on Amazon MQ (good), but then uses EC2 Auto Scaling groups for the PostgreSQL database. Managing a database cluster on EC2 across AZs adds significant operational overhead and complexity compared to a managed service. Auto Scaling groups are not designed for stateful databases; they can’t guarantee zero data loss or seamless failover the way Amazon RDS Multi-AZ does. Thus, this fails the requirement for least operational overhead and optimal HA for the database layer. Option C (INCORRECT): This uses an EC2-based RabbitMQ cluster with a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group. Running a stateful queue on EC2 and scaling it automatically across AZs leads to complexity in clustering, failover, and message durability. While the database migration to Multi-AZ Amazon RDS is correct, the queue layer still incurs high operational overhead and risk. Therefore, it does not meet the “least operational overhead” requirement for the messaging tier. Option D (INCORRECT): Here, all three components—RabbitMQ, application, and database—are run on EC2 Auto Scaling groups. This design maximizes operational burden by requiring you to build, monitor, patch, and orchestrate HA for every tier. It also fails to leverage managed services that provide built-in multi-AZ redundancy, driving up both cost and complexity. Option B (CORRECT): Use Amazon MQ for RabbitMQ in an active/standby configuration. This offloads broker management, automates failover, and ensures high availability. Place the application servers behind an Auto Scaling group spanning multiple AZs for fault tolerance and scalability. Run PostgreSQL on Amazon RDS with Multi-AZ deployment to provide automated failover, backups, and minimal operational overhead. This design achieves the highest availability while minimizing the operational burden by leveraging fully managed AWS services. Summary: We’ve learned that for a resilient, highly available architecture with minimal operational overhead, you should leverage managed services (Amazon MQ and RDS Multi-AZ) for stateful tiers and Auto Scaling groups for stateless tiers. This question belongs to Domain 2 – Design Resilient Architectures.

question: An ecommerce company runs several internal applications in multiple AWS accounts. The company uses AWS Organizations to manage its AWS accounts. A security appliance in the company's networking account must inspect interactions between applications across AWS accounts. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Deploy a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in the networking account to send traffic to the security appliance. Configure the application accounts to send traffic to the NLB by using an interface VPC endpoint in the application accounts.
Deploy an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in the application accounts to send traffic directly to the security appliance.

Deploy a Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) in the networking account to send traffic to the security appliance. Configure the application accounts to send traffic to the GWLB by using an interface GWLB endpoint in the application accounts.
Deploy an interface VPC endpoint in the application accounts to send traffic directly to the security appliance.
explanation: The correct answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): “Deploy a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in the networking account to send traffic to the security appliance. Configure the application accounts to send traffic to the NLB by using an interface VPC endpoint in the application accounts.” NLB operates at Layer 4 and does not support the transparent tunneling (GENEVE) required for third-party inspection appliances. Interface VPC endpoints cannot target an NLB across accounts in this scenario—interface endpoints are meant for AWS service targets, not custom NLBs for traffic inspection. Option B (INCORRECT): “Deploy an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in the application accounts to send traffic directly to the security appliance.” ALBs are HTTP/HTTPS (Layer 7) load balancers and do not provide the required network-level tunneling for transparent inspection appliances. Scaling and centralized management of a security appliance across multiple accounts cannot be accomplished by deploying separate ALBs in each account. Option D (INCORRECT): “Deploy an interface VPC endpoint in the application accounts to send traffic directly to the security appliance.” Interface VPC endpoints (powered by AWS PrivateLink) only work for AWS services or supported partner services, not for arbitrary network inspection appliances. They cannot enforce route-table based redirection of cross-account traffic through a centralized appliance. Option C (CORRECT): “Deploy a Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) in the networking account to send traffic to the security appliance. Configure the application accounts to send traffic to the GWLB by using an interface GWLB endpoint in the application accounts.” GWLB is designed for transparent, scale-out inspection of network flows by third-party virtual appliances (uses GENEVE tunneling). Gateway Load Balancer Endpoints (GWLBe) allow you to configure route tables in each application VPC to redirect traffic into the GWLB—works seamlessly across AWS accounts. Provides central management, automatic scaling of the inspection fleet, and minimal changes in application VPCs. In summary, we learned that for centrally inspecting cross-account application traffic with a virtual security appliance, the correct pattern is to use AWS Gateway Load Balancer with Gateway Load Balancer Endpoints. This approach falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company is implementing new data retention policies for all databases that run on Amazon RDS DB instances. The company must retain daily backups for a minimum period of 2 years. The backups must be consistent and restorable. Which solution should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?
options: Create a backup vault in AWS Backup to retain RDS backups. Create a new backup plan with a daily schedule and an expiration period of 2 years after creation. Assign the RDS DB instances to the backup plan.

Configure a backup window for the RDS DB instances for daily snapshots. Assign a snapshot retention policy of 2 years to each RDS DB instance. Use Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (Amazon DLM) to schedule snapshot deletions.
Configure database transaction logs to be automatically backed up to Amazon CloudWatch Logs with an expiration period of 2 years.

Configure an AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) replication task. Deploy a replication instance, and configure a change data capture (CDC) task to stream database changes to Amazon S3 as the target. Configure S3 Lifecycle policies to delete the snapshots after 2 years.
explanation: The correct answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): “Configure a backup window for the RDS DB instances for daily snapshots. Assign a snapshot retention policy of 2 years to each RDS DB instance. Use Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (Amazon DLM) to schedule snapshot deletions.” Amazon RDS automated backups retention period is limited to 35 days; manual snapshots do not support an automated “2-year” retention via RDS settings. Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager manages EBS volume snapshots, not RDS snapshots. You cannot use DLM to schedule deletions of RDS snapshots. Option C (INCORRECT): “Configure database transaction logs to be automatically backed up to Amazon CloudWatch Logs with an expiration period of 2 years.” Transaction log shipping to CloudWatch Logs does not produce a full, restorable backup of the database. You cannot restore an RDS instance from just transaction logs in CloudWatch; you need consistent snapshots or point-in-time restored from automated backups. Option D (INCORRECT): “Configure an AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) replication task. Deploy a replication instance, and configure a change data capture (CDC) task to stream database changes to Amazon S3 as the target. Configure S3 Lifecycle policies to delete the snapshots after 2 years.” AWS DMS CDC streams data changes but is not intended to produce full, consistent database backups for long-term retention. Reconstructing a restorable database from CDC data in S3 is complex and error-prone; it does not meet the requirement for consistent, restorable daily backups. Option A (CORRECT): “Create a backup vault in AWS Backup to retain RDS backups. Create a new backup plan with a daily schedule and an expiration period of 2 years after creation. Assign the RDS DB instances to the backup plan.” AWS Backup natively supports Amazon RDS and allows you to define daily backup schedules with retention up to many years. Backups stored in the AWS Backup vault are consistent, managed, and easily restored. You can centrally manage, monitor, and automate retention policies for all RDS instances via AWS Backup. Summary: We learned that to meet a two-year retention requirement for consistent, restorable RDS backups, the recommended solution is to use AWS Backup with a custom backup vault and plan. This question falls under Domain 2 - Design Resilient Architectures, as it focuses on designing backup and recovery strategies to ensure data durability and recoverability.

question: A company recently migrated its web application to the AWS Cloud. The company uses an Amazon EC2 instance to run multiple processes to host the application. The processes include an Apache web server that serves static content. The Apache web server makes requests to a PHP application that uses a local Redis server for user sessions. The company wants to redesign the architecture to be highly available and to use AWS managed solutions. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Use AWS Elastic Beanstalk to host the static content and the PHP application. Configure Elastic Beanstalk to deploy its EC2 instance into a public subnet. Assign a public IP address.

Use AWS Lambda to host the static content and the PHP application. Use an Amazon API Gateway REST API to proxy requests to the Lambda function. Set the API Gateway CORS configuration to respond to the domain name. Configure Amazon ElastiCache for Redis to handle session information.

Keep the backend code on the EC2 instance. Create an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster that has Multi-AZ enabled. Configure the ElastiCache for Redis cluster in cluster mode. Copy the frontend resources to Amazon S3. Configure the backend code to reference the EC2 instance.

Configure an Amazon CloudFront distribution with an Amazon S3 endpoint to an S3 bucket that is configured to host the static content. Configure an Application Load Balancer that targets an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) service that runs AWS Fargate tasks for the PHP application. Configure the PHP application to use an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster that runs in multiple Availability Zones.
explanation: The correct answer is D Option A (INCORRECT): This keeps everything in one Elastic Beanstalk environment on EC2—you still have a single point of failure unless you explicitly configure multiple instances and AZs. Serving static content via Elastic Beanstalk is suboptimal compared to S3 + CloudFront for performance, scalability, and cost. No managed session store—Redis is still local to the instance, which is not HA. Option B (INCORRECT): Lambda isn’t ideal for serving static files—S3 + CloudFront is the AWS‐managed best practice. Running PHP in Lambda requires custom runtimes and breaks request‐response semantics (cold starts, concurrency limits). This design also introduces an API Gateway in front of every request and more complexity without clear HA benefits for the application runtime. Option C (INCORRECT): You still rely on a single EC2 instance for your backend code—no high availability at the application layer. While ElastiCache for Redis Multi-AZ is good, the compute tier remains a point of failure. Frontend in S3 is good, but the overall architecture is not fully resilient or managed for the PHP application. Option D (CORRECT): Static content is offloaded to Amazon S3 with Amazon CloudFront in front—highly available, globally distributed, and cost‐effective. PHP application runs in containers on Amazon ECS (Fargate) behind an Application Load Balancer—tasks can span multiple AZs for true HA. Sessions stored in an ElastiCache for Redis cluster deployed Multi-AZ—fully managed, replicated, and fault-tolerant. All components used are AWS managed services, reducing operational overhead and improving resilience. In summary, we’ve moved static assets to S3/CloudFront, containerized the PHP app on Fargate behind an ALB, and used Multi-AZ ElastiCache for session state—achieving high availability and leveraging AWS managed services. This question belongs to Domain 2 – Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company is planning to move its data to an Amazon S3 bucket. The data must be encrypted when it is stored in the S3 bucket. Additionally, the encryption key must be automatically rotated every year.Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Move the data to the S3 bucket. Use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed encryption keys (SSE-S3). Use the built-in key rotation behavior of SSE-S3 encryption keys.

Create an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key. Enable automatic key rotation. Set the S3 bucket’s default encryption behavior to use the customer managed KMS key. Move the data to the S3 bucket.

Create an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key. Set the S3 bucket’s default encryption behavior to use the customer managed KMS key. Move the data to the S3 bucket. Manually rotate the KMS key every year.

Encrypt the data with customer key material before moving the data to the S3 bucket. Create an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key without key material. Import the customer key material into the KMS key. Enable automatic key rotation.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): Move the data to the S3 bucket and use SSE-S3. Although S3-managed keys are rotated by AWS, you cannot configure the rotation period to exactly one year. The rotation process is entirely managed by AWS and does not guarantee a yearly rotation schedule, so this does not meet the requirement. Option C (INCORRECT): Create a customer-managed KMS key, set the bucket default encryption to use it, and then manually rotate the key every year. This meets the encryption and rotation period, but manual rotation adds unnecessary operational overhead. Option D (INCORRECT): Encrypt data with customer key material, import it into KMS, and enable automatic rotation. Imported key material keys in KMS do not support automatic rotation—you must re-import new key material yourself. This adds significant operational complexity and fails the “least operational overhead” requirement. Option B (CORRECT): Create an AWS KMS customer-managed key, enable its built-in automatic annual rotation, and set the S3 bucket’s default encryption to use that CMK. When you move your data to S3, it is encrypted at rest with your CMK, and KMS handles key rotation every year without any manual intervention, satisfying both encryption and rotation requirements with minimal overhead. Summary: We learned that for server-side encryption with an annual rotation requirement and minimal operational overhead, using an AWS KMS customer-managed key with automatic rotation is the optimal solution. This question falls under Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company uses a popular content management system (CMS) for its corporate website. However, the required patching and maintenance are burdensome. The company is redesigning its website and wants anew solution. The website will be updated four times a year and does not need to have any dynamic content available. The solution must provide high scalability and enhanced security. Which combination of changes will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose two.)
options: Configure Amazon CloudFront in front of the website to use HTTPS functionality.
Deploy an AWS WAF web ACL in front of the website to provide HTTPS functionality.
Create and deploy an AWS Lambda function to manage and serve the website content.
Create the new website and an Amazon S3 bucket. Deploy the website on the S3 bucket with static website hosting enabled.
Create the new website. Deploy the website by using an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer.
explanation: The correct answer is A and D. Option B (INCORRECT): “Deploy an AWS WAF web ACL in front of the website to provide HTTPS functionality.” AWS WAF provides protection against common web exploits (SQL injection, XSS, etc.), but it does not itself terminate HTTPS or deliver content. You would still need CloudFront or another HTTPS endpoint. Introducing WAF alone adds complexity without solving static‐hosting or HTTPS termination by itself. Option C (INCORRECT): “Create and deploy an AWS Lambda function to manage and serve the website content.” Using Lambda to serve static files is unnecessary overhead: you’d pay for invocation time, cold starts, and add complexity in maintenance. Static content is best served from S3 (a fully managed object store), not from compute resources. Option E (INCORRECT): “Deploy the website by using an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer.” EC2 instances require patching, scaling policies, AMI maintenance, and load-balancer configuration—far more operational overhead than S3 + CloudFront. For purely static content with only quarterly updates, EC2 is overkill and less cost-efficient. Option A (CORRECT): “Configure Amazon CloudFront in front of the website to use HTTPS functionality.” CloudFront provides global edge caching for low latency and high scalability without you managing servers. It terminates HTTPS (SSL/TLS) at edge locations and can enforce TLS protocols and ciphers, enhancing security. Option D (CORRECT): “Create the new website and an Amazon S3 bucket. Deploy the website on the S3 bucket with static website hosting enabled.” S3 static website hosting is a fully managed service—no patching or servers. It scales automatically to handle any request volume, and you only pay for storage and data transfer. Pairing S3 with CloudFront ensures both high performance and secure HTTPS delivery. Summary: By choosing S3 static website hosting (Option D) and fronting it with CloudFront for HTTPS and caching (Option A), you achieve maximum scalability, security, and minimal operational overhead. This question aligns with Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company needs to implement a new data retention policy for regulatory compliance. As part of this policy, sensitive documents that are stored in an Amazon S3 bucket must be protected from deletion or modification for a fixed period of time. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Activate S3 Object Lock on the required objects and enable governance mode.
Activate S3 Object Lock on the required objects and enable compliance mode.
Enable versioning on the S3 bucket. Set a lifecycle policy to delete the objects after a specified period.
Configure an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition objects to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval for the retention duration.
explanation: The correct answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): “Activate S3 Object Lock on the required objects and enable governance mode.” Governance mode allows privileged users (with the s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permission) to alter or delete locked objects. This does not fully enforce immutability for regulatory compliance, since certain roles can still override the lock. Option C (INCORRECT): “Enable versioning on the S3 bucket. Set a lifecycle policy to delete the objects after a specified period.” Versioning alone does not prevent deletion or modification; it just keeps older versions. A lifecycle policy that deletes objects conflicts with the requirement to protect them from deletion for a fixed retention period. Option D (INCORRECT): “Configure an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition objects to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval for the retention duration.” Transitioning to Glacier only changes storage class; it does not prevent object deletion or modification. Lifecycle transitions can still be overridden or deleted unless combined with Object Lock compliance mode. Option B (CORRECT): “Activate S3 Object Lock on the required objects and enable compliance mode.” Compliance mode enforces Write-Once-Read-Many (WORM) and blocks all object modification or deletion, even by the root user, for the retention period. Once set, retention cannot be shortened or removed, satisfying strict regulatory requirements. S3 Object Lock in compliance mode is the AWS-recommended way to meet immutable data retention policies. In summary, we learned that for regulatory compliance requiring immutable storage S3 Object Lock in compliance mode is the correct solution. This question belongs to Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A global marketing company has applications that run in the ap-southeast-2 Region and the eu-west-1 Region. Applications that run in a VPC in eu-west-1 need to communicate securely with databases that run in a VPC in ap-southeast-2. Which network design will meet these requirements?
options: Create a VPC peering connection between the eu-west-1 VPC and the ap-southeast-2 VPC. Create an inbound rule in the eu-west-1 application security group that allows traffic from the database server IP addresses in the ap-southeast-2 security group.

Configure a VPC peering connection between the ap-southeast-2 VPC and the eu-west-1 VPC. Update the subnet route tables. Create an inbound rule in the ap-southeast-2 database security group that references the security group ID of the application servers in eu-west-1.

Configure a VPC peering connection between the ap-southeast-2 VPC and the eu-west-1 VPUpdate the subnet route tables. Create an inbound rule in the ap-southeast-2 database security group that allows traffic from the eu-west-1 application server IP addresses.

Create a transit gateway with a peering attachment between the eu-west-1 VPC and the ap-southeast-2 VPC. After the transit gateways are properly peered and routing is configured, create an inbound rule in the database security group that references the security group ID of the application servers in eu-west-1.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): Opens an inbound rule on the application side instead of on the database side—traffic needs to be allowed into the database SG, not the app SG. Does not mention updating route tables to enable cross-region routing over the peering connection. You cannot reference a security group in a different region in an inbound rule. Option B (INCORRECT): Although it mentions peering and route-table updates (good), it suggests referencing the application security group in a different region—AWS does not support cross-region SG references. This would fail validation because SG-to-SG rules only work within the same region. Option D (INCORRECT): Introduces a Transit Gateway (TGW) peering attachment—a heavy, costly solution for just two VPCs. Still suggests cross-region SG referencing, which is not supported. A TGW would work, but the question does not call for multi-VPC scalability or advanced routing features. Option C (CORRECT): Creates a cross-region VPC peering connection (supported between ap-southeast-2 and eu-west-1). Updates the subnet route tables so that each VPC can route traffic to the other over the peering link. In the ap-southeast-2 database security group, allows inbound from the eu-west-1 application servers’ IP addresses or CIDR, which is valid across regions. Does not rely on unsupported cross-region SG-to-SG rules, keeping the design secure and simple. In summary, we learned that for cross-region VPC communication: Use cross-region VPC peering (or Transit Gateway if you need more scale). Always update route tables to send traffic over the peering link. Reference CIDR blocks or IP addresses across regions—security group-to-security group references only work within the same region. This question belongs to Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company's HTTP application is behind a Network Load Balancer (NLB). The NLB's target group is configured to use an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group with multiple EC2 instances that run the web service. The company notices that the NLB is not detecting HTTP errors for the application. These errors require a manual restart of the EC2 instances that run the web service. The company needs to improve the application's availability without writing custom scripts or code. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
options: Enable HTTP health checks on the NLB, supplying the URL of the company's application.
Add a cron job to the EC2 instances to check the local application's logs once each minute. If HTTP errors are detected. the application will restart.
Replace the NLB with an Application Load Balancer. Enable HTTP health checks by supplying the URL of the company's application. Configure an Auto Scaling action to replace unhealthy instances.
Create an Amazon Cloud Watch alarm that monitors the UnhealthyHostCount metric for the NLB. Configure an Auto Scaling action to replace unhealthy instances when the alarm is in the ALARM state.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): “Enable HTTP health checks on the NLB, supplying the URL of the company's application.” While NLB now supports HTTP health checks, the setup in the question indicates it’s currently using only TCP health checks and not detecting HTTP 5xx errors. The more straightforward solution is to use a load balancer designed for HTTP/HTTPS applications that natively handles application-level health checks without having to retrofit NLB settings. Option B (INCORRECT): “Add a cron job to the EC2 instances to check the local application's logs once each minute. If HTTP errors are detected, the application will restart.” This requires custom scripting and maintenance on each instance, which the company wants to avoid. Cron-based self-healing is error-prone and not a native AWS solution for improving availability. Option D (INCORRECT): “Create a CloudWatch alarm that monitors the UnhealthyHostCount metric for the NLB. Configure an Auto Scaling action to replace unhealthy instances when the alarm is in the ALARM state.” The UnhealthyHostCount metric never increases because the NLB is using TCP checks and not detecting HTTP errors. Even if you alarm on UnhealthyHostCount, you would still need HTTP-level checks to mark instances unhealthy in the first place. Option C (CORRECT): “Replace the NLB with an Application Load Balancer. Enable HTTP health checks by supplying the URL of the company's application. Configure an Auto Scaling action to replace unhealthy instances.” ALB is designed for HTTP/HTTPS traffic and provides robust application-level health checks (return codes, path checks). When the ALB detects HTTP 5xx errors on a target, it marks the instance unhealthy and Auto Scaling can automatically replace it. No custom scripts or manual intervention are required — this leverages native AWS features to improve availability. In summary, we learned that for application-level error detection and automated instance replacement, an Application Load Balancer’s HTTP health checks combined with Auto Scaling is the correct AWS-native solution. This question belongs to Domain 2 - Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company runs a global web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The application stores data in Amazon Aurora. The company needs to create a disaster recovery solution and can tolerate up to 30 minutes of downtime and potential data loss. The solution does not need to handle the load when the primary infrastructure is healthy.What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
options: Deploy the application with the required infrastructure elements in place. Use Amazon Route 53 to configure active-passive failover. Create an Aurora Replica in a second AWS Region.
Host a scaled-down deployment of the application in a second AWS Region. Use Amazon Route 53 to configure active-active failover. Create an Aurora Replica in the second Region.
Replicate the primary infrastructure in a second AWS Region. Use Amazon Route 53 to configure active-active failover. Create an Aurora database that is restored from the latest snapshot.

Back up data with AWS Backup. Use the backup to create the required infrastructure in a second AWS Region. Use Amazon Route 53 to configure active-passive failover. Create an Aurora second primary instance in the second Region.
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): This suggests an active-active failover with a “scaled-down” deployment always running in the secondary Region, which increases cost during normal operation. It also misuses an Aurora Replica for write workloads in active-active mode—Aurora Replicas are read-only and cannot serve as a live writable primary without promotion. Does not meet the requirement of minimizing ongoing cost when the primary infrastructure is healthy. Option C (INCORRECT): Restoring an Aurora database from a snapshot in the second Region at failover time can take well over 30 minutes, violating the RTO requirement. Snapshot-based restore also risks more than 30 minutes of data loss (RPO), since snapshots are taken at discrete intervals. This approach requires fully duplicating the primary infrastructure, driving up cost unnecessarily during normal operations. Option D (INCORRECT): Relying on AWS Backup to restore Aurora data in a secondary Region is too slow to meet the 30-minute RTO. Manual recovery from backup also risks significant data loss if backups run only periodically, exceeding the 30-minute RPO. Additionally, backing up and restoring compute and networking infrastructure adds complexity and further delay. Option A (CORRECT): Deploys only a passive (scaled-down or no-load) setup in the secondary Region, minimizing cost during normal operations. Uses an Aurora Global Database or cross-Region Aurora Replica which replicates asynchronously, achieving an RPO well within 30 minutes. Amazon Route 53 active-passive failover allows quick redirection of traffic, meeting the 30-minute RTO requirement. Simple to monitor and automate failover when the primary Region becomes unavailable. In summary, Option A meets the disaster-recovery requirements by using asynchronous cross-Region replication (Aurora Replica) and Route 53 active-passive failover, keeping cost low when the primary is healthy and ensuring RTO/RPO within 30 minutes. This question belongs to Domain 2 – Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company has deployed its newest product on AWS. The product runs in an Auto Scaling group behind a Network Load Balancer. The company stores the product’s objects in an Amazon S3 bucket. The company recently experienced malicious attacks against its systems. The company needs a solution that continuously monitors for malicious activity in the AWS account, workloads, and access patterns to the S3 bucket. The solution must also report suspicious activity and display the information on a dashboard.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Configure Amazon Macie to monitor and report findings to AWS Config.
Configure Amazon Inspector to monitor and report findings to AWS CloudTrail.
Configure Amazon GuardDuty to monitor and report findings to AWS Security Hub.
Configure AWS Config to monitor and report findings to Amazon EventBridge.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): Configure Amazon Macie to monitor and report findings to AWS Config. Amazon Macie is designed for discovering and protecting sensitive data in Amazon S3 (PII detection), not for continuous threat detection across AWS accounts and workloads. Macie integrates with AWS Security Hub, not AWS Config, for centralizing findings. Option B (INCORRECT): Configure Amazon Inspector to monitor and report findings to AWS CloudTrail. Amazon Inspector performs automated security assessments on EC2 instances and container images, focusing on vulnerabilities and deviations from best practices. It does not provide continuous monitoring of account-level malicious activity or S3 access patterns, nor does it report findings to CloudTrail. Option D (INCORRECT): Configure AWS Config to monitor and report findings to Amazon EventBridge. AWS Config tracks and records AWS resource configurations and changes, not runtime malicious activity or unauthorized access attempts. While Config can send compliance events to EventBridge, it doesn’t analyze traffic patterns or detect threats. Option C (CORRECT): Configure Amazon GuardDuty to monitor and report findings to AWS Security Hub. Amazon GuardDuty continuously monitors for malicious or unauthorized behavior across AWS accounts, workloads, and S3 data events. It can detect unusual API calls, reconnaissance, instance compromise, and anomalous access to S3 buckets. GuardDuty findings can be aggregated and visualized in AWS Security Hub dashboards, providing centralized reporting and alerts. In summary, we learned that GuardDuty is the AWS service purpose-built for continuous threat detection across AWS accounts, workloads, and S3 access patterns, with built-in integration to Security Hub for visualization and alerting. This question belongs to Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company has an AWS account used for software engineering. The AWS account has access to the company’s on-premises data center through a pair of AWS Direct Connect connections. All non-VPC traffic routes to the virtual private gateway. A development team recently created an AWS Lambda function through the console. The development team needs to allow the function to access a database that runs in a private subnet in the company’s data center.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Configure the Lambda function to run in the VPC with the appropriate security group.
Set up a VPN connection from AWS to the data center. Route the traffic from the Lambda function through the VPN.
Update the route tables in the VPC to allow the Lambda function to access the on-premises data center through Direct Connect.
Create an Elastic IP address. Configure the Lambda function to send traffic through the Elastic IP address without an elastic network interface.
explanation: The correct Answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): “Set up a VPN connection from AWS to the data center. Route the traffic from the Lambda function through the VPN.” The account already has Direct Connect, so adding a VPN is redundant and increases complexity and cost. Lambda functions by default do not attach to a network interface that could use this VPN; you would still need to place the function in a VPC first. Option C (INCORRECT): “Update the route tables in the VPC to allow the Lambda function to access the on-premises data center through Direct Connect.” Lambda functions created without VPC configuration do not have ENIs in your VPC, so changing route tables alone has no effect. You must first attach the Lambda to your VPC (via subnet and security group) before it can honor any VPC route table entries. Option D (INCORRECT): “Create an Elastic IP address. Configure the Lambda function to send traffic through the Elastic IP address without an elastic network interface.” Lambda functions need ENIs in order to have static IPs; you cannot bind an EIP without placing the function in a VPC and associating it to an ENI. There is no native mechanism for a Lambda to “send traffic through an EIP” without VPC networking. Option A (CORRECT): “Configure the Lambda function to run in the VPC with the appropriate security group.” Once the function is placed in the private subnets of your VPC and given a security group, its ENIs will use the VPC routing. All non-VPC traffic is already routed to the Virtual Private Gateway, which sits behind your Direct Connect links to on-prem. This setup lets your Lambda function transparently reach the on-prem database over the existing Direct Connect connection. In summary, we learned that to give a Lambda function access to on-premises resources via Direct Connect, you must configure the function to run inside your VPC with proper subnet and security group settings so that VPC routing—and, by extension, the Virtual Private Gateway—can carry traffic over Direct Connect. This question falls under Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A solutions architect is designing a three-tier web application. The architecture consists of an internet-facing Application Load Balancer (ALB) and a web tier that is hosted on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets. The application tier with the business logic runs on EC2 instances in private subnets. The database tier consists of Microsoft SQL Server that runs on EC2 instances in private subnets. Security is a high priority for the company. Which combination of security group configurations should the solutions architect use? (Choose three.)
options: Configure the security group for the web tier to allow inbound HTTPS traffic from the security group for the ALB.
Configure the security group for the web tier to allow outbound HTTPS traffic to 0.0.0.0/0.
Configure the security group for the database tier to allow inbound Microsoft SQL Server traffic from the security group for the application tier.
Configure the security group for the database tier to allow outbound HTTPS traffic and Microsoft SQL Server traffic to the security group for the web tier.
Configure the security group for the application tier to allow inbound HTTPS traffic from the security group for the web tier.
Configure the security group for the application tier to allow outbound HTTPS traffic and Microsoft SQL Server traffic to the security group for the web tier.
explanation: The correct answer is A, C, E. Option B (INCORRECT): “Configure the security group for the web tier to allow outbound HTTPS traffic to 0.0.0.0/0.” Allows the web tier to make arbitrary outbound calls to the internet, which violates the principle of least privilege. The web tier only needs to communicate with the application tier, not the public internet. Option D (INCORRECT): “Configure the security group for the database tier to allow outbound HTTPS traffic and Microsoft SQL Server traffic to the security group for the web tier.” The database tier should not initiate communication to the web tier; it only needs to accept inbound SQL connections from the application tier. Outbound rules on the DB SG are unnecessary here (default allows all outbound), but you certainly wouldn’t open traffic back to the web tier. Option F (INCORRECT): “Configure the security group for the application tier to allow outbound HTTPS traffic and Microsoft SQL Server traffic to the security group for the web tier.” The application tier does not talk to the web tier; it receives inbound requests from the web tier. Outbound SQL traffic should go to the database tier, not the web tier. Option A (CORRECT): “Configure the security group for the web tier to allow inbound HTTPS traffic from the security group for the ALB.” Allows only the ALB to reach the web tier on port 443, enforcing tier-to-tier traffic rules. Keeps the web servers isolated from the internet except through the ALB. Option E (CORRECT): “Configure the security group for the application tier to allow inbound HTTPS traffic from the security group for the web tier.” Enables the web tier to communicate securely with the application tier over port 443. Ensures only the web tier can invoke the business logic, locking down any other access. Option C (CORRECT): “Configure the security group for the database tier to allow inbound Microsoft SQL Server traffic from the security group for the application tier.” Allows only the application tier to connect on the SQL Server port (1433), protecting the database from unauthorized access. Follows the least-privilege model by restricting inbound DB traffic to a known source SG. Summary: We learned how to enforce strict security group rules by permitting only tier-to-tier communication on the required ports and from specific security groups, adhering to the principle of least privilege. This question belongs to Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A solutions architect needs to host a high performance computing (HPC) workload in the AWS Cloud. The workload will run on hundreds of Amazon EC2 instances and will require parallel access to a shared file system to enable distributed processing of large datasets. Datasets will be accessed across multiple instances simultaneously. The workload requires access latency within 1 ms. After processing has completed, engineers will need access to the dataset for manual postprocessing.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Use Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) as a shared file system. Access the dataset from Amazon EFS.
Mount an Amazon S3 bucket to serve as the shared file system. Perform postprocessing directly from the S3 bucket.
Use Amazon FSx for Lustre as a shared file system. Link the file system to an Amazon S3 bucket for postprocessing.
Configure AWS Resource Access Manager to share an Amazon S3 bucket so that it can be mounted to all instances for processing and postprocessing.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): Use Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) as a shared file system. EFS provides scalable NFS storage but cannot consistently deliver sub-1 ms latency for hundreds of EC2 instances in an HPC environment. Throughput and IOPS are lower compared to specialized parallel file systems needed for high-performance computing. Option B (INCORRECT): Mount an Amazon S3 bucket to serve as the shared file system. S3 is object storage and does not natively support POSIX semantics or low-latency file operations. Mounting wrappers introduce additional latency and are not suitable for sub-1 ms I/O requirements. Option D (INCORRECT): Configure AWS Resource Access Manager to share an Amazon S3 bucket so that it can be mounted to all instances. Again, S3 is object storage and not a parallel file system—latency is too high and semantics are different from POSIX file systems. RAM sharing does not change performance characteristics of S3 and cannot deliver the required HPC throughput or latency. Option C (CORRECT): Use Amazon FSx for Lustre as a shared file system. Link the file system to an Amazon S3 bucket for postprocessing. FSx for Lustre is a fully managed, high-performance parallel file system designed for HPC workloads, with sub-millisecond latencies. It can be linked to S3 so that data is transparently imported/exported, enabling fast processing and later manual postprocessing from S3. Provides the required POSIX compliance, massive throughput, and low latencies across hundreds of EC2 instances. In summary, we learned that Amazon FSx for Lustre is the optimal choice for sub-millisecond, parallel file I/O in HPC scenarios, with seamless integration to S3 for postprocessing. This question belongs to Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company performs monthly maintenance on its AWS infrastructure. During these maintenance activities, the company needs to rotate the credentials for its Amazon RDS for MySQL databases across multiple AWS Regions.Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Store the credentials as secrets in AWS Secrets Manager. Use multi-Region secret replication for the required Regions. Configure Secrets Manager to rotate the secrets on a schedule.

Store the credentials as secrets in AWS Systems Manager by creating a secure string parameter. Use multi-Region secret replication for the required Regions. Configure Systems Manager to rotate the secrets on a schedule.

Store the credentials in an Amazon S3 bucket that has server-side encryption (SSE) enabled. Use Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) to invoke an AWS Lambda function to rotate the credentials.

Encrypt the credentials as secrets by using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) multi-Region customer managed keys. Store the secrets in an Amazon DynamoDB global table. Use an AWS Lambda function to retrieve the secrets from DynamoDB. Use the RDS API to rotate the secrets.
explanation: The correct Answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): Store the credentials as secrets in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Parameter Store secure strings do not offer built-in rotation for RDS credentials. There is no native multi-Region secret replication in Systems Manager Parameter Store. You would need to build and maintain custom Lambda functions and EventBridge rules—higher operational overhead. Option C (INCORRECT): Store encrypted credentials in an S3 bucket and use EventBridge + Lambda to rotate. This requires custom code to retrieve, decrypt, rotate, and store secrets in each region. EventBridge triggers and Lambda implementations must be developed and operated across regions. Higher complexity and maintenance compared to a managed service. Option D (INCORRECT): Use KMS multi-Region Customer Managed Keys and DynamoDB global tables with Lambda. Also demands custom logic to encrypt/decrypt, rotate, and distribute credentials. DynamoDB global tables add cost and complexity for storing secrets. No native RDS-secret rotation integration—full operational burden on your team. Option A (CORRECT): Use AWS Secrets Manager with multi-Region secret replication and built-in rotation. Secrets Manager natively supports RDS credential rotation on a schedule. Multi-Region secret replication automatically replicates secrets to target regions. Eliminates custom code and reduces operational overhead by leveraging a fully managed service. In summary, leveraging AWS Secrets Manager for automated, multi-Region rotation of RDS credentials provides the least operational overhead. This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures, as it focuses on secure credential management and rotation.

question: A company's solutions architect is designing an AWS multi-account solution that uses AWS Organizations. The solutions architect has organized the company's accounts into organizational units (OUs). The solutions architect needs a solution that will identify any changes to the OU hierarchy. The solution also needs to notify the company's operations team of any changes. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Provision the AWS accounts by using AWS Control Tower. Use account drift notifications to identify the changes to the OU hierarchy.
Provision the AWS accounts by using AWS Control Tower. Use AWS Config aggregated rules to identify the changes to the OU hierarchy.
Use AWS Service Catalog to create accounts in Organizations. Use an AWS CloudTrail organization trail to identify the changes to the OU hierarchy.
Use AWS CloudFormation templates to create accounts in Organizations. Use the drift detection operation on a stack to identify the changes to the OU hierarchy.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): “Provision the AWS accounts by using AWS Control Tower. Use account drift notifications to identify the changes to the OU hierarchy.” AWS Control Tower’s drift detection is focused on the landing zone’s guardrail compliance and account factory provisioning settings, not on arbitrary changes in the OU structure. Control Tower does not generate automatic notifications for OU‐level changes in AWS Organizations. Option B (INCORRECT): “Provision the AWS accounts by using AWS Control Tower. Use AWS Config aggregated rules to identify the changes to the OU hierarchy.” AWS Config does not natively track AWS Organizations’ OU hierarchy changes as a resource type in an aggregated account setup. You would need custom lambda functions or custom config rules, which increases operational overhead and complexity. Option D (INCORRECT): “Use AWS CloudFormation templates to create accounts in Organizations. Use the drift detection operation on a stack to identify the changes to the OU hierarchy.” CloudFormation does not directly support AWS::Organizations::OrganizationalUnit resources for full hierarchy modeling. Stack drift detection must be manually initiated or scheduled, and CloudFormation drift doesn’t alert via SNS out-of-the-box without additional automation. This approach adds significant operational overhead compared to a simple CloudTrail organization trail. Option C (CORRECT): “Use AWS Service Catalog to create accounts in Organizations. Use an AWS CloudTrail organization trail to identify the changes to the OU hierarchy.” CloudTrail organization-level trails capture all AWS Organizations API calls (CreateOrganizationalUnit, MoveAccount, etc.) across every account. You can configure the trail to deliver logs to CloudWatch Logs or S3 and set up CloudWatch metric filters and SNS notifications to alert the operations team immediately on any OU change. This solution requires minimal ongoing maintenance and leverages AWS-managed services for auditing and notification. In summary, we learned that tracking AWS Organizations OU hierarchy changes is best done with a CloudTrail organization trail combined with automated alerts. This approach provides a fully managed, low-overhead solution. This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company is building a mobile app on AWS. The company wants to expand its reach to millions of users. The company needs to build a platform so that authorized users can watch the company’s content on their mobile devices. What should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?
options: Publish content to a public Amazon S3 bucket. Use AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) keys to stream content.
Set up IPsec VPN between the mobile app and the AWS environment to stream content.
Use Amazon CloudFront. Provide signed URLs to stream content.
Set up AWS Client VPN between the mobile app and the AWS environment to stream content.
explanation: The correct answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): “Publish content to a public Amazon S3 bucket. Use AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) keys to stream content.” Making the bucket public exposes content to everyone; it does not restrict to authorized users. AWS KMS is for encrypting data at rest or in transit but does not provide streaming access control or URL signing for clients. It lacks the performance and global edge‐caching benefits that CloudFront provides for millions of users. Option B (INCORRECT): “Set up IPsec VPN between the mobile app and the AWS environment to stream content.” IPsec VPN is designed for site-to-site or client-to-site connectivity, not for mobile app content streaming at scale. Managing millions of VPN connections from mobile devices is operationally complex and costly. It adds latency and bottlenecks at the VPN termination points instead of leveraging global edge locations. Option D (INCORRECT): “Set up AWS Client VPN between the mobile app and the AWS environment to stream content.” AWS Client VPN is similar to IPsec VPN and is meant for secure access to AWS resources from clients, not high-volume content delivery. It does not provide caching, URL signing, or content distribution optimizations. Scaling to millions of mobile users through a VPN endpoint is impractical and expensive. Option C (CORRECT): “Use Amazon CloudFront. Provide signed URLs to stream content.” CloudFront is a global content distribution network that caches content at edge locations, delivering low latency and high throughput to users worldwide. Signed URLs allow you to restrict access to only authorized users for a defined time period, ensuring secure streaming. It seamlessly integrates with origin stores like S3 or MediaStore, scales automatically to millions of requests, and provides detailed logging and monitoring. From this discussion we learned that for large-scale, secure content streaming to mobile devices, Amazon CloudFront with signed URLs is the optimal solution. This question belongs to Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company wants to manage Amazon Machine Images (AMIs). The company currently copies AMIs to the same AWS Region where the AMIs were created. The company needs to design an application that captures AWS API calls and sends alerts whenever the Amazon EC2 CreateImage API operation is called within the company’s account. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Create an AWS Lambda function to query AWS CloudTrail logs and to send an alert when a CreateImage API call is detected.

Configure AWS CloudTrail with an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) notification that occurs when updated logs are sent to Amazon S3. Use Amazon Athena to create a new table and to query on CreateImage when an API call is detected.

Create an Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) rule for the CreateImage API call. Configure the target as an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to send an alert when a CreateImage API call is detected.

Configure an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue as a target for AWS CloudTrail logs. Create an AWS Lambda function to send an alert to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic when a CreateImage API call is detected.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): “Create an AWS Lambda function to query AWS CloudTrail logs and to send an alert when a CreateImage API call is detected.” You’d have to schedule the Lambda (e.g., via CloudWatch Events) to poll CloudTrail logs in S3, adding complexity and delays. This approach introduces extra operational overhead—managing schedules, retries, parsing logs—rather than real-time alerting. Option B (INCORRECT): “Configure AWS CloudTrail with an Amazon SNS notification when updated logs land in S3. Use Amazon Athena to query CreateImage calls.” Athena queries are ad hoc or scheduled, not immediate; you won’t get near real-time alerts. Setting up SNS on S3 log delivery plus Athena table definitions and scheduled queries increases operational complexity. Option D (INCORRECT): “Send CloudTrail logs to an SQS FIFO queue, then have a Lambda read from SQS and alert via SNS on CreateImage.” Managing SQS, Lambda polling logic, error handling, and scaling adds overhead. It’s more complex than using a native event‐driven pattern that directly filters the API call. Option C (CORRECT): “Create an EventBridge rule for the CreateImage API call and target an SNS topic for alerts.” EventBridge (formerly CloudWatch Events) can natively filter AWS API calls in real time. You simply define a rule on the CreateImage operation and attach an SNS topic—no servers or polling required. This solution delivers alerts immediately and has minimal operational overhead. In summary, we want real-time notifications with minimal operational overhead. EventBridge rules provide exactly that by filtering and routing API events without custom polling or log-parsing code. This question belongs to Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures, as it focuses on auditing and alerting on sensitive API operations.

question: A company wants to migrate 100 GB of historical data from an on-premises location to an Amazon S3 bucket. The company has a 100 megabits per second (Mbps) internet connection on premises. The company needs to encrypt the data in transit to the S3 bucket. The company will store new data directly in Amazon S3. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Use the s3 sync command in the AWS CLI to move the data directly to an S3 bucket
Use AWS DataSync to migrate the data from the on-premises location to an S3 bucket
Use AWS Snowball to move the data to an S3 bucket
Set up an IPsec VPN from the on-premises location to AWS. Use the s3 cp command in the AWS CLI to move the data directly to an S3 bucket
explanation: The correct answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): “Use the aws s3 sync command in the AWS CLI to move the data directly to an S3 bucket.” The AWS CLI s3 sync does encrypt data in transit via HTTPS, but this approach requires you to script, monitor, retry failures, and handle partial uploads manually. Operational overhead is higher compared to a fully managed service that handles performance tuning, error handling, and monitoring. Option C (INCORRECT): “Use AWS Snowball to move the data to an S3 bucket.” Snowball is designed for large data sets (multiple TBs or PBs) and involves shipping physical devices back and forth. For only 100 GB over a 100 Mbps link, shipping a device adds unnecessary time, cost, and operational steps. Option D (INCORRECT): “Set up an IPsec VPN from the on-premises location to AWS. Use the aws s3 cp command in the AWS CLI to move the data directly to an S3 bucket.” While a VPN plus CLI approach secures data in transit, it requires network configuration (VPN gateways, routing) and ongoing management. This increases operational overhead relative to a managed data-transfer service that natively encrypts in transit. Option B (CORRECT): “Use AWS DataSync to migrate the data from the on-premises location to an S3 bucket.” DataSync automatically encrypts data in transit (TLS 1.2) without additional network setup. It’s a fully managed service that handles network optimization, error retries, and logging—minimizing operational overhead. DataSync can efficiently transfer 100 GB over a 100 Mbps link in roughly 24 hours, with built-in monitoring and reporting. Summary: We’ve reviewed why direct CLI approaches (Options A and D) incur more scripting and operational burden, and why Snowball (Option C) is overkill for just 100 GB. AWS DataSync (Option B) meets the encryption, performance, and low-overhead requirements most effectively. This question falls under Domain 4 – Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company wants to provide data scientists with near real-time read-only access to the company's production Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL database. The database is currently configured as a Single-AZ database. The data scientists use complex queries that will not affect the production database. The company needs a solution that is highly available.Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Scale the existing production database in a maintenance window to provide enough power for the data scientists.
Change the setup from a Single-AZ to a Multi-AZ instance deployment with a larger secondary standby instance. Provide the data scientists access to the secondary instance.
Change the setup from a Single-AZ to a Multi-AZ instance deployment. Provide two additional read replicas for the data scientists.
Change the setup from a Single-AZ to a Multi-AZ cluster deployment with two readable standby instances. Provide read endpoints to the data scientists.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): “Scale the existing production database in a maintenance window to provide enough power for the data scientists.” • This does not isolate the heavy analytical queries from production, risking performance impact. • It doesn’t provide high availability or offload reads. • Scaling in a maintenance window still leaves you with a single point of failure. Option B (INCORRECT): “Change the setup from a Single-AZ to a Multi-AZ instance deployment with a larger secondary standby instance. Provide the data scientists access to the secondary instance.” • In RDS Multi-AZ, the standby is not readable—AWS does not allow read traffic on the synchronous standby. • You cannot offload read workloads to the standby in a Multi-AZ configuration. Option D (INCORRECT): “Change the setup from a Single-AZ to a Multi-AZ cluster deployment with two readable standby instances. Provide read endpoints to the data scientists.” • This describes Amazon Aurora (cluster deployment), not standard RDS for PostgreSQL. Migrating to Aurora has additional licensing and conversion overhead. • Aurora clusters are more costly than RDS + read replicas unless you need advanced Aurora features. Option C (CORRECT): “Change the setup from a Single-AZ to a Multi-AZ instance deployment.
