Provide two additional read replicas for the data scientists.” • You get high availability for the primary (automatic failover to the standby). • Multiple read replicas offload complex, read-only analytical queries without impacting production. • Read replicas support near real-time replication and can be placed in different AZs for improved availability. • This approach is more cost-effective than migrating to Aurora or over-provisioning the primary database. In summary, by combining Multi-AZ for automated failover with dedicated read replicas for analytics traffic, we meet the requirements for high availability, near real-time read access, and cost efficiency. This question belongs to Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company has an on-premises server that uses an Oracle database to process and store customer information. The company wants to use an AWS database service to achieve higher availability and to improve application performance. The company also wants to offload reporting from its primary database system.Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way?
options: Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to create an Amazon RDS DB instance in multiple AWS Regions. Point the reporting functions toward a separate DB instance from the primary DB instance.
Use Amazon RDS in a Single-AZ deployment to create an Oracle database. Create a read replica in the same zone as the primary DB instance. Direct the reporting functions to the read replica.
Use Amazon RDS deployed in a Multi-AZ cluster deployment to create an Oracle database. Direct the reporting functions to use the reader instance in the cluster deployment.
Use Amazon RDS deployed in a Multi-AZ instance deployment to create an Amazon Aurora database. Direct the reporting functions to the reader instances.
explanation: The correct answer is D. Option A (INCORRECT): Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to create an Amazon RDS DB instance in multiple AWS Regions. Point the reporting functions toward a separate DB instance from the primary DB instance. AWS DMS is designed for one-time or ongoing migrations, not active–active multi-region high-availability for production databases. Managing cross-region replication with DMS adds complexity and operational overhead. It does not provide native reader endpoints for reporting, so you’d still need to manage separate instances manually. Option B (INCORRECT): Use Amazon RDS in a Single-AZ deployment to create an Oracle database. Create a read replica in the same zone as the primary DB instance. Direct the reporting functions to the read replica. Single-AZ RDS offers no automatic failover—if the AZ fails, the database goes down. Amazon RDS for Oracle does not support read replicas in the same way as MySQL/Aurora—it only supports Multi-AZ synchronous failover. This design fails the high-availability requirement and still leaves you managing primary and reporting instances yourself. Option C (INCORRECT): Use Amazon RDS deployed in a Multi-AZ cluster deployment to create an Oracle database. Direct the reporting functions to use the reader instance in the cluster deployment. “Multi-AZ cluster deployment” and reader endpoints are features of Amazon Aurora, not of RDS for Oracle. RDS for Oracle only provides a standby for failover in Multi-AZ, not reader nodes you can offload reporting to. This option is not supported by the Oracle engine on RDS and adds confusion without operational benefit. Option D (CORRECT): Use Amazon RDS deployed in a Multi-AZ instance deployment to create an Amazon Aurora database. Direct the reporting functions to the reader instances. Amazon Aurora automatically replicates data across multiple Availability Zones to ensure high availability and fast failover. The cluster endpoints (writer and reader) let you offload reporting and read-intensive workloads to up to 15 low-latency reader instances. Aurora is fully managed—patching, scaling, backups, and failover are handled by AWS, delivering the most operationally efficient solution. In summary, migrating to Amazon Aurora in a Multi-AZ cluster meets all requirements—high availability, improved performance, and offloaded reporting—in the most operationally efficient way. This question belongs to Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company is deploying an application in three AWS Regions using an Application Load Balancer. Amazon Route 53 will be used to distribute traffic between these Regions. Which Route 53 configuration should a solutions architect use to provide the MOST high-performing experience?
options: Create an A record with a latency policy.
Create an A record with a geolocation policy.
Create a CNAME record with a failover policy.
Create a CNAME record with a geoproximity policy.
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): “Create an A record with a geolocation policy.” • Geolocation routing directs users based on their physical location, not on network performance. • It ensures compliance or content localization, but it does not guarantee the lowest latency path. Option C (INCORRECT): “Create a CNAME record with a failover policy.” • Failover routing is designed for high availability by routing traffic to a standby endpoint when the primary is unhealthy. • It does not optimize for performance or latency under normal operating conditions. Option D (INCORRECT): “Create a CNAME record with a geoproximity policy.” • Geoproximity routing lets you shift traffic based on geographic bias and endpoint weight, but it isn’t the best choice purely for minimizing latency. • It requires Route 53 Traffic Flow and is more complex, without the direct latency optimization provided by latency-based routing. Option A (CORRECT): “Create an A record with a latency policy.” • Latency-based routing directs each user’s DNS query to the Region that provides the lowest network latency. • By using an A (alias) record pointing to the regional Application Load Balancers, Route 53 automatically measures latency to each Region and routes traffic accordingly. • This ensures the most high-performing experience for users distributed globally. In summary, we learned that for GLOBAL PERFORMANCE optimization, Route 53’s Latency-based Routing is the most appropriate choice. This question falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company is creating a prototype of an ecommerce website on AWS. The website consists of an Application Load Balancer, an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 instances for web servers, and an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance that runs with the Single-AZ configuration. The website is slow to respond during searches of the product catalog. The product catalog is a group of tables in the MySQL database that the company does not update frequently. A solutions architect has determined that the CPU utilization on the DB instance is high when product catalog searches occur. What should the solutions architect recommend to improve the performance of the website during searches of the product catalog?
options: Migrate the product catalog to an Amazon Redshift database. Use the COPY command to load the product catalog tables.
Implement an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster to cache the product catalog. Use lazy loading to populate the cache.
Add an additional scaling policy to the Auto Scaling group to launch additional EC2 instances when database response is slow.
Turn on the Multi-AZ configuration for the DB instance. Configure the EC2 instances to throttle the product catalog queries that are sent to the database.
explanation: The correct answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): “Migrate the product catalog to an Amazon Redshift database. Use the COPY command to load the product catalog tables.” Amazon Redshift is designed for large-scale data warehousing and analytics, not for serving high-throughput, low-latency application queries in real time. Moving the catalog into Redshift adds complexity and latency when loading and querying small tables that change infrequently. Redshift incurs higher costs and is not optimized for the pattern of dozens or hundreds of small, repeated catalog lookups from web servers. Option C (INCORRECT): “Add an additional scaling policy to the Auto Scaling group to launch additional EC2 instances when database response is slow.” Adding web servers does nothing to reduce the load on the single-node MySQL database; it only increases concurrent queries to an already CPU-bound database. This does not address the core issue—high CPU on the RDS instance when running catalog searches. Scaling web tier without offloading or caching the database queries will only exacerbate database contention. Option D (INCORRECT): “Turn on the Multi-AZ configuration for the DB instance. Configure the EC2 instances to throttle the product catalog queries that are sent to the database.” Multi-AZ provides high availability and failover but does not improve read-query performance on the primary instance. Throttling queries only slows the application further and degrades user experience rather than improving search latency. Multi-AZ increases cost without addressing the CPU bottleneck during read operations. Option B (CORRECT): “Implement an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster to cache the product catalog. Use lazy loading to populate the cache.” Amazon ElastiCache for Redis provides in-memory caching and sub-millisecond latency, offloading read queries from the MySQL database. With lazy loading, the cache is populated on the first read and subsequently serves frequent catalog lookups without hitting the DB. This solution directly reduces CPU utilization on the RDS instance and improves website performance for product searches. In summary, caching the infrequently updated product catalog in ElastiCache reduces load on the MySQL database and delivers faster, scalable read performance. This question falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company hosts a three-tier web application that includes a PostgreSQL database. The database stores the metadata from documents. The company searches the metadata for key terms to retrieve documents that the company reviews in a report each month. The documents are stored in Amazon S3. The documents are usually written only once, but they are updated frequently. The reporting process takes a few hours with the use of relational queries. The reporting process must not prevent any document modifications or the addition of new documents. A solutions architect needs to implement a solution to speed up the reporting process.Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST amount of change to the application code?
options: Set up a new Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) cluster that includes a read replica. Scale the read replica to generate the reports.
Set up a new Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster that includes an Aurora Replica. Issue queries to the Aurora Replica to generate the reports.
Set up a new Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL Multi-AZ DB instance. Configure the reporting module to query the secondary RDS node so that the reporting module does not affect the primary node.
Set up a new Amazon DynamoDB table to store the documents. Use a fixed write capacity to support new document entries. Automatically scale the read capacity to support the reports.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): Setting up Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) requires migrating from PostgreSQL to a document‐style database. This involves significant application‐level changes (queries, drivers, schema design). DocumentDB is optimized for JSON-style documents rather than relational metadata queries. It does not offer the same SQL capabilities for complex relational reports. Option C (INCORRECT): Using Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL in Multi-AZ mode provides a synchronous standby for failover—but that standby is not open for read traffic. You cannot direct read/reporting queries to the standby in a Multi-AZ RDS configuration. All read/write traffic still hits the primary, so reporting would continue to compete with writes. Option D (INCORRECT): Migrating the metadata and documents into DynamoDB would be a major rewrite of your application logic. DynamoDB is a NoSQL key-value store, not designed for complex relational queries. Frequent schema changes and scanning large tables for monthly reports would be inefficient and costly. Option B (CORRECT): Deploy an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster with an Aurora Replica, and run the reporting queries against that read replica. Aurora Replicas are designed for high-performance, low-latency reads and can offload heavy reporting workloads. No major application code changes are needed—just point the reporting module at the reader endpoint. Writes and document updates continue on the primary without interference from read queries. Summary: Offloading reporting to an Aurora Replica speeds up complex queries with minimal code change. This solution falls squarely into Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures, as it optimizes read performance while preserving write availability.

question: A company is launching a new application deployed on an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster and is using the Fargate launch type for ECS tasks. The company is monitoring CPU and memory usage because it is expecting high traffic to the application upon its launch. However, the company wants to reduce costs when utilization decreases. What should a solutions architect recommend?
options: Use Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling to scale at certain periods based on previous traffic patterns.
Use an AWS Lambda function to scale Amazon ECS based on metric breaches that trigger an Amazon CloudWatch alarm.
Use Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling with simple scaling policies to scale when ECS metric breaches trigger an Amazon CloudWatch alarm.
Use AWS Application Auto Scaling with target tracking policies to scale when ECS metric breaches trigger an Amazon CloudWatch alarm.
explanation: The correct answer is D Option A (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling to scale at certain periods based on previous traffic patterns.” • With Fargate you don’t manage EC2 instances directly, so EC2 Auto Scaling does not apply. • You need a serverless scaling approach tied to your ECS service, not scheduling EC2 capacity. Option B (INCORRECT): “Use an AWS Lambda function to scale Amazon ECS based on metric breaches that trigger an Amazon CloudWatch alarm.” • Introducing Lambda adds unnecessary complexity; AWS Application Auto Scaling natively integrates with ECS. • You’d have to write, maintain and secure custom scaling logic instead of using a managed service. Option C (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling with simple scaling policies to scale when ECS metric breaches trigger an Amazon CloudWatch alarm.” • Again, EC2 Auto Scaling is for instance fleets, not Fargate tasks. • Fargate tasks are scaled via ECS service Auto Scaling, not by EC2 Auto Scaling groups. Option D (CORRECT): “Use AWS Application Auto Scaling with target tracking policies to scale when ECS metric breaches trigger an Amazon CloudWatch alarm.” • AWS Application Auto Scaling is the built-in service for scaling ECS (including Fargate) services. • Target tracking policies let you specify a desired CPU or memory utilization percentage and automatically add or remove tasks to maintain that target. • This serverless scaling model ensures you run just enough Fargate tasks to meet demand—optimizing performance and cost. In summary, we learned that for ECS on Fargate you should use AWS Application Auto Scaling with target tracking to automatically adjust the number of tasks based on resource utilization. This question belongs to Domain 4 – Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company hosts a frontend application that uses an Amazon API Gateway API backend that is integrated with AWS Lambda. When the API receives requests, the Lambda function loads many libraries. Then the Lambda function connects to an Amazon RDS database, processes the data, and returns the data to the frontend application. The company wants to ensure that response latency is as low as possible for all its users with the fewest number of changes to the company's operations.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Establish a connection between the frontend application and the database to make queries faster by bypassing the API.
Configure provisioned concurrency for the Lambda function that handles the requests.
Cache the results of the queries in Amazon S3 for faster retrieval of similar datasets.
Increase the size of the database to increase the number of connections Lambda can establish at one time.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): Bypassing API Gateway and Lambda to hit the database directly: Breaks the existing architecture and security boundary provided by API Gateway. Exposes your RDS publicly or requires managing additional credentials and VPC-to-internet configurations. Does not address Lambda cold-start latency or library-loading overhead. Option C (INCORRECT): “Cache the results of the queries in Amazon S3” is not optimal because: Amazon S3 has higher retrieval latency than in-memory caches or pre-warmed functions. S3 is object storage, not a real-time query cache—you’d need to build your own indexing and invalidation logic. Complexity and latency of fetching from S3 can exceed the original Lambda cold-start plus RDS query time. Option D (INCORRECT): “Increase the size of the database to support more connections” misses the mark because: Scaling your RDS instance only affects throughput and connection limits, not Lambda cold-start delays. Does nothing to reduce the latency caused by loading large libraries or initializing the function. Introduces cost and operational overhead without solving the primary latency issue. Option B (CORRECT): “Configure provisioned concurrency for the Lambda function” is the right choice: Provisioned Concurrency keeps function instances initialized and libraries loaded, eliminating cold starts. Ensures consistent, low-latency responses for all users with minimal operational changes. Requires only a configuration change in Lambda—no new services or architectural overhaul. In summary, we learned that to minimize response latency—especially cold-start overhead when loading libraries and connecting to RDS—you should use Lambda Provisioned Concurrency. This question falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company uses 50 TB of data for reporting. The company wants to move this data from on premises to AWS. A custom application in the company’s data center runs a weekly data transformation job. The company plans to pause the application until the data transfer is complete and needs to begin the transfer process as soon as possible. The data center does not have any available network bandwidth for additional workloads. A solutions architect must transfer the data and must configure the transformation job to continue to run in the AWS Cloud. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Use AWS DataSync to move the data. Create a custom transformation job by using AWS Glue.
Order an AWS Snowcone device to move the data. Deploy the transformation application to the device.
Order an AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device. Copy the data to the device. Create a custom transformation job by using AWS Glue.
Order an AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device that includes Amazon EC2 compute. Copy the data to the device. Create a new EC2 instance on AWS to run the transformation application.
explanation: The correct answer is D. Option A (INCORRECT): Use AWS DataSync to move the data. DataSync requires available network bandwidth, but the data center has no spare bandwidth for this transfer. You cannot begin immediately without impacting existing workloads. Option B (INCORRECT): Order an AWS Snowcone device to move the data. Snowcone’s capacity (up to ~8 TB) is far below the 50 TB requirement. It cannot hold all of the data, so multiple shipments would be needed—adding complexity and delay. Option C (INCORRECT): Order an AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device. Copy the data to the device. Create a custom transformation job by using AWS Glue. Snowball Edge Storage Optimized (≈80 TB) can transfer the data, but using AWS Glue requires rewriting your existing application into ETL jobs. This refactoring adds considerable operational and development overhead compared to simply running your current application. Option D (CORRECT): Order an AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device that includes Amazon EC2 compute. Copy the data to the device. Create a new EC2 instance on AWS to run the transformation application. Snowball Edge Storage Optimized handles the full 50 TB offline transfer without using on-premises network bandwidth. You can immediately spin up an EC2 instance in AWS and deploy your existing transformation application—no refactoring into another service needed. This approach minimizes operational overhead while meeting the requirement to run the transformation job in the AWS Cloud. In summary, we learned how to choose the right Snowball device for large-scale data migration when bandwidth is constrained, and how to minimize operational overhead by leveraging EC2 for existing applications. This question belongs to Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: The customers of a finance company request appointments with financial advisors by sending text messages. A web application that runs on Amazon EC2 instances accepts the appointment requests. The text messages are published to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue through the web application. Another application that runs on EC2 instances then sends meeting invitations and meeting confirmation email messages to the customers. After successful scheduling, this application stores the meeting information in an Amazon DynamoDB database. As the company expands, customers report that their meeting invitations are taking longer to arrive. What should a solutions architect recommend to resolve this issue?
options: Add a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster in front of the DynamoDB database.
Add an Amazon API Gateway API in front of the web application that accepts the appointment requests.
Add an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Set the origin as the web application that accepts the appointment requests.
Add an Auto Scaling group for the application that sends meeting invitations. Configure the Auto Scaling group to scale based on the depth of the SQS queue.
explanation: The correct answer is D. Option A (INCORRECT): Adding a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster improves read performance from DynamoDB, but the slowdown is in processing and sending meeting invitations (the consumer application), not in reading from the database. Caching reads won’t speed up the invitation workflow. Option B (INCORRECT): Placing Amazon API Gateway in front of the web application does not address the bottleneck. API Gateway adds a managed API layer, but the delay is happening downstream when processing SQS messages and sending invitations, not at request ingestion. Option C (INCORRECT): An Amazon CloudFront distribution is for caching and delivering static or dynamic HTTP content closer to users. It won’t accelerate the backend processing of SQS messages or the sending of emails and invites. Option D (CORRECT): By placing the invitation-sending application in an Auto Scaling group that scales based on the depth of the SQS queue, you ensure that as more messages queue up, additional EC2 instances come online to process them. This directly addresses the increasing latency in sending meeting invitations. In summary, we learned that when a queue-based workload experiences growing delays, the correct solution is to scale the consumers automatically according to the queue depth. This question belongs to Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company hosts an application on Amazon EC2 instances that run in a single Availability Zone. The application is accessible by using the transport layer of the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model. The company needs the application architecture to have high availability.Which combination of steps will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively? (Choose two.)
options: Configure new EC2 instances in a different Availability Zone. Use Amazon Route 53 to route traffic to all instances.
Configure a Network Load Balancer in front of the EC2 instances.
Configure a Network Load Balancer for TCP traffic to the instances. Configure an Application Load Balancer for HTTP and HTTPS traffic to the instances.

Create an Auto Scaling group for the EC2 instances. Configure the Auto Scaling group to use multiple Availability Zones. Configure the Auto Scaling group to run application health checks on the instances.
Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm. Configure the alarm to restart EC2 instances that transition to a stopped state.
explanation: The correct answer is B, D. Option A (INCORRECT): “Configure new EC2 instances in a different Availability Zone. Use Amazon Route 53 to route traffic to all instances.” Using Route 53 alone means DNS-based routing; it cannot perform fine‐grained transport-layer health checks or real-time failover as effectively as an NLB. Route 53 DNS records are cached by clients, which adds latency to failover and does not guarantee session-sticky TCP connections. This approach does not automatically replace unhealthy instances or scale based on demand. Option C (INCORRECT): “Configure a Network Load Balancer for TCP traffic to the instances. Configure an Application Load Balancer for HTTP and HTTPS traffic to the instances.” This solution adds unnecessary cost and complexity by running two load balancers when only TCP-level access is required. An ALB works at layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) and offers no benefit if the application uses only TCP. Option E (INCORRECT): “Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm. Configure the alarm to restart EC2 instances that transition to a stopped state.” Restarting a stopped instance does not protect against AZ failures or system faults—it is a reactive manual step. It does not provide true high availability across multiple AZs or automatic replacement of unhealthy instances. Option B (CORRECT): “Configure a Network Load Balancer in front of the EC2 instances.” Network Load Balancer (NLB) operates at transport layer (TCP/UDP) and can distribute TCP traffic across multiple targets. NLB supports cross-zone load balancing and health checks to detect and remove unhealthy instances automatically. It is cost-effective for non-HTTP workloads and scales automatically with traffic. Option D (CORRECT): “Create an Auto Scaling group for the EC2 instances. Configure the Auto Scaling group to use multiple Availability Zones. Configure the Auto Scaling group to run application health checks on the instances.” An Auto Scaling group spread across multiple AZs ensures high availability and fault tolerance. ASG health checks replace unhealthy instances automatically, maintaining the desired capacity. It provides automatic scaling in or out based on demand, which is cost-optimized and resilient. In summary, by combining an NLB (Option B) with an Auto Scaling group across multiple AZs (Option D), you achieve a highly available, fault‐tolerant, and cost-effective architecture for TCP-based applications. This question belongs to Domain 2 – Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A media company uses an Amazon CloudFront distribution to deliver content over the internet. The company wants only premium customers to have access to the media streams and file content. The company stores all content in an Amazon S3 bucket. The company also delivers content on demand to customers for a specific purpose, such as movie rentals or music downloads.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Generate and provide S3 signed cookies to premium customers.
Generate and provide CloudFront signed URLs to premium customers.
Use origin access control (OAC) to limit the access of non-premium customers.
Generate and activate field-level encryption to block non-premium customers.
explanation: The correct Answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): Generate and provide S3 signed cookies to premium customers. S3 signed cookies are used to grant time-limited access directly to S3 objects, bypassing CloudFront. When you deliver through CloudFront, you should use CloudFront signed cookies or signed URLs, not S3 cookies. This option wouldn’t leverage CloudFront’s edge caching or georestriction features for premium users. Option C (INCORRECT): Use origin access control (OAC) to limit the access of non-premium customers. Origin Access Control (OAC) secures CloudFront → S3 communication by preventing direct S3 URL access, but it does not differentiate between premium and non-premium users. OAC ensures that only CloudFront can fetch from the bucket, not end-user authentication or authorization. It does not provide per-user, time-limited access to media content. Option D (INCORRECT): Generate and activate field-level encryption to block non-premium customers. Field-level encryption protects specific data fields in POST requests from untrusted intermediaries; it’s not an access-control mechanism for content distribution. It does not issue credentials or URLs to end users, nor enforce time-based or user-based access to media streams. Therefore, it cannot restrict content delivery to premium customers. Option B (CORRECT): Generate and provide CloudFront signed URLs to premium customers. CloudFront signed URLs allow you to grant time-limited, per-user access to specific objects distributed via your CloudFront distribution. By generating a signed URL for each rental or download, you ensure only premium customers can fetch the media during the allowed time window. Signed URLs integrate seamlessly with S3 origins and CloudFront origin access identities (or OAC) to keep your bucket private. In summary, controlling on-demand access for premium users is best achieved with CloudFront signed URLs, which provide secure, time-bounded links to your S3-backed content. This question falls under Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures, as it focuses on restricting and securing content delivery.

question: A company uses Amazon S3 as its data lake. The company has a new partner that must use SFTP to upload data files. A solutions architect needs to implement a highly available SFTP solution that minimizes operational overhead. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Use AWS Transfer Family to configure an SFTP-enabled server with a publicly accessible endpoint. Choose the S3 data lake as the destination.
Use Amazon S3 File Gateway as an SFTP server. Expose the S3 File Gateway endpoint URL to the new partner. Share the S3 File Gateway endpoint with the new partner.

Launch an Amazon EC2 instance in a private subnet in a VPInstruct the new partner to upload files to the EC2 instance by using a VPN. Run a cron job script, on the EC2 instance to upload files to the S3 data lake.

Launch Amazon EC2 instances in a private subnet in a VPC. Place a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in front of the EC2 instances. Create an SFTP listener port for the NLB. Share the NLB hostname with the new partner. Run a cron job script on the EC2 instances to upload files to the S3 data lake.
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon S3 File Gateway as an SFTP server.” S3 File Gateway provides NFS/SMB access to S3, not an SFTP interface. It cannot natively speak the SFTP protocol, so the partner cannot upload over SFTP directly. Therefore, it does not meet the requirement for an SFTP endpoint. Option C (INCORRECT): “Launch an EC2 instance in a private subnet and use a VPN plus a cron job.” This approach requires building and maintaining the VPN infrastructure. The EC2 instance is a single point of failure unless you architect for high availability yourself. Operational overhead is high due to server maintenance, patching, and custom scripting. Option D (INCORRECT): “Deploy EC2 instances behind an NLB with an SFTP listener and cron jobs.” You must manage EC2 fleet scaling, patching, and availability across AZs. Building SFTP on EC2 and tying it to an NLB adds complexity and operational burden. It does not minimize operational overhead compared to a managed service. Option A (CORRECT): “Use AWS Transfer Family to configure a fully managed SFTP server with a public endpoint and point it directly at the S3 data lake.” AWS Transfer Family is a fully managed service that provides SFTP, FTPS, and FTP endpoints. It automatically scales across multiple Availability Zones for high availability. No EC2 management or custom scripting is needed, minimizing operational overhead. It integrates directly with S3, so uploaded files land in the data lake instantly. In summary, we learned that AWS Transfer Family is the best choice for a highly available, managed SFTP solution with minimal operational overhead. This question falls under Domain 2 - Design Resilient Architectures, as it focuses on achieving high availability and resilience.

question: A company uses AWS Organizations to manage multiple AWS accounts for different departments. The management account has an Amazon S3 bucket that contains project reports. The company wants to limit access to this S3 bucket to only users of accounts within the organization in AWS Organizations. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST amount of operational overhead?
options: Add the aws PrincipalOrgID global condition key with a reference to the organization ID to the S3 bucket policy.
Create an organizational unit (OU) for each department. Add the aws:PrincipalOrgPaths global condition key to the S3 bucket policy.
Use AWS CloudTrail to monitor the CreateAccount, InviteAccountToOrganization, LeaveOrganization, and RemoveAccountFromOrganization events. Update the S3 bucket policy accordingly.
Tag each user that needs access to the S3 bucket. Add the aws:PrincipalTag global condition key to the S3 bucket policy.
explanation: The correct answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): “Create an organizational unit (OU) for each department. Add the aws:PrincipalOrgPaths global condition key to the S3 bucket policy.” The aws:PrincipalOrgPaths condition key evaluates the full path of the principal in the organization and is intended for more granular OU-level control, not just membership. Defining and maintaining separate OUs for every department adds extra operational overhead, which is not required for a simple “organization-wide” restriction. Option C (INCORRECT): “Use AWS CloudTrail to monitor the CreateAccount, InviteAccountToOrganization, LeaveOrganization, and RemoveAccountFromOrganization events. Update the S3 bucket policy accordingly.” CloudTrail can audit account changes, but reacting to events by updating the bucket policy is manual and error-prone. This approach introduces significant operational overhead and lag between account changes and policy updates. Option D (INCORRECT): “Tag each user that needs access to the S3 bucket. Add the aws:PrincipalTag global condition key to the S3 bucket policy.” Tagging every user individually and maintaining those tags is high maintenance. This does not automatically cover all new or removed accounts in the organization—tags must be managed constantly. Option A (CORRECT): “Add the aws:PrincipalOrgID global condition key with a reference to the organization ID to the S3 bucket policy.” The aws:PrincipalOrgID condition key restricts access to principals that belong to the specified AWS Organization. This requires a one-time policy configuration and automatically covers all current and future accounts in the organization, minimizing operational overhead. From this discussion, we learned how to use AWS Organizations global condition keys—specifically aws:PrincipalOrgID—to centrally restrict S3 bucket access to an entire organization with minimal ongoing maintenance. This question falls under Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company recently signed a contract with an AWS Managed Service Provider (MSP) Partner for help with an application migration initiative. A solutions architect needs ta share an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) from an existing AWS account with the MSP Partner's AWS account. The AMI is backed by Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) and uses an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key to encrypt EBS volume snapshots. What is the MOST secure way for the solutions architect to share the AMI with the MSP Partner's AWS account?
options: Make the encrypted AMI and snapshots publicly available. Modify the key policy to allow the MSP Partner's AWS account to use the key.
Modify the launchPermission property of the AMI. Share the AMI with the MSP Partner's AWS account only. Modify the key policy to allow the MSP Partner's AWS account to use the key.
Modify the launchPermission property of the AMI. Share the AMI with the MSP Partner's AWS account only. Modify the key policy to trust a new KMS key that is owned by the MSP Partner for encryption.

Export the AMI from the source account to an Amazon S3 bucket in the MSP Partner's AWS account, Encrypt the S3 bucket with a new KMS key that is owned by the MSP Partner. Copy and launch the AMI in the MSP Partner's AWS account.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): Making the AMI and its snapshots publicly available exposes your proprietary data and configuration to anyone on AWS, violating the principle of least privilege. Even if you modify the KMS key policy, public access undermines the security boundary you need for controlled sharing. Option C (INCORRECT): You cannot simply “trust” another KMS key to decrypt or re-encrypt snapshots owned by your customer-managed key. AWS does not automatically re-encrypt EBS snapshots with a third-party key without an explicit copy operation. This approach would fail because the snapshots remain encrypted under your original CMK, not the partner’s key. Option D (INCORRECT): Exporting the AMI to Amazon S3 and re-importing it is an overly complex workaround that isn’t necessary for cross-account AMI sharing. Snapshot export/import works only for certain virtualization types and adds operational overhead, while direct AMI sharing with proper KMS permissions is simpler and more secure. Option B (CORRECT): Use modify-image-attribute --launch-permission to share the AMI privately with the MSP Partner’s AWS account. Adjust your customer-managed KMS key policy to grant the MSP Partner’s account kms:Decrypt (and related) permissions on the key that encrypts your EBS snapshots. This maintains strict access control, follows the principle of least privilege, and avoids making your AMI public or performing unnecessary export/import steps. In summary, we learned how to securely share an EBS-backed, KMS-encrypted AMI across AWS accounts by combining AMI launch permissions with precise KMS key policy grants. This question belongs to Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company runs its production workload on Amazon EC2 instances with Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes. A solutions architect needs to analyze the current EBS volume cost and to recommend optimizations. The recommendations need to include estimated monthly saving opportunities.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Use Amazon Inspector reporting to generate EBS volume recommendations for optimization.
Use AWS Systems Manager reporting to determine EBS volume recommendations for optimization.
Use Amazon CloudWatch metrics reporting to determine EBS volume recommendations for optimization.
Use AWS Compute Optimizer to generate EBS volume recommendations for optimization.
explanation: The correct answer is D Option A (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon Inspector reporting to generate EBS volume recommendations for optimization.” Amazon Inspector is a security assessment service—it identifies vulnerabilities and deviations from best practices in your EC2 instances and container images, not cost-related configurations of EBS volumes. It cannot estimate monthly savings or provide right-sizing suggestions for storage volumes. Option B (INCORRECT): “Use AWS Systems Manager reporting to determine EBS volume recommendations for optimization.” AWS Systems Manager Inventory can collect metadata about EBS volumes (tags, attachments), and Run Command can automate tasks, but it does not analyze volume utilization patterns or estimate cost savings. There is no built-in cost-optimization recommendation engine for EBS in Systems Manager. Option C (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon CloudWatch metrics reporting to determine EBS volume recommendations for optimization.” CloudWatch can show metrics like VolumeReadOps, VolumeWriteOps, and VolumeIdleTime, but it won’t translate those into storage-type or size recommendations. You would need to manually interpret metrics and calculate savings; there’s no automated monthly savings estimate. Option D (CORRECT): “Use AWS Compute Optimizer to generate EBS volume recommendations for optimization.” AWS Compute Optimizer analyzes historical utilization data for your EBS volumes and provides right-sizing recommendations (e.g., downsizing volume types, changing to Provisioned IOPS SSD, etc.). It includes estimated monthly savings for each recommendation, making it ideal for cost-optimization exercises. Compute Optimizer supports both EC2 instance and EBS volume recommendations, delivering a consolidated view of optimization opportunities. In this discussion, we learned how to identify the appropriate AWS service for analyzing EBS volume usage and generating cost-saving recommendations. This question falls under Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company is migrating a three-tier application to AWS. The application requires a MySQL database. In the past, the application users reported poor application performance when creating new entries. These performance issues were caused by users generating different real-time reports from the application during working hours.Which solution will improve the performance of the application when it is moved to AWS?
options: Import the data into an Amazon DynamoDB table with provisioned capacity. Refactor the application to use DynamoDB for reports.
Create the database on a compute optimized Amazon EC2 instance. Ensure compute resources exceed the on-premises database.
Create an Amazon Aurora MySQL Multi-AZ DB cluster with multiple read replicas. Configure the application to use the reader endpoint for reports.
Create an Amazon Aurora MySQL Multi-AZ DB cluster. Configure the application to use the backup instance of the cluster as an endpoint for the reports.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): Importing the data into DynamoDB and refactoring the application for reports is a major architectural change. The application already uses MySQL, and moving only reporting workloads to DynamoDB adds complexity and data‐synchronization overhead. It’s not necessary to introduce a NoSQL store just to offload reads. Option B (INCORRECT): Running MySQL on a compute-optimized EC2 instance merely ups the CPU capacity but does not address read-scaling or workload isolation. Real-time reporting queries will still compete with transactional writes on the single database, so performance issues can persist. Option D (INCORRECT): Aurora’s “backup instance” (the standby in a Multi-AZ configuration) is not accessible for reads. It exists solely for high availability and failover, not for offloading read traffic. You cannot point reporting queries to the standby. Option C (CORRECT): Creating an Amazon Aurora MySQL Multi-AZ DB cluster with multiple read replicas and using the reader endpoint for reports offloads read traffic from the primary writer. This separation of transactional writes and analytical reads significantly improves performance. Aurora’s reader endpoint automatically load-balances queries across replicas and provides near-real-time data, making it the optimal choice for scaling read-heavy workloads. In summary, we learned that for read-intensive reporting workloads on a relational database, the best practice is to offload reads to read replicas rather than over-provisioning a single instance or introducing an entirely new database engine. This question belongs to Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company is concerned that two NAT instances in use will no longer be able to support the traffic needed for the company’s application. A solutions architect wants to implement a solution that is highly available, fault tolerant, and automatically scalable. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Remove the two NAT instances and replace them with two NAT gateways in the same Availability Zone.
Use Auto Scaling groups with Network Load Balancers for the NAT instances in different Availability Zones.
Remove the two NAT instances and replace them with two NAT gateways in different Availability Zones.
Replace the two NAT instances with Spot Instances in different Availability Zones and deploy a Network Load Balancer.
explanation: The correct Answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): “Remove the two NAT instances and replace them with two NAT gateways in the same Availability Zone.” Deploying both NAT Gateways in the same AZ creates a single point of failure—if that AZ fails, connectivity for all private subnets is lost. A highly available design requires NAT Gateways in multiple AZs so that traffic can fail over if one AZ goes down. Option B (INCORRECT): “Use Auto Scaling groups with Network Load Balancers for the NAT instances in different Availability Zones.” Managing your own NAT instances adds operational overhead (OS patching, scaling policies) versus using a managed service. You cannot easily place NAT instances behind an NLB for private-subnet egress—the routing and health-check mechanisms become complex and error-prone. NAT Gateways auto-scale and are fully managed, eliminating the need to build your own Auto Scaling solution. Option D (INCORRECT): “Replace the two NAT instances with Spot Instances in different Availability Zones and deploy a Network Load Balancer.” Spot Instances can be reclaimed by AWS at any time, making them unsuitable for reliable egress (NAT) traffic handling. Combining Spot Instances with an NLB does not guarantee uninterrupted connectivity, nor does it simplify maintenance compared to NAT Gateways. Option C (CORRECT): “Remove the two NAT instances and replace them with two NAT gateways in different Availability Zones.” NAT Gateways are a fully managed AWS service that automatically scale to accommodate bursts in traffic without any instance management. Deploying one NAT Gateway per AZ ensures high availability and fault tolerance—if one AZ becomes unreachable, private subnets in other AZs still have egress access. This design is both simple to operate (no OS/patching) and performant, meeting the requirement for automatic scalability. In summary, we learned that AWS NAT Gateways provide a resilient, fully managed, and auto-scaling solution for outbound internet access. By placing NAT Gateways in multiple Availability Zones, you achieve fault tolerance and high availability without the operational complexity of managing instances. This question falls under Domain 2 - Design Resilient Architectures, as it focuses on ensuring availability and fault-tolerance for network egress.

question: A company has an ordering application that stores customer information in Amazon RDS for MySQL. During regular business hours, employees run one-time queries for reporting purposes. Timeouts are occurring during order processing because the reporting queries are taking a long time to run. The company needs to eliminate the timeouts without preventing employees from performing queries.What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
options: Create a read replica. Move reporting queries to the read replica.
Create a read replica. Distribute the ordering application to the primary DB instance and the read replica.
Migrate the ordering application to Amazon DynamoDB with on-demand capacity.
Schedule the reporting queries for non-peak hours.
explanation: The correct answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): “Create a read replica. Distribute the ordering application to the primary DB instance and the read replica.” You cannot run write operations (order processing) on a read replica—replicas are read‐only. Distributing the ordering application across both instances would break transactional consistency for order writes. Option C (INCORRECT): “Migrate the ordering application to Amazon DynamoDB with on-demand capacity.” This is a disruptive migration; not required just to separate reporting workloads. DynamoDB isn’t needed for one-time reporting queries against an existing MySQL schema. Option D (INCORRECT): “Schedule the reporting queries for non-peak hours.” This approach delays reporting and doesn’t meet the requirement of allowing employees to query during business hours. It’s a workaround rather than a scalable solution to eliminate timeouts in real time. Option A (CORRECT): “Create a read replica. Move reporting queries to the read replica.” Offloads heavy, long-running read queries to a replica so the primary handles transactional writes without contention. Eliminates timeouts on the primary during business hours while still allowing employees to run ad-hoc reports. Is simple to implement with Amazon RDS MySQL read replicas and maintains replication lag within seconds. In summary, we learned that offloading read-intensive reporting queries to an RDS read replica eliminates timeouts and keeps the primary instance focused on transactional workloads. This question falls under Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company recently launched a new application for its customers. The application runs on multiple Amazon EC2 instances across two Availability Zones. End users use TCP to communicate with the application. The application must be highly available and must automatically scale as the number of users increases. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively? (Choose two.)
options: Add a Network Load Balancer in front of the EC2 instances.
Configure an Auto Scaling group for the EC2 instances.
Add an Application Load Balancer in front of the EC2 instances.
Manually add more EC2 instances for the application.
Add a Gateway Load Balancer in front of the EC2 instances.
explanation: The correct answer is A, B Option C (INCORRECT): An Application Load Balancer operates at Layer 7 and supports HTTP/HTTPS, WebSocket and gRPC protocols. It does not handle raw TCP traffic, so it cannot be used for this TCP‐based application. Option D (INCORRECT): Manually adding more EC2 instances does not provide automatic scaling and is operationally intensive. It cannot respond dynamically to changing traffic patterns and is not cost-effective. Option E (INCORRECT): A Gateway Load Balancer is designed for deploying, scaling, and managing third-party virtual appliances (firewalls, intrusion detection systems, etc.). It is not intended for general application load-balancing or auto-scaling of EC2 instances. Option A (CORRECT): Add a Network Load Balancer in front of the EC2 instances. Operates at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP) and is ideal for raw TCP traffic. Provides cross-AZ high availability and handles millions of requests per second with ultra-low latency. Cost-effective for high-throughput, non-HTTP workloads. Option B (CORRECT): Configure an Auto Scaling group for the EC2 instances. Automatically scales the number of instances in response to demand (e.g., CPU, network). Maintains application availability by replacing unhealthy instances and distributing across AZs. Optimizes costs by running only the required capacity at any given time. In summary, combining a Network Load Balancer with an Auto Scaling group ensures the TCP-based application is highly available, scales automatically, and remains cost-efficient. This question falls under Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company wants to direct its users to a backup static error page if the company's primary website is unavailable. The primary website's DNS records are hosted in Amazon Route 53. The domain is pointing to an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The company needs a solution that minimizes changes and infrastructure overhead.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Update the Route 53 records to use a latency routing policy. Add a static error page that is hosted in an Amazon S3 bucket to the records so that the traffic is sent to the most responsive endpoints.

Set up a Route 53 active-passive failover configuration. Direct traffic to a static error page that is hosted in an Amazon S3 bucket when Route 53 health checks determine that the ALB endpoint is unhealthy.

Set up a Route 53 active-active configuration with the ALB and an Amazon EC2 instance that hosts a static error page as endpoints. Configure Route 53 to send requests to the instance only if the health checks fail for the ALB.

Update the Route 53 records to use a multivalue answer routing policy. Create a health check. Direct traffic to the website if the health check passes. Direct traffic to a static error page that is hosted in Amazon S3 if the health check does not pass.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): Latency routing policy directs traffic based on latency, not availability. You cannot simply add an S3-hosted static error page as a latency endpoint for the ALB. This solution does not perform failover when the primary ALB is down. Option C (INCORRECT): Active-active with an EC2 instance introduces unnecessary server management and cost. Overhead of running and monitoring an EC2 just for an error page is higher than using S3. Failover routing (active-passive) is simpler and more appropriate for a backup error page. Option D (INCORRECT): Multi-value answer routing is meant for DNS-level load distribution, not true failover. It returns multiple healthy records rather than switching entirely to a backup. Complex to configure for a single static error page compared to Route 53 failover. Option B (CORRECT): Uses Route 53 active-passive failover routing: primary alias to the ALB, secondary alias to an S3 static website. Attach a health check to the ALB record—when it fails, Route 53 automatically routes to the S3 error page. Requires minimal changes and no extra servers, leveraging S3 for the static error page. In summary, we learned that for simple failover to a static error page with minimal infrastructure, Route 53 active-passive failover is the ideal solution. This question belongs to Domain 2 - Design Resilient Architectures, as it focuses on ensuring high availability and automatic failover.

question: A media company is evaluating the possibility of moving its systems to the AWS Cloud. The company needs at least 10 TB of storage with the maximum possible I/O performance for video processing, 300 TB of very durable storage for storing media content, and 900 TB of storage to meet requirements for archival media that is not in use anymore.Which set of services should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?
options: Amazon EBS for maximum performance, Amazon S3 for durable data storage, and Amazon S3 Glacier for archival storage
Amazon EBS for maximum performance, Amazon EFS for durable data storage, and Amazon S3 Glacier for archival storage
Amazon EC2 instance store for maximum performance, Amazon EFS for durable data storage, and Amazon S3 for archival storage
Amazon EC2 instance store for maximum performance, Amazon S3 for durable data storage, and Amazon S3 Glacier for archival storage
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): Uses Amazon EFS for the 300 TB of durable storage, but EFS is a POSIX‐compliant filesystem service and is significantly more expensive than Amazon S3 for large‐scale object storage. EFS is optimized for shared file access rather than as a cost‐effective, highly durable object store for media content. Option C (INCORRECT): Relies on EC2 instance store for the 10 TB scratch space. Instance store is ephemeral—data is lost if the instance stops or fails—so it’s not suitable unless you replicate or back up constantly. Chooses Amazon S3 (standard) for the 900 TB archival tier, but standard S3 is not a true archival class; you’d incur higher storage costs compared to S3 Glacier or Glacier Deep Archive. Option D (INCORRECT): Again uses EC2 instance store for the 10 TB scratch volume—it cannot guarantee persistence or the required capacity across instance types. While it picks S3 and S3 Glacier for durable and archival, the scratch‐disk choice remains flawed. Option A (CORRECT): Amazon EBS: Provides the highest I/O performance volumes (e.g., gp3 or io2) and can easily scale to ≥10 TB for video processing scratch storage. Amazon S3 Standard: Delivers 99.999999999% durability for 300 TB of frequently accessed media content at a cost‐effective rate. Amazon S3 Glacier: Offers low‐cost, highly durable archival storage for 900 TB of media that is infrequently accessed. In summary, we learned how to match AWS storage services to workload requirements—high-performance scratch (EBS), durable object storage (S3 Standard), and cost-optimized archival (S3 Glacier). This scenario falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company wants to monitor its AWS costs for financial review. The cloud operations team is designing an architecture in the AWS Organizations management account to query AWS Cost and Usage Reports for all member accounts. The team must run this query once a month and provide a detailed analysis of the bill.Which solution is the MOST scalable and cost-effective way to meet these requirements?
options: Enable Cost and Usage Reports in the management account. Deliver reports to Amazon Kinesis. Use Amazon EMR for analysis.
Enable Cost and Usage Reports in the management account. Deliver the reports to Amazon S3 Use Amazon Athena for analysis.
Enable Cost and Usage Reports for member accounts. Deliver the reports to Amazon S3 Use Amazon Redshift for analysis.
Enable Cost and Usage Reports for member accounts. Deliver the reports to Amazon Kinesis. Use Amazon QuickSight tor analysis.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Let’s step through why Option A, Option C, and Option D are not correct, and why Option B is the right choice: Option A (INCORRECT): Delivers Cost and Usage Reports into Amazon Kinesis, which is intended for streaming data, not bulk monthly report files. Requires running an Amazon EMR cluster for analysis—this adds provisioning overhead and ongoing cost even though queries run only once a month. Overkill for static, monthly billing data; not the most cost-effective or simplest architecture. Option C (INCORRECT): Enables Cost and Usage Reports per member account, leading to multiple report files and extra management complexity. Loads data into Amazon Redshift, which requires cluster provisioning, vacuuming, resizing, and continuous costs regardless of query frequency. Less scalable and more expensive compared to a serverless, pay-per-query solution. Option D (INCORRECT): Again splits reports per member account and uses Amazon Kinesis—unsuited for batch monthly data delivery. Using QuickSight directly on a Kinesis stream is not a standard pattern for Cost and Usage reports; QuickSight is also licensed per user or capacity, adding cost. Introduces unnecessary streaming infrastructure and BI licensing costs for a simple monthly analysis. Option B (CORRECT): Centralizes Cost and Usage Reports in the AWS Organizations management account and delivers them to an S3 bucket. Uses Amazon Athena, a serverless, pay-per-query service that spins up resources on demand—no provisioned infrastructure to manage. Highly scalable for any data volume and very cost-effective for infrequent, ad hoc or scheduled monthly queries. In summary, using a single, centralized Cost and Usage Report delivered to S3 combined with Amazon Athena provides the most scalable and cost-optimized solution for monthly billing analysis. This question belongs to Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company wants to migrate two DNS servers to AWS. The servers host a total of approximately 200 zones and receive 1 million requests each day on average. The company wants to maximize availability while minimizing the operational overhead that is related to the management of the two servers. What should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?
options: Create 200 new hosted zones in the Amazon Route 53 console Import zone files.
Launch a single large Amazon EC2 instance Import zone tiles. Configure Amazon CloudWatch alarms and notifications to alert the company about any downtime.
Migrate the servers to AWS by using AWS Server Migration Service (AWS SMS). Configure Amazon CloudWatch alarms and notifications to alert the company about any downtime.

Launch an Amazon EC2 instance in an Auto Scaling group across two Availability Zones. Import zone files. Set the desired capacity to 1 and the maximum capacity to 3 for the Auto Scaling group. Configure scaling alarms to scale based on CPU utilization.
explanation: The correct answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): Launching a single large EC2 instance and importing zone files still leaves you with a single point of failure. Even with CloudWatch alarms, you must manage OS updates, patching, scaling, and worry about instance health. This does not minimize operational overhead nor maximize availability. Option C (INCORRECT): AWS Server Migration Service is for lift-and-shift of on-premises servers to EC2. You would still be running and managing DNS software on EC2 instances (with all associated maintenance), so operational overhead remains high and you’re not leveraging a managed DNS service. Option D (INCORRECT): An Auto Scaling group across AZs improves availability, but you still manage EC2 instances, DNS software, patching, scaling policies (CPU-based alarms don’t necessarily reflect DNS query load), and failover. This solution is more complex and has higher operational overhead than a managed service. Option A (CORRECT): Creating 200 hosted zones in Amazon Route 53 and importing your zone files gives you a fully managed, highly available, and globally distributed DNS service. You no longer manage servers or worry about scaling; Route 53 automatically handles query volume, redundancy, and health checks, minimizing operational overhead while maximizing availability. Summary: By migrating your DNS hosting to Amazon Route 53, you offload server management and gain built-in high availability and scalability. This question belongs to Domain 2 – Design Resilient Architectures, as it focuses on maximizing availability and reducing operational complexity.

question: A company uses Amazon RDS with default backup settings for its database tier. The company needs to make a daily backup of the database to meet regulatory requirements. The company must retain the backups for 30 days.Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Write an AWS Lambda function to create an RDS snapshot every day.
Modify the RDS database to have a retention period of 30 days for automated backups.
Use AWS Systems Manager Maintenance Windows to modify the RDS backup retention period.
Create a manual snapshot every day by using the AWS CLI. Modify the RDS backup retention period.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): Writing an AWS Lambda function to create an RDS snapshot every day adds unnecessary operational overhead (managing, monitoring, and error-handling the Lambda and its schedule) when RDS already provides automated daily backups. Option C (INCORRECT): Using AWS Systems Manager Maintenance Windows to modify the RDS backup retention period is overly complex. The retention setting is a native RDS parameter that can be adjusted directly, without involving Systems Manager. Option D (INCORRECT): Creating a manual snapshot every day via the AWS CLI still requires you to manage snapshot lifecycles (no built-in retention), which increases operational burden. Also, modifying the automated backup retention period separately is redundant if you’re relying on manual snapshots. Option B (CORRECT): By simply setting the RDS automated backup retention period to 30 days, Amazon RDS will automatically take daily backups and retain them for the required duration. This approach leverages built-in functionality, requires no additional scripts or manual tasks, and minimizes operational overhead. In summary, adjusting the RDS automated backup retention period is the easiest and most operationally efficient way to meet a 30-day daily backup requirement. This scenario falls under Domain 2 - Design Resilient Architectures, as it focuses on backup and recovery strategies.

question: A hospital is designing a new application that gathers symptoms from patients. The hospital has decided to use Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) and Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) in the architecture. A solutions architect is reviewing the infrastructure design. Data must be encrypted at rest and in transit. Only authorized personnel of the hospital should be able to access the data. Which combination of steps should the solutions architect take to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
options: Turn on server-side encryption on the SQS components. Update the default key policy to restrict key usage to a set of authorized principals.
Turn on server-side encryption on the SNS components by using an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key. Apply a key policy to restrict key usage to a set of authorized principals.

Turn on encryption on the SNS components. Update the default key policy to restrict key usage to a set of authorized principals. Set a condition in the topic policy to allow only encrypted connections over TLS.

Turn on server-side encryption on the SQS components by using an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key. Apply a key policy to restrict key usage to a set of authorized principals. Set a condition in the queue policy to allow only encrypted connections over TLS.

Turn on server-side encryption on the SQS components by using an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key. Apply an IAM policy to restrict key usage to a set of authorized principals. Set a condition in the queue policy to allow only encrypted connections over TLS.
explanation: The correct answer is C, D. Option A (INCORRECT): “Turn on server-side encryption on the SQS components. Update the default key policy to restrict key usage to a set of authorized principals.” Missing enforcement of encryption in transit (TLS) via a queue policy condition. You also need to specify using a customer-managed AWS KMS key to meet the requirement of controlling key usage. Option B (INCORRECT): “Turn on server-side encryption on the SNS components by using an AWS KMS customer managed key. Apply a key policy to restrict key usage to a set of authorized principals.” It secures data at rest but does not enforce encryption in transit (TLS) on the SNS topic. You must add a condition in the SNS topic policy (SecureTransport) to block non-TLS connections. Option E (INCORRECT): “Turn on server-side encryption on the SQS components by using an AWS KMS customer managed key. Apply an IAM policy to restrict key usage to a set of authorized principals. Set a condition in the queue policy to allow only encrypted connections over TLS.” Key restrictions should be managed in the KMS key policy (not only via IAM policies) to ensure only authorized principals can use the CMK. Best practice is to enforce both data-at-rest (SSE with customer-managed CMK) and in-transit (SecureTransport) via queue policy. Option C (CORRECT): “Turn on encryption on the SNS components. Update the default key policy to restrict key usage to a set of authorized principals. Set a condition in the topic policy to allow only encrypted connections over TLS.” Enables server-side encryption for SNS using a customer-managed AWS KMS key, ensuring data at rest is encrypted. Updates the KMS key policy to restrict encryption/decryption to authorized personnel. Enforces TLS (SecureTransport) in the SNS topic policy, ensuring data in transit is encrypted. Option D (CORRECT): “Turn on server-side encryption on the SQS components by using an AWS KMS customer managed key. Apply a key policy to restrict key usage to a set of authorized principals. Set a condition in the queue policy to allow only encrypted connections over TLS.” Applies SSE for SQS with a customer-managed CMK, encrypting messages at rest. KMS key policy restricts which IAM principals can use the key. Queue policy condition SecureTransport=true ensures only TLS-encrypted connections, satisfying in-transit encryption. In summary, we must secure both Amazon SNS and SQS by enabling server-side encryption with customer-managed KMS keys (and appropriate key policies) and enforce TLS-only traffic via resource policies. This question belongs to Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A social media company allows users to upload images to its website. The website runs on Amazon EC2 instances. During upload requests, the website resizes the images to a standard size and stores the resized images in Amazon S3. Users are experiencing slow upload requests to the website. The company needs to reduce coupling within the application and improve website performance. A solutions architect must design the most operationally efficient process for image uploads. Which combination of actions should the solutions architect take to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
options: Configure the application to upload images to S3 Glacier.
Configure the web server to upload the original images to Amazon S3.
Configure the application to upload images directly from each user's browser to Amazon S3 through the use of a presigned URL
Configure S3 Event Notifications to invoke an AWS Lambda function when an image is uploaded. Use the function to resize the image.
Create an Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) rule that invokes an AWS Lambda function on a schedule to resize uploaded images.
explanation: The correct answer is C, D. Option A (INCORRECT): “Configure the application to upload images to S3 Glacier.” S3 Glacier is designed for long-term, cold storage with retrieval delays of minutes to hours. It is not suitable for serving images or supporting real-time upload workflows. Option B (INCORRECT): “Configure the web server to upload the original images to Amazon S3.” Although this would offload storage from EC2, the web servers still handle upload and image resizing synchronously. It does not reduce coupling or significantly improve upload latency, because EC2 remains in the critical path. Option E (INCORRECT): “Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that invokes a Lambda function on a schedule to resize uploaded images.” Scheduled processing introduces unpredictable delays between upload and availability of resized images. Users would not get immediate feedback, and the system remains batch-oriented rather than event-driven. Option C (CORRECT): “Configure the application to upload images directly from each user's browser to Amazon S3 through the use of a presigned URL.” Offloads file transfer traffic from EC2 instances, reducing server load and improving upload performance. Decouples the web tier from the data storage tier, enhancing scalability and operational efficiency. Option D (CORRECT): “Configure S3 Event Notifications to invoke an AWS Lambda function when an image is uploaded. Use the function to resize the image.” Enables asynchronous, event-driven processing of images without impacting the user upload flow. Further decouples resizing logic from the web application, simplifying maintenance and scaling. Summary: By using presigned URLs (Option C) and S3 Event Notifications with Lambda (Option D), we decouple the upload and processing steps, dramatically reduce load on EC2, and deliver better upload performance. This question falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company is running an online transaction processing (OLTP) workload on AWS. This workload uses an unencrypted Amazon RDS DB instance in a Multi-AZ deployment. Daily database snapshots are taken from this instance.What should a solutions architect do to ensure the database and snapshots are always encrypted moving forward?
options: Encrypt a copy of the latest DB snapshot. Replace existing DB instance by restoring the encrypted snapshot.
Create a new encrypted Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume and copy the snapshots to it. Enable encryption on the DB instance.
Copy the snapshots and enable encryption using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) Restore encrypted snapshot to an existing DB instance.
Copy the snapshots to an Amazon S3 bucket that is encrypted using server-side encryption with AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) managed keys (SSE-KMS).
explanation: The Correct Answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): “Create a new encrypted Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume and copy the snapshots to it. Enable encryption on the DB instance.” You cannot convert or attach RDS snapshots to an EBS volume; snapshots are managed by the RDS service, not directly by EBS. Encryption must be enabled at the time of DB creation or via snapshot copy—there is no direct “enable encryption” toggle on an existing unencrypted RDS instance. Option C (INCORRECT): “Copy the snapshots and enable encryption using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS). Restore encrypted snapshot to an existing DB instance.” While you can copy an unencrypted snapshot and apply encryption via KMS, you cannot restore a snapshot into an existing DB instance—you must launch a new RDS instance from that snapshot. The wording “restore to an existing DB instance” is technically invalid in RDS workflows. Option D (INCORRECT): “Copy the snapshots to an Amazon S3 bucket that is encrypted using server-side encryption with AWS Key Management Service (SSE-KMS).” RDS snapshots aren’t directly stored in your own S3 bucket; AWS manages them behind the scenes. You can export snapshot data to S3 for analytics, but this does not change the encryption state of the RDS snapshot or the running DB instance. Option A (CORRECT): “Encrypt a copy of the latest DB snapshot. Replace existing DB instance by restoring the encrypted snapshot.” RDS does not allow enabling encryption on an existing unencrypted DB instance directly. Instead, you copy the latest unencrypted DB snapshot and specify a KMS key to encrypt the copy. You then restore the encrypted snapshot to spin up a new DB instance (Multi-AZ as before), and decommission the old unencrypted instance—ensuring all future snapshots and the running DB are encrypted. In summary, the only supported way to encrypt both the database and its snapshots moving forward is to copy your existing snapshot with encryption enabled and restore from that encrypted copy. This ensures encryption at rest for the new RDS instance and any snapshots taken thereafter. This question falls under Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures, as it deals with implementing encryption to safeguard data at rest.

question: A city has deployed a web application running on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The application's users have reported sporadic performance, which appears to be related to DDoS attacks originating from random IP addresses. The city needs a solution that requires minimal configuration changes and provides an audit trail for the DDoS sources.Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Enable an AWS WAF web ACL on the ALB, and configure rules to block traffic from unknown sources.
Subscribe to Amazon Inspector. Engage the AWS DDoS Response Team (DRT) to integrate mitigating controls into the service.
Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced. Engage the AWS DDoS Response Team (DRT) to integrate mitigating controls into the service.
Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution for the application, and set the ALB as the origin. Enable an AWS WAF web ACL on the distribution, and configure rules to block traffic from unknown sources
explanation: The correct answer is D. Option A (INCORRECT): “Enable an AWS WAF web ACL on the ALB, and configure rules to block traffic from unknown sources.” AWS WAF at the ALB operates at Layer 7 (HTTP/S) and helps block malicious requests, but it does not protect against large-scale Layer 3/4 DDoS floods. By itself, WAF on the ALB won’t mitigate transport-level DDoS events, and you’d need to enable and manage WAF logging separately for an audit trail. Option B (INCORRECT): “Subscribe to Amazon Inspector. Engage the AWS DDoS Response Team (DRT) to integrate mitigating controls into the service.” Amazon Inspector is a vulnerability assessment service, not a DDoS mitigation solution. Engaging the DDoS Response Team (DRT) requires AWS Shield Advanced, not Inspector. Option C (INCORRECT): “Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced. Engage the AWS DDoS Response Team (DRT) to integrate mitigating controls into the service.” Shield Advanced provides 24x7 DRT access and mitigates large-scale Layer 3/4 and some Layer 7 attacks, but it does not automatically give you a simple HTTP request audit trail—you must separately enable logs (e.g., VPC Flow Logs, WAF logs). Although powerful, this incurs additional cost and configuration beyond what the city requested (“minimal configuration changes”). Option D (CORRECT): “Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution for the application, and set the ALB as the origin. Enable an AWS WAF web ACL on the distribution, and configure rules to block traffic from unknown sources.” CloudFront includes built-in AWS Shield Standard protection at the edge, mitigating most Layer 3/4 DDoS attacks automatically—no extra subscription required. Adding WAF to the CloudFront distribution lets you block or rate-limit malicious HTTP/S traffic (Layer 7). CloudFront access logs (and WAF logs) can be enabled with minimal effort to record the source IPs and request details, providing a full audit trail of the attack traffic. This approach requires only spinning up a CloudFront distribution and attaching WAF, achieving DDoS mitigation and logging with minimal configuration changes. In summary, by fronting the ALB with Amazon CloudFront you leverage Shield Standard edge protection, add WAF rules for Layer 7 filtering, and capture CloudFront logs for auditing the malicious IPs. This solution meets the requirements with minimal changes. This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company wants to deploy its containerized application workloads to a VPC across three Availability Zones. The company needs a solution that is highly available across Availability Zones. The solution must require minimal changes to the application.Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
