Option C (INCORRECT): “Create an Amazon S3 bucket and an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Import the data into the S3 bucket. Copy the data from the S3 bucket to the EFS file system. Access the EFS file system from the HPC cluster instances.” Amazon EFS is a general-purpose NFS file system. Even in the Provisioned Throughput mode, its latencies are typically a few milliseconds. EFS cannot deliver sub-millisecond latency required by high-performance computing clusters. Throughput and IO operations per second are also lower compared to a parallel file system like Lustre. Option D (INCORRECT): “Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system. Import the data directly into the FSx for Lustre file system. Access the FSx for Lustre file system from the HPC cluster instances.” While FSx for Lustre is indeed a high-performance parallel file system with sub-millisecond latencies, importing 200 TB directly into Lustre without an S3 data repository integration is operationally complex. You lose the seamless data synchronization and lifecycle management that FSx for Lustre’s S3 integration provides. This option does not leverage AWS’s recommended pattern of linking S3 as the durable data repository. Option B (CORRECT): “Create an Amazon S3 bucket. Import the data into the S3 bucket. Configure an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system, and integrate it with the S3 bucket. Access the FSx for Lustre file system from the HPC cluster instances.” Amazon FSx for Lustre provides a high-performance parallel file system designed for HPC workloads, delivering consistent sub-millisecond latencies and massive throughput. The native integration with Amazon S3 allows you to import and export data seamlessly, keeping S3 as the durable repository while providing your cluster low-latency, high-throughput access. This pattern is AWS’s recommended solution for HPC data processing, ensuring you meet both latency and throughput requirements at scale. In summary, by integrating Amazon S3 with Amazon FSx for Lustre you achieve both sub-millisecond latency and high throughput for your AWS-hosted HPC cluster. This question belongs to Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A data analytics company has 80 offices that are distributed globally. Each office hosts 1 PB of data and has between 1 and 2 Gbps of internet bandwidth. The company needs to perform a one-time migration of a large amount of data from its offices to Amazon S3. The company must complete the migration within 4 weeks. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Establish a new 10 Gbps AWS Direct Connect connection to each office. Transfer the data to Amazon S3.
Use multiple AWS Snowball Edge storage-optimized devices to store and transfer the data to Amazon S3.
Use an AWS Snowmobile to store and transfer the data to Amazon S3.
Set up an AWS Storage Gateway Volume Gateway to transfer the data to Amazon S3.
explanation: The correct answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): Establishing a new 10 Gbps AWS Direct Connect link to each of the 80 offices would be extremely expensive and time-consuming. Physical Direct Connect circuits take weeks to provision and require onsite setup per location. Monthly port fees for 80 separate 10 Gbps connections would be very high, defeating the cost-optimization goal. Option C (INCORRECT): AWS Snowmobile is designed for exabyte-scale transfers (up to 100 PB+) via a truck-sized shipping container. One Snowmobile can carry ~45 PB, but it must physically drive to a single data center—not 80 global offices. Coordinating Snowmobile visits worldwide within four weeks is logistically impractical and overkill for 80 PB. Option D (INCORRECT): AWS Storage Gateway (Volume Gateway) continuously syncs data over the internet, but it is not optimized for a one-time bulk export of 1 PB per site. Limited by each office’s 1–2 Gbps bandwidth—transferring 1 PB would take many weeks or months. Storage Gateway caches blocks but is intended for hybrid ongoing workloads, not large one-off migrations. Option B (CORRECT): Use multiple AWS Snowball Edge storage-optimized devices at each office to capture, ship, and import the data into Amazon S3. Each Snowball Edge offers up to 80 TB of rugged, high-speed storage—multiple devices can be issued per office to aggregate 1 PB. Devices can be loaded in parallel over available 1–2 Gbps links, returned by courier, and imported into S3 within the 4-week window. This avoids recurring connectivity fees, leverages physical transport for cost-effective throughput, and scales globally. In summary, we learned how to choose the most cost-effective, scalable one-time data migration method for distributed offices. This scenario falls under Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company has hundreds of Amazon EC2 Linux-based instances in the AWS Cloud. Systems administrators have used shared SSH keys to manage the instances. After a recent audit, the company’s security team is mandating the removal of all shared keys. A solutions architect must design a solution that provides secure access to the EC2 instances. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST amount of administrative overhead?
options: Use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager to connect to the EC2 instances.
Use AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) to generate one-time SSH keys on demand.
Allow shared SSH access to a set of bastion instances. Configure all other instances to allow only SSH access from the bastion instances.
Use an Amazon Cognito custom authorizer to authenticate users. Invoke an AWS Lambda function to generate a temporary SSH key.
explanation: The correct Answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): • AWS STS issues temporary AWS credentials (access keys, secret keys, session tokens) for API calls, not SSH key pairs. • You’d need to build and maintain custom logic to generate, distribute, and install one‐time SSH keys on each EC2 instance, which adds significant operational overhead. Option C (INCORRECT): • A bastion host still relies on SSH key management (and likely shared keys) for admins to log into it. • This design centralizes risk on the bastion and does not eliminate key rotation or audit requirements on the underlying instances. Option D (INCORRECT): • Using Amazon Cognito custom authorizers and Lambda to generate SSH keys introduces custom development, deployment, and maintenance overhead. • It’s a complex, bespoke solution that duplicates existing AWS capabilities and increases points of failure. Option A (CORRECT): • AWS Systems Manager Session Manager provides browser‐based or CLI shell access to Linux instances without opening SSH ports or managing SSH keys. • Access is controlled via IAM policies, enabling fine-grained permissions and audit logging through AWS CloudTrail and Session Manager logs. • No bastion hosts or custom key-generation workflows are required, minimizing administrative overhead. Summary: We’ve learned that eliminating shared SSH keys in favor of AWS Systems Manager Session Manager streamlines secure access, leverages IAM for authentication and authorization, and provides comprehensive logging without manual key rotation. This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer that has sticky sessions enabled. The web server currently hosts the user session state. The company wants to ensure high availability and avoid user session state loss in the event of a web server outage.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Use an Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached instance to store the session data. Update the application to use ElastiCache for Memcached to store the session state.
Use Amazon ElastiCache for Redis to store the session state. Update the application to use ElastiCache for Redis to store the session state.
Use an AWS Storage Gateway cached volume to store session data. Update the application to use AWS Storage Gateway cached volume to store the session state.
Use Amazon RDS to store the session state. Update the application to use Amazon RDS to store the session state.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): Use an Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached instance to store the session data. Memcached is a simple, in-memory key–value store that does not support replication or persistence across AZs. If a node fails or is replaced, all session data in Memcached is lost, leading to user session state loss. It does not meet the high‐availability and durability requirements for session state. Option C (INCORRECT): Use an AWS Storage Gateway cached volume to store session data. Storage Gateway is designed to integrate on‐premises environments with AWS Storage Services; it is not optimized for high‐performance, low‐latency session lookups. It introduces additional network hops and latency unsuitable for real‐time web session management. Complexity and cost are higher compared to in-memory caching solutions. Option D (INCORRECT): Use Amazon RDS to store the session state. Although RDS provides durability, it adds significant read/write latency for each HTTP request. Database connections scale poorly under high session churn, leading to potential performance bottlenecks. Suboptimal for low-latency session management compared with in-memory data stores. Option B (CORRECT): Use Amazon ElastiCache for Redis to store the session state. Redis supports replication across multiple AZs and can be configured for automatic failover, ensuring high availability. It offers optional AOF/RDB persistence so that session data can survive node restarts. Low-latency, in-memory operations suit real-time session lookups, decoupling state from individual web servers. Scales easily with Auto Scaling Groups and ALBs without sticky sessions, avoiding single points of failure. From this discussion, we’ve learned that decoupling session state from web servers into a highly available, in-memory data store with replication and optional persistence ensures sessions survive server outages. This solution belongs to Domain 2 – Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company hosts its application on AWS. The company uses Amazon Cognito to manage users. When users log in to the application, the application fetches required data from Amazon DynamoDB by using a REST API that is hosted in Amazon API Gateway. The company wants an AWS managed solution that will control access to the REST API to reduce development efforts.Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Configure an AWS Lambda function to be an authorizer in API Gateway to validate which user made the request.
For each user, create and assign an API key that must be sent with each request. Validate the key by using an AWS Lambda function.
Send the user’s email address in the header with every request. Invoke an AWS Lambda function to validate that the user with that email address has proper access.
Configure an Amazon Cognito user pool authorizer in API Gateway to allow Amazon Cognito to validate each request.
explanation: The correct answer is D Option A (INCORRECT): Configure an AWS Lambda function as a custom authorizer. This adds custom code to maintain, deploy, and scale—higher operational overhead. You’re reinventing what a managed authorizer (Cognito) already provides. Option B (INCORRECT): Issue API keys per user and validate them via Lambda. API keys are for throttling and metering, not user authentication. You’d still build and manage Lambda logic to validate keys—extra effort. Option C (INCORRECT): Send the user’s email in a header and validate access via Lambda. Trusting a client-supplied header is insecure without JWT validation. Requires custom code to parse and authorize—higher development and maintenance. Option D (CORRECT): Use an Amazon Cognito user pool authorizer in API Gateway. API Gateway natively validates the JSON Web Token (JWT) issued by Cognito. No custom authorizer code—AWS fully manages the authentication flow. Least operational overhead while enforcing secure, user-based access. In summary, integrating API Gateway with a Cognito user pool authorizer offloads authentication to a fully managed service, minimizes custom code, and enforces user-based access controls. This question belongs to Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company has NFS servers in an on-premises data center that need to periodically back up small amounts of data to Amazon S3. Which solution meets these requirements and is MOST cost-effective?
options: Set up AWS Glue to copy the data from the on-premises servers to Amazon S3.
Set up an AWS DataSync agent on the on-premises servers, and sync the data to Amazon S3.
Set up an SFTP sync using AWS Transfer for SFTP to sync data from on premises to Amazon S3.
Set up an AWS Direct Connect connection between the on-premises data center and a VPC, and copy the data to Amazon S3.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): Set up AWS Glue to copy the data from the on-premises servers to Amazon S3. AWS Glue is an ETL service for data discovery, cataloging, and transformation—not optimized for simple file-level backups. It incurs extra costs for crawlers, jobs, and data catalog storage, making it overkill for small periodic transfers. Option C (INCORRECT): Set up an SFTP sync using AWS Transfer for SFTP to sync data from on premises to Amazon S3. AWS Transfer for SFTP requires managing SFTP endpoints, user authentication, and might introduce additional monthly endpoint costs. For small periodic backups, the endpoint charges and management overhead make it less cost-effective than a direct sync solution. Option D (INCORRECT): Set up an AWS Direct Connect connection between the on-premises data center and a VPC, and copy the data to Amazon S3. AWS Direct Connect provides dedicated bandwidth but comes with fixed port-hour fees and long-term commitments. For occasional, small data transfers, Direct Connect is underutilized and significantly more expensive than pay-per-use services. Option B (CORRECT): Set up an AWS DataSync agent on the on-premises servers, and sync the data to Amazon S3. AWS DataSync is purpose-built for automated, incremental transfers from NFS/SMB to AWS storage with built-in scheduling and monitoring. It offers pay-per-GB pricing, encryption in transit, bandwidth control, and automatic retries—minimizing operational overhead. Ideal for small periodic backups, it optimizes network usage and costs without the need for long-term commitments. In summary, AWS DataSync delivers the most cost-effective, secure, and easy-to-manage solution for periodic backups from on-premises NFS servers to Amazon S3. This question belongs to Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures, emphasizing the selection of AWS services that balance functionality with minimal cost.

question: A business application is hosted on Amazon EC2 and uses Amazon S3 for encrypted object storage. The chief information security officer has directed that no application traffic between the two services should traverse the public internet.Which capability should the solutions architect use to meet the compliance requirements?
options: AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS)
VPC endpoint
Private subnet
Virtual private gateway
explanation: The correct Answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) KMS provides encryption key management and cryptographic operations, but it does not control network paths or ensure that S3 traffic stays off the public internet. While you can use KMS to encrypt S3 objects, it has no bearing on the routing of requests between EC2 and S3. Option C (INCORRECT): Private Subnet Putting your EC2 instance in a private subnet prevents direct Internet access, but does not by itself guarantee that calls to S3 remain within the AWS network. You would still need a route (e.g., Internet Gateway, NAT Gateway, or VPC Endpoint) for S3 access; a private subnet alone is insufficient to meet the requirement. Option D (INCORRECT): Virtual Private Gateway A Virtual Private Gateway is used to connect your VPC to an on-premises network via VPN or AWS Direct Connect, not to access AWS services like S3 privately. It does not provide a mechanism to keep EC2-to-S3 traffic within the AWS backbone. Option B (CORRECT): VPC Endpoint A Gateway VPC Endpoint for Amazon S3 allows instances in your VPC to privately communicate with S3 without traversing the public internet. Traffic between EC2 and S3 remains on the AWS global network, satisfying the chief information security officer’s requirement. No Internet Gateway, NAT device, VPN connection, or proxy is required—just the VPC Endpoint and an appropriate route table entry. Summary: By using a Gateway VPC Endpoint for S3, you ensure that all traffic between EC2 and S3 remains on the AWS network, fulfilling strict compliance requirements. This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company is required to use cryptographic keys in its on-premises key manager. The key manager is outside of the AWS Cloud because of regulatory and compliance requirements. The company wants to manage encryption and decryption by using cryptographic keys that are retained outside of the AWS Cloud and that support a variety of external key managers from different vendors. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Use AWS CloudHSM key store backed by a CloudHSM cluster.
Use an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) external key store backed by an external key manager.
Use the default AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) managed key store.
Use a custom key store backed by an AWS CloudHSM cluster.
explanation: The correct answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): “Use AWS CloudHSM key store backed by a CloudHSM cluster.” CloudHSM clusters run inside AWS and manage keys within AWS CloudHSM appliances, not on-premises. They do not integrate with existing external key managers from various vendors. Operational overhead is higher—you must deploy, scale, and maintain the HSM cluster in your VPC. Option C (INCORRECT): “Use the default AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) managed key store.” The default KMS store keeps keys fully managed by AWS inside the AWS Cloud. It cannot use keys residing outside AWS or integrate with on-prem key management systems. Fails the requirement to retain cryptographic keys in an external, on-premises key manager. Option D (INCORRECT): “Use a custom key store backed by an AWS CloudHSM cluster.” Custom key stores also rely on AWS CloudHSM appliances hosted in your VPC, not on-prem. They do not support external, heterogeneous key managers outside AWS Cloud. Maintaining and operating your own CloudHSM cluster adds more overhead, not less. Option B (CORRECT): “Use an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) external key store backed by an external key manager.” KMS External Key Store (XKS) lets you keep your key material in an on-premises HSM or any supported external key manager. AWS KMS handles the API layer for encryption and decryption while forwarding cryptographic operations to your external key manager. Supports multiple vendors and requires minimal changes to applications—AWS manages the infrastructure overhead. In summary, AWS KMS External Key Store meets the requirement to retain keys outside the AWS Cloud and supports a variety of external key managers with the least operational overhead. This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company has AWS Lambda functions that use environment variables. The company does not want its developers to see environment variables in plaintext. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Deploy code to Amazon EC2 instances instead of using Lambda functions.
Configure SSL encryption on the Lambda functions to use AWS CloudHSM to store and encrypt the environment variables.
Create a certificate in AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Configure the Lambda functions to use the certificate to encrypt the environment variables.
Create an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key. Enable encryption helpers on the Lambda functions to use the KMS key to store and encrypt the environment variables.
explanation: The correct answer is D. Let’s step through why A, B, and C are not correct, and why D is the right choice: Option A (INCORRECT): “Deploy code to Amazon EC2 instances instead of using Lambda functions.” This does not address the requirement to hide environment variables—on EC2 you’d still need to manage secrets yourself (e.g., via user data, SSM Parameter Store, or manual injection). It also discards the benefit of Lambda’s built-in encryption-at-rest and serverless deployment model. Option B (INCORRECT): “Configure SSL encryption on the Lambda functions to use AWS CloudHSM to store and encrypt the environment variables.” Lambda environment variables are stored at rest and can be encrypted by KMS; there is no mechanism to attach a CloudHSM-backed SSL certificate to encrypt env vars within Lambda. SSL/TLS certificates and CloudHSM are for securing network traffic, not for transparent at-rest encryption of Lambda environment variables. Option C (INCORRECT): “Create a certificate in AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Configure the Lambda functions to use the certificate to encrypt the environment variables.” ACM issues and manages TLS certificates for endpoints and load balancers—it is not used for data-at-rest encryption in Lambda. Lambda does not support using ACM certificates to encrypt environment variables; only AWS KMS keys are supported for that purpose. Option D (CORRECT): “Create an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key. Enable encryption helpers on the Lambda functions to use the KMS key to store and encrypt the environment variables.” Lambda natively supports encrypting environment variables at rest using a customer-managed KMS key. When you configure a Lambda function with a KMS key, the service automatically encrypts/decrypts the variables—developers without KMS Decrypt permissions cannot view the plaintext values. This meets the requirement of hiding environment variables from developers while still allowing runtime access within the function. In summary, we learned how Lambda integrates with AWS KMS to securely encrypt environment variables at rest, preventing unauthorized users from viewing sensitive data. This question belongs to Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company runs a three-tier web application in a VPC across multiple Availability Zones. Amazon EC2 instances run in an Auto Scaling group for the application tier. The company needs to make an automated scaling plan that will analyze each resource's daily and weekly historical workload trends. The configuration must scale resources appropriately according to both the forecast and live changes in utilization. Which scaling strategy should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?
options: Implement dynamic scaling with step scaling based on average CPU utilization from the EC2 instances.
Enable predictive scaling to forecast and scale. Configure dynamic scaling with target tracking
Create an automated scheduled scaling action based on the traffic patterns of the web application.
Set up a simple scaling policy. Increase the cooldown period based on the EC2 instance startup time.
explanation: The correct answer is Option B. Option A (INCORRECT): Implementing dynamic step scaling based solely on average CPU utilization does not incorporate any forecasting of daily or weekly trends. Step policies only react when thresholds are crossed, so you miss proactive scaling ahead of anticipated workload peaks. Option C (INCORRECT): Scheduled scaling can handle predictable traffic patterns by executing scaling actions at fixed times, but it will not respond to unexpected surges or drops in utilization. It lacks real‐time responsiveness and does not use historical metrics to forecast future needs. Option D (INCORRECT): A simple scaling policy with an increased cooldown period is too rudimentary. It neither forecasts based on historical trends nor provides fine‐grained target tracking. Cooldown adjustments simply delay subsequent scaling actions, but don’t anticipate workload changes. Option B (CORRECT): Combining predictive scaling with target tracking meets both requirements: Predictive Scaling uses machine learning to analyze daily and weekly historical utilization, forecasting the number of instances needed ahead of time. Target Tracking dynamically adjusts capacity in real time to maintain a specified metric (for example, CPU utilization at 50%), handling unexpected traffic spikes or drops. This hybrid strategy ensures you are both proactive (forecast-driven) and reactive (live changes) in your scaling approach, optimizing performance and reliability. In summary, we’ve learned that to satisfy both historical forecasting and real‐time responsiveness, predictive scaling with target tracking is the ideal solution. This scenario falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures, as it focuses on ensuring the application scales efficiently to meet performance demands.

question: A company has a three-tier application on AWS that ingests sensor data from its users’ devices. The traffic flows through a Network Load Balancer (NLB), then to Amazon EC2 instances for the web tier, and finally to EC2 instances for the application tier. The application tier makes calls to a database. What should a solutions architect do to improve the security of the data in transit?
options: Configure a TLS listener. Deploy the server certificate on the NLB.
Configure AWS Shield Advanced. Enable AWS WAF on the NLB.
Change the load balancer to an Application Load Balancer (ALB). Enable AWS WAF on the ALB.
Encrypt the Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume on the EC2 instances by using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS).
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): Configuring AWS Shield Advanced and enabling AWS WAF on the NLB helps protect against DDoS and web exploits, but it does not provide encryption for the data in transit. Shield and WAF are security controls for threat mitigation, not for TLS encryption. Option C (INCORRECT): Switching to an Application Load Balancer and enabling WAF can give you Layer 7 filtering, but by itself it does not ensure end-to-end encryption of the traffic between clients, load balancer, and EC2 instances unless you explicitly configure TLS listeners and install certificates on the targets. The option as stated focuses on WAF, not on TLS. Option D (INCORRECT): Encrypting Amazon EBS volumes via AWS KMS protects data at rest on the EC2 instances’ storage, but it does not affect the security of data moving between clients, load balancers, and servers. This does not address the in-transit encryption requirement. Option A (CORRECT): By configuring a TLS listener on the Network Load Balancer and deploying a valid server certificate, you ensure that traffic from clients to the load balancer is encrypted using TLS. You can further secure the back-end path by using TLS target groups (protocol TLS) and installing certificates on your EC2 instances, enabling end-to-end encryption from client through NLB to your web tier. This approach directly addresses the requirement to improve the security of data in transit. In summary, we learned that to secure data in transit on AWS you must implement TLS/SSL at the load balancer and optionally between the load balancer and targets. Other services like Shield, WAF, or EBS encryption protect different layers (DDoS, application filtering, or data at rest). This question falls under Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A solutions architect needs to copy files from an Amazon S3 bucket to an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system and another S3 bucket. The files must be copied continuously. New files are added to the original S3 bucket consistently. The copied files should be overwritten only if the source file changes.Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Create an AWS DataSync location for both the destination S3 bucket and the EFS file system. Create a task for the destination S3 bucket and the EFS file system. Set the transfer mode to transfer only data that has changed.

Create an AWS Lambda function. Mount the file system to the function. Set up an S3 event notification to invoke the function when files are created and changed in Amazon S3. Configure the function to copy files to the file system and the destination S3 bucket.

Create an AWS DataSync location for both the destination S3 bucket and the EFS file system. Create a task for the destination S3 bucket and the EFS file system. Set the transfer mode to transfer all data.

Launch an Amazon EC2 instance in the same VPC as the file system. Mount the file system. Create a script to routinely synchronize all objects that changed in the origin S3 bucket to the destination S3 bucket and the mounted file system.
explanation: The correct answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): “Create an AWS Lambda function, mount the EFS file system, and use S3 event notifications to invoke it.” Lambda has a 10 GB mount limit and cold-start latency; it isn’t ideal for continuous, high-throughput file sync. Managing retries, error handling, concurrency, and idempotence adds significant operational overhead. S3 event notifications may be lost or reordered under high volume, risking missed files. Option C (INCORRECT): “Use AWS DataSync with transfer mode set to transfer all data.” Transfers every object on each run—even unchanged ones—incurring unnecessary data transfer costs and longer sync times. Violates the requirement to overwrite only when the source file changes. Option D (INCORRECT): “Launch an EC2 instance, mount EFS, and run a custom sync script.” Requires you to manage the EC2 instance, OS updates, script logic, monitoring, and scaling—high operational overhead. Custom scripting is error-prone and less reliable compared to a fully managed service. Option A (CORRECT): “Create AWS DataSync locations for the destination S3 bucket and the EFS file system, then create DataSync tasks with the transfer mode set to send only changed data.” Fully managed, serverless service with built-in scheduling, monitoring, and automatic retries. Incremental sync mode ensures that only modified files are transferred, minimizing cost and time. Supports both S3 and EFS targets in a single solution with minimal configuration. Summary: We’ve learned that AWS DataSync is the most operationally efficient way to continuously copy files from S3 to both another S3 bucket and an EFS file system, performing only incremental transfers when files change. This question aligns with Domain 4 – Design Cost-Optimized Architectures, as it evaluates minimizing data transfer costs and reducing operational overhead.

question: A weather forecasting company collects temperature readings from various sensors on a continuous basis. An existing data ingestion process collects the readings and aggregates the readings into larger Apache Parquet files. Then the process encrypts the files by using client-side encryption with KMS managed keys (CSE-KMS). Finally, the process writes the files to an Amazon S3 bucket with separate prefixes for each calendar day. The company wants to run occasional SQL queries on the data to take sample moving averages for a specific calendar day. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Configure Amazon Athena to read the encrypted files. Run SQL queries on the data directly in Amazon S3.
Use Amazon S3 Select to run SQL queries on the data directly in Amazon S3.
Configure Amazon Redshift to read the encrypted files. Use Redshift Spectrum and Redshift query editor v2 to run SQL queries on the data directly in Amazon S3.
Configure Amazon EMR Serverless to read the encrypted files. Use Apache SparkSQL to run SQL queries on the data directly in Amazon S3.
explanation: The correct answer is D Option A (INCORRECT): Configure Amazon Athena to read the encrypted files. Athena is serverless and queries Parquet on S3, but it only supports server-side encryption (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS), not client-side encryption (CSE-KMS). Since the files are encrypted client-side, Athena cannot decrypt them and therefore cannot read the data. Option B (INCORRECT): Use Amazon S3 Select to run SQL queries on the data directly in Amazon S3. S3 Select can push down SQL for specific object ranges, reducing data scanning—but it also only supports server-side encryption. It cannot decrypt client-side encrypted objects, so you cannot query the CSE-KMS–encrypted Parquet files. Option C (INCORRECT): Configure Amazon Redshift with Redshift Spectrum to read the encrypted files. Redshift Spectrum also relies on server-side decryption (SSE-KMS), and it cannot handle client-side encrypted data. Even if it could, running Redshift clusters for occasional queries is significantly more expensive than other serverless or on-demand options. Option D (CORRECT): Configure Amazon EMR Serverless to read the encrypted files. Use Apache SparkSQL to run SQL queries on the data directly in Amazon S3. EMR (even serverless) can be extended with the AWS Encryption SDK or Hadoop-compatible KMS client libraries to decrypt CSE-KMS files at runtime. SparkSQL on EMR Serverless allows you to run ad-hoc SQL against Parquet with built-in support for custom decryption logic. You pay only for the EMR resources used during query execution—ideal for occasional workloads—making this the most cost-effective approach. In summary, only Amazon EMR Serverless can decrypt client-side (CSE-KMS) Parquet files and run on-demand SQL queries without incurring the cost of a long-running cluster. This question falls under Domain 4 – Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company is creating an application. The company stores data from tests of the application in multiple on-premises locations. The company needs to connect the on-premises locations to VPCs in an AWS Region in the AWS Cloud. The number of accounts and VPCs will increase during the next year. The network architecture must simplify the administration of new connections and must provide the ability to scale. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST administrative overhead?
options: Create a peering connection between the VPCs. Create a VPN connection between the VPCs and the on-premises locations.
Launch an Amazon EC2 instance. On the instance, include VPN software that uses a VPN connection to connect all VPCs and on-premises locations.
Create a transit gateway. Create VPC attachments for the VPC connections. Create VPN attachments for the on-premises connections.
Create an AWS Direct Connect connection between the on-premises locations and a central VPC. Connect the central VPC to other VPCs by using peering connections.
explanation: The correct answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): “Create a peering connection between the VPCs. Create a VPN connection between the VPCs and the on-premises locations.” VPC peering is a 1:1 non-transitive relationship and does not scale as the number of VPCs grows. Managing individual VPN connections between each VPC and every on-premises site quickly becomes an operational burden. Peering across AWS accounts adds complexity and does not simplify administration as requirements grow. Option B (INCORRECT): “Launch an Amazon EC2 instance. On the instance, include VPN software that uses a VPN connection to connect all VPCs and on-premises locations.” This is a self-managed VPN solution that introduces a single point of failure unless you architect HA yourself. You must patch, scale and monitor the EC2 instance(s) and VPN software—significantly increasing administrative overhead. Performance and throughput are limited by the EC2 instance size, and scaling out is manual and error-prone. Option D (INCORRECT): “Create an AWS Direct Connect connection between the on-premises locations and a central VPC. Connect the central VPC to other VPCs by using peering connections.” Though Direct Connect provides high throughput, using VPC peering for transit is not supported (peering is non-transitive). Managing a mesh of peering links as VPC count grows is administratively complex. You’d still need additional VPN or DX private virtual interfaces per on-prem site if peering doesn’t cover all routes. Option C (CORRECT): “Create a transit gateway. Create VPC attachments for the VPC connections. Create VPN attachments for the on-premises connections.” AWS Transit Gateway provides a central hub that supports thousands of VPCs and VPN connections. It’s fully managed, simplifies routing (no transitive peering), and scales elastically as you add accounts, VPCs, or sites. Administration is minimal: you just attach or detach VPCs and VPNs, and propagate routes via route tables. Supports both VPN and Direct Connect attachments, giving flexibility for performance or cost needs. In summary, using an AWS Transit Gateway (Option C) meets the requirements for simplified administration, scalability, and support for multiple VPCs and on-premises connections with minimal overhead. This question falls under Domain 2 – Design Resilient Architectures, as it focuses on a highly available, scalable, and easy-to-manage network topology.

question: A company runs an application on AWS. The application receives inconsistent amounts of usage. The application uses AWS Direct Connect to connect to an on-premises MySQL-compatible database. The on-premises database consistently uses a minimum of 2 GiB of memory. The company wants to migrate the on-premises database to a managed AWS service. The company wants to use auto scaling capabilities to manage unexpected workload increases. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST administrative overhead?
options: Provision an Amazon DynamoDB database with default read and write capacity settings.
Provision an Amazon Aurora database with a minimum capacity of 1 Aurora capacity unit (ACU).
Provision an Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 database with a minimum capacity of 1 Aurora capacity unit (ACU).
Provision an Amazon RDS for MySQL database with 2 GiB of memory.
explanation: The correct answer is Option C. Option A (INCORRECT): • Amazon DynamoDB is a NoSQL service and not MySQL-compatible. • While it can auto scale its read/write capacity, it does not natively support MySQL wire protocol or SQL semantics. • Migrating a MySQL application to DynamoDB would require significant schema and application changes, increasing administrative overhead. Option B (INCORRECT): • A provisioned Amazon Aurora cluster requires you to choose instance classes up front; it does not auto scale compute capacity on demand. • You cannot set a “minimum ACU” on provisioned Aurora: you must manually resize the DB instance to change memory/CPU. • This lacks the automatic scaling needed for unpredictable workloads. Option D (INCORRECT): • Amazon RDS for MySQL requires you to pick an instance type with fixed memory (e.g. 2 GiB). • There is no built-in auto scaling of instance size or memory; you’d have to manually modify the instance class. • It does not meet the requirement for automatic capacity adjustment with minimal administrative overhead. Option C (CORRECT): • Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 supports MySQL compatibility and scales compute capacity (in Aurora Capacity Units) automatically in fine-grained increments. • You can define a minimum capacity of 1 ACU and Aurora Serverless v2 will scale up and down seamlessly to accommodate workload spikes. • It is a fully managed solution with minimal operational overhead and no need to provision or manage fixed instance types. Summary: We have learned that when migrating a MySQL-compatible database with unpredictable workloads and minimal administrative overhead, Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 is the ideal choice due to its automatic, on-demand scaling of compute capacity. This question belongs to Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company hosts a multiplayer gaming application on AWS. The company wants the application to read data with sub-millisecond latency and run one-time queries on historical data. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Use Amazon RDS for data that is frequently accessed. Run a periodic custom script to export the data to an Amazon S3 bucket.

Store the data directly in an Amazon S3 bucket. Implement an S3 Lifecycle policy to move older data to S3 Glacier Deep Archive for long-term storage. Run one-time queries on the data in Amazon S3 by using Amazon Athena.

Use Amazon DynamoDB with DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) for data that is frequently accessed. Export the data to an Amazon S3 bucket by using DynamoDB table export. Run one-time queries on the data in Amazon S3 by using Amazon Athena.

Use Amazon DynamoDB for data that is frequently accessed. Turn on streaming to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to read the data from Kinesis Data Streams. Store the records in an Amazon S3 bucket.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): Amazon RDS delivers millisecond-level latency, not guaranteed sub-millisecond reads. Maintaining and scheduling a custom export script adds operational overhead. This approach does not natively support one-time ad hoc queries on historical data without additional tooling. Option B (INCORRECT): Storing active game data directly in S3 cannot achieve sub-millisecond read latency. Moving older data into Glacier Deep Archive increases retrieval time and complexity. While Athena is great for queries, S3-only storage fails the real-time performance requirement. Option D (INCORRECT): DynamoDB alone can serve low-latency reads, but without DAX you won’t hit sub-millisecond consistently. Streaming through Kinesis Data Streams and Firehose adds components and operational overhead. There’s no built-in, one-step Athena integration—data formatting and delivery require extra setup. Option C (CORRECT): DynamoDB provides single-digit millisecond latency; DAX adds an in-memory cache for sub-millisecond reads. DynamoDB table export to S3 is a fully managed feature—no servers or custom scripts needed. Amazon Athena can perform one-time ad hoc queries on the exported historical dataset with zero infrastructure management. Overall, this delivers the required performance and analytics with the least operational overhead. In summary, deploying DynamoDB with DAX meets the sub-millisecond read requirement, and exporting to S3 for Athena queries covers one-time historical analysis while minimizing operations. This question falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company's near-real-time streaming application is running on AWS. As the data is ingested, a job runs on the data and takes 30 minutes to complete. The workload frequently experiences high latency due to large amounts of incoming data. A solutions architect needs to design a scalable and serverless solution to enhance performance.Which combination of steps should the solutions architect take? (Choose two.)
options: Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to ingest the data.
Use AWS Lambda with AWS Step Functions to process the data.
Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to ingest the data.
Use Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group to process the data.
Use AWS Fargate with Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) to process the data.
explanation: The correct answer is A, E. Option B (INCORRECT): Use AWS Lambda with AWS Step Functions to process the data. AWS Lambda has a maximum execution time of 15 minutes—your job takes 30 minutes, so it cannot complete in one invocation. Orchestrating many small Lambdas via Step Functions adds complexity and overhead, and may not suit heavy, long-running processing. Concurrency limits and cold-start unpredictability can increase latency under high load. Option C (INCORRECT): Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to ingest the data. AWS DMS is designed for migrating databases, not for real-time streaming ingestion of application data. It does not provide the low-latency, scalable streaming pipeline required for near-real-time processing. Option D (INCORRECT): Use Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group to process the data. EC2-based solutions are not serverless; you must manage instance provisioning, patching, and scaling policies. This adds operational overhead and increases latency during scale-out events compared to a fully managed service. Option A (CORRECT): Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to ingest the data. Kinesis Data Firehose is a fully managed, serverless ingestion service that automatically scales to handle high-throughput streams. It can deliver data to multiple destinations (S3, Redshift, etc.) with configurable buffering intervals for near-real-time delivery. Option E (CORRECT): Use AWS Fargate with Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) to process the data. AWS Fargate provides serverless container compute, handling provisioning and scaling automatically. Containers can run arbitrarily long tasks without the 15-minute limit of Lambda, ideal for 30-minute long jobs. You can integrate an ECS service on Fargate to poll the ingestion stream (or process batches in S3) and scale out as needed. In summary, by combining Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose for scalable, serverless ingestion with AWS Fargate for long-running, container-based processing, you address the high-latency issue and avoid managing infrastructure. This solution demonstrates best practices in Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A gaming company uses Amazon DynamoDB to store user information such as geographic location, player data, and leaderboards. The company needs to configure continuous backups to an Amazon S3 bucket with a minimal amount of coding. The backups must not affect availability of the application and must not affect the read capacity units (RCUs) that are defined for the table.Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Use an Amazon EMR cluster. Create an Apache Hive job to back up the data to Amazon S3.
Export the data directly from DynamoDB to Amazon S3 with continuous backups. Turn on point-in-time recovery for the table.
Configure Amazon DynamoDB Streams. Create an AWS Lambda function to consume the stream and export the data to an Amazon S3 bucket.
Create an AWS Lambda function to export the data from the database tables to Amazon S3 on a regular basis. Turn on point-in-time recovery for the table.
explanation: The correct Answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): “Use an Amazon EMR cluster. Create an Apache Hive job to back up the data to Amazon S3.” • Provisioning and managing an EMR cluster adds operational overhead and complexity. • Hive on EMR will perform table scans that consume your table’s read capacity units (RCUs), impacting application performance. • This approach is not truly continuous and requires custom coding and scheduling logic. Option C (INCORRECT): “Configure Amazon DynamoDB Streams. Create an AWS Lambda function to consume the stream and export the data to an Amazon S3 bucket.” • Although Streams + Lambda avoids RCUs, it only captures item-level changes (inserts/updates/deletes), not full table snapshots. • Building and maintaining the Lambda export logic incurs additional coding and operational complexity. • It does not provide a point-in-time continuous backup capability out of the box. Option D (INCORRECT): “Create an AWS Lambda function to export the data from the database tables to Amazon S3 on a regular basis. Turn on point-in-time recovery for the table.” • Scheduled Lambda exports require scanning the table or using queries, which consume read capacity units (RCUs). • You still need to write, deploy, and maintain custom code. • Regular snapshots are not truly continuous and can miss high-frequency updates between runs. Option B (CORRECT): “Export the data directly from DynamoDB to Amazon S3 with continuous backups. Turn on point-in-time recovery for the table.” • DynamoDB’s native point-in-time recovery (PITR) automatically captures continuous backups without consuming your provisioned RCUs. • The new “Export to S3” feature lets you export data snapshots directly to S3 with zero custom code. • There is no impact on table availability or read/write throughput, and AWS manages all the infrastructure for you. Summary: We learned that Amazon DynamoDB’s built-in PITR and Export to S3 capabilities provide continuous, zero-impact backups without custom code or RCU consumption. This question falls under Domain 2 – Design Resilient Architectures, as it addresses high availability and data protection strategies.

question: A company has an on-premises SFTP file transfer solution. The company is migrating to the AWS Cloud to scale the file transfer solution and to optimize costs by using Amazon S3. The company's employees will use their credentials for the on-premises Microsoft Active Directory (AD) to access the new solution. The company wants to keep the current authentication and file access mechanisms. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Configure an S3 File Gateway. Create SMB file shares on the file gateway that use the existing Active Directory to authenticate.
Configure an Auto Scaling group with Amazon EC2 instances to run an SFTP solution. Configure the group to scale up at 60% CPU utilization.
Create an AWS Transfer Family server with SFTP endpoints. Choose the AWS Directory Service option as the identity provider. Use AD Connector to connect the on-premises Active Directory.
Create an AWS Transfer Family SFTP endpoint. Configure the endpoint to use the AWS Directory Service option as the identity provider to connect to the existing Active Directory.
explanation: The correct answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): “Configure an S3 File Gateway. Create SMB file shares on the file gateway that use the existing Active Directory to authenticate.” S3 File Gateway with SMB is for Windows-based file shares, not SFTP protocol. Does not natively support SFTP clients, so you’d still need to manage an SFTP server or gateway for SFTP access. Operationally, you’d introduce extra components without meeting the SFTP requirement. Option B (INCORRECT): “Configure an Auto Scaling group with Amazon EC2 instances to run an SFTP solution. Configure the group to scale up at 60% CPU utilization.” Requires you to deploy, patch, and maintain EC2-based SFTP servers (OS, security, high availability). More operational overhead compared to a fully managed service. Does not leverage built-in integration with on-prem AD without additional configuration. Option D (INCORRECT): “Create an AWS Transfer Family SFTP endpoint. Configure the endpoint to use the AWS Directory Service option as the identity provider to connect to the existing Active Directory.” Conceptually close, but incomplete—AWS Directory Service must be set up via AD Connector if you want to federate to on-prem AD. The option as stated does not explicitly mention AD Connector, which is required to link the Transfer Family server to on-prem AD credentials. Option C (CORRECT): “Create an AWS Transfer Family server with SFTP endpoints. Choose the AWS Directory Service option as the identity provider. Use AD Connector to connect the on-premises Active Directory.” Fully managed SFTP service—no EC2 instances to provision or maintain. AD Connector federates authentication requests directly to on-prem AD, keeping existing credentials and policies. Stores files in Amazon S3, providing scalable, durable, and cost-effective storage. Minimal operational overhead and integrates seamlessly with AWS IAM for logging and monitoring. In summary, we learned how AWS Transfer Family combined with AD Connector provides a fully managed, low-overhead SFTP solution that reuses on-premises Active Directory for authentication and stores files in S3. This question belongs to Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A solutions architect needs to ensure that API calls to Amazon DynamoDB from Amazon EC2 instances in a VPC do not travel across the internet. Which combination of steps should the solutions architect take to meet this requirement? (Choose two.)
options: Create a route table entry for the endpoint.
Create a gateway endpoint for DynamoDB.
Create an interface endpoint for Amazon EC2.
Create an elastic network interface for the endpoint in each of the subnets of the VPC.
Create a security group entry in the endpoint's security group to provide access.
explanation: The correct answer is A, B. Option C (INCORRECT): “Create an interface endpoint for Amazon EC2.” Interface endpoints (powered by AWS PrivateLink) are used to privately connect to supported AWS services—but EC2 itself isn’t a service target for PrivateLink. DynamoDB supports a gateway endpoint, not an interface endpoint. Option D (INCORRECT): “Create an elastic network interface for the endpoint in each of the subnets of the VPC.” When you create an interface endpoint, AWS automatically provisions the required ENIs—you don’t create them yourself. Gateway endpoints (the correct type for DynamoDB) do not use ENIs at all. Option E (INCORRECT): “Create a security group entry in the endpoint's security group to provide access.” Gateway endpoints are route-based and do not have security groups. Only interface endpoints are associated with ENIs and security groups. Option A (CORRECT): “Create a route table entry for the endpoint.” Gateway VPC endpoints require you to add a route in your VPC route table that points DynamoDB’s prefix list (pl-xxxx) to the endpoint. Once the route is in place, all traffic to DynamoDB will stay within the AWS network. Option B (CORRECT): “Create a gateway endpoint for DynamoDB.” DynamoDB supports gateway endpoints, which provide private, secure access from your VPC directly to DynamoDB without using the internet. No NAT gateway, Internet Gateway, or public IP is needed—traffic stays on Amazon’s private backbone. Summary: We learned that to prevent DynamoDB API calls from leaving the AWS network, you must use a gateway VPC endpoint (Option B) and configure the appropriate route table entry (Option A). This question falls under Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures, as it focuses on securing service access and keeping traffic off the public internet.

question: QUESTION: A company runs workloads on AWS. The company needs to connect to a service from an external provider. The service is hosted in the provider's VPC. According to the company’s security team, the connectivity must be private and must be restricted to the target service. The connection must be initiated only from the company’s VPC. Which solution will mast these requirements?
options: Create a VPC peering connection between the company's VPC and the provider's VPC. Update the route table to connect to the target service.
Ask the provider to create a virtual private gateway in its VPC. Use AWS PrivateLink to connect to the target service.
Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet of the company’s VPUpdate the route table to connect to the target service.
Ask the provider to create a VPC endpoint for the target service. Use AWS PrivateLink to connect to the target service.
explanation: The correct answer is D. Option A (INCORRECT): VPC Peering creates a full mesh between two VPCs and is not limited to a single service. You cannot restrict the peering connection to only the target service. It also requires non‐overlapping CIDRs and does not support advanced access control for specific service endpoints. Option B (INCORRECT): A Virtual Private Gateway is used for VPN or AWS Direct Connect, not for AWS PrivateLink. AWS PrivateLink does not require the provider to create a Virtual Private Gateway—rather, the provider must register a Network Load Balancer-backed Endpoint Service. Option C (INCORRECT): A NAT Gateway routes traffic to the internet and is not a private connectivity solution. This would expose traffic to the public internet and cannot be restricted to a single external service privately. Option D (CORRECT): The provider creates an AWS PrivateLink Endpoint Service in their VPC (backed by a Network Load Balancer). The company then creates an Interface VPC Endpoint in its VPC to connect privately to that service. All traffic remains on the AWS network, is restricted to that specific service, and is initiated only from the company’s VPC. In summary, AWS PrivateLink is the appropriate solution for private, service-specific connectivity where the provider publishes an endpoint service and the consumer connects via an Interface VPC Endpoint. This question belongs to Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures, as it focuses on secure, private access to external services.

question: A company runs a production application on a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances. The application reads the data from an Amazon SQS queue and processes the messages in parallel. The message volume is unpredictable and often has intermittent traffic. This application should continually process messages without any downtime.Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Use Spot Instances exclusively to handle the maximum capacity required.
Use Reserved Instances exclusively to handle the maximum capacity required.
Use Reserved Instances for the baseline capacity and use Spot Instances to handle additional capacity.
Use Reserved Instances for the baseline capacity and use On-Demand Instances to handle additional capacity.
explanation: The correct answer is D. Option A (INCORRECT): Use Spot Instances exclusively to handle the maximum capacity required. Spot Instances are the cheapest, but they can be terminated by AWS with little notice. This unpredictability can lead to application downtime when traffic spikes and spot instances get reclaimed. The requirement explicitly states “continually process messages without any downtime,” so Spot‐only is too risky. Option B (INCORRECT): Use Reserved Instances exclusively to handle the maximum capacity required. Reserved Instances provide cost savings for steady state usage but assume you run at that level 24/7. Provisioning for peak capacity with RIs means you pay for unused capacity during low-traffic periods. This approach is not the most cost‐effective for unpredictable, intermittent workloads. Option C (INCORRECT): Use Reserved Instances for the baseline capacity and use Spot Instances to handle additional capacity. You get cost benefits on baseline, and cheap Spot Instances for peaks. However, Spot Instances can still be terminated, risking message processing interruptions. Since the application must “continually process messages without any downtime,” relying on Spot for overflow is unacceptable. Option D (CORRECT): Use Reserved Instances for the baseline capacity and use On-Demand Instances to handle additional capacity. Reserved Instances cover the steady, predictable workload at the lowest hourly cost. On-Demand Instances instantly scale up for traffic spikes without risk of termination. This combination ensures both cost optimization and continuous availability—meeting the “no downtime” requirement. In summary, we learned that mixing Reserved Instances for predictable load with On-Demand Instances for unpredictable peaks delivers the best balance of cost-efficiency and reliability. This question belongs to Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A solutions architect needs to review a company's Amazon S3 buckets to discover personally identifiable information (PII). The company stores the PII data in the us-east-1 Region and us-west-2 Region. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Configure Amazon Macie in each Region. Create a job to analyze the data that is in Amazon S3.
Configure AWS Security Hub for all Regions. Create an AWS Config rule to analyze the data that is in Amazon S3.
Configure Amazon Inspector to analyze the data that is in Amazon S3.
Configure Amazon GuardDuty to analyze the data that is in Amazon S3.
explanation: The correct answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): “Configure AWS Security Hub for all Regions. Create an AWS Config rule to analyze the data that is in Amazon S3.” AWS Security Hub aggregates findings from other services and does not natively inspect S3 objects for sensitive data. AWS Config rules evaluate resource compliance and configuration, but they don’t scan object contents for PII. Option C (INCORRECT): “Configure Amazon Inspector to analyze the data that is in Amazon S3.” Amazon Inspector is designed to assess security vulnerabilities in EC2 instances, container images, and Lambda functions—not to scan S3 object contents. Option D (INCORRECT): “Configure Amazon GuardDuty to analyze the data that is in Amazon S3.” GuardDuty detects threats in account activity, VPC flow logs, and DNS logs. It does not inspect S3 objects for PII. Option A (CORRECT): “Configure Amazon Macie in each Region. Create a job to analyze the data that is in Amazon S3.” Amazon Macie is purpose‐built to discover, classify, and protect sensitive data such as PII in S3 buckets. Macie can be enabled in multiple Regions (us-east-1 and us-west-2) with minimal setup and provides automated, scheduled jobs to scan for PII. This solution requires the least operational overhead compared to custom rules or manual processes. In summary, we learned that identifying and classifying PII in S3 requires a dedicated data-inspection service. Amazon Macie is the AWS service designed for this purpose and can operate across Regions with minimal management. This question belongs to Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A university research laboratory needs to migrate 30 TB of data from an on-premises Windows file server to Amazon FSx for Windows File Server. The laboratory has a 1 Gbps network link that many other departments in the university share. The laboratory wants to implement a data migration service that will maximize the performance of the data transfer. However, the laboratory needs to be able to control the amount of bandwidth that the service uses to minimize the impact on other departments. The data migration must take place within the next 5 days. Which AWS solution will meet these requirements?
options: AWS Snowcone
Amazon FSx File Gateway
AWS DataSync
AWS Transfer Family
explanation: The correct Answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): AWS Snowcone • AWS Snowcone is a small, portable edge computing and data transfer device designed for up to 8 TB of data per device. It does not meet the 30 TB requirement without using multiple devices, which increases complexity and shipping time. • The laboratory needs to complete migration within 5 days. Relying on physical shipment and multiple devices is unpredictable and could exceed the time window. • Snowcone cannot throttle network bandwidth because data transfer occurs offline (by shipping the device). Option B (INCORRECT): Amazon FSx File Gateway • The FSx File Gateway presents an SMB/NFS file interface backed by FSx in AWS, primarily for hybrid access and caching rather than bulk migration. • It is designed to give on-premises applications low-latency access to FSx data with local caching, not for one-time transfer of large datasets. • It does not provide built-in bandwidth shaping controls for a large bulk migration scenario. Option D (INCORRECT): AWS Transfer Family • AWS Transfer Family (SFTP/FTPS/FTP) is used to migrate files into Amazon S3 or EFS via standard file-transfer protocols. It does not integrate directly with Amazon FSx for Windows File Server. • This service is aimed at replacing legacy file-transfer servers, not at high-speed SMB data migration to FSx. • You cannot throttle Transfer Family bandwidth in the same way you can with DataSync for controlled migration. Option C (CORRECT): AWS DataSync • AWS DataSync automates and accelerates moving large datasets—up to hundreds of petabytes—between on-premises storage and AWS, including FSx for Windows File Server. • It uses parallel, multi-threaded transfer engines to maximize throughput over your existing 1 Gbps link, helping you meet the 5-day window for 30 TB. • DataSync provides built-in bandwidth throttling controls so you can limit transfer rate and minimize impact on other departments sharing the network. In summary, AWS DataSync is the ideal solution because it meets the 30 TB transfer requirement within 5 days over a shared 1 Gbps link and allows precise bandwidth control to avoid impacting other users. This question belongs to Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company hosts a multi-tier web application that uses an Amazon Aurora MySQL DB cluster for storage. The application tier is hosted on Amazon EC2 instances. The company's IT security guidelines mandate that the database credentials be encrypted and rotated every 14 days.What should a solutions architect do to meet this requirement with the LEAST operational effort?
options: Create a new AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption key. Use AWS Secrets Manager to create a new secret that uses the KMS key with the appropriate credentials. Associate the secret with the Aurora DB cluster. Configure a custom rotation period of 14 days.

Create two parameters in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store: one for the user name as a string parameter and one that uses the SecureString type for the password. Select AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption for the password parameter, and load these parameters in the application tier. Implement an AWS Lambda function that rotates the password every 14 days.

Store a file that contains the credentials in an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encrypted Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Mount the EFS file system in all EC2 instances of the application tier. Restrict the access to the file on the file system so that the application can read the file and that only super users can modify the file. Implement an AWS Lambda function that rotates the key in Aurora every 14 days and writes new credentials into the file.

Store a file that contains the credentials in an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encrypted Amazon S3 bucket that the application uses to load the credentials. Download the file to the application regularly to ensure that the correct credentials are used. Implement an AWS Lambda function that rotates the Aurora credentials every 14 days and uploads these credentials to the file in the S3 bucket.
explanation: The correct Answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): This approach uses AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store plus a custom Lambda to rotate credentials every 14 days. Parameter Store SecureString can store secrets, but you must build, maintain, and schedule the Lambda rotation logic yourself. This adds significant operational effort compared to a fully managed rotation solution. Option C (INCORRECT): Storing credentials in an EFS file system and mounting it on EC2 instances is overly complex. You’d need to manage file permissions, EFS performance, and write custom rotation code in Lambda. This violates the “least operational effort” requirement. Option D (INCORRECT): Putting encrypted files in S3 and writing custom rotation Lambdas is also a self-managed solution. It requires orchestrating downloads, decryption, uploads, and scheduling—adding undue operational overhead. Option A (CORRECT): AWS Secrets Manager natively integrates with Amazon Aurora MySQL for credential storage and rotation. You can specify a 14-day rotation interval, and AWS handles rotation via built-in Lambda functions. Using a dedicated KMS key for encryption meets security guidelines with minimal manual work. In summary, AWS Secrets Manager (Option A) offers fully managed secret storage and automatic rotation, satisfying the encryption and 14-day rotation requirements with the least operational effort. This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company is deploying an application that processes streaming data in near-real time. The company plans to use Amazon EC2 instances for the workload. The network architecture must be configurable to provide the lowest possible latency between nodes. Which combination of network solutions will meet these requirements?(Choose two.)
options: Enable and configure enhanced networking on each EC2 instance.
Group the EC2 instances in separate accounts.
Run the EC2 instances in a cluster placement group.
Attach multiple elastic network interfaces to each EC2 instance.
Use Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) optimized instance types.
explanation: The correct answer is A, C. Option B (INCORRECT): “Group the EC2 instances in separate accounts.” AWS account boundaries do not influence network proximity or latency. Separating instances into different accounts only adds management complexity, without reducing inter-node latency. Option D (INCORRECT): “Attach multiple elastic network interfaces to each EC2 instance.” Multiple ENIs can increase network segmentation or bandwidth, but they do not inherently lower latency between instances. Adding ENIs introduces more network interfaces rather than optimizing the physical placement or packet path. Option E (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) optimized instance types.” EBS-optimized instances improve disk I/O performance, not network performance. This setting is for storage throughput and does nothing to reduce network latency between EC2 nodes. Option A (CORRECT): “Enable and configure enhanced networking on each EC2 instance.” Enhanced networking (ENA or Intel 82599 VF) provides higher packet‐per‐second (PPS) performance and lower latency. It reduces jitter and delivers consistent, low-latency connectivity crucial for near-real-time streaming workloads. Option C (CORRECT): “Run the EC2 instances in a cluster placement group.” Cluster placement groups place instances physically close within an Availability Zone, minimizing network hops. This optimized placement yields ultra-low latency and high throughput, ideal for tightly coupled, real-time processing. In summary, the lowest possible latency between EC2 nodes is achieved by combining enhanced networking with a cluster placement group. This question falls under Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures, as it focuses on network performance optimizations for near-real-time workloads.

question: A company that is in the ap-northeast-1 Region has a fleet of thousands of AWS Outposts servers. The company has deployed the servers at remote locations around the world. All the servers regularly download new software versions that consist of 100 files. There is significant latency before all servers run the new software versions. The company must reduce the deployment latency for new software versions.Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Create an Amazon S3 bucket in ap-northeast-1. Set up an Amazon CloudFront distribution in ap-northeast-1 that includes a CachingDisabled cache policy. Configure the S3 bucket as the origin. Download the software by using signed URLs.

Create an Amazon S3 bucket in ap-northeast-1. Create a second S3 bucket in the us-east-1 Region. Configure replication between the buckets. Set up an Amazon CloudFront distribution that uses ap-northeast-1 as the primary origin and us-east-1 as the secondary origin. Download the software by using signed URLs.
Create an Amazon S3 bucket in ap-northeast-1. Configure Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration. Download the software by using the S3 Transfer Acceleration endpoint.
Create an Amazon S3 bucket in ap-northeast-1. Set up an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Configure the S3 bucket as the origin. Download the software by using signed URLs.
explanation: The correct answer is D Option A (INCORRECT): Using a CloudFront distribution with a CachingDisabled policy completely negates the benefit of edge caching. Every request still goes back to the S3 origin in ap-northeast-1, so global servers will continue to experience high latency. This fails the requirement to reduce deployment latency. Option B (INCORRECT): Introducing a second S3 bucket in us-east-1 and replicating data adds significant operational overhead. You must manage replication rules, monitor consistency, and maintain multiple buckets. The complexity outweighs the benefit, and CloudFront will still fetch from the primary origin until the cache is primed. Option C (INCORRECT): S3 Transfer Acceleration optimizes network paths for uploading and downloading to a single bucket, but it does not provide persistent edge caching. Every download still traverses back to the origin via an optimized path, which helps performance marginally but doesn’t achieve the low-latency, globally cached distribution that CloudFront provides. Option D (CORRECT): Deploying a CloudFront distribution in front of the S3 bucket leverages edge caching worldwide. Once the 100 files are fetched the first time, subsequent downloads by remote Outposts servers are served directly from the nearest edge location, dramatically cutting latency. The operational overhead is minimal: you configure the distribution, set S3 as the origin, and issue signed URLs. In summary, by placing a CloudFront distribution in front of your S3 bucket, you achieve globally distributed caching with virtually no extra management tasks. This solution belongs to Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures, since it optimizes performance and reduces latency for worldwide deployments.

question: A company is migrating an application from an on-premises environment to AWS. The application will store sensitive data in Amazon S3. The company must encrypt the data before storing the data in Amazon S3.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Encrypt the data by using client-side encryption with customer managed keys.
Encrypt the data by using server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS).
Encrypt the data by using server-side encryption with customer-provided keys (SSE-C).
Encrypt the data by using client-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys.
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): Encrypt the data by using server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS). With SSE-KMS, encryption happens after the data reaches S3. The requirement specifies encrypting data before storing it in S3. Server-side encryption still means unencrypted data is sent to S3, which does not meet the “encrypt before storing” rule. Option C (INCORRECT): Encrypt the data by using server-side encryption with customer-provided keys (SSE-C). SSE-C also performs encryption on the server side, not on the client side. Although you supply the key, the data is transmitted in plain text to S3 first and then encrypted—so it’s not encrypted before storage. Option D (INCORRECT): Encrypt the data by using client-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys. This option is not valid because Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3) are used for server-side encryption, not for client-side. You cannot perform client-side encryption with S3-managed keys; those keys are never exposed outside of AWS. Option A (CORRECT): Encrypt the data by using client-side encryption with customer managed keys. Client-side encryption ensures data is encrypted within your application or on your servers before it is sent to S3. Using customer managed keys (for example, keys you control in AWS KMS or your own key management system) lets you maintain full ownership and management of the encryption keys. This meets the explicit requirement to encrypt data before storing it in Amazon S3. In summary, only client-side encryption meets the requirement to encrypt data prior to storing it in S3. This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A development team has launched a new application that is hosted on Amazon EC2 instances inside a development VPC. A solutions architect needs to create a new VPC in the same account. The new VPC will be peered with the development VPC. The VPC CIDR block for the development VPC is 192.168.0.0/24. The solutions architect needs to create a CIDR block for the new VPC. The CIDR block must be valid for a VPC peering connection to the development VPC.What is the SMALLEST CIDR block that meets these requirements?
explanation: The correct answer is D. Option A (INCORRECT): “10.0.1.0/32” A /32 mask represents a single IP address, not a network block. AWS VPC CIDR blocks must be between /16 and /28—you cannot create a /32 VPC. Option B (INCORRECT): “192.168.0.0/24” This CIDR exactly matches the development VPC’s 192.168.0.0/24 block. VPC peering requires non‐overlapping CIDR ranges, so this would be invalid. Option C (INCORRECT): “192.168.1.0/32” Again, /32 is a single IP, too small for a VPC. Even though it doesn’t overlap, it fails the AWS requirement of a /16–/28 block size. Option D (CORRECT): “10.0.1.0/24” /24 is within the supported VPC range (/16 to /28). 10.0.1.0/24 does not overlap with 192.168.0.0/24. Of the valid options provided, it is the smallest acceptable CIDR block. In summary, when peering VPCs the CIDR blocks must not overlap and must adhere to AWS’s /16–/28 size restrictions. We chose 10.0.1.0/24 as the smallest valid network that meets these criteria. This question falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures, focusing on proper network design and addressing.

question: A company hosts an application on multiple Amazon EC2 instances. The application processes messages from an Amazon SQS queue, writes to an Amazon RDS table, and deletes the message from the queue. Occasional duplicate records are found in the RDS table. The SQS queue does not contain any duplicate messages. What should a solutions architect do to ensure messages are being processed once only?
options: Use the CreateQueue API call to create a new queue.
Use the AddPermission API call to add appropriate permissions.
Use the ReceiveMessage API call to set an appropriate wait time.
Use the ChangeMessageVisibility API call to increase the visibility timeout.
explanation: The correct answer is D Option A (INCORRECT): “Use the CreateQueue API call to create a new queue.” The CreateQueue API simply provisions a new SQS queue; it does not adjust any visibility or processing behavior. Creating a new queue will not prevent duplicate records in RDS if the processing logic and timeouts remain unchanged. Option B (INCORRECT): “Use the AddPermission API call to add appropriate permissions.” AddPermission grants cross-account or cross-service access to the queue, but it has no effect on message visibility or processing guarantees. Permissions do not influence duplicate handling in your consumer application or SQS message lifecycle. Option C (INCORRECT): “Use the ReceiveMessage API call to set an appropriate wait time.” Setting WaitTimeSeconds (long polling) reduces empty responses and lowers cost, but it does not affect how long a message remains invisible after being received. Long polling improves efficiency but does not address duplicate processing when a consumer fails to delete within the visibility window.
