It cannot satisfy a long-term retention requirement of 7 years. Therefore, it does not meet the business requirement. Option C (INCORRECT): Create an on-demand backup of the table by using the DynamoDB console. Store the backup in an Amazon S3 bucket. Set an S3 Lifecycle configuration for the S3 bucket. This is a manual, one-off operation unless scripted, which is not operationally efficient. You would need to remember to schedule backups yourself or build a custom process. AWS Backup provides a managed service for scheduling and retention instead. Option D (INCORRECT): Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to invoke a Lambda function to back up the table to S3 with a lifecycle policy. This introduces custom code and infrastructure to manage backups. You are responsible for writing, deploying, and maintaining the Lambda function and EventBridge rule. AWS Backup does all of this out of the box, which is more operationally efficient. Option B (CORRECT): Use AWS Backup to create backup schedules and retention policies for the table. AWS Backup natively supports DynamoDB and lets you define automated backup plans. You can specify retention periods up to 7 years (or longer) directly in the policy. No custom scripts or manual steps are required—AWS Backup handles scheduling, storage, and lifecycle. This is the most operationally efficient solution to meet the 7-year retention requirement. In summary, AWS Backup provides a fully managed, policy-driven way to schedule and retain DynamoDB backups for long periods, eliminating the need for custom code or manual processes. This question falls under Domain 2 - Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company wants to use high performance computing (HPC) infrastructure on AWS for financial risk modeling. The company’s HPC workloads run on Linux. Each HPC workflow runs on hundreds of Amazon EC2 Spot Instances, is short-lived, and generates thousands of output files that are ultimately stored in persistent storage for analytics and long-term future use. The company seeks a cloud storage solution that permits the copying of on-premises data to long-term persistent storage to make data available for processing by all EC2 instances. The solution should also be a high performance file system that is integrated with persistent storage to read and write datasets and output files.Which combination of AWS services meets these requirements?
options: Amazon FSx for Lustre integrated with Amazon S3
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server integrated with Amazon S3
Amazon S3 Glacier integrated with Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS)
Amazon S3 bucket with a VPC endpoint integrated with an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) General Purpose SSD (gp2) volume
explanation: The correct Answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): Amazon FSx for Windows File Server integrated with Amazon S3 FSx for Windows File Server is designed for Windows-based workloads and SMB protocol, not optimized for Linux-based HPC environments. It does not provide the high‐throughput, low‐latency parallel file system needed for HPC workloads. Option C (INCORRECT): Amazon S3 Glacier integrated with Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) S3 Glacier is for long‐term archival storage with retrieval times in minutes to hours, unsuitable for active HPC workflows that need rapid I/O. EBS volumes attach to individual instances and do not provide a shared parallel file system across hundreds of Spot Instances. Option D (INCORRECT): Amazon S3 bucket with a VPC endpoint integrated with an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) General Purpose SSD (gp2) volume This combination does not provide a unified POSIX‐compliant, high‐performance parallel file system for all compute nodes. Accessing S3 via a VPC endpoint is object‐based, and EBS is single‐attach per volume, so it can’t be shared across hundreds of instances simultaneously. Option A (CORRECT): Amazon FSx for Lustre integrated with Amazon S3 FSx for Lustre delivers a high‐performance, POSIX‐compliant parallel file system ideal for Linux‐based HPC workloads. It can transparently ingest data from and write output back to S3, providing seamless integration between compute and persistent object storage. Hundreds of EC2 Spot Instances can mount the same FSx for Lustre file system concurrently for low‐latency, high‐throughput I/O. Output files are persisted to S3 for long‐term analytics and archiving once the short‐lived cluster completes its tasks. Summary: We learned that Amazon FSx for Lustre is the best choice for Linux‐based HPC workloads requiring a shared, high‐performance file system tightly integrated with persistent S3 storage. This question falls under Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: QUESTION: An application that is hosted on Amazon EC2 instances needs to access an Amazon S3 bucket. Traffic must not traverse the internet. How should a solutions architect configure access to meet these requirements?
options: Create a private hosted zone by using Amazon Route 53.
Set up a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3 in the VPC.
Configure the EC2 instances to use a NAT gateway to access the S3 bucket.
Establish an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection between the VPC and the S3 bucket.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): Creating a private hosted zone in Amazon Route 53 only affects DNS resolution. It does not provide a private network path to S3, so traffic would still traverse the internet unless another mechanism is used. Option C (INCORRECT): Configuring a NAT gateway routes S3 requests through the internet gateway. Although EC2 instances in private subnets can reach S3, the traffic still goes out to the internet and back, violating the “no internet traversal” requirement. Option D (INCORRECT): An AWS Site-to-Site VPN connects your VPC to an on-premises network—not directly to S3. You can’t establish a VPN between a VPC and S3, and this solution would be overkill even if possible. Option B (CORRECT): A Gateway VPC Endpoint for Amazon S3 enables private connectivity between your VPC and S3 without using an internet gateway, NAT device, VPN connection, or AWS Direct Connect. It adds a route in your VPC route table so that requests to S3 remain on the AWS network. Summary: We’ve learned that to keep S3 traffic within AWS’s private network, you must use a Gateway VPC Endpoint. DNS tricks or VPNs don’t address the requirement, and a NAT gateway still routes via the internet. This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company is designing a web application with an internet-facing Application Load Balancer (ALB). The company needs the ALB to receive HTTPS web traffic from the public internet. The ALB must send only HTTPS traffic to the web application servers hosted on the Amazon EC2 instances on port 443. The ALB must perform a health check of the web application servers over HTTPS on port 8443. Which combination of configurations of the security group that is associated with the ALB will meet these requirements? (Choose three.)
options: Allow HTTPS inbound traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 for port 443.
Allow all outbound traffic to 0.0.0.0/0 for port 443.
Allow HTTPS outbound traffic to the web application instances for port 443.
Allow HTTPS inbound traffic from the web application instances for port 443.
Allow HTTPS outbound traffic to the web application instances for the health check on port 8443.
Allow HTTPS inbound traffic from the web application instances for the health check on port 8443.
explanation: The correct answer is A, C, E Option B (INCORRECT): • This rule would allow outbound HTTPS traffic to any IP on the internet (0.0.0.0/0) on port 443. You only need to allow outbound traffic to your EC2 instances, not everywhere. Overly permissive and not aligned with the principle of least privilege. Option D (INCORRECT): • This inbound rule suggests that the ALB would receive HTTPS connections from the application servers on port 443. In reality, the ALB initiates connections to the instances (outbound from the ALB’s perspective) and the instances respond. You do not need inbound rules from the instances on port 443. Option F (INCORRECT): • This rule implies that health checks on port 8443 arrive inbound from the instances. Actually, the ALB sends the health check (outbound from the ALB) to the instances on port 8443. Therefore you need an outbound rule, not an inbound one. Option A (CORRECT): • Allows the ALB to receive HTTPS (port 443) traffic from any client on the internet (0.0.0.0/0). This satisfies the requirement to accept public HTTPS requests. Option C (CORRECT): • Permits the ALB to initiate outbound HTTPS connections to your web application instances on port 443. This enables secure backend communication from the ALB to the EC2 instances. Option E (CORRECT): • Enables the ALB to perform health checks by sending outbound HTTPS requests on port 8443 to the instances. This meets the requirement for HTTPS health checks over port 8443. Summary: We’ve learned that for an internet-facing Application Load Balancer you must configure inbound rules to accept public HTTPS traffic and outbound rules to allow both application traffic and health-check traffic to your EC2 instances. This question falls under Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company has an on-premises volume backup solution that has reached its end of life. The company wants to use AWS as part of a new backup solution and wants to maintain local access to all the data while it is backed up on AWS. The company wants to ensure that the data backed up on AWS is automatically and securely transferred.Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Use AWS Snowball to migrate data out of the on-premises solution to Amazon S3. Configure on-premises systems to mount the Snowball S3 endpoint to provide local access to the data.
Use AWS Snowball Edge to migrate data out of the on-premises solution to Amazon S3. Use the Snowball Edge file interface to provide on-premises systems with local access to the data.

Use AWS Storage Gateway and configure a cached volume gateway. Run the Storage Gateway software appliance on premises and configure a percentage of data to cache locally. Mount the gateway storage volumes to provide local access to the data.

Use AWS Storage Gateway and configure a stored volume gateway. Run the Storage Gateway software appliance on premises and map the gateway storage volumes to on-premises storage. Mount the gateway storage volumes to provide local access to the data.
explanation: The correct answer is D Option A (INCORRECT): “Use AWS Snowball to migrate data out of the on-premises solution to Amazon S3. Configure on-premises systems to mount the Snowball S3 endpoint to provide local access to the data.” Snowball is a one-time physical data-transfer appliance, not a continuous backup solution. You cannot “mount” Snowball’s S3 endpoint as a persistent volume for on-going local access. It won’t automatically and securely transfer incremental changes over time. Option B (INCORRECT): “Use AWS Snowball Edge to migrate data out of the on-premises solution to Amazon S3. Use the Snowball Edge file interface to provide on-premises systems with local access to the data.” Snowball Edge similarly is a batch-style device; it does not serve as a continuously available volume gateway. You must ship the device back and forth—there is no ongoing sync service. It’s not designed for automated, continuous backup with seamless local mounting. Option C (INCORRECT): “Use AWS Storage Gateway and configure a cached volume gateway. Run the Storage Gateway software appliance on premises and configure a percentage of data to cache locally. Mount the gateway storage volumes to provide local access to the data.” Cached volumes keep only a subset (cache) of your data locally; the master copy resides in AWS S3. If you need access to “all” data locally, uncached portions must be fetched over the network, adding latency. Does not satisfy requirement to maintain local access to the entire dataset at all times. Option D (CORRECT): “Use AWS Storage Gateway and configure a stored volume gateway. Run the Storage Gateway software appliance on premises and map the gateway storage volumes to on-premises storage. Mount the gateway storage volumes to provide local access to the data.” Stored volumes keep the primary data copy locally on-premises, so you have full local access at all times. All writes are asynchronously and securely backed up to AWS as EBS snapshots in Amazon S3. Provides continuous, automated transfer of data to AWS without manual intervention. In summary, a stored-volume AWS Storage Gateway meets both requirements: full local access to all on-premises data and automatic, secure backups to AWS. This question falls under Domain 2 - Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company has an Amazon S3 data lake. The company needs a solution that transforms the data from the data lake and loads the data into a data warehouse every day. The data warehouse must have massively parallel processing (MPP) capabilities. Data analysts then need to create and train machine learning (ML) models by using SQL commands on the data. The solution must use serverless AWS services wherever possible. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Run a daily Amazon EMR job to transform the data and load the data into Amazon Redshift. Use Amazon Redshift ML to create and train the ML models.
Run a daily Amazon EMR job to transform the data and load the data into Amazon Aurora Serverless. Use Amazon Aurora ML to create and train the ML models.
Run a daily AWS Glue job to transform the data and load the data into Amazon Redshift Serverless. Use Amazon Redshift ML to create and train the ML models.
Run a daily AWS Glue job to transform the data and load the data into Amazon Athena tables. Use Amazon Athena ML to create and train the ML models.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): • Uses Amazon EMR for the daily job, which is not fully serverless. • Loads into provisioned Amazon Redshift (not Redshift Serverless), so it does not meet the “serverless wherever possible” requirement. • EMR clusters introduce management overhead and cost that can be avoided with AWS Glue. Option B (INCORRECT): • Amazon Aurora Serverless is not a massively parallel processing (MPP) data warehouse. • Aurora ML can invoke ML models, but it does not provide the scale or SQL-based ML integration for large analytic workloads. • Fails the requirement for an MPP data warehouse. Option D (INCORRECT): • AWS Glue → Amazon Athena is fully serverless, but Athena is a query service, not an MPP data warehouse for large-scale loading and storage. • Athena ML exists as a preview feature but is not designed for large-scale model training directly within a data warehouse. • Does not satisfy the requirement to load transformed data into an MPP data warehouse. Option C (CORRECT): Uses AWS Glue (serverless ETL) to transform data daily from Amazon S3. Loads into Amazon Redshift Serverless, providing a fully managed, serverless MPP data warehouse. Leverages Amazon Redshift ML so data analysts can create and train ML models using SQL commands directly in the data warehouse. Meets all requirements: serverless services, daily transformation and load, MPP architecture, and SQL-based ML. In summary, this question tests your ability to design a serverless, high-performing analytics and ML pipeline. We learned how to choose AWS Glue for serverless ETL, Redshift Serverless for a scalable MPP warehouse, and Redshift ML for SQL-based model training. This scenario falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company runs a critical, customer-facing application on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). The application has a microservices architecture. The company needs to implement a solution that collects, aggregates, and summarizes metrics and logs from the application in a centralized location. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Run the Amazon CloudWatch agent in the existing EKS cluster. View the metrics and logs in the CloudWatch console.
Run AWS App Mesh in the existing EKS cluster. View the metrics and logs in the App Mesh console.
Configure AWS CloudTrail to capture data events. Query CloudTrail by using Amazon OpenSearch Service.
Configure Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights in the existing EKS cluster. View the metrics and logs in the CloudWatch console.
explanation: The correct answer is D. Option A (INCORRECT): Run the Amazon CloudWatch agent in the existing EKS cluster. The CloudWatch agent can collect host-level metrics and logs, but it does not provide Kubernetes-native insights such as per-pod, per-node, or per-service metrics out of the box. Without Container Insights, you must build and maintain custom dashboards and queries to correlate logs and metrics across microservices, which is operationally heavy. Option B (INCORRECT): Run AWS App Mesh in the existing EKS cluster. AWS App Mesh is a service mesh for controlling and securing traffic between microservices. It does emit metrics via Envoy proxies, but it’s not a centralized logging and metrics aggregation solution by itself. App Mesh helps with traffic shaping, retries, and security policies, but you still need a monitoring solution such as Container Insights or Prometheus to view and analyze logs and metrics centrally. Option C (INCORRECT): Configure AWS CloudTrail to capture data events and query with Amazon OpenSearch Service. CloudTrail captures AWS API calls (control plane events), not application-level metrics or container logs. OpenSearch Service can index and search logs, but you would still lack out-of-the-box Kubernetes performance metrics (CPU, memory, network) without additional instrumentation. Option D (CORRECT): Configure Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights in the existing EKS cluster. Container Insights automatically collects CPU, memory, disk, and network metrics at the cluster, node, pod, and service levels. It also collects and aggregates container logs. You get built-in dashboards and the ability to create custom CloudWatch dashboards, alarms, and insights queries without additional agent management. This solution centralizes metrics and logs in CloudWatch, meeting the requirement for aggregated and summarised visibility across all microservices. In summary, Container Insights is the AWS-managed observability solution tailored for EKS and other container platforms. It simplifies the deployment of agents, automates the collection of key performance and operational data, and provides centralized dashboards and alerts. This question falls under Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures, as it focuses on implementing an efficient monitoring and observability strategy for containerized applications.

question: A financial company needs to handle highly sensitive data. The company will store the data in an Amazon S3 bucket. The company needs to ensure that the data is encrypted in transit and at rest. The company must manage the encryption keys outside the AWS Cloud.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Encrypt the data in the S3 bucket with server-side encryption (SSE) that uses an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key.
Encrypt the data in the S3 bucket with server-side encryption (SSE) that uses an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) AWS managed key.
Encrypt the data in the S3 bucket with the default server-side encryption (SSE).
Encrypt the data at the company's data center before storing the data in the S3 bucket.
explanation: The correct answer is D. Option A (INCORRECT): Encrypt the data in the S3 bucket with server-side encryption (SSE) that uses an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer-managed key. This still uses AWS KMS inside the AWS Cloud to manage keys. The requirement specifies that the encryption keys must be managed outside of the AWS Cloud. Option B (INCORRECT): Encrypt the data in the S3 bucket with server-side encryption (SSE) that uses an AWS KMS AWS-managed key. AWS-managed KMS keys are fully controlled by AWS, not by your organization. Keys remain inside AWS, violating the “manage keys outside AWS Cloud” requirement. Option C (INCORRECT): Encrypt the data in the S3 bucket with the default server-side encryption (SSE-S3). SSE-S3 uses keys managed by AWS internally. No control over key lifecycle, rotation, or storage outside AWS. Option D (CORRECT): Encrypt the data at the company's data center before storing the data in the S3 bucket. Client-side encryption ensures data is encrypted before it ever leaves your premises. You manage encryption keys entirely outside of AWS, meeting the key-management requirement. Data is protected in transit (using HTTPS) and remains encrypted at rest in S3 (AWS stores only the ciphertext). Summary: We reviewed the options for encrypting data in Amazon S3 while managing keys outside AWS. Only client-side encryption (Option D) fully satisfies encryption in transit, encryption at rest, and external key management. This question falls under Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company runs a three-tier web application in the AWS Cloud that operates across three Availability Zones. The application architecture has an Application Load Balancer, an Amazon EC2 web server that hosts user session states, and a MySQL database that runs on an EC2 instance. The company expects sudden increases in application traffic. The company wants to be able to scale to meet future application capacity demands and to ensure high availability across all three Availability Zones. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Migrate the MySQL database to Amazon RDS for MySQL with a Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment. Use Amazon ElastiCache for Redis with high availability to store session data and to cache reads. Migrate the web server to an Auto Scaling group that is in three Availability Zones.

Migrate the MySQL database to Amazon RDS for MySQL with a Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment. Use Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached with high availability to store session data and to cache reads. Migrate the web server to an Auto Scaling group that is in three Availability Zones.

Migrate the MySQL database to Amazon DynamoDB Use DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) to cache reads. Store the session data in DynamoDB. Migrate the web server to an Auto Scaling group that is in three Availability Zones.

Migrate the MySQL database to Amazon RDS for MySQL in a single Availability Zone. Use Amazon ElastiCache for Redis with high availability to store session data and to cache reads. Migrate the web server to an Auto Scaling group that is in three Availability Zones.
explanation: The correct Answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): Using Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached to store session data and cache reads introduces the following issues: Memcached is a simple, in-memory key-value store that shards data without replication. If a node or an Availability Zone fails, all session data on that node is lost. Memcached does not provide automatic failover or persistence, so you cannot guarantee high availability for user sessions. The requirement is to maintain session state reliably across AZs; Memcached alone cannot meet that SLA. Option C (INCORRECT): Migrating the relational MySQL database to Amazon DynamoDB and using DAX plus DynamoDB for session state has drawbacks in this context: This represents a major database paradigm shift (relational → NoSQL), requiring extensive application rewrites and redesign of the data model. DynamoDB Accelerators (DAX) provide in-memory caching for read-heavy workloads, but DAX clusters have specific consistency and availability trade-offs that complicate session handling. The question explicitly calls out a MySQL database; replacing it with DynamoDB isn’t the simplest path to high availability and scalability for an existing relational application. Option D (INCORRECT): Keeping Amazon RDS for MySQL in a single Availability Zone fails to meet the high-availability requirement: A single-AZ RDS instance has no standby for failover—if that AZ goes down, the database becomes unavailable. This design does not provide the resilience needed across three Availability Zones. Option A (CORRECT): This solution addresses both scaling and high availability for all tiers: Amazon RDS for MySQL with Multi-AZ automatically provisions a synchronous standby in a separate AZ and handles failover seamlessly. Amazon ElastiCache for Redis (in a replication group with Multi-AZ) stores session state and caches reads, ensuring that session data survives node or AZ failures. Web servers in an Auto Scaling group spread across three AZs behind an Application Load Balancer automatically scale out to meet traffic spikes and provide redundancy. Summary: We learned how to build a three-tier, highly available, and auto-scaling web application by leveraging RDS Multi-AZ for database resilience, ElastiCache Redis for fault-tolerant session storage and caching, and EC2 Auto Scaling across multiple AZs for the web tier. This question falls under Domain 2 – Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company is designing an event-driven order processing system. Each order requires multiple validation steps after the order is created. An idempotent AWS Lambda function performs each validation step. Each validation step is independent from the other validation steps. Individual validation steps need only a subset of the order event information. The company wants to ensure that each validation step Lambda function has access to only the information from the order event that the function requires. The components of the order processing system should be loosely coupled to accommodate future business changes. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue for each validation step. Create a new Lambda function to transform the order data to the format that each validation step requires and to publish the messages to the appropriate SQS queues. Subscribe each validation step Lambda function to its corresponding SQS queue.

Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic. Subscribe the validation step Lambda functions to the SNS topic. Use message body filtering to send only the required data to each subscribed Lambda function.
Create an Amazon EventBridge event bus. Create an event rule for each validation step. Configure the input transformer to send only the required data to each target validation step Lambda function.

Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Create a new Lambda function to subscribe to the SQS queue and to transform the order data to the format that each validation step requires. Use the new Lambda function to perform synchronous invocations of the validation step Lambda functions in parallel on separate threads.
explanation: The correct answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): Create an Amazon SQS queue for each validation step, plus a Lambda “fan-out” transformer that reads the original order and publishes to each queue. This design adds an extra Lambda just to reshape and route messages—unnecessary overhead in both code maintenance and cost. Using SQS alone does not natively support payload transformation; you must write and manage that transformer function yourself. Fan-out via multiple queues is more complex than needed for simple, independent validation steps. Option B (INCORRECT): Create a single SNS topic, subscribe each validation Lambda, and use message‐body filtering. SNS message filtering only works on message attributes, not on the JSON body fields—so you cannot selectively strip out unused data. There’s no built-in SNS feature to transform or reshape the payload per subscriber; each function still receives the full event. This fails the requirement to expose only the subset of order attributes needed by each validation step. Option D (INCORRECT): Use a single SQS queue, a transformer Lambda, and then synchronously invoke each validation Lambda in parallel threads. Synchronous invocation from one Lambda breaks loose coupling and introduces complexity in error handling and scaling. Managing threads or parallel invocations inside a Lambda is non-idiomatic and can lead to throttling or resource contention. You lose the simplicity and native decoupling that an event-driven, rule-based system provides. Option C (CORRECT): Create an Amazon EventBridge event bus, define one rule per validation step, and use each rule’s input transformer to send only the required data to its target Lambda. EventBridge natively supports multiple, independent event rules that route to different targets—perfect for loose coupling. Each rule’s input transformer can select and reshape only the subset of event fields needed by its validation Lambda. No extra “dispatcher” Lambda is required; EventBridge handles fan-out, transformation, and routing at scale. In summary, using Amazon EventBridge with per‐rule input transformers satisfies all requirements: loose coupling, scalable fan-out, and selective data exposure. This question falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company wants to build a map of its IT infrastructure to identify and enforce policies on resources that pose security risks. The company's security team must be able to query data in the IT infrastructure map and quickly identify security risks.Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Use Amazon RDS to store the data. Use SQL to query the data to identify security risks.
Use Amazon Neptune to store the data. Use SPARQL to query the data to identify security risks.
Use Amazon Redshift to store the data. Use SQL to query the data to identify security risks.
Use Amazon DynamoDB to store the data. Use PartiQL to query the data to identify security risks.
explanation: The correct answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): Use Amazon RDS to store the data. While a relational database can hold infrastructure data, modeling complex relationships (such as network paths, security group associations, IAM roles, etc.) requires many JOINs and schema changes. This leads to high operational overhead and poor query performance for graph-style queries. Option C (INCORRECT): Use Amazon Redshift to store the data. Redshift is designed for analytical workloads on large tabular datasets, not for traversing highly connected graph data. Querying relationships in a star schema adds complexity and maintenance effort, increasing operational overhead. Option D (INCORRECT): Use Amazon DynamoDB to store the data. DynamoDB is a key-value and document database. Although you can store graph data in a single table, querying multi-hop relationships requires complex data modeling or multiple requests, which increases development and operational burden. Option B (CORRECT): Use Amazon Neptune to store the data. Neptune is a fully managed graph database service that natively supports fast traversal of relationships using SPARQL or Gremlin. It minimizes operational overhead because Amazon handles backups, scaling, patching, and high availability. Security teams can efficiently query the graph to identify risky resource connections and enforce policies. In summary, we learned that for building and querying an IT-infrastructure map—where relationships between resources are critical—a purpose-built graph database like Amazon Neptune provides the least operational overhead and best performance. This question belongs to Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: An ecommerce company is running a multi-tier application on AWS. The front-end and backend tiers both run on Amazon EC2, and the database runs on Amazon RDS for MySQL. The backend tier communicates with the RDS instance. There are frequent calls to return identical datasets from the database that are causing performance slowdowns. Which action should be taken to improve the performance of the backend?
options: Implement Amazon SNS to store the database calls.
Implement Amazon ElastiCache to cache the large datasets.
Implement an RDS for MySQL read replica to cache database calls.
Implement Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to stream the calls to the database.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): “Implement Amazon SNS to store the database calls.” Amazon SNS is a pub/sub messaging service—it does not cache or accelerate database query results. SNS is used for notifications and message fan-out, not for reducing read latency from an RDS database. Option C (INCORRECT): “Implement an RDS for MySQL read replica to cache database calls.” Read replicas help with horizontal scaling of read traffic, but they do not cache repeated identical queries at the application tier. Each query still goes over the network to the replica, so latency improvements are modest compared to an in-memory cache. Option D (INCORRECT): “Implement Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to stream the calls to the database.” Kinesis Data Firehose is for streaming and loading data into destinations such as S3, Redshift, or Elasticsearch—it is not a caching or performance-boosting layer for real-time query results. This does not address the need to reduce repeated read latency on the backend tier. Option B (CORRECT): “Implement Amazon ElastiCache to cache the large datasets.” ElastiCache (Redis or Memcached) provides an in-memory caching layer, which can store frequently accessed query results close to your application. Caching reduces the number of direct calls to RDS, greatly improving read performance and lowering database load. This approach is the standard AWS solution for accelerating read-heavy workloads with identical datasets. In summary, by introducing ElastiCache you can serve repeat reads from memory instead of querying RDS each time, yielding significant performance gains for your backend tier. This question belongs to Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company is building a microservices-based application that will be deployed on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). The microservices will interact with each other. The company wants to ensure that the application is observable to identify performance issues in the future.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Configure the application to use Amazon ElastiCache to reduce the number of requests that are sent to the microservices.
Configure Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights to collect metrics from the EKS clusters. Configure AWS X-Ray to trace the requests between the microservices.
Configure AWS CloudTrail to review the API calls. Build an Amazon QuickSight dashboard to observe the microservice interactions.
Use AWS Trusted Advisor to understand the performance of the application.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Let’s step through why A, C, and D are not correct, and why B is the right choice: Option A (INCORRECT): • Amazon ElastiCache is a caching solution to reduce backend load, not an observability tool. • It does not provide metrics, logs, or traces of inter-service calls. • Caching addresses performance optimization, not visibility into microservice interactions. Option C (INCORRECT): • AWS CloudTrail records AWS API calls (who, when, what), not intra-cluster HTTP/gRPC calls between your pods. • Amazon QuickSight is a BI/dashboard tool, but you’d first need logs or metrics; it doesn’t collect them itself. • You would not capture service-to-service traces or performance metrics with this approach. Option D (INCORRECT): • AWS Trusted Advisor provides recommendations on cost, security, performance best practices for AWS resources—but it does not instrument or trace your application. • It cannot collect real-time metrics or distributed traces of your microservices. Option B (CORRECT): • Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights automatically collects CPU, memory, disk, and network metrics from your EKS clusters and nodes. • AWS X-Ray instruments your application to record distributed traces, showing latency and error rates across microservice calls. • Together, they provide both cluster-level metrics and end-to-end request tracing—fulfilling the observability requirement. Summary: We’ve learned that effective observability for a microservices application on EKS requires both metrics (via CloudWatch Container Insights) and distributed tracing (via AWS X-Ray). This question falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures, since it focuses on monitoring performance and identifying bottlenecks.

question: The DNS provider that hosts a company's domain name records is experiencing outages that cause service disruption for a website running on AWS. The company needs to migrate to a more resilient managed DNS service and wants the service to run on AWS. What should a solutions architect do to rapidly migrate the DNS hosting service?
options: Create an Amazon Route 53 public hosted zone for the domain name. Import the zone file containing the domain records hosted by the previous provider.
Create an Amazon Route 53 private hosted zone for the domain name. Import the zone file containing the domain records hosted by the previous provider.
Create a Simple AD directory in AWS. Enable zone transfer between the DNS provider and AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory for the domain records.

Create an Amazon Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint in the VPC. Specify the IP addresses that the provider's DNS will forward DNS queries to. Configure the provider's DNS to forward DNS queries for the domain to the IP addresses that are specified in the inbound endpoint.
explanation: The correct Answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): Creates a private hosted zone, which is only accessible within specified VPCs. It cannot serve public internet DNS queries and therefore cannot replace a public DNS provider. Option C (INCORRECT): Involves AWS Directory Service for Microsoft AD and zone transfers—this setup is aimed at Active Directory workloads, not hosting public DNS records for a website. Option D (INCORRECT): A Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint allows on-premises resolvers to query private zones in your VPC. It does not host or serve public DNS records for an internet-facing domain. Option A (CORRECT): Create an Amazon Route 53 public hosted zone for the domain and import the existing zone file. This rapidly migrates all DNS records to a highly available, managed AWS service that serves the internet. In summary, importing your DNS zone file into a Route 53 public hosted zone is the fastest way to replace an external DNS provider and ensure resilient, globally distributed name resolution. This question falls under Domain 2 – Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company wants to host a scalable web application on AWS. The application will be accessed by users from different geographic regions of the world. Application users will be able to download and upload unique data up to gigabytes in size. The development team wants a cost-effective solution to minimize upload and download latency and maximize performance. What should a solutions architect do to accomplish this?
options: Use Amazon S3 with Transfer Acceleration to host the application.
Use Amazon S3 with CacheControl headers to host the application.
Use Amazon EC2 with Auto Scaling and Amazon CloudFront to host the application.
Use Amazon EC2 with Auto Scaling and Amazon ElastiCache to host the application.
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): Use Amazon S3 with CacheControl headers to host the application. Cache-Control headers only instruct browsers and intermediate caches how long to keep objects—they do not speed up uploads or optimize global network paths. This approach helps with download caching for static content, but it provides no benefit for large uploads or cross-continent latency reductions. Option C (INCORRECT): Use Amazon EC2 with Auto Scaling and Amazon CloudFront to host the application. CloudFront accelerates content delivery (downloads) by caching at edge locations, but it does not accelerate uploads. Users uploading gigabytes of data back to EC2 instances would still face high latency and variable performance because uploads traverse the public internet directly to your EC2 fleet. Option D (INCORRECT): Use Amazon EC2 with Auto Scaling and Amazon ElastiCache to host the application. ElastiCache is an in-memory caching service for database query results and session data, not for large file storage or transfer optimization. This setup neither addresses global upload/download latency nor provides a cost‐effective mechanism for distributing multi‐gigabyte file transfers. Option A (CORRECT): Use Amazon S3 with Transfer Acceleration to host the application. S3 Transfer Acceleration leverages Amazon CloudFront’s globally distributed edge locations to optimize network path and routing for both uploads and downloads. Clients upload data to the nearest edge location over a long-lived optimized connection, and AWS’s backbone network delivers it to the S3 bucket, minimizing latency. This solution is fully managed, scales automatically to handle gigabyte‐sized transfers, and only incurs modest per-GB acceleration fees on top of standard S3 storage. In summary, Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration is the most cost-effective way to minimize upload and download latency and maximize performance for a global audience handling large files. This question falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company has multiple Amazon RDS DB instances that run in a development AWS account. All the instances have tags to identify them as development resources. The company needs the development DB instances to run on a schedule only during business hours.Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to identify RDS instances that need to be stopped. Create an AWS Lambda function to start and stop the RDS instances.
Create an AWS Trusted Advisor report to identify RDS instances to be started and stopped. Create an AWS Lambda function to start and stop the RDS instances.
Create AWS Systems Manager State Manager associations to start and stop the RDS instances.
Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that invokes AWS Lambda functions to start and stop the RDS instances.
explanation: The correct answer is D. Option A (INCORRECT): CloudWatch alarms monitor metrics, not schedules. You cannot directly schedule start/stop actions by tags using CloudWatch alarms. You would still need a scheduler (like EventBridge) to trigger the alarm or Lambda, adding extra complexity and overhead. Option B (INCORRECT): AWS Trusted Advisor provides best-practice recommendations, not operational scheduling or tagging-driven instance actions. Trusted Advisor reports are not designed to trigger automated start/stop operations on resources. Option C (INCORRECT): Systems Manager State Manager is intended for enforcing configuration state on managed instances (EC2/on-prem servers), not for controlling Amazon RDS lifecycle. RDS instances are not managed nodes under SSM State Manager, so you cannot directly start/stop them via State Manager associations. Option D (CORRECT): EventBridge supports cron or rate expressions to schedule events. You can create two rules—one for starting and one for stopping—during business hours. Each rule invokes a Lambda function that uses the RDS APIs (StartDBInstance/StopDBInstance). The function can filter by the “development” tag to target only the dev instances. This solution is fully serverless, requires minimal operational overhead, and scales automatically as you add more tagged instances. In summary, using an Amazon EventBridge scheduled rule paired with AWS Lambda to filter by tags and start/stop RDS instances satisfies the requirement with the least operational overhead. This question falls under Domain 4 – Design Cost-Optimized Architectures, since you’re optimizing costs by running development databases only during business hours.

question: A company stores user data in AWS. The data is used continuously with peak usage during business hours. Access patterns vary, with some data not being used for months at a time. A solutions architect must choose a cost-effective solution that maintains the highest level of durability while maintaining high availability. Which storage solution meets these requirements?
options: Amazon S3 Standard
Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering
Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive
Amazon S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA)
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): Amazon S3 Standard Offers 99.99% availability and 11 9’s durability. Costs are high for data that goes unused for long periods. Does not automatically optimize for infrequent access patterns, so not cost‐effective when usage varies widely. Option C (INCORRECT): Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive Provides lowest-cost storage for long-term archives. Retrieval times can range from 12 hours to 48 hours—unsuitable for data that may be needed on demand. Designed for rarely accessed archives, not for continuous or unpredictable access during business hours. Option D (INCORRECT): Amazon S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access Reduces cost by storing data in a single Availability Zone. Lower durability (single AZ) and lower availability compared to multi-AZ classes. Does not meet the requirement for “highest level of durability” or full availability. Option B (CORRECT): Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering Automatically moves objects between frequent and infrequent access tiers based on usage. Maintains 11 9’s durability and 99.9% availability for the infrequent tier (and 99.99% for the frequent tier). Eliminates retrieval fees and operational overhead—ideal for unpredictable access patterns and cost optimization. Summary: We have learned that S3 Intelligent-Tiering is the best fit when you need high durability, high availability, and automated cost optimization for data with varying and unpredictable access patterns. This question belongs to Domain 4 – Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company deployed a serverless application that uses Amazon DynamoDB as a database layer. The application has experienced a large increase in users. The company wants to improve database response time from milliseconds to microseconds and to cache requests to the database. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Use DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX).
Migrate the database to Amazon Redshift.
Migrate the database to Amazon RDS.
Use Amazon ElastiCache for Redis.
explanation: The correct Answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): “Migrate the database to Amazon Redshift.” Amazon Redshift is a data warehousing solution optimized for complex analytical queries on large datasets, not for low-latency, microsecond‐level lookups. It introduces significant operational overhead and cost, and does not provide an integrated, transparent cache for DynamoDB workloads. Option C (INCORRECT): “Migrate the database to Amazon RDS.” Amazon RDS is a managed relational database service with typical response times in the single‐ to low-millisecond range. It requires schema redesign, data migration, and additional maintenance overhead, and still won’t meet microsecond‐level latency requirements. Option D (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon ElastiCache for Redis.” While ElastiCache can cache data and reduce latency, you must build, maintain, and synchronize a separate caching layer in your application logic. This adds operational complexity (key management, cache invalidation, failover) rather than providing a seamless, low-overhead integration with DynamoDB. Option A (CORRECT): “Use DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX).” DAX is a fully managed, in-memory cache designed specifically for DynamoDB. It accelerates reads from milliseconds to microseconds. It offers transparent, write-through and read-through caching with minimal application changes and near-zero operational overhead. No additional cache-management code or infrastructure is needed—DAX handles replication, failover, and maintenance for you. In this discussion we learned that DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is the ideal choice to achieve microsecond-level latency and caching with the least operational overhead. This question belongs to Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A startup company is hosting a website for its customers on an Amazon EC2 instance. The website consists of a stateless Python application and a MySQL database. The website serves only a small amount of traffic. The company is concerned about the reliability of the instance and needs to migrate to a highly available architecture. The company cannot modify the application code.Which combination of actions should a solutions architect take to achieve high availability for the website? (Choose two.)
options: Provision an internet gateway in each Availability Zone in use.
Migrate the database to an Amazon RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ DB instance.
Migrate the database to Amazon DynamoDB, and enable DynamoDB auto scaling.
Use AWS DataSync to synchronize the database data across multiple EC2 instances.
Create an Application Load Balancer to distribute traffic to an Auto Scaling group of EC2 instances that are distributed across two Availability Zones.
explanation: The correct answer is B, E Option A (INCORRECT): • You do not need to provision an Internet Gateway in each Availability Zone. An Internet Gateway is a VPC-level construct that provides Internet access for the entire VPC, not per-AZ. • This action does not address high availability of the application or the database. Option C (INCORRECT): • Migrating the database to DynamoDB would require code changes (to use a NoSQL API instead of MySQL). • The requirement states you cannot modify the application code. Option D (INCORRECT): • AWS DataSync is not used for live, multi-AZ replication of a running MySQL database. • It is designed for data transfer and periodic synchronization— it cannot replace real database replication for high availability. Option B (CORRECT): • Amazon RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ provides synchronous standby replication in a different Availability Zone, ensuring automatic failover without code changes. • This meets the requirement for a highly available database. Option E (CORRECT): • An Application Load Balancer distributes traffic across an Auto Scaling group of EC2 instances in multiple Availability Zones, providing fault tolerance at the compute layer. • Because the Python app is stateless, you can scale out/in and handle instance failures automatically. In summary, migrating the database to an Amazon RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ instance (Option B) and placing the stateless application behind an ALB with EC2 Auto Scaling across two AZs (Option E) ensures high availability without modifying application code. This question belongs to Domain 2 – Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company is creating a new application that will store a large amount of data. The data will be analyzed hourly and will be modified by several Amazon EC2 Linux instances that are deployed across multiple Availability Zones. The needed amount of storage space will continue to grow for the next 6 months. Which storage solution should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?
options: Store the data in Amazon S3 Glacier. Update the S3 Glacier vault policy to allow access to the application instances.
Store the data in an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. Mount the EBS volume on the application instances.
Store the data in an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Mount the file system on the application instances.
Store the data in an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) Provisioned IOPS volume shared between the application instances.
explanation: The correct answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): “Store the data in Amazon S3 Glacier. Update the S3 Glacier vault policy to allow access to the application instances.” Amazon S3 Glacier is designed for long-term archival and infrequent access. It is not suitable for hourly analysis or frequent read/write operations. Glacier retrievals introduce significant delays (minutes to hours) and costs, which violate the requirement for hourly analysis and regular modifications. Option B (INCORRECT): “Store the data in an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. Mount the EBS volume on the application instances.” An EBS volume can only be attached to a single EC2 instance at a time (per AZ). It does not support concurrent mounts across multiple Availability Zones. The application needs to share and modify data across several instances in multiple AZs, which EBS by itself cannot handle. Option D (INCORRECT): “Store the data in an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) Provisioned IOPS volume shared between the application instances.” Even Provisioned IOPS EBS volumes cannot be concurrently mounted by multiple EC2 instances across AZs. It would require complex clustering solutions (e.g., EBS Multi-Attach with Nitro-based instances), but still limited to a single AZ—failing the multi-AZ requirement. Option C (CORRECT): “Store the data in an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Mount the file system on the application instances.” Amazon EFS provides a fully managed, NFS-based file system that can be mounted concurrently on multiple EC2 Linux instances across Availability Zones. EFS automatically scales storage capacity as data grows—perfect for a dataset that “will continue to grow for the next 6 months.” It supports low-latency access and consistent performance suitable for hourly data analysis and frequent modifications. Summary: We learned that for shared, scalable, and multi-AZ file storage with frequent read/write access, Amazon EFS is the ideal choice. This question falls under Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures, as it focuses on selecting a storage solution that delivers performance, scalability, and availability across multiple instances and Availability Zones.

question: A solutions architect is designing an asynchronous application to process credit card data validation requests for a bank. The application must be secure and be able to process each request at least once. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Use AWS Lambda event source mapping. Set Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) standard queues as the event source. Use AWS Key Management Service (SSE-KMS) for encryption. Add the kms:Decrypt permission for the Lambda execution role.

Use AWS Lambda event source mapping. Use Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queues as the event source. Use SQS managed encryption keys (SSE-SQS) for encryption. Add the encryption key invocation permission for the Lambda function.

Use the AWS Lambda event source mapping. Set Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queues as the event source. Use AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS). Add the kms:Decrypt permission for the Lambda execution role.

Use the AWS Lambda event source mapping. Set Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) standard queues as the event source. Use AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS) for encryption. Add the encryption key invocation permission for the Lambda function.
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): “Use AWS Lambda event source mapping. Use Amazon SQS FIFO queues as the event source. Use SQS managed encryption keys (SSE-SQS) for encryption. Add the encryption key invocation permission for the Lambda function.” SSE-SQS already uses an AWS-managed key so you do not need to grant any decryption permissions to your Lambda — AWS handles that automatically. FIFO queues incur additional per-request charges compared to standard queues, yet the requirement only calls for at-least-once processing, not strict ordering. Option C (INCORRECT): “Use AWS Lambda event source mapping. Set Amazon SQS FIFO queues as the event source. Use AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS). Add the kms:Decrypt permission for the Lambda execution role.” This ties you to the higher cost of FIFO queues plus AWS KMS request fees — not cost-effective when FIFO ordering isn’t required. Option D (INCORRECT): “Use AWS Lambda event source mapping. Set Amazon SQS standard queues as the event source. Use AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS). Add the encryption key invocation permission for the Lambda function.” The permission description is vague — you must explicitly grant kms:Decrypt to the Lambda role. Still uses SSE-KMS (with per-request charges) when SSE-SQS or standard queue-only encryption could reduce cost. Option A (CORRECT): “Use AWS Lambda event source mapping. Set Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) standard queues as the event source. Use AWS Key Management Service (SSE-KMS) for encryption. Add the kms:Decrypt permission for the Lambda execution role.” SQS standard queues provide the required at-least-once delivery at the lowest per-request cost. SSE-KMS meets the security requirement with customer-controlled encryption keys, and granting kms:Decrypt to Lambda enables decryption during processing. No extra FIFO charges or unnecessary IAM permissions — this is the most cost-effective secure solution. In summary, we evaluated queue types (standard vs FIFO), encryption options (SSE-SQS vs SSE-KMS), and IAM permissions to ensure secure, at-least-once processing at minimal cost. This question belongs to Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company is implementing a shared storage solution for a gaming application that is hosted in the AWS Cloud. The company needs the ability to use Lustre clients to access data. The solution must be fully managed.Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Create an AWS DataSync task that shares the data as a mountable file system. Mount the file system to the application server.
Create an AWS Storage Gateway file gateway. Create a file share that uses the required client protocol. Connect the application server to the file share.
Create an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system, and configure it to support Lustre. Attach the file system to the origin server. Connect the application server to the file system.
Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system. Attach the file system to the origin server. Connect the application server to the file system.
explanation: The correct answer is D. Option A (INCORRECT): “Create an AWS DataSync task that shares the data as a mountable file system. Mount the file system to the application server.” DataSync is a data transfer service, not a managed file system. You cannot mount a DataSync task as a live, shared file system. It simply moves or replicates data between storage locations; it does not provide POSIX-compliant file access or Lustre protocol support. Option B (INCORRECT): “Create an AWS Storage Gateway file gateway. Create a file share that uses the required client protocol. Connect the application server to the file share.” Storage Gateway File Gateway supports NFS and SMB, but not the Lustre protocol. It caches data locally for on-premises workloads; it’s not a pure, fully managed Lustre file system in the cloud. Option C (INCORRECT): “Create an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system, and configure it to support Lustre. Attach the file system to the origin server. Connect the application server to the file system.” Amazon EFS provides NFS v4.1/4.2 access, but it does not natively support the Lustre protocol. You cannot “configure” EFS as a Lustre file system; that capability is provided by Amazon FSx for Lustre. Option D (CORRECT): “Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system. Attach the file system to the origin server. Connect the application server to the file system.” Amazon FSx for Lustre is a fully managed service that provides a high-performance, POSIX-compliant file system accessible via the native Lustre protocol. It integrates seamlessly with compute instances and supports multiple Lustre clients, making it ideal for shared gaming workloads. In summary, we learned that Amazon FSx for Lustre is the only fully managed AWS service that offers native Lustre protocol support and POSIX-compliant shared storage. This question falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures, as it requires selecting a storage solution optimized for performance and shared access.

question: A company is using a SQL database to store movie data that is publicly accessible. The database runs on an Amazon RDS Single-AZ DB instance. A script runs queries at random intervals each day to record the number of new movies that have been added to the database. The script must report a final total during business hours. The company's development team notices that the database performance is inadequate for development tasks when the script is running. A solutions architect must recommend a solution to resolve this issue. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Modify the DB instance to be a Multi-AZ deployment.
Create a read replica of the database. Configure the script to query only the read replica.
Instruct the development team to manually export the entries in the database at the end of each day.
Use Amazon ElastiCache to cache the common queries that the script runs against the database.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): “Modify the DB instance to be a Multi-AZ deployment.” • Multi-AZ provides high availability and automatic failover, but it does not offload read traffic—every query still hits the primary. Performance under load remains the same. • This fails to isolate the heavy reporting script from the development workload. Option C (INCORRECT): “Instruct the development team to manually export the entries in the database at the end of each day.” • Manual exports introduce human error and operational overhead. • They do not address real-time performance degradation during the script run. Option D (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon ElastiCache to cache the common queries that the script runs against the database.” • Caching helps only if queries are repeated and cache-friendly. A script counting “new movies” at random intervals will likely bust the cache frequently. • You must design invalidation strategies and manage cluster sizing—additional operational complexity. Option B (CORRECT): “Create a read replica of the database. Configure the script to query only the read replica.” • Read replicas offload read traffic from the primary, isolating the heavy reporting script from development queries. • Amazon RDS manages replication and failover automatically with minimal operational overhead. • This approach meets the requirement to keep production performance high while the script runs. In summary, offloading read-only workloads to a read replica is the simplest, lowest-overhead way to preserve production performance. This question falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company has multiple AWS accounts in an organization in AWS Organizations that different business units use. The company has multiple offices around the world. The company needs to update security group rules to allow new office CIDR ranges or to remove old CIDR ranges across the organization. The company wants to centralize the management of security group rules to minimize the administrative overhead that updating CIDR ranges requires. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Create VPC security groups in the organization's management account. Update the security groups when a CIDR range update is necessary.

Create a VPC customer managed prefix list that contains the list of CIDRs. Use AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) to share the prefix list across the organization. Use the prefix list in the security groups across the organization.

Create an AWS managed prefix list. Use an AWS Security Hub policy to enforce the security group update across the organization. Use an AWS Lambda function to update the prefix list automatically when the CIDR ranges change.

Create security groups in a central administrative AWS account. Create an AWS Firewall Manager common security group policy for the whole organization. Select the previously created security groups as primary groups in the policy.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): Create VPC security groups in the management account and update them when CIDR ranges change. This does not scale across multiple AWS accounts—each account would need its own security group references or peering, increasing overhead. Changes in the management account won’t automatically propagate to other accounts’ security groups. Administrative overhead remains high because you’d still need to update multiple resources manually or with custom tooling. Option C (INCORRECT): Create an AWS managed prefix list and use Security Hub policies plus Lambda to auto-update it. You cannot create or modify AWS managed prefix lists—they are read-only lists provided by AWS (e.g., for Amazon services). Security Hub is for security posture and compliance checks, not for enforcing or auto-updating VPC configurations. Introducing Lambda functions and custom automation adds complexity and cost compared to a simple prefix list share. Option D (INCORRECT): Use Firewall Manager to deploy a common security group policy from a central account. AWS Firewall Manager can audit or enforce security group rules but primarily for AWS WAF, Shield Advanced, or AWS Network Firewall—its VPC SG support is limited. Firewall Manager policies add service costs and complexity; they are overkill for just sharing CIDR sets. Updating CIDRs would still require updating the policy in Firewall Manager, not as seamless as a shared prefix list. Option B (CORRECT): Create a customer-managed prefix list with all office CIDRs, share it via AWS RAM, and reference it in security groups in every account. Customer-managed prefix lists let you centrally maintain your CIDR entries in one place. AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) allows you to share that prefix list across all AWS accounts in your Organization with no additional cost. Every security group using the shared prefix list automatically sees updates—minimizing administrative overhead and keeping costs lowest. In summary, using a shared customer-managed prefix list via AWS RAM (Option B) centralizes CIDR management, reduces manual updates, and is the most cost-effective approach. This question falls under Domain 4 – Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company has an application that ingests incoming messages. Dozens of other applications and microservices then quickly consume these messages. The number of messages varies drastically and sometimes increases suddenly to 100,000 each second. The company wants to decouple the solution and increase scalability. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Persist the messages to Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics. Configure the consumer applications to read and process the messages.
Deploy the ingestion application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group to scale the number of EC2 instances based on CPU metrics.

Write the messages to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with a single shard. Use an AWS Lambda function to preprocess messages and store them in Amazon DynamoDB. Configure the consumer applications to read from DynamoDB to process the messages.

Publish the messages to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic with multiple Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SOS) subscriptions. Configure the consumer applications to process the messages from the queues.
explanation: The correct answer is D. Option A (INCORRECT): Persisting messages to Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics is not appropriate because Kinesis Data Analytics is used for real-time analytics on streaming data, not for durable message ingestion and fan-out to multiple consumers. Consumer applications cannot directly subscribe to Kinesis Data Analytics; they need a proper streaming platform like Kinesis Data Streams or a pub/sub service. Option B (INCORRECT): Scaling the ingestion application on EC2 instances with Auto Scaling based on CPU does not decouple producers and consumers. This approach ties message ingestion tightly to compute resources, making it harder to handle sudden spikes of 100,000 messages per second and complicating consumer scaling. Option C (INCORRECT): Using a single-shard Kinesis Data Stream cannot support 100,000 messages per second (a single shard handles up to 1 MB/sec or 1,000 records/sec). Additionally, writing to DynamoDB and having consumers poll it adds unnecessary latency and complexity. This design fails both scalability and decoupling goals. Option D (CORRECT): Publishing messages to an SNS topic with multiple SQS subscriptions provides a fully managed pub/sub fan-out pattern. Each consumer queue (SQS) scales independently, handles sudden spikes, and ensures reliable delivery. Decoupling is achieved as producers publish to SNS and consumers process messages from their own SQS queues at their own pace. In summary, we've learned that for high-throughput, highly scalable, and decoupled message ingestion with many consumers, the SNS-to-SQS fan-out pattern is the optimal AWS solution. This question belongs to Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A news company that has reporters all over the world is hosting its broadcast system on AWS. The reporters send live broadcasts to the broadcast system. The reporters use software on their phones to send live streams through the Real Time Messaging Protocol (RTMP). A solutions architect must design a solution that gives the reporters the ability to send the highest quality streams. The solution must provide accelerated TCP connections back to the broadcast system.What should the solutions architect use to meet these requirements?
options: Amazon CloudFront
AWS Global Accelerator
AWS Client VPN
Amazon EC2 instances and AWS Elastic IP addresses
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): Amazon CloudFront CloudFront’s RTMP distribution is deprecated and only supports on-demand streaming from S3 to clients, not real-time broadcaster push. It’s optimized for HTTP content delivery rather than bidirectional TCP acceleration required for live RTMP feeds. Option C (INCORRECT): AWS Client VPN AWS Client VPN delivers secure network access via SSL VPN but does not provide global TCP acceleration. It adds encryption overhead and is not designed for optimizing real-time media traffic performance. Option D (INCORRECT): Amazon EC2 Instances and Elastic IP Addresses Manually provisioning EC2 servers with Elastic IPs globally doesn’t leverage AWS’s Anycast network or performance-based routing. This approach increases operational complexity and cannot guarantee the lowest latency or best path for live RTMP streams. Option B (CORRECT): AWS Global Accelerator Provides static Anycast IP addresses that route TCP traffic over AWS’s optimized global network, reducing latency, jitter, and packet loss. Automatically directs reporters’ RTMP streams to the nearest healthy endpoint, ensuring the highest quality live broadcasts. Fully managed service simplifies architecture and delivers consistent performance for real-time streaming worldwide. In summary, AWS Global Accelerator is the optimal choice for accelerating TCP-based RTMP streams from global reporters, offering low latency and resilient routing over the AWS backbone. This scenario falls under Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A global company runs its workloads on AWS. The company's application uses Amazon S3 buckets across AWS Regions for sensitive data storage and analysis. The company stores millions of objects in multiple S3 buckets daily. The company wants to identify all S3 buckets that are not versioning-enabled. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Set up an AWS CloudTrail event that has a rule to identify all S3 buckets that are not versioning-enabled across Regions.
Use Amazon S3 Storage Lens to identify all S3 buckets that are not versioning-enabled across Regions.
Enable IAM Access Analyzer for S3 to identify all S3 buckets that are not versioning-enabled across Regions.
Create an S3 Multi-Region Access Point to identify all S3 buckets that are not versioning-enabled across Regions.
explanation: The correct Answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): “Set up an AWS CloudTrail event that has a rule to identify all S3 buckets that are not versioning-enabled across Regions.” CloudTrail records API calls and configuration changes, but it does not provide an out-of-the-box report or dashboard summarizing which buckets currently have versioning disabled. You would need custom processing of CloudTrail logs or Athena queries to derive bucket configuration state—there’s no native “non-versioned buckets” alert in CloudTrail. Option C (INCORRECT): “Enable IAM Access Analyzer for S3 to identify all S3 buckets that are not versioning-enabled across Regions.” IAM Access Analyzer for S3 evaluates resource policies to flag overly permissive access (public or cross-account), not bucket versioning status. It does not scan or report configuration features like versioning—its focus is on access policies and security findings. Option D (INCORRECT): “Create an S3 Multi-Region Access Point to identify all S3 buckets that are not versioning-enabled across Regions.” S3 Multi-Region Access Points provide a single global endpoint for read/write operations across multiple buckets, simplifying data access but not auditing configurations. They do not include any mechanism to report which buckets have versioning disabled. Option B (CORRECT): “Use Amazon S3 Storage Lens to identify all S3 buckets that are not versioning-enabled across Regions.” S3 Storage Lens automatically collects organization- or account-level usage and activity metrics, including bucket configuration metrics such as “Buckets without versioning.” It provides a dashboard and the ability to export daily metrics (in CSV/Parquet) to S3, so you can see exactly which buckets are non-versioned across all Regions. No custom parsing or additional infrastructure is required—Storage Lens is designed for large-scale, cross-region insights into S3 best practices. In summary, S3 Storage Lens is the simplest, native AWS service that delivers a consolidated view of bucket versioning status across Regions without the need for custom log processing or policy checks. This question falls under Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company is building a new furniture inventory application. The company has deployed the application on a fleet ofAmazon EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zones. The EC2 instances run behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in their VPC. A solutions architect has observed that incoming traffic seems to favor one EC2 instance, resulting in latency for some requests. What should the solutions architect do to resolve this issue?
options: Disable session affinity (sticky sessions) on the ALB
Replace the ALB with a Network Load Balancer
Increase the number of EC2 instances in each Availability Zone
Adjust the frequency of the health checks on the ALB's target group
explanation: The correct answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): Replace the ALB with a Network Load Balancer An NLB operates at Layer 4 (transport layer) and doesn’t provide HTTP-aware routing features like stickiness out of the box. Switching to an NLB will not inherently balance traffic more evenly—if session affinity or other config issues remain, you’ll still see hot-spots. The requirement is to fix uneven distribution at the ALB level, not to change to a different load balancer type. Option C (INCORRECT): Increase the number of EC2 instances in each Availability Zone Adding more instances can improve overall capacity but will not address why one node is being favored. Even with more back-end servers, if the load balancer uses session affinity, new or sticky sessions can still go to the same instance. Option D (INCORRECT): Adjust the frequency of the health checks on the ALB’s target group Health checks determine whether an instance is considered healthy, not how traffic is distributed. Changing health-check intervals won’t rebalance existing connections or remove the bias toward one instance. Option A (CORRECT): Disable session affinity (sticky sessions) on the ALB Session affinity (also called “stickiness”) pins a client’s requests to the same target for the duration of a session cookie. When stickiness is enabled, new or returning clients will often hit the same instance, causing uneven load and latency spikes on that host. Disabling sticky sessions lets the ALB distribute each request evenly across all healthy targets, reducing hotspots and latency. In summary, we learned that session affinity can cause one server to become a bottleneck under an ALB—disabling stickiness restores true round-robin (or least-outstanding-requests) distribution. This question maps to Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures, since it focuses on optimizing request distribution and reducing latency.

question: A solutions architect is creating a data processing job that runs once daily and can take up to 2 hours to complete. If the job is interrupted, it has to restart from the beginning. How should the solutions architect address this issue in the MOST cost-effective manner?
options: Create a script that runs locally on an Amazon EC2 Reserved Instance that is triggered by a cron job.
Create an AWS Lambda function triggered by an Amazon EventBridge scheduled event.
Use an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) Fargate task triggered by an Amazon EventBridge scheduled event.
Use an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task running on Amazon EC2 triggered by an Amazon EventBridge scheduled event.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): “Create a script that runs locally on an Amazon EC2 Reserved Instance that is triggered by a cron job.” Reserved Instances require you to pay for capacity whether you're using it or not, leading to unnecessary costs since the job only runs 2 hours per day. If the instance goes down or the script fails, you still need to restart the entire job manually. Option B (INCORRECT): “Create an AWS Lambda function triggered by an Amazon EventBridge scheduled event.” AWS Lambda has a maximum execution timeout of 15 minutes, but the job can take up to 2 hours, so Lambda cannot complete the task. If the function fails partway, it would restart from the beginning, but you cannot extend Lambda beyond its timeout. Option D (INCORRECT): “Use an Amazon ECS task running on Amazon EC2 triggered by an Amazon EventBridge scheduled event.” You must keep EC2 instances running (or in auto-scaling groups) to host ECS tasks, incurring cost even when the job is idle. Managing the EC2 fleet adds operational overhead and does not optimize for a once-daily, 2-hour workload. Option C (CORRECT): “Use an Amazon ECS Fargate task triggered by an Amazon EventBridge scheduled event.” Fargate is a serverless compute engine for containers—there is no EC2 to manage or pay for when the task isn’t running. You pay only for the vCPU and memory resources consumed during the actual 2-hour job, making it highly cost-effective. If the job is interrupted, Fargate will stop the task and you can schedule it to restart at the next daily trigger, restarting from the beginning as required.
