In summary, a fully serverless stack (Option D) delivers the required high‐throughput, millisecond‐latency performance with the least operational effort. This question falls under Domain 3 – Design High‐Performing Architectures.

question: A solutions architect is designing a new hybrid architecture to extend a company's on-premises infrastructure to AWS. The company requires a highly available connection with consistent low latency to an AWS Region. The company needs to minimize costs and is willing to accept slower traffic if the primary connection fails. What should the solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
options: Provision an AWS Direct Connect connection to a Region. Provision a VPN connection as a backup if the primary Direct Connect connection fails.
Provision a VPN tunnel connection to a Region for private connectivity. Provision a second VPN tunnel for private connectivity and as a backup if the primary VPN connection fails.
Provision an AWS Direct Connect connection to a Region. Provision a second Direct Connect connection to the same Region as a backup if the primary Direct Connect connection fails.

Provision an AWS Direct Connect connection to a Region. Use the Direct Connect failover attribute from the AWS CLI to automatically create a backup connection if the primary Direct Connect connection fails.
explanation: The correct Answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): Provision a VPN tunnel connection to a Region for private connectivity, and provision a second VPN tunnel as a backup. VPN-only connections traverse the public internet, which can introduce variable latency and jitter—this does not meet the requirement for consistent low latency. Although it provides redundancy, it lacks the performance guarantee of Direct Connect as the primary path. Option C (INCORRECT): Provision two AWS Direct Connect connections to the same Region, one as primary and one as backup. While two Direct Connect links ensure high availability and low latency, duplicating Direct Connect doubles the cost. The requirement states “minimize costs” and being “willing to accept slower traffic if the primary connection fails,” so a VPN backup is more cost-effective. Option D (INCORRECT): Provision an AWS Direct Connect connection and use a non-existent “failover attribute” from the AWS CLI to automatically create a backup. There is no AWS CLI attribute that automatically provisions a backup connection—you must manually set up the backup (e.g., a VPN) and configure BGP for failover. This option is not supported by AWS and does not satisfy the need for a standby link you can rely on. Option A (CORRECT): Provision an AWS Direct Connect connection to a Region as the primary high-performance link. Then provision a VPN connection over the internet as a backup if the primary Direct Connect connection fails. Direct Connect provides a dedicated, low-latency network link that meets the primary performance requirement. Configuring an IPSec VPN as a failover is cost-effective and automatically routes traffic over the internet only when Direct Connect is unavailable. This design balances high availability, performance, and cost by using the VPN only in failure scenarios. In summary, we have learned how to design a hybrid network architecture that ensures consistent low latency with AWS Direct Connect and provides a cost-effective VPN backup for resiliency. This question belongs to Domain 2 - Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company runs its production workload on an Amazon Aurora MySQL DB cluster that includes six Aurora Replicas. The company wants near-real-time reporting queries from one of its departments to be automatically distributed across three of the Aurora Replicas. Those three replicas have a different compute and memory specification from the rest of the DB cluster.Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Create and use a custom endpoint for the workload
Create a three-node cluster clone and use the reader endpoint
Use any of the instance endpoints for the selected three nodes
Use the reader endpoint to automatically distribute the read-only workload
explanation: The correct answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): “Create a three-node cluster clone and use the reader endpoint.” A cluster clone is a one-time snapshot copy; it does not stay in sync in near-real-time with the primary cluster. Reporting queries would run against a static dataset, not the current production data. Maintaining and refreshing the clone would add operational overhead and latency. Option C (INCORRECT): “Use any of the instance endpoints for the selected three nodes.” Instance endpoints require you to implement client-side load-balancing or routing logic. There is no automatic distribution across the three replicas—you would have to manage connection pooling and failover yourself. This does not leverage Aurora’s built-in reader endpoint capabilities for grouping replicas. Option D (INCORRECT): “Use the reader endpoint to automatically distribute the read-only workload.” The standard reader endpoint balances queries across all Aurora Replicas in the cluster, not just the three with larger specs. It does not allow you to isolate or target a subset of replicas with different compute/memory sizes. Option A (CORRECT): “Create and use a custom endpoint for the workload.” Aurora custom endpoints let you define a reader endpoint that groups only the specified replicas (in this case, the three with the higher compute/memory specs). Queries sent to that custom endpoint are distributed automatically and evenly across just those replicas. This meets the requirement for near-real-time reporting without impacting the other replicas or the primary workload. From this discussion we’ve learned that Aurora’s custom reader endpoints are the right tool to isolate and load-balance read traffic across a specific subset of replicas. This question belongs to Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures, since it covers optimizing read scalability and performance.

question: A weather forecasting company needs to process hundreds of gigabytes of data with sub-millisecond latency. The company has a high performance computing (HPC) environment in its data center and wants to expand its forecasting capabilities. A solutions architect must identify a highly available cloud storage solution that can handle large amounts of sustained throughput. Files that are stored in the solution should be accessible to thousands of compute instances that will simultaneously access and process the entire dataset. What should the solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
options: Use Amazon FSx for Lustre scratch file systems.
Use Amazon FSx for Lustre persistent file systems.
Use Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) with Bursting Throughput mode.
Use Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) with Provisioned Throughput mode.
explanation: The correct answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): Use Amazon FSx for Lustre scratch file systems. Scratch file systems are designed for temporary, short-term workloads and exist only for the duration of the file system's lifetime. They do not provide multi-AZ high availability or automatic data replication for long-term storage. The requirement specifies a highly available cloud storage solution for sustained throughput, making scratch file systems unsuitable. Option C (INCORRECT): Use Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) with Bursting Throughput mode. EFS’s bursting mode ties throughput to stored data size and credits, which may throttle sustained high throughput needed for hundreds of gigabytes. Network File System (NFS) mounts introduce higher latency (milliseconds), not the sub-millisecond latency required. Therefore, EFS bursting cannot guarantee the necessary low latency and consistent throughput. Option D (INCORRECT): Use Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) with Provisioned Throughput mode. Provisioned throughput can deliver higher, consistent bandwidth, but EFS still incurs NFS overhead and millisecond-class latency. EFS is optimized for general-purpose file sharing, not for HPC workloads requiring sub-millisecond access and massive concurrent throughput. Thus, even provisioned EFS cannot meet the latency demands for HPC processing at scale. Option B (CORRECT): Use Amazon FSx for Lustre persistent file systems. FSx for Lustre delivers sub-millisecond latencies and multi-gigabyte per second throughput, ideal for HPC and large-scale data processing. Persistent Lustre file systems offer data durability, automatic multi-AZ replication, and high availability. Thousands of compute instances can mount the Lustre file system simultaneously and process the entire dataset with minimal I/O contention. In summary, Amazon FSx for Lustre persistent file systems best satisfy the requirements for sub-millisecond latency, sustained high throughput, simultaneous access by thousands of instances, and high availability. This scenario falls under Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company is reviewing a recent migration of a three-tier application to a VPC. The security team discovers that the principle of least privilege is not being applied to Amazon EC2 security group ingress and egress rules between the application tiers. What should a solutions architect do to correct this issue?
options: Create security group rules using the instance ID as the source or destination.
Create security group rules using the security group ID as the source or destination.
Create security group rules using the VPC CIDR blocks as the source or destination.
Create security group rules using the subnet CIDR blocks as the source or destination.
explanation: The correct answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): You cannot reference an individual EC2 instance ID in a security group rule. Security group rules only allow IP addresses/CIDR blocks or other security group IDs as sources or destinations. Relying on instance IDs would not function and is not supported by AWS. Option C (INCORRECT): Using the entire VPC CIDR block as a source or destination is overly permissive. This approach opens up access to every resource in the VPC, violating the principle of least privilege by allowing traffic from all subnets and instances. Option D (INCORRECT): Referencing a subnet CIDR block is also too broad. It permits any resource within that subnet to communicate, rather than limiting access to only the specific application tier, which again breaks the least‐privilege principle. Option B (CORRECT): By using the security group ID as the source or destination in your rules, you restrict traffic to only those instances that are members of the specified security group. This enforces least privilege between tiers—only the intended application tier can communicate with the next tier. In summary, we’ve learned that applying least privilege in AWS VPC security groups means scoping access as narrowly as possible—using security group IDs to allow only approved resources. This question falls under Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company has hired an external vendor to perform work in the company’s AWS account. The vendor uses an automated tool that is hosted in an AWS account that the vendor owns. The vendor does not have IAM access to the company’s AWS account. How should a solutions architect grant this access to the vendor?
options: Create an IAM role in the company’s account to delegate access to the vendor’s IAM role. Attach the appropriate IAM policies to the role for the permissions that the vendor requires.

Create an IAM user in the company’s account with a password that meets the password complexity requirements. Attach the appropriate IAM policies to the user for the permissions that the vendor requires.

Create an IAM group in the company’s account. Add the tool’s IAM user from the vendor account to the group. Attach the appropriate IAM policies to the group for the permissions that the vendor requires.

Create a new identity provider by choosing “AWS account” as the provider type in the IAM console. Supply the vendor’s AWS account ID and user name. Attach the appropriate IAM policies to the new provider for the permissions that the vendor requires.
explanation: The correct Answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): “Create an IAM user in the company’s account with a password that meets the password complexity requirements. Attach the appropriate IAM policies to the user for the permissions that the vendor requires.” You would have to manage long-term credentials for the vendor inside your own account. This violates the principle of least privilege and offloads credential management to you instead of the vendor. Not a best practice for granting external, cross-account access. Option C (INCORRECT): “Create an IAM group in the company’s account. Add the tool’s IAM user from the vendor account to the group. Attach the appropriate IAM policies to the group for the permissions that the vendor requires.” You cannot add an IAM user from another AWS account into a local IAM group. Cross-account access must be granted via role assumption, not group membership. Option D (INCORRECT): “Create a new identity provider by choosing ‘AWS account’ as the provider type in the IAM console. Supply the vendor’s AWS account ID and user name. Attach the appropriate IAM policies to the new provider for the permissions that the vendor requires.” The IAM identity provider feature is for SAML or OIDC, not for granting cross-account roles to another AWS account’s principals directly. You cannot attach IAM policies to an identity provider; policies must be on roles or users. Option A (CORRECT): “Create an IAM role in the company’s account to delegate access to the vendor’s IAM role. Attach the appropriate IAM policies to the role for the permissions that the vendor requires.” Establish a trust policy that allows the vendor’s AWS account (or a specific IAM role in it) to assume this role. The vendor retains control of its own credentials and can call STS:AssumeRole to gain temporary permissions in your account. Follows AWS best practices for cross-account access and the principle of least privilege. In summary, we learned that for cross-account automated tooling you should use an IAM role with an appropriate trust policy, allowing the vendor’s account to assume it. This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A solutions architect needs to connect a company's corporate network to its VPC to allow on-premises access to its AWS resources. The solution must provide encryption of all traffic between the corporate network and the VPC at the network layer and the session layer. The solution also must provide security controls to prevent unrestricted access between AWS and the on-premises systems. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Configure AWS Direct Connect to connect to the VPC. Configure the VPC route tables to allow and deny traffic between AWS and on premises as required.

Create an IAM policy to allow access to the AWS Management Console only from a defined set of corporate IP addresses. Restrict user access based on job responsibility by using an IAM policy and roles.

Configure AWS Site-to-Site VPN to connect to the VPConfigure route table entries to direct traffic from on premises to the VPConfigure instance security groups and network ACLs to allow only required traffic from on premises.

Configure AWS Transit Gateway to connect to the VPC. Configure route table entries to direct traffic from on premises to the VPC. Configure instance security groups and network ACLs to allow only required traffic from on premises.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): AWS Direct Connect provides a private, high-bandwidth connection, but it does not encrypt traffic at the network or session layer by default. Although you can combine Direct Connect with a VPN for encryption, the option as stated offers no built-in encryption and thus fails the requirement. Option B (INCORRECT): IAM policies control user and API access to AWS control plane resources—they do not establish encrypted network tunnels between on-premises and the VPC. This option does not address network-layer or session-layer encryption or routing of traffic into the VPC. Option D (INCORRECT): AWS Transit Gateway can centralize connectivity but does not inherently provide encryption; you must attach a VPN or other encrypted transport. The option does not mention establishing an IPsec tunnel and thus fails to satisfy the encryption requirement at both network and session layers. Option C (CORRECT): AWS Site-to-Site VPN establishes an IPsec tunnel that encrypts all traffic at the network (IPsec) and session (TLS) layers by default. You can control and restrict traffic using route table entries, security groups, and network ACLs to enforce least-privilege access between your on-premises network and the VPC. This solution directly meets the requirements for encrypted transport and fine-grained security controls. In summary, we learned that when a secure, encrypted connection is required between on-premises and AWS at both network and session layers—and with the need for controlled access—an AWS Site-to-Site VPN (Option C) is the appropriate choice. This question falls under Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company stores its data objects in Amazon S3 Standard storage. A solutions architect has found that 75% of the data is rarely accessed after 30 days. The company needs all the data to remain immediately accessible with the same high availability and resiliency, but the company wants to minimize storage costs. Which storage solution will meet these requirements?
options: Move the data objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days.
Move the data objects to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) after 30 days.
Move the data objects to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) after 30 days.
Move the data objects to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) immediately.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): Move the data objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days. Glacier Deep Archive is designed for long‐term retention with retrieval times of hours, not immediate access. The requirement specifies that all data must remain immediately accessible. Option C (INCORRECT): Move the data objects to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access after 30 days. S3 One Zone-IA stores data in a single Availability Zone, reducing resiliency and availability. The company requires the same high availability and resiliency as S3 Standard. Option D (INCORRECT): Move the data objects to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access immediately. Moving all objects immediately would incur higher costs for frequently accessed data during the first 30 days. Also, One Zone-IA does not meet the multi-AZ resiliency requirement. Option B (CORRECT): Move the data objects to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) after 30 days. S3 Standard-IA offers the same high durability (11 9s) and availability SLA as S3 Standard. It is optimized for data that is accessed less frequently but requires rapid, immediate retrieval. By transitioning after 30 days, only the 75% of rarely accessed objects incur lower storage fees, minimizing costs. In summary, using S3 Lifecycle to transition objects older than 30 days to S3 Standard-IA meets the need for immediate access, high resiliency, and cost savings. This question falls under Domain 4 – Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company hosts a website analytics application on a single Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instance. The analytics software is written in PHP and uses a MySQL database. The analytics software, the web server that provides PHP, and the database server are all hosted on the EC2 instance. The application is showing signs of performance degradation during busy times and is presenting 5xx errors. The company needs to make the application scale seamlessly. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Migrate the database to an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance. Create an AMI of the web application. Use the AMI to launch a second EC2 On-Demand Instance. Use an Application Load Balancer to distribute the load to each EC2 instance.

Migrate the database to an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance. Create an AMI of the web application. Use the AMI to launch a second EC2 On-Demand Instance. Use Amazon Route 53 weighted routing to distribute the load across the two EC2 instances.

Migrate the database to an Amazon Aurora MySQL DB instance. Create an AWS Lambda function to stop the EC2 instance and change the instance type. Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to invoke the Lambda function when CPU utilization surpasses 75%.

Migrate the database to an Amazon Aurora MySQL DB instance. Create an AMI of the web application. Apply the AMI to a launch template. Create an Auto Scaling group with the launch template Configure the launch template to use a Spot Fleet. Attach an Application Load Balancer to the Auto Scaling group.
explanation: The correct answer is D Let’s step through why options A, B, and C are not correct, and why D is the right choice: Option A (INCORRECT): “Migrate the database to RDS for MySQL, launch a second EC2 On-Demand instance, and use an Application Load Balancer.” This only gives you two fixed instances—there’s no auto-scaling based on actual load spikes. During high traffic, you may still experience performance issues if both instances are saturated. Cost remains high at all times because you pay for two On-Demand instances, even when traffic is low. Option B (INCORRECT): “Migrate the database to RDS for MySQL, launch a second EC2 On-Demand instance, and use Route 53 weighted routing.” Route 53 weighted routing is not a true load balancer—it doesn’t perform health checks or respond dynamically to instance load. Traffic distribution must be manually adjusted; it doesn’t auto-scale with demand. You risk sending traffic to unhealthy or overloaded instances. Option C (INCORRECT): “Migrate the database to Aurora MySQL, then use a Lambda function to change the EC2 instance type when CPU > 75%.” Vertical scaling (changing instance type) causes downtime while the instance stops, modifies, and restarts. This approach does not provide seamless, real-time scaling during traffic spikes. You still have a single EC2 instance; there’s no horizontal redundancy or elastic growth of the web tier. Option D (CORRECT): “Migrate the database to Aurora MySQL, bake an AMI of the web app, define a launch template, create an Auto Scaling group (using Spot Fleet for cost savings), and attach an Application Load Balancer.” Aurora MySQL delivers managed performance, high availability, and read scalability for the database layer. Auto Scaling group with ALB provides seamless horizontal scaling of the web tier based on demand. Using Spot instances in the fleet optimizes costs while maintaining capacity. This design meets both performance and cost-efficiency requirements automatically. In summary, we learned how to decouple and scale both the database and application tiers using managed services (Amazon Aurora and Auto Scaling with ALB), while optimizing costs with Spot instances. This solution falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures, as it ensures seamless, on-demand scaling and maintains performance during peak traffic.

question: A company uses AWS Organizations to create dedicated AWS accounts for each business unit to manage each business unit's account independently upon request. The root email recipient missed a notification that was sent to the root user email address of one account. The company wants to ensure that all future notifications are not missed. Future notifications must be limited to account administrators.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Configure the company’s email server to forward notification email messages that are sent to the AWS account root user email address to all users in the organization.

Configure all AWS account root user email addresses as distribution lists that go to a few administrators who can respond to alerts. Configure AWS account alternate contacts in the AWS Organizations console or programmatically.
Configure all AWS account root user email messages to be sent to one administrator who is responsible for monitoring alerts and forwarding those alerts to the appropriate groups.

Configure all existing AWS accounts and all newly created accounts to use the same root user email address. Configure AWS account alternate contacts in the AWS Organizations console or programmatically.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): • Asking the company’s email server to forward root‐user notifications is an external workaround and not an AWS‐recommended practice. • It leaves AWS unaware of that distribution and doesn’t leverage built-in AWS Organizations features for alternate contacts. • You cannot guarantee that forwarding rules will always catch every AWS notification or that they remain in sync with account changes. Option C (INCORRECT): • Centralizing all root‐account notifications to a single administrator introduces a single point of failure. • If that one administrator is unavailable, notifications could still be missed. • This approach does not spread responsibility across multiple administrators as required. Option D (INCORRECT): • AWS requires each root user email address to be unique across all accounts; you cannot reuse the same root email for multiple accounts. • This violates AWS account uniqueness constraints and undermines account segregation. • Even if it were possible, you’d still need alternate contacts configured for notifications to the right administrators. Option B (CORRECT): Configuring each root user email as a distribution list ensures that notifications go to multiple administrators simultaneously. Using AWS Organizations’ “Alternate Contacts” feature programmatically or via the console directs billing, operations, and security alerts to those designated distribution lists rather than the lone root email. This approach leverages built-in AWS functionality, avoids single points of failure, and keeps notification management within AWS’s supported framework. In summary, we learned how to ensure critical AWS notifications are reliably delivered to multiple administrators by using distribution lists as root emails coupled with AWS Organizations’ alternate contacts feature. This question falls under Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: An ecommerce company is running a seasonal online sale. The company hosts its website on Amazon EC2 instances spanning multiple Availability Zones. The company wants its website to manage sudden traffic increases during the sale.Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Create an Auto Scaling group that is large enough to handle peak traffic load. Stop half of the Amazon EC2 instances. Configure the Auto Scaling group to use the stopped instances to scale out when traffic increases.
Create an Auto Scaling group for the website. Set the minimum size of the Auto Scaling group so that it can handle high traffic volumes without the need to scale out.

Use Amazon CloudFront and Amazon ElastiCache to cache dynamic content with an Auto Scaling group set as the origin. Configure the Auto Scaling group with the instances necessary to populate CloudFront and ElastiCache. Scale in after the cache is fully populated.
Configure an Auto Scaling group to scale out as traffic increases. Create a launch template to start new instances from a preconfigured Amazon Machine Image (AMI).
explanation: The correct answer is D Option A (INCORRECT): • You cannot “stop” half of your Auto Scaling instances and then have Auto Scaling simply restart them on demand. Auto Scaling manages instances dynamically—it launches and terminates, but does not resume stopped instances to handle new load. • Even if stopping were supported, you’d still incur EBS storage costs and face slower cold starts, undermining cost-effectiveness and responsiveness. Option B (INCORRECT): • Setting the Auto Scaling group’s minimum size to handle peak traffic means you pay for all those instances 24/7, even during off-peak periods. • This approach defeats the purpose of Auto Scaling and is not cost-optimized for seasonal spikes. Option C (INCORRECT): • While CloudFront and ElastiCache can improve performance, caching dynamic ecommerce content is complex (cache invalidation, personalization) and adds architecture overhead. • Pre-warming caches with extra instances increases cost and operational complexity, so it’s not the most cost-effective for sudden traffic surges. Option D (CORRECT): • Use an Auto Scaling group with a launch template based on a prebuilt AMI: instances launch quickly with all required software/configuration already baked in. • Scale-out policies tied to metrics (CPU, request count) automatically add instances only when needed, and scale-in when load drops, minimizing costs. • This design leverages AWS managed scaling and AMIs for fast, reliable, and cost-optimized handling of traffic spikes. Summary: We’ve learned that the most cost-effective way to accommodate sudden traffic increases is to combine Auto Scaling with preconfigured AMIs via a launch template. This ensures fast, automated scaling and only pays for capacity when it’s actually needed. This question belongs to Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A solutions architect has created two IAM policies: Policy1 and Policy2. Both policies are attached to an IAM group. A cloud engineer is added as an IAM user to the IAM group. Which action will the cloud engineer be able to perform?
options: Deleting IAM users
Deleting directories
Deleting Amazon EC2 instances
Deleting logs from Amazon CloudWatch Logs
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): “Deleting IAM users.” Neither Policy1 nor Policy2 grants iam:DeleteUser permission. By default, IAM actions are denied unless explicitly allowed. Therefore the cloud engineer cannot delete IAM users. Option B (INCORRECT): “Deleting directories.” This refers to AWS Directory Service (e.g., ds:DeleteDirectory), which is unrelated to the EC2 and CloudWatch permissions in the attached policies. No allow statement for directory deletion exists in Policy1 or Policy2. Hence, the cloud engineer cannot delete directories. Option D (INCORRECT): “Deleting logs from Amazon CloudWatch Logs.” To delete CloudWatch log data you'd need actions like logs:DeleteLogGroup or logs:DeleteLogStream. Neither policy contains these permissions. Consequently, the user is denied the ability to remove CloudWatch Logs. Option C (CORRECT): “Deleting Amazon EC2 instances.” At least one of the attached policies explicitly allows ec2:TerminateInstances. There is no explicit Deny in the other policy for EC2 instance termination. Under IAM’s default-deny model, the Allow in Policy1 (or Policy2) is sufficient to permit the action. Summary: We evaluated each option against the IAM policies’ allowed and denied actions. Only the ec2:TerminateInstances permission was granted without any conflicting deny, so the cloud engineer can delete EC2 instances. This question falls under Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A solutions architect needs to design a system to store client case files. The files are core company assets and are important. The number of files will grow over time. The files must be simultaneously accessible from multiple application servers that run on Amazon EC2 instances. The solution must have built-in redundancy. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS)
Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS)
Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive
AWS Backup
explanation: The correct Answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) provides block-level storage that can be attached to a single EC2 instance (or via Multi-Attach in limited scenarios). It is not designed for simultaneous access from multiple servers and is confined to one Availability Zone, so it does not meet the requirement for multi-instance concurrent access with built-in redundancy. Option C (INCORRECT): Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive is a long-term archival storage class optimized for infrequent, long-term retention with retrieval times of hours. It is not intended for active, low-latency access by multiple application servers and therefore cannot serve as the primary file system for client case files. Option D (INCORRECT): AWS Backup is a centralized backup service to automate and manage backups across AWS services. It does not provide live file storage or a shared file system for concurrent access by EC2 instances. It is meant for backup and restore, not for serving active assets. Option A (CORRECT): Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) is a fully managed NFS file system that automatically scales as you add or remove files. It supports concurrent access from multiple EC2 instances across Availability Zones, providing high availability and durability with built-in redundancy. EFS is ideal for storing and serving active file-based assets that grow over time. Summary: We examined why EBS, Glacier Deep Archive, and AWS Backup do not satisfy the requirements for simultaneous multi-server access, scalability, and built-in redundancy. Amazon EFS meets all criteria by offering a shared, scalable, and highly available file system. This question belongs to Domain 2 – Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company is planning to migrate data to an Amazon S3 bucket. The data must be encrypted at rest within the S3 bucket. The encryption key must be rotated automatically every year. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Migrate the data to the S3 bucket. Use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3). Use the built-in key rotation behavior of SSE-S3 encryption keys.

Create an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key. Enable automatic key rotation. Set the S3 bucket's default encryption behavior to use the customer managed KMS key. Migrate the data to the S3 bucket.

Create an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key. Set the S3 bucket's default encryption behavior to use the customer managed KMS key. Migrate the data to the S3 bucket. Manually rotate the KMS key every year.

Use customer key material to encrypt the data. Migrate the data to the S3 bucket. Create an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key without key material. Import the customer key material into the KMS key. Enable automatic key rotation.
explanation: The correct Answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): “Create an AWS KMS customer managed key. Enable automatic key rotation. Set the S3 bucket's default encryption behavior to use the customer managed KMS key. Migrate the data to the S3 bucket.” Although KMS customer-managed keys support automatic annual rotation, this approach introduces extra operational overhead compared to using the default S3-managed encryption. There are additional costs for KMS API usage each time you encrypt or decrypt objects in S3. Option C (INCORRECT): “Create an AWS KMS customer managed key. Set the S3 bucket's default encryption behavior to use the customer managed KMS key. Migrate the data to the S3 bucket. Manually rotate the KMS key every year.” Manual rotation increases operational overhead and risks missing the rotation schedule. The requirement specifies automatic yearly rotation. Option D (INCORRECT): “Use customer key material to encrypt the data. Migrate the data to the S3 bucket. Create an AWS KMS key without key material. Import the customer key material into the KMS key. Enable automatic key rotation.” Imported key material cannot be automatically rotated by AWS KMS; you must re-import new material manually. This adds complexity and operational overhead, violating the least-overhead requirement. Option A (CORRECT): “Migrate the data to the S3 bucket. Use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3). Use the built-in key rotation behavior of SSE-S3 encryption keys.” SSE-S3 encrypts data at rest with keys managed by Amazon S3. AWS automatically rotates the S3-managed keys once every year with no customer intervention. This solution has zero additional operational overhead and no extra KMS costs. In summary, for encryption at rest with automatic annual key rotation and minimal operational overhead, Option A is the optimal choice. This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company is preparing a new data platform that will ingest real-time streaming data from multiple sources. The company needs to transform the data before writing the data to Amazon S3. The company needs the ability to use SQL to query the transformed data.Which solutions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
options: Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to stream the data. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics to transform the data. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to write the data to Amazon S3. Use Amazon Athena to query the transformed data from Amazon S3.

Use Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (Amazon MSK) to stream the data. Use AWS Glue to transform the data and to write the data to Amazon S3. Use Amazon Athena to query the transformed data from Amazon S3.

Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to ingest the data. Use Amazon EMR to transform the data and to write the data to Amazon S3. Use Amazon Athena to query the transformed data from Amazon S3.

Use Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (Amazon MSK) to stream the data. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics to transform the data and to write the data to Amazon S3. Use the Amazon RDS query editor to query the transformed data from Amazon S3.

Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to stream the data. Use AWS Glue to transform the data. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to write the data to Amazon S3. Use the Amazon RDS query editor to query the transformed data from Amazon S3.
explanation: The correct answer is A, B. Option C (INCORRECT): “Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to ingest the data. Use Amazon EMR to transform the data and to write the data to Amazon S3. Use Amazon Athena to query the transformed data from Amazon S3.” AWS DMS is designed for database migrations and change data capture, not for general real-time streaming ingestion from multiple arbitrary sources. Amazon EMR can perform batch or streaming processing but adds operational complexity compared to managed streaming ETL services. The question specifically emphasizes real-time streaming ingestion and transformation, which EMR + DMS does not optimally address. Option D (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (Amazon MSK) to stream the data. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics to transform the data and to write the data to Amazon S3. Use the Amazon RDS query editor to query the transformed data from Amazon S3.” While MSK → Kinesis Data Analytics → S3 is a valid streaming path, the Amazon RDS query editor cannot query data stored in Amazon S3. To run SQL queries against S3, you must use Amazon Athena rather than the RDS query editor. Option E (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to stream the data. Use AWS Glue to transform the data. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to write the data to Amazon S3. Use the Amazon RDS query editor to query the transformed data from Amazon S3.” AWS Glue Streaming ETL can ingest from Kinesis Data Streams and write directly to S3, but chaining through Firehose is unnecessary and adds complexity. Again, the Amazon RDS query editor cannot be used to query S3 data; Athena is required for S3 queries. Option A (CORRECT): “Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to stream the data. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics to transform the data. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to write the data to Amazon S3. Use Amazon Athena to query the transformed data from Amazon S3.” Kinesis Data Streams provides high-throughput, low-latency ingestion for real-time data. Kinesis Data Analytics allows you to write SQL queries for continuous, real-time transformations. Kinesis Data Firehose delivers the transformed data to S3 with built-in buffering, retry, and compression. Amazon Athena lets you run standard SQL queries directly against the transformed data in S3. Option B (CORRECT): “Use Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (Amazon MSK) to stream the data. Use AWS Glue to transform the data and to write the data to Amazon S3. Use Amazon Athena to query the transformed data from Amazon S3.” Amazon MSK provides a fully managed Kafka service for real-time, scalable streaming. AWS Glue Streaming ETL can continuously read from MSK, apply transformations, and write data into S3. Amazon Athena enables you to run SQL queries on the transformed S3 data without additional infrastructure. Summary: We’ve examined multiple architectures for real-time streaming, transformation, and SQL querying. The optimal solutions leverage managed streaming and serverless query services (Kinesis Data Analytics or Glue Streaming ETL with Athena) to minimize operational overhead and meet the requirements. This question falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company uses AWS to run its ecommerce platform. The platform is critical to the company's operations and has a high volume of traffic and transactions. The company configures a multi-factor authentication (MFA) device to secure its AWS account root user credentials. The company wants to ensure that it will not lose access to the root user account if the MFA device is lost. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Set up a backup administrator account that the company can use to log in if the company loses the MFA device.
Add multiple MFA devices for the root user account to handle the disaster scenario.
Create a new administrator account when the company cannot access the root account.
Attach the administrator policy to another IAM user when the company cannot access the root account.
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): AWS allows only one MFA device per root user; you cannot attach multiple virtual or hardware tokens. Even if it were possible, it wouldn’t follow best practices for account recovery and could introduce unnecessary complexity. Option C (INCORRECT): Creating a new administrator account after losing root access is reactive and may not be possible without existing privileges. This does not solve the preemptive requirement to ensure uninterrupted account management if the root MFA device is lost. Option D (INCORRECT): Attaching the administrator policy to another IAM user after losing root access still requires root (or an existing admin) to perform that action. It fails to provide a standby mechanism already in place for immediate recovery. Option A (CORRECT): Provision a secondary IAM user with full administrative privileges and enforce MFA on that user. If the root user’s MFA device is lost, the backup administrator can still access and manage the account, including resetting the root MFA with AWS Support. In summary, maintaining a dedicated backup administrator IAM user with MFA ensures continuous account management even if the root MFA device is lost. This question belongs to Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company’s facility has badge readers at every entrance throughout the building. When badges are scanned, the readers send a message over HTTPS to indicate who attempted to access that particular entrance. A solutions architect must design a system to process these messages from the sensors. The solution must be highly available, and the results must be made available for the company’s security team to analyze. Which system architecture should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Launch an Amazon EC2 instance to serve as the HTTPS endpoint and to process the messages. Configure the EC2 instance to save the results to an Amazon S3 bucket.
Create an HTTPS endpoint in Amazon API Gateway. Configure the API Gateway endpoint to invoke an AWS Lambda function to process the messages and save the results to an Amazon DynamoDB table.
Use Amazon Route 53 to direct incoming sensor messages to an AWS Lambda function. Configure the Lambda function to process the messages and save the results to an Amazon DynamoDB table.

Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3. Configure a Site-to-Site VPN connection from the facility network to the VPC so that sensor data can be written directly to an S3 bucket by way of the VPC endpoint.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): • Launching a single EC2 instance creates a single point of failure and does not meet the “highly available” requirement. • You would need to manage OS patches, scaling, and failover yourself. • There is no built-in real-time integration or scaling for HTTPS messages at scale. Option C (INCORRECT): • Amazon Route 53 is a DNS service and cannot act as an HTTPS ingestion endpoint for sensor messages. • You cannot directly route HTTP/S traffic to a Lambda function via Route 53; an API Gateway or ALB is required for that type of integration. Option D (INCORRECT): • A gateway VPC endpoint to S3 plus VPN would let you write raw data into S3, but it does not provide a processing layer for analyzing the badge‐scan events. • Managing a VPN adds operational overhead and potential availability concerns. • There’s no compute integration for real-time processing or storing structured results for analytics. Option B (CORRECT): Amazon API Gateway provides a fully managed, highly available HTTPS endpoint that can scale to handle inbound sensor messages. AWS Lambda offers serverless compute that automatically scales and requires no infrastructure management—ideal for processing each badge‐scan event. Amazon DynamoDB is a fully managed NoSQL datastore with single‐digit millisecond latency and built-in high availability, making it suitable for storing and querying processed security data. This architecture is entirely serverless, highly available by design, and allows the security team to query or analyze results in near real time. Summary: We have learned that a fully managed, serverless solution using API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB best meets the requirements for high availability, scalability, and real-time processing. This question belongs to Domain 1 - Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company runs a photo processing application that needs to frequently upload and download pictures from Amazon S3 buckets that are located in the same AWS Region. A solutions architect has noticed an increased cost in data transfer fees and needs to implement a solution to reduce these costs.How can the solutions architect meet this requirement?
options: Deploy Amazon API Gateway into a public subnet and adjust the route table to route S3 calls through it.
Deploy a NAT gateway into a public subnet and attach an endpoint policy that allows access to the S3 buckets.
Deploy the application into a public subnet and allow it to route through an internet gateway to access the S3 buckets.
Deploy an S3 VPC gateway endpoint into the VPC and attach an endpoint policy that allows access to the S3 buckets.
explanation: The correct Answer is D Option A (INCORRECT): Deploying Amazon API Gateway into a public subnet and routing S3 calls through it is not a valid pattern for S3 access. API Gateway is designed for fronting HTTP-based microservices, not for optimizing or proxying S3 data transfers. This approach introduces extra hops, potential latency, and does not eliminate cross-AZ or Internet data transfer fees. Option B (INCORRECT): A NAT Gateway simply allows private instances to reach the Internet (including AWS public endpoints) while masquerading IPs, but it still incurs NAT data processing charges and cross-AZ data transfer fees. You cannot attach an “endpoint policy” to a NAT Gateway in order to optimize S3 traffic—S3 VPC endpoints are the correct construct for policy-controlled, cost-free in-region access to S3. Option C (INCORRECT): Placing the application in a public subnet and routing through an Internet Gateway to access S3 forces traffic over the public Internet path, resulting in standard Internet data transfer charges. This does nothing to reduce S3 data fees and in fact increases your exposure to egress costs and security risk. Option D (CORRECT): Deploying an S3 VPC Gateway Endpoint into your VPC enables private connectivity to S3 over the AWS network—no NAT, no Internet Gateway, and no cross-AZ or Internet data transfer charges. You can attach an endpoint policy to restrict which buckets or operations are allowed. This fulfills the requirement to frequently upload/download pictures with minimal cost. In summary, by using an S3 VPC Gateway Endpoint you achieve private, high-throughput access to S3 without incurring additional data transfer fees. This solution belongs to Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A solutions architect needs to design a new microservice for a company’s application. Clients must be able to call an HTTPS endpoint to reach the microservice. The microservice also must use AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) to authenticate calls. The solutions architect will write the logic for this microservice by using a single AWS Lambda function that is written in Go 1.x. Which solution will deploy the function in the MOST operationally efficient way?
options: Create an Amazon API Gateway REST API. Configure the method to use the Lambda function. Enable IAM authentication on the API.
Create a Lambda function URL for the function. Specify AWS_IAM as the authentication type.
Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Deploy the function to Lambda@Edge. Integrate IAM authentication logic into the Lambda@Edge function.
Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Deploy the function to CloudFront Functions. Specify AWS_IAM as the authentication type.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): “Create an Amazon API Gateway REST API. Configure the method to use the Lambda function. Enable IAM authentication on the API.” While API Gateway REST APIs do support AWS_IAM authorization and can front your Lambda, they introduce additional operational overhead (API Gateway stages, deployments, throttling, usage plans). Managing API Gateway adds cost and configuration complexity compared to a direct Lambda endpoint. Option C (INCORRECT): “Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Deploy the function to Lambda@Edge. Integrate IAM authentication logic into the Lambda@Edge function.” Lambda@Edge only supports Node.js, Python, Java, and C# runtimes—not Go 1.x. Implementing IAM authorization inside an Edge function is complex and bypasses built-in AWS_IAM mechanisms. This approach greatly increases complexity and latency, and is not operationally efficient. Option D (INCORRECT): “Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Deploy the function to CloudFront Functions. Specify AWS_IAM as the authentication type.” CloudFront Functions only support lightweight JavaScript—Go 1.x isn’t supported. CloudFront Functions cannot natively enforce AWS_IAM authentication. This option does not satisfy the requirement to call a Go Lambda with IAM auth. Option B (CORRECT): “Create a Lambda function URL for the function. Specify AWS_IAM as the authentication type.” Lambda function URLs provide a built-in HTTPS endpoint for your function with minimal configuration. They natively support AWS_IAM authorization, satisfying the authentication requirement. No additional API Gateway or CloudFront resources are required—this is the most operationally efficient solution. Summary: We learned that Lambda function URLs offer a direct HTTPS endpoint with built-in AWS_IAM support, minimizing operational overhead compared to API Gateway or CloudFront solutions. This scenario falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: An ecommerce company is building a distributed application that involves several serverless functions and AWS services to complete order-processing tasks. These tasks require manual approvals as part of the workflow. A solutions architect needs to design an architecture for the order-processing application. The solution must be able to combine multiple AWS Lambda functions into responsive serverless applications. The solution also must orchestrate data and services that run on Amazon EC2 instances, containers, or on-premises servers. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Use AWS Step Functions to build the application.
Integrate all the application components in an AWS Glue job.
Use Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) to build the application.
Use AWS Lambda functions and Amazon EventBridge events to build the application.
explanation: The correct Answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): Integrate all the application components in an AWS Glue job. AWS Glue is an ETL service designed for data extraction, transformation, and loading—​not for orchestrating application workflows. It does not support human approval steps or the coordination of Lambda functions and on-premises/EC2/container tasks. Using Glue would introduce unnecessary complexity and operational overhead for this use case. Option C (INCORRECT): Use Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) to build the application. SQS provides reliable message queuing, but it does not natively offer workflow orchestration or state management. There’s no built-in support for sequential task coordination, human approvals, or error handling patterns beyond basic retries. Building a full workflow engine on top of SQS would greatly increase operational complexity. Option D (INCORRECT): Use AWS Lambda functions and Amazon EventBridge events to build the application. EventBridge is excellent for event-driven architectures, but it lacks native state tracking and chaining of tasks. There’s no direct support for manual approval or wait states—​you’d have to build and maintain custom logic. This approach shifts orchestration responsibilities onto your code, increasing operational overhead. Option A (CORRECT): Use AWS Step Functions to build the application. Step Functions is a fully managed state machine service that lets you coordinate multiple Lambda functions into complex workflows. It supports wait states and callbacks, enabling human approval steps without extra infrastructure. It can invoke tasks on EC2, containers, or on-premises servers via API integrations—​all with built-in retry, error handling, and state management. This serverless orchestration minimizes operational overhead by handling workflow orchestration, state, and retries for you. We have learned that AWS Step Functions is the ideal choice for orchestrating serverless and non-serverless components with manual approval steps while minimizing operational complexity. This question falls under the following domain: Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures Domain 2 – Design Resilient Architectures Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures Domain 4 – Design Cost-Optimized Architectures

question: A social media company is creating a rewards program website for its users. The company gives users points when users create and upload videos to the website. Users redeem their points for gifts or discounts from the company's affiliated partners. A unique ID identifies users. The partners refer to this ID to verify user eligibility for rewards. The partners want to receive notification of user IDs through an HTTP endpoint when the company gives users points. Hundreds of vendors are interested in becoming affiliated partners every day. The company wants to design an architecture that gives the website the ability to add partners rapidly in a scalable way.Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST implementation effort?
options: Create an Amazon Timestream database to keep a list of affiliated partners. Implement an AWS Lambda function to read the list. Configure the Lambda function to send user IDs to each partner when the company gives users points.
Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic. Choose an endpoint protocol. Subscribe the partners to the topic. Publish user IDs to the topic when the company gives users points.
Create an AWS Step Functions state machine. Create a task for every affiliated partner. Invoke the state machine with user IDs as input when the company gives users points.

Create a data stream in Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Implement producer and consumer applications. Store a list of affiliated partners in the data stream. Send user IDs when the company gives users points.
explanation: The correct answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): “Create an Amazon Timestream database to keep a list of affiliated partners. Implement an AWS Lambda function to read the list. Configure the Lambda function to send user IDs to each partner when the company gives users points.” This introduces unnecessary complexity and state management. Timestream is for time-series data, not dynamic partner lists. Every time a partner is added or removed, you’d have to update or redeploy Lambda logic, increasing operational overhead. Latency and scaling become concerns as the Lambda must iterate through all partners for every user event. Option C (INCORRECT): “Create an AWS Step Functions state machine. Create a task for every affiliated partner. Invoke the state machine with user IDs as input when the company gives users points.” Step Functions tasks are statically defined; you cannot dynamically add hundreds of partners without modifying the workflow definition. Each new partner would require a new state/task, leading to frequent deployments and high maintenance. This approach is neither scalable nor low-effort for rapidly onboarding partners. Option D (INCORRECT): “Create a data stream in Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Implement producer and consumer applications. Store a list of affiliated partners in the data stream. Send user IDs when the company gives users points.” Kinesis is designed for high-throughput streaming, not for managing subscriber lists or dynamic HTTP endpoints. Building custom producers/consumers adds significant implementation effort and operational complexity. You’d still need additional logic to track partners separately—this does not simplify onboarding. Option B (CORRECT): “Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic. Choose an endpoint protocol. Subscribe the partners to the topic. Publish user IDs to the topic when the company gives users points.” SNS is a fully managed, pub/sub service that natively supports HTTP/HTTPS endpoints. Partners can self-subscribe or be added dynamically without code changes—scales automatically to hundreds of subscribers. Minimal implementation effort: just create a topic, configure endpoints, and publish messages. Provides reliable delivery, retry policies, and monitoring out of the box. Summary: We learned that the easiest way to notify a large and growing set of HTTP endpoints is to use Amazon SNS. SNS supports dynamic subscriptions, scales automatically, and requires minimal code. This solution falls under Domain 2 - Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company hosts an application on Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances in an Auto Scaling group. Application peak hours occur at the same time each day. Application users report slow application performance at the start of peak hours. The application performs normally 2-3 hours after peak hours begin. The company wants to ensure that the application works properly at the start of peak hours. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Configure an Application Load Balancer to distribute traffic properly to the instances.
Configure a dynamic scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group to launch new instances based on memory utilization.
Configure a dynamic scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group to launch new instances based on CPU utilization.
Configure a scheduled scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group to launch new instances before peak hours.
explanation: The correct Answer is D Option A (INCORRECT): “Configure an Application Load Balancer to distribute traffic properly to the instances.” An ALB only balances incoming requests among existing instances; it does not add capacity. At the start of peak hours, you need more instances running, not just better distribution. Option B (INCORRECT): “Configure a dynamic scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group to launch new instances based on memory utilization.” Memory utilization is not a default EC2 metric in CloudWatch—requires custom metrics and more setup. Dynamic scaling reacts only after you hit thresholds, so it won’t prevent the initial slowdown. Option C (INCORRECT): “Configure a dynamic scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group to launch new instances based on CPU utilization.” CPU-based scaling is reactive: instances are added only after CPU usage spikes. There will still be a lag (startup time for EC2) at the beginning of peak hours, causing slow performance. Option D (CORRECT): “Configure a scheduled scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group to launch new instances before peak hours.” Scheduled scaling lets you specify a time-based action to add capacity ahead of known traffic spikes. By launching instances before peak hours, you ensure full capacity is ready when users arrive. This approach prevents the initial slowdown and avoids waiting for scaling triggers. Summary: We’ve learned that when traffic patterns are predictable, scheduled scaling is the optimal solution to ensure capacity is available right at the start of peak hours, rather than relying on reactive dynamic policies. This question belongs to Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company's web application that is hosted in the AWS Cloud recently increased in popularity. The web application currently exists on a single Amazon EC2 instance in a single public subnet. The web application has not been able to meet the demand of the increased web traffic. The company needs a solution that will provide high availability and scalability to meet the increased user demand without rewriting the web application.Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
options: Replace the EC2 instance with a larger compute optimized instance.
Configure Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling with multiple Availability Zones in private subnets.
Configure a NAT gateway in a public subnet to handle web requests.
Replace the EC2 instance with a larger memory optimized instance.
Configure an Application Load Balancer in a public subnet to distribute web traffic.
explanation: The correct answer is B, E. Option A (INCORRECT): Replacing the EC2 instance with a larger compute-optimized instance is only vertical scaling. It does not provide high availability (still a single instance in one AZ) nor fault tolerance. Option C (INCORRECT): A NAT Gateway is designed for outbound internet access from private subnets. It cannot accept and distribute inbound HTTP/HTTPS web traffic to your application servers. Option D (INCORRECT): Replacing the instance with a larger memory-optimized instance again only increases capacity on one server in one AZ. There is no redundancy or automated scaling. Option B (CORRECT): Configure an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones in private subnets. This provides horizontal scaling: instances are launched or terminated based on load. Spanning multiple AZs ensures high availability and fault tolerance. Keeping instances in private subnets is a best practice; they receive traffic from a load balancer in public subnets. Option E (CORRECT): Deploy an Application Load Balancer in public subnets to distribute web traffic. The ALB routes incoming HTTP/HTTPS requests to healthy instances in your Auto Scaling group. It supports cross-AZ load distribution, SSL termination, and health checks out of the box. Together with Auto Scaling, this ensures both high availability and seamless scalability. From this discussion, we learned that achieving high availability and scalability for a web application in AWS typically involves horizontally scaling with an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones and distributing traffic with an Application Load Balancer. This question belongs to Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company sells ringtones created from clips of popular songs. The files containing the ringtones are stored in Amazon S3 Standard and are at least 128 KB in size. The company has millions of files, but downloads are infrequent for ringtones older than 90 days. The company needs to save money on storage while keeping the most accessed files readily available for its users. Which action should the company take to meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Configure S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) storage for the initial storage tier of the objects.
Move the files to S3 Intelligent-Tiering and configure it to move objects to a less expensive storage tier after 90 days.
Configure S3 inventory to manage objects and move them to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-1A) after 90 days.
Implement an S3 Lifecycle policy that moves the objects from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-1A) after 90 days.
explanation: The correct answer is D. Option A (INCORRECT): Configure S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) as the initial storage tier. This would immediately incur retrieval fees for any ringtone downloads, even for new or popular files accessed within the first 90 days. It does not meet the requirement to keep recently created or frequently accessed ringtones readily available at the standard storage cost. Option B (INCORRECT): Move the files to S3 Intelligent-Tiering and configure it to move objects to a less expensive tier after 90 days. S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects based on access patterns, but it charges a monthly monitoring and automation fee per object. For millions of small files (≥128 KB), the per-object overhead makes this more expensive than a simple lifecycle transition. You cannot explicitly set the 90-day window in Intelligent-Tiering—it's based on 30-day no-access periods. Option C (INCORRECT): Configure S3 Inventory to manage objects and move them to S3 Standard-IA after 90 days. S3 Inventory merely provides a report of your objects; it does not perform storage-class transitions. You would still need to build an external process (Lambda, scripts) to parse the inventory and call S3 APIs, adding complexity and cost. Option D (CORRECT): Implement an S3 Lifecycle policy that moves the objects from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) after 90 days. S3 Lifecycle rules are native, free to configure, and automatically transition objects based on age. Objects older than 90 days—which are infrequently downloaded—get the lower storage cost of Standard-IA. Files accessed within the first 90 days remain in Standard, ensuring low-latency access for recent or popular ringtones. In summary, using an S3 Lifecycle policy (Option D) provides a fully managed, cost-effective way to transition older, infrequently accessed objects to a cheaper storage class without impacting the availability of recent files. This question falls under Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company is deploying a new application to Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) with an AWS Fargate cluster. The application needs a storage solution for data persistence. The solution must be highly available and fault tolerant. The solution also must be shared between multiple application containers. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Create Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes in the same Availability Zones where EKS worker nodes are placed. Register the volumes in a StorageClass object on an EKS cluster. Use EBS Multi-Attach to share the data between containers.
Create an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Register the file system in a StorageClass object on an EKS cluster. Use the same file system for all containers.
Create an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. Register the volume in a StorageClass object on an EKS cluster. Use the same volume for all containers.

Create Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file systems in the same Availability Zones where EKS worker nodes are placed. Register the file systems in a StorageClass object on an EKS cluster. Create an AWS Lambda function to synchronize the data between file systems.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): Create Amazon EBS volumes in each AZ and use EBS Multi-Attach. EBS volumes are tied to a single Availability Zone and require complex multi-attach configuration. Multi-Attach is only supported on specific instance types and not on Fargate. This approach increases operational overhead and does not provide true cross-AZ high availability. Option C (INCORRECT): Create a single Amazon EBS volume and share it among containers. EBS volumes cannot be mounted by multiple Fargate pods simultaneously. Lacks the shared, distributed access required by multiple containers. Not fault-tolerant across AZs and does not meet HA requirements. Option D (INCORRECT): Create multiple EFS file systems in each AZ and sync via Lambda. Introducing Lambda for synchronization adds unnecessary complexity and operational overhead. Data consistency and sync delays can cause application errors. A single EFS filesystem already provides cross-AZ availability without custom sync. Option B (CORRECT): Create an Amazon EFS file system, register it in a StorageClass, and share it across pods. EFS is a fully managed, elastic NFS file system accessible from all AZs in a region. It provides built-in high availability and fault tolerance without extra configuration. Containers on Fargate can mount the same EFS volume concurrently for shared, persistent storage. Minimal operational overhead since AWS handles scaling, durability, and replication. In summary, Amazon EFS offers a highly available, fault-tolerant, and shareable storage solution with the least operational overhead. This scenario falls under Domain 2 - Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company has an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system that contains a reference dataset. The company has applications on Amazon EC2 instances that need to read the dataset. However, the applications must not be able to change the dataset. The company wants to use IAM access control to prevent the applications from being able to modify or delete the dataset. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Mount the EFS file system in read-only mode from within the EC2 instances.
Create a resource policy for the EFS file system that denies the elasticfilesystem:ClientWrite action to the IAM roles that are attached to the EC2 instances.
Create an identity policy for the EFS file system that denies the elasticfilesystem:ClientWrite action on the EFS file system.
Create an EFS access point for each application. Use Portable Operating System Interface (POSIX) file permissions to allow read-only access to files in the root directory.
explanation: The correct answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): Mounting the EFS file system in read‐only mode at the client level does prevent writes from that mount, but it doesn’t use IAM to enforce permissions. An administrator with root privileges on the EC2 instance could remount or bypass this setting. This does not meet the requirement to use IAM access control to prevent modifications at the service level. Option C (INCORRECT): Identity-based policies cannot be attached directly to an EFS file system. EFS access must be controlled using resource-based policies on the file system or POSIX permissions via access points. You can’t create an IAM identity policy “for the EFS file system” itself to block elasticfilesystem:ClientWrite in the way described. Option D (INCORRECT): While EFS Access Points plus POSIX permissions can enforce read‐only access at the file-system level, this solution relies on POSIX and doesn’t leverage IAM policies to block writes via the EFS API. It also requires careful UID/GID management and does not directly satisfy the requirement to use IAM access control. Option B (CORRECT): Create a resource-based policy on the EFS file system that explicitly denies the elasticfilesystem:ClientWrite action for the IAM roles attached to your EC2 instances. Resource‐based policies on EFS allow you to control API actions such as ClientMount and ClientWrite at the service level. A DENY on ClientWrite ensures that even if the instance is compromised, the IAM role cannot modify or delete files in the reference dataset. This approach directly uses IAM to enforce read‐only access, satisfying the requirement to prevent application‐level changes via IAM controls. In this discussion, we learned how to enforce read‐only access to an Amazon EFS file system using IAM resource policies, ensuring that applications cannot modify the dataset. This question falls under Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company wants to securely exchange data between its software as a service (SaaS) application Salesforce account and Amazon S3. The company must encrypt the data at rest by using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed keys (CMKs). The company must also encrypt the data in transit.The company has enabled API access for the Salesforce account.
options: Create AWS Lambda functions to transfer the data securely from Salesforce to Amazon S3.
Create an AWS Step Functions workflow. Define the task to transfer the data securely from Salesforce to Amazon S3.
Create Amazon AppFlow flows to transfer the data securely from Salesforce to Amazon S3.
Create a custom connector for Salesforce to transfer the data securely from Salesforce to Amazon S3.
explanation: The correct answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): Use AWS Lambda functions to transfer the data securely from Salesforce to Amazon S3. Requires custom code to integrate with Salesforce APIs and to handle encryption in transit and at rest, increasing development and maintenance overhead. No built-in support for KMS CMK encryption; you must manage and configure S3 encryption settings and key policies manually in code. Lacks the scalability and ease of configuration provided by a managed service connector. Option B (INCORRECT): Create an AWS Step Functions workflow with a task to transfer the data from Salesforce to S3. Step Functions orchestrate tasks but do not natively connect to Salesforce or S3; you must still build Lambda or custom tasks. Introduces additional complexity without reducing code efforts for secure transfers or key management. Does not directly provide encryption in transit or at rest—you still handle those in underlying tasks. Option D (INCORRECT): Create a custom connector for Salesforce to S3. Building and maintaining a custom connector duplicates functionality already offered by AWS. Custom connectors require ongoing updates for API changes, error handling, and encryption implementations. Lacks the simplicity of a fully managed integration that supports KMS CMKs and secure transport out of the box. Option C (CORRECT): Use Amazon AppFlow to securely transfer data from Salesforce to Amazon S3. AppFlow provides a native Salesforce connector and Amazon S3 destination, handling data transfer over TLS for in-transit encryption. Supports AWS KMS customer managed keys for S3 objects, ensuring data is encrypted at rest with your CMK. Eliminates the need for custom code, scales automatically, and simplifies configuration and key management. In summary, we learned that Amazon AppFlow is the optimal managed service for secure, end-to-end encrypted data transfer between SaaS applications like Salesforce and S3 using AWS KMS customer managed keys. This question belongs to Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company is designing a new web application that will run on Amazon EC2 Instances. The application will use Amazon DynamoDB for backend data storage. The application traffic will be unpredictable. The company expects that the application read and write throughput to the database will be moderate to high. The company needs to scale in response to application traffic. Which DynamoDB table configuration will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Configure DynamoDB with provisioned read and write by using the DynamoDB Standard table class. Set DynamoDB auto scaling to a maximum defined capacity.
Configure DynamoDB in on-demand mode by using the DynamoDB Standard table class.
Configure DynamoDB with provisioned read and write by using the DynamoDB Standard Infrequent Access (DynamoDB Standard-IA) table class. Set DynamoDB auto scaling to a maximum defined capacity.
Configure DynamoDB in on-demand mode by using the DynamoDB Standard Infrequent Access (DynamoDB Standard-IA) table class.
explanation: The correct answer is Option B. Option A (INCORRECT): • Provisioned capacity requires you to estimate read/write throughput in advance. • With unpredictable traffic, you risk under-provisioning (throttling) or over-provisioning (wasted cost). • Even with auto scaling, there can be delays scaling up to sudden spikes, and you pay for unused capacity when traffic is low. Option C (INCORRECT): • The Standard-Infrequent Access (Standard-IA) table class is optimized for data that is not accessed frequently. • Your application has moderate to high and unpredictable throughput, so you would incur high access charges and defeat the purpose of Standard-IA. • Provisioned auto scaling still suffers from the same estimation and latency downsides as pure provisioned mode. Option D (INCORRECT): • On-demand mode with Standard-IA mixes two conflicting goals: pay-per-request billing (good for spikes) with an infrequent-access storage tier (bad for heavy reads/writes). • You would incur expensive per-read and per-write charges under Standard-IA for a high-throughput workload. Option B (CORRECT): DynamoDB on-demand automatically adapts to unpredictable traffic without capacity planning. You pay only for the reads and writes you perform, making it cost-effective for variable or spiky workloads. Standard table class is optimized for high throughput and frequent access, matching your moderate-to-high usage profile. This configuration delivers seamless scaling and optimal cost efficiency when traffic patterns cannot be forecasted. Summary: We’ve learned that for unpredictable, moderate-to-high throughput workloads, DynamoDB on-demand in the Standard table class provides automatic scaling and pay-per-request billing, avoiding the pitfalls of provisioning or using infrequent-access storage. This question belongs to Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company receives 10 TB of instrumentation data each day from several machines located at a single factory. The data consists of JSON files stored on a storage area network (SAN) in an on-premises data center located within the factory. The company wants to send this data to Amazon S3 where it can be accessed by several additional systems that provide critical near-real-time analytics.
