Attach a security configuration to each job that uses client-side encryption with AWS KMS managed keys (CSE-KMS) to encrypt the data.” CSE-KMS performs encryption on the client side (in the Glue job) using customer-specific KMS keys, ensuring data is encrypted before it leaves the processing environment. Glue is serverless—no cluster management—and you simply supply the per-customer KMS key in the security configuration. Meets both requirements: encryption at processing time with customer-specific keys and minimal operational effort. Summary: We learned how to choose a serverless, client-side encryption approach with AWS Glue and per-customer KMS keys to minimize operations while ensuring data is encrypted during processing and at rest. This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A 4-year-old media company is using the AWS Organizations all features feature set to organize its AWS accounts. According to the company's finance team, the billing information on the member accounts must not be accessible to anyone, including the root user of the member accounts. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Add all finance team users to an IAM group. Attach an AWS managed policy named Billing to the group.
Attach an identity-based policy to deny access to the billing information to all users, including the root user.
Create a service control policy (SCP) to deny access to the billing information. Attach the SCP to the root organizational unit (OU).
Convert from the Organizations all features feature set to the Organizations consolidated billing feature set.
explanation: The correct Answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): “Add all finance team users to an IAM group. Attach an AWS managed policy named Billing to the group.” This actually grants billing permissions rather than restricts them. It does nothing to prevent the root user or other member-account principals from viewing billing details. Option B (INCORRECT): “Attach an identity-based policy to deny access to the billing information to all users, including the root user.” Identity-based policies cannot restrict the root user of an AWS account. Service Control Policies (SCPs) are required to impose restrictions on root or any IAM principals across an OU. Option D (INCORRECT): “Convert from the Organizations all features feature set to the Organizations consolidated billing feature set.” The consolidated billing feature set is legacy and does not provide finer control over member-account billing access. This change does not prevent the root user of each member account from viewing billing data. Option C (CORRECT): “Create a Service Control Policy (SCP) to deny access to the billing information. Attach the SCP to the root organizational unit (OU).” SCPs apply at the organization or OU level and can explicitly deny billing-related actions (e.g. aws-portal:*, awsbillingconsole:*). They affect all IAM principals, including the root user of each member account. This ensures that no one in the member accounts can view or manage billing details. In summary, we learned that to restrict access to billing details even from root users in member accounts, you must use Service Control Policies in AWS Organizations. This question falls under Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company is designing a shared storage solution for a gaming application that is hosted in the AWS Cloud. The company needs the ability to use SMB clients to access data. The solution must be fully managed. Which AWS solution meets these requirements?
options: Create an AWS DataSync task that shares the data as a mountable file system. Mount the file system to the application server.
Create an Amazon EC2 Windows instance. Install and configure a Windows file share role on the instance. Connect the application server to the file share.
Create an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system. Attach the file system to the origin server. Connect the application server to the file system.
Create an Amazon S3 bucket. Assign an IAM role to the application to grant access to the S3 bucket. Mount the S3 bucket to the application server.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): AWS DataSync is designed for one-time or scheduled data transfers between on-premises storage and AWS, not for presenting a continuously available SMB file share. Option B (INCORRECT): Launching a Windows EC2 instance and configuring a file-share role is a self-managed solution. It requires you to handle OS patching, scaling, high-availability, and backups, so it isn’t fully managed by AWS. Option D (INCORRECT): Amazon S3 is an object store and does not natively support the SMB protocol. Mounting an S3 bucket requires third-party or custom tools, so it’s not a fully managed SMB file system. Option C (CORRECT): Amazon FSx for Windows File Server provides a fully managed, native SMB file share with integration into AWS Directory Service. It offers Windows ACLs, automatic backups, multi-AZ redundancy, and the performance characteristics required by file-based workloads. Supports SMB protocol out of the box for seamless Windows and Linux SMB clients. Fully managed by AWS—no OS management, patching, or scaling tasks required. Offers high throughput, low latency, and enterprise-grade features (snapshots, replication). In summary, for a fully managed SMB-accessible shared storage solution in AWS, Amazon FSx for Windows File Server is the optimal choice. This question belongs to Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company uses AWS and sells access to copyrighted images. The company’s global customer base needs to be able to access these images quickly. The company must deny access to users from specific countries. The company wants to minimize costs as much as possible. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Use Amazon S3 to store the images. Turn on multi-factor authentication (MFA) and public bucket access. Provide customers with a link to the S3 bucket.
Use Amazon S3 to store the images. Create an IAM user for each customer. Add the users to a group that has permission to access the S3 bucket.

Use Amazon EC2 instances that are behind Application Load Balancers (ALBs) to store the images. Deploy the instances only in the countries the company services. Provide customers with links to the ALBs for their specific country's instances.
Use Amazon S3 to store the images. Use Amazon CloudFront to distribute the images with geographic restrictions. Provide a signed URL for each customer to access the data in CloudFront.
explanation: The correct Answer is: D Option A (INCORRECT): Making the S3 bucket public with MFA does not restrict access by geography. Public bucket access cannot enforce country-level blocking. There is no way to deny specific countries or provide signed URLs for secure, time-limited access. Option B (INCORRECT): Creating an IAM user per customer is operationally heavy and does not address geo-restriction. IAM policies cannot easily block users based on their source country. This approach increases management overhead and cost. Option C (INCORRECT): Using EC2 instances around the globe is costly to deploy and maintain. Managing ALBs in multiple countries drives up both infrastructure and operational expenses. Does not natively provide easy country-based blocking without additional software. Option D (CORRECT): Amazon S3 stores the images centrally and cost-effectively. Amazon CloudFront delivers images from edge locations for low latency and global performance. CloudFront’s geo-restriction feature blocks users from specified countries. Signed URLs ensure only authorized customers can access the content, with time-limited validity. This solution balances performance, security, and cost optimization. In summary, we learned how to securely distribute copyrighted images globally while blocking access from unwanted countries, all at minimal cost by leveraging Amazon S3 and CloudFront with geo-restriction and signed URLs. This question falls under Domain 3 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company uses Amazon EC2, AWS Fargate, and AWS Lambda to run multiple workloads in the company's AWS account. The company wants to fully make use of its Compute Savings Plans. The company wants to receive notification when coverage of the Compute Savings Plans drops.Which solution will meet these requirements with the MOST operational efficiency?
options: Create a daily budget for the Savings Plans by using AWS Budgets. Configure the budget with a coverage threshold to send notifications to the appropriate email message recipients.
Create a Lambda function that runs a coverage report against the Savings Plans. Use Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) to email the report to the appropriate email message recipients.
Create an AWS Budgets report for the Savings Plans budget. Set the frequency to daily.
Create a Savings Plans alert subscription. Enable all notification options. Enter an email address to receive notifications.
explanation: The correct Answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): “Create a Lambda function that runs a coverage report against the Savings Plans. Use Amazon SES to email the report.” This introduces custom code and maintenance overhead. SES integration, error handling, retries and scaling all add operational complexity. AWS provides native alerting for Savings Plans coverage via AWS Budgets—no need to reinvent the wheel. Option C (INCORRECT): “Create an AWS Budgets report for the Savings Plans budget. Set the frequency to daily.” Budget reports deliver periodic summaries, not threshold-based alerts. You need a coverage budget with alert thresholds to get notified when utilization falls below a target. Daily reports alone won’t trigger notifications on coverage breaches. Option D (INCORRECT): “Create a Savings Plans alert subscription. Enable all notification options. Enter an email address.” AWS Cost Explorer supports notifications for upcoming purchase recommendations, not real-time coverage drops. There is no direct “Savings Plans alert subscription” feature that monitors coverage thresholds. It cannot meet the requirement to alert on coverage dropping below your defined threshold. Option A (CORRECT): “Create a daily budget for the Savings Plans by using AWS Budgets. Configure the budget with a coverage threshold to send notifications to the appropriate email recipients.” AWS Budgets supports Savings Plans coverage budgets natively. You can define a percentage-coverage threshold (e.g. 80%) and get an email or SNS notification when actual coverage falls below that threshold. This solution requires no custom code, offers automated alerts, and is fully managed—maximizing operational efficiency. Summary: We’ve learned that AWS Budgets provides built-in coverage thresholds and automated alerts for Compute Savings Plans, making it the simplest, most operationally efficient way to monitor coverage drops. This question belongs to Domain 4 – Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company runs an AWS Lambda function in private subnets in a VPC. The subnets have a default route to the internet through an Amazon EC2 NAT instance. The Lambda function processes input data and saves its output as an object to Amazon S3. Intermittently, the Lambda function times out while trying to upload the object because of saturated traffic on the NAT instance's network. The company wants to access Amazon S3 without traversing the internet.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Replace the EC2 NAT instance with an AWS managed NAT gateway.
Increase the size of the EC2 NAT instance in the VPC to a network optimized instance type.
Provision a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3 in the VPUpdate the route tables of the subnets accordingly.
Provision a transit gateway. Place transit gateway attachments in the private subnets where the Lambda function is running.
explanation: The correct answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): Replace the EC2 NAT instance with an AWS managed NAT gateway. While a NAT Gateway is fully managed and can scale better than a NAT instance, it still routes traffic over the internet to reach public AWS services like S3. The requirement is to access S3 without traversing the internet, which a NAT Gateway does not solve. Option B (INCORRECT): Increase the size of the EC2 NAT instance in the VPC to a network optimized instance type. Upsizing the NAT instance may relieve network saturation temporarily, but traffic still goes through the internet. This does not eliminate internet traversal and adds operational overhead and cost of larger EC2 instances. Option D (INCORRECT): Provision a transit gateway. Place transit gateway attachments in the private subnets where the Lambda function is running. Transit Gateway is used to interconnect VPCs and on-premises networks, not for direct access to AWS public services like S3. This adds unnecessary complexity and does not prevent internet egress for S3 traffic. Option C (CORRECT): Provision a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3 in the VPC and update the route tables of the subnets accordingly. A VPC gateway endpoint for S3 enables private connectivity between your VPC and S3 without requiring internet access, NAT devices, or VPN. Traffic to S3 stays within the AWS backbone, reducing latency, improving reliability, and avoiding NAT saturation. It is simple to set up and cost-effective, as there are no data processing charges for gateway endpoints. From this discussion, we learned that using a VPC gateway endpoint is the best way to privately and reliably access S3 without traversing the internet or managing additional NAT infrastructure. This question belongs to Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures, as it focuses on optimizing network performance and reliability for AWS Lambda to Amazon S3 communication.

question: A company needs to connect several VPCs in the us-east-1 Region that span hundreds of AWS accounts. The company's networking team has its own AWS account to manage the cloud network. What is the MOST operationally efficient solution to connect the VPCs?
options: Set up VPC peering connections between each VPC. Update each associated subnet’s route table
Configure a NAT gateway and an internet gateway in each VPC to connect each VPC through the internet
Create an AWS Transit Gateway in the networking team’s AWS account. Configure static routes from each VPC.
Deploy VPN gateways in each VPC. Create a transit VPC in the networking team’s AWS account to connect to each VPC.
explanation: The correct answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): VPC peering requires setting up a peering connection between every pair of VPCs (N*(N-1)/2), which becomes operationally overwhelming when you have hundreds of VPCs. Peering does not support transitive routing—each route table must be updated individually, and you cannot centralize connectivity easily. Option B (INCORRECT): Using Internet Gateways and NAT Gateways to route between VPCs sends traffic over the public internet, introducing security risks and higher latency. This approach incurs egress data-transfer costs and does not provide private, scalable, or manageable inter-VPC connectivity. Option D (INCORRECT): The “transit VPC” pattern with VPN gateways and EC2-based routers is a legacy solution that requires managing VPN connections and EC2 instances at scale. It adds operational overhead (patching, scaling, HA) and is more complex and costly versus a native AWS service. Option C (CORRECT): AWS Transit Gateway provides a central hub for inter-VPC connectivity, supports transitive routing, and scales to thousands of attachments. You can share a single Transit Gateway across hundreds of AWS accounts using AWS RAM, letting the networking team manage one resource. Route tables on the Transit Gateway allow you to control traffic flows centrally, greatly reducing manual route management and operational complexity. Summary: AWS Transit Gateway is the most operationally efficient way to connect many VPCs across multiple accounts in a single region, offering centralized management, scalability, and transitive routing. This question falls under Domain 2 - Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company has a business system that generates hundreds of reports each day. The business system saves the reports to a network share in CSV format. The company needs to store this data in the AWS Cloud in near-real time for analysis. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST administrative overhead?
options: Use AWS DataSync to transfer the files to Amazon S3. Create a scheduled task that runs at the end of each day.
Create an Amazon S3 File Gateway. Update the business system to use a new network share from the S3 File Gateway.
Use AWS DataSync to transfer the files to Amazon S3. Create an application that uses the DataSync API in the automation workflow.
Deploy an AWS Transfer for SFTP endpoint. Create a script that checks for new files on the network share and uploads the new files by using SFTP.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): Using AWS DataSync with a daily scheduled task moves files only once per day, which fails the near-real-time requirement. It also adds extra overhead for scheduling and monitoring the DataSync task. Option C (INCORRECT): While AWS DataSync can transfer files continuously, building a custom application to invoke the DataSync API increases administrative overhead. This approach is more complex than necessary for simply mirroring a network share to S3. Option D (INCORRECT): Deploying AWS Transfer for SFTP and writing a script to poll and upload adds significant operational complexity. It requires maintaining scripts, handling retries, and does not integrate as seamlessly as a file gateway for near-real-time ingestion. Option B (CORRECT): An Amazon S3 File Gateway presents a standard network share (SMB/NFS) backed by S3. The business system can continue writing CSV files to a local mount, and the gateway uploads each file to S3 in near-real time. This solution requires minimal configuration and no custom coding, meeting the requirement with the least administrative overhead. In summary, we learned that when ingesting files in near-real time with minimal operational burden, an S3 File Gateway is the simplest choice. This question maps to Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures, as it focuses on real-time data transfer and scalability.

question: A company is creating an application that runs on containers in a VPC. The application stores and accesses data in an Amazon S3 bucket. During the development phase, the application will store and access 1 TB of data in Amazon S3 each day. The company wants to minimize costs and wants to prevent traffic from traversing the internet whenever possible. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering for the S3 bucket
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration for the S3 bucket
Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3. Associate this endpoint with all route tables in the VPC
Create an interface endpoint for Amazon S3 in the VPC. Associate this endpoint with all route tables in the VPC
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): “Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering for the S3 bucket.” S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between access tiers to reduce storage cost—it does not affect network routing. It does not prevent data from traversing the internet or reduce data-transfer charges when accessing S3 from within a VPC. Option B (INCORRECT): “Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration for the S3 bucket.” Transfer Acceleration speeds up transfers by routing through CloudFront edge locations over the public internet. This incurs additional cost and does not keep traffic entirely within the AWS backbone. It contradicts the requirement to avoid internet traversal and minimize cost. Option D (INCORRECT): “Create an interface endpoint for Amazon S3 in the VPC. Associate this endpoint with all route tables in the VPC.” Amazon S3 supports only gateway VPC endpoints, not interface endpoints via PrivateLink. Interface endpoints (if they existed for S3) would incur hourly and data-processing charges, increasing cost. This option is not valid for S3 and would not be the most cost-effective solution. Option C (CORRECT): “Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3. Associate this endpoint with all route tables in the VPC.” Gateway VPC endpoints for S3 are free and allow private connectivity between your VPC and S3 without an internet gateway, NAT, or public IPs. All S3 traffic stays within the AWS network, eliminating internet egress charges and improving security. This meets both requirements: minimizing costs and preventing traffic from traversing the internet. In summary, using a gateway VPC endpoint for S3 ensures private, cost-efficient access to S3 from within your VPC. This solution aligns with Domain 4 – Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company has a large dataset for its online advertising business stored in an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance in a single Availability Zone. The company wants business reporting queries to run without impacting the write operations to the production DB instance.Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Deploy RDS read replicas to process the business reporting queries.
Scale out the DB instance horizontally by placing it behind an Elastic Load Balancer.
Scale up the DB instance to a larger instance type to handle write operations and queries.
Deploy the DB instance in multiple Availability Zones to process the business reporting queries.
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): “Scale out the DB instance horizontally by placing it behind an Elastic Load Balancer.” Elastic Load Balancer is used for distributing incoming application or network traffic across multiple targets, such as EC2 instances, containers, and IP addresses, not RDS instances. RDS does not support placing database instances behind an ELB for query load distribution. This approach cannot offload read traffic from the primary instance and would not prevent reporting queries from impacting writes. Option C (INCORRECT): “Scale up the DB instance to a larger instance type to handle write operations and queries.” Scaling vertically (bigger instance) can improve capacity but doesn’t isolate reporting workload from writes. All reads and writes still contend on the same instance resources, so heavy reporting can still impact write performance. This does not provide the separation needed for high-performing, non-disruptive analytics queries. Option D (INCORRECT): “Deploy the DB instance in multiple Availability Zones to process the business reporting queries.” Multi-AZ deployments create a synchronous standby for high availability and failover, not for read scaling. The standby instance is not open for read operations; it only serves as a failover target. This configuration improves resilience, but cannot serve reporting queries without impacting the primary. Option A (CORRECT): “Deploy RDS read replicas to process the business reporting queries.” Read replicas provide one or more read-only copies of the primary database, isolating read-heavy workloads. Reporting queries run against the replica(s), so the primary instance’s write performance is unaffected. MySQL read replicas are easy to set up in RDS and can be placed in the same or different Availability Zones for additional resiliency and performance. Summary: We learned that to offload read-heavy reporting workloads without impacting the production writer, Amazon RDS Read Replicas are the ideal solution. This question belongs to Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company runs an Oracle database on premises. As part of the company’s migration to AWS, the company wants to upgrade the database to the most recent available version. The company also wants to set up disaster recovery (DR) for the database. The company needs to minimize the operational overhead for normal operations and DR setup. The company also needs to maintain access to the database's underlying operating system. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Migrate the Oracle database to an Amazon EC2 instance. Set up database replication to a different AWS Region.
Migrate the Oracle database to Amazon RDS for Oracle. Activate Cross-Region automated backups to replicate the snapshots to another AWS Region.
Migrate the Oracle database to Amazon RDS Custom for Oracle. Create a read replica for the database in another AWS Region.
Migrate the Oracle database to Amazon RDS for Oracle. Create a standby database in another Availability Zone.
explanation: The correct Answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): “Migrate the Oracle database to an Amazon EC2 instance. Set up database replication to a different AWS Region.” You must fully manage the OS, patching, backups, and Oracle installation yourself—this fails the requirement to minimize operational overhead. Replicating at the database level on EC2 involves significant manual setup and maintenance. No built-in AWS automated minor-version upgrades or managed DR features are available. Option B (INCORRECT): “Migrate the Oracle database to Amazon RDS for Oracle. Activate Cross-Region automated backups to replicate the snapshots to another AWS Region.” RDS for Oracle does not provide underlying OS access, so you cannot meet the requirement to maintain OS‐level control. Cross-Region automated backups only copy snapshots, which leads to longer recovery times and manual restores. This approach reduces DR RTO/RPO guarantees compared to replication or read replicas. Option D (INCORRECT): “Migrate the Oracle database to Amazon RDS for Oracle. Create a standby database in another Availability Zone.” Multi-AZ in the same region is High Availability, not full DR—if the region fails, you lose access. RDS for Oracle does not expose the OS, so you cannot administer the host directly. No cross-Region failover; you cannot meet a true DR requirement. Option C (CORRECT): “Migrate the Oracle database to Amazon RDS Custom for Oracle. Create a read replica for the database in another AWS Region.” RDS Custom gives you managed database operations plus direct OS access for any required customizations. You can upgrade to the latest Oracle version with minimal operational overhead, since RDS handles patching and minor-version upgrades. Cross-Region read replicas provide near-real-time replication for DR, and you can promote a replica if the primary region fails. Overall, this meets the need for OS access, the latest DB version, minimal ops overhead, and reliable DR. Summary: We’ve learned that Amazon RDS Custom for Oracle strikes the right balance between managed operations and OS-level control, while cross-Region read replicas deliver effective disaster recovery. This scenario falls under Domain 2 - Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A solutions architect observes that a nightly batch processing job is automatically scaled up for 1 hour before the desired Amazon EC2 capacity is reached. The peak capacity is the ‘same every night and the batch jobs always start at 1 AM. The solutions architect needs to find a cost-effective solution that will allow for the desired EC2 capacity to be reached quickly and allow the Auto Scaling group to scale down after the batch jobs are complete. What should the solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
options: Increase the minimum capacity for the Auto Scaling group.
Increase the maximum capacity for the Auto Scaling group.
Configure scheduled scaling to scale up to the desired compute level.
Change the scaling policy to add more EC2 instances during each scaling operation.
explanation: The correct answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): “Increase the minimum capacity for the Auto Scaling group.” Raising the minimum capacity would keep instances running even when not needed, increasing costs. It does not address the timing of scale-out; it just ensures a floor, not a scheduled peak. Option B (INCORRECT): “Increase the maximum capacity for the Auto Scaling group.” The group is already capable of reaching the needed peak; the problem is that scaling up takes too long. Raising the maximum limit alone won’t make instances launch faster at 1 AM. Option D (INCORRECT): “Change the scaling policy to add more EC2 instances during each scaling operation.” Adjusting step or simple scaling policies may speed up growth slightly but still relies on CloudWatch metrics reacting to load. Because the batch job always starts at 1 AM with predictable demand, reactive policies can lag behind and incur delays. Option C (CORRECT): “Configure scheduled scaling to scale up to the desired compute level.” Scheduled scaling lets you pre-emptively launch the exact number of EC2 instances at 1 AM, ensuring capacity is ready when the batch job starts. After the job completes, the Auto Scaling group can automatically scale down, preventing unnecessary uptime and reducing cost. This approach is both predictable and cost-effective for fixed, recurring workloads. In summary, we learned that when you have a predictable, nightly batch workload, using AWS Auto Scaling’s scheduled scaling is the most cost-optimized way to ensure capacity is available right when you need it and to release resources afterward. This question falls under Domain 4 – Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company hosts an application in a private subnet. The company has already integrated the application with Amazon Cognito. The company uses an Amazon Cognito user pool to authenticate users. The company needs to modify the application so the application can securely store user documents in an Amazon S3 bucket.Which combination of steps will securely integrate Amazon S3 with the application? (Choose two.)
options: Create an Amazon Cognito identity pool to generate secure Amazon S3 access tokens for users when they successfully log in.
Use the existing Amazon Cognito user pool to generate Amazon S3 access tokens for users when they successfully log in.
Create an Amazon S3 VPC endpoint in the same VPC where the company hosts the application.
Create a NAT gateway in the VPC where the company hosts the application. Assign a policy to the S3 bucket to deny any request that is not initiated from Amazon Cognito.
Attach a policy to the S3 bucket that allows access only from the users' IP addresses.
explanation: The correct answer is A, C. Option B (INCORRECT): Using the existing Amazon Cognito user pool alone cannot generate AWS credentials for S3 access. User pools only handle authentication (username/password), but do not issue temporary IAM roles or AWS access tokens. You must use an identity pool to obtain AWS credentials. Option D (INCORRECT): While a NAT gateway allows outbound internet access from a private subnet, it is not required if you use a VPC endpoint to reach S3 privately. Moreover, you cannot write an S3 bucket policy that reliably detects “requests initiated from Cognito” alone—authentication comes from IAM roles assumed via an identity pool, not directly from Cognito user pools. Option E (INCORRECT): Restricting S3 access by the users’ IP addresses is brittle and insecure. End-user IPs are dynamic, VPNs may change addresses, and this approach does not integrate with Cognito for fine-grained access control. Option A (CORRECT): Create a Cognito Identity Pool. Identity pools federate identities from your user pool and issue temporary AWS credentials (via IAM roles) so authenticated users can directly call S3. This is the standard method for granting least-privilege S3 access to Cognito-authenticated users. Option C (CORRECT): Deploy an S3 VPC endpoint (Gateway endpoint) in the application’s VPC. This allows the private-subnet application to reach S3 without traversing the internet or NAT gateway, and you can enforce aws:sourceVpce in the bucket policy to permit access only via that endpoint. In summary, by combining A (Cognito Identity Pool for IAM credentials) with C (VPC Endpoint for private connectivity), you securely integrate S3 with your private-subnet application. This question tests your ability to design secure, private access to AWS services and therefore falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company runs workloads in the AWS Cloud. The company wants to centrally collect security data to assess security across the entire company and to improve workload protection.Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?
options: Configure a data lake in AWS Lake Formation. Use AWS Glue crawlers to ingest the security data into the data lake.
Configure an AWS Lambda function to collect the security data in .csv format. Upload the data to an Amazon S3 bucket.
Configure a data lake in Amazon Security Lake to collect the security data. Upload the data to an Amazon S3 bucket.
Configure an AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) replication instance to load the security data into an Amazon RDS cluster.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): “Configure a data lake in AWS Lake Formation. Use AWS Glue crawlers to ingest the security data into the data lake.” Lake Formation is a general-purpose data-lake service. It requires defining schemas, building ETL, and managing crawlers for each data source. This approach involves significant development and configuration effort to normalize and ingest multiple security log formats. It is not tailored for security data, so you would still have to build connectors or parsers for each service’s logs. Option B (INCORRECT): “Configure an AWS Lambda function to collect the security data in .csv format. Upload the data to an Amazon S3 bucket.” This is a custom‐built solution requiring you to write, deploy, and maintain Lambdas for every log source. Parsing, error-handling, schema management, and format conversions all add to the development burden. It lacks the out-of-the-box normalization and enrichment that a security-focused service provides. Option D (INCORRECT): “Configure an AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) replication instance to load the security data into an Amazon RDS cluster.” DMS is designed for database replication and migration, not for streaming or batch-ingesting log files and security events. Security logs are typically in JSON, text, or proprietary formats—not relational tables—making DMS unsuitable. You would need to build or configure additional agents to convert and feed your logs into a supported database schema, increasing development effort. Option C (CORRECT): “Configure a data lake in Amazon Security Lake to collect the security data. Upload the data to an Amazon S3 bucket.” Amazon Security Lake is a purpose-built service that automatically centralizes and normalizes security logs from AWS sources and supported third-party tools. It requires minimal setup—enabling Security Lake in your AWS Organizations accounts—and then it automatically delivers data in a standardized schema to your designated S3 buckets. This out-of-the-box integration minimizes custom development, operational maintenance, and schema-management work. Summary: We have evaluated why generic data-lake (Lake Formation), custom Lambda scripts, and DMS-based approaches introduce unnecessary development and operational complexity. Amazon Security Lake provides a turnkey solution for aggregating, normalizing, and storing security data across multiple accounts with minimal effort. This question belongs to Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures, as it focuses on centralized security data collection and workload protection.

question: A company has applications that run on Amazon EC2 instances. The EC2 instances connect to Amazon RDS databases by using an IAM role that has associated policies. The company wants to use AWS Systems Manager to patch the EC2 instances without disrupting the running applications.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Create a new IAM role. Attach the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy to the new IAM role. Attach the new IAM role to the EC2 instances and the existing IAM role.
Create an IAM user. Attach the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy to the IAM user. Configure Systems Manager to use the IAM user to manage the EC2 instances.
Enable Default Host Configuration Management in Systems Manager to manage the EC2 instances.
Remove the existing policies from the existing IAM role. Add the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy to the existing IAM role.
explanation: The correct answer is D Option A (INCORRECT): Suggests creating a second IAM role and attaching it alongside the existing one. EC2 instances can only have one IAM instance profile (one role) at launch. You cannot attach two separate IAM roles to the same running EC2 instance—this makes A invalid. Option B (INCORRECT): Proposes using an IAM user for Systems Manager. SSM Patch Manager requires the EC2 instance to be registered with an IAM role, not an IAM user. Systems Manager agents authenticate via the instance profile, so a user‐based approach will not work. Option C (INCORRECT): “Default Host Configuration Management” in Systems Manager refers to State Manager for applying configuration documents, not Patch Manager for OS patching. That feature does not by itself grant the EC2 instances the required SSM permissions to download and apply patches. Option D (CORRECT): Modify the existing EC2 instance role to include the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy. This grants the SSM agent permission to communicate with Systems Manager for patching. By updating the same IAM role, you retain the current RDS-access policies and seamlessly add SSM Patch Manager permissions without disrupting your applications. In summary, you should simply augment the existing EC2 instance IAM role with the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy so the instances can register with Systems Manager and receive patch instructions. This question tests your ability to design secure and operationally resilient architectures by leveraging IAM and Systems Manager correctly. This belongs to Domain 2 – Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company's infrastructure consists of hundreds of Amazon EC2 instances that use Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) storage. A solutions architect must ensure that every EC2 instance can be recovered after a disaster.What should the solutions architect do to meet this requirement with the LEAST amount of effort?
options: Take a snapshot of the EBS storage that is attached to each EC2 instance. Create an AWS CloudFormation template to launch new EC2 instances from the EBS storage.
Take a snapshot of the EBS storage that is attached to each EC2 instance. Use AWS Elastic Beanstalk to set the environment based on the EC2 template and attach the EBS storage.
Use AWS Backup to set up a backup plan for the entire group of EC2 instances. Use the AWS Backup API or the AWS CLI to speed up the restore process for multiple EC2 instances.

Create an AWS Lambda function to take a snapshot of the EBS storage that is attached to each EC2 instance and copy the Amazon Machine Images (AMIs). Create another Lambda function to perform the restores with the copied AMIs and attach the EBS storage.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): “Take a snapshot of the EBS storage that is attached to each EC2 instance. Create an AWS CloudFormation template to launch new EC2 instances from the EBS storage.” Manually managing snapshots and building CloudFormation templates for hundreds of instances adds significant operational overhead. CloudFormation automates infrastructure provisioning, but it does not natively manage snapshot scheduling, retention, or cross-region replication out of the box. Recovery would still require manual adjustment of templates and parameters for each instance type, making this approach labor-intensive. Option B (INCORRECT): “Take a snapshot of the EBS storage that is attached to each EC2 instance. Use AWS Elastic Beanstalk to set the environment based on the EC2 template and attach the EBS storage.” AWS Elastic Beanstalk is a PaaS service for deploying and scaling web applications, not for orchestrating low-level EBS snapshot backups. Elastic Beanstalk environments are designed around application platforms (e.g., Java, Node.js) and not for arbitrary EC2 + EBS configurations at scale. This detours from the requirement to protect existing EC2 instances and increases complexity without adding backup automation benefits. Option D (INCORRECT): “Create an AWS Lambda function to take a snapshot of the EBS storage that is attached to each EC2 instance and copy the Amazon Machine Images (AMIs). Create another Lambda function to perform the restores with the copied AMIs and attach the EBS storage.” While feasible, this custom solution requires writing, testing, and maintaining Lambda code for backup scheduling, snapshot lifecycle, and restores. Handling errors, retries, cross-region copies, and retention policies in custom code is error-prone and adds ongoing maintenance tasks. The “least amount of effort” requirement rules out heavy custom automation when AWS Backup provides built-in capabilities. Option C (CORRECT): “Use AWS Backup to set up a backup plan for the entire group of EC2 instances. Use the AWS Backup API or the AWS CLI to speed up the restore process for multiple EC2 instances.” AWS Backup provides centralized, automated backup management for EBS volumes, EC2 instances, RDS, DynamoDB, and more. You can define backup plans with scheduling, retention, lifecycle rules, and cross-region replication—no custom code required. Restores can be orchestrated via the AWS Backup console, API, or CLI, simplifying recovery for multiple instances with minimal manual effort. In summary, AWS Backup delivers an out-of-the-box, policy-driven solution to protect your EC2/EBS infrastructure with the least operational effort. This question falls under Domain 2 – Design Resilient Architectures, as it focuses on disaster recovery and ensuring recoverability of compute resources.

question: A company that hosts its web application on AWS wants to ensure all Amazon EC2 instances. Amazon RDS DB instances. and Amazon Redshift clusters are configured with tags. The company wants to minimize the effort of configuring and operating this check. What should a solutions architect do to accomplish this?
options: Use AWS Config rules to define and detect resources that are not properly tagged.
Use Cost Explorer to display resources that are not properly tagged. Tag those resources manually.
Write API calls to check all resources for proper tag allocation. Periodically run the code on an EC2 instance.
Write API calls to check all resources for proper tag allocation. Schedule an AWS Lambda function through Amazon CloudWatch to periodically run the code.
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): “Use Cost Explorer to display resources that are not properly tagged. Tag those resources manually.” Cost Explorer is intended for analyzing and visualizing cost and usage data, not for enforcing or detecting tagging compliance in real time. It does not provide automated checks or continuous evaluation of tag presence—manual intervention is required, increasing operational overhead. Option C (INCORRECT): “Write API calls to check all resources for proper tag allocation. Periodically run the code on an EC2 instance.” This solution requires you to develop, deploy, and maintain custom scripts on an EC2 instance, adding undifferentiated heavy lifting. Scheduling, scaling, error handling, and patching the EC2 instance are all your responsibility, which increases effort and risk. Option D (INCORRECT): “Write API calls to check all resources for proper tag allocation. Schedule an AWS Lambda function through Amazon CloudWatch to periodically run the code.” While Lambda is serverless, you still must write, test, and maintain custom code and a CloudWatch Events (EventBridge) schedule. This approach lacks the built-in compliance reporting and remediation capabilities that a managed service like AWS Config provides. Option A (CORRECT): “Use AWS Config rules to define and detect resources that are not properly tagged.” AWS Config offers a managed rule (e.g., required-tags) that continuously checks your EC2, RDS, and Redshift resources for specific tag keys. No custom code or infrastructure is required—Config automatically evaluates compliance and can trigger notifications or automated remediation. This solution minimizes operational effort, provides audit history, and integrates with AWS Organizations for account-wide governance. In summary, AWS Config rules offer a fully managed, continuous, and scalable way to enforce tagging standards across AWS resources with minimal operational overhead. This question belongs to Domain 4 – Design Cost-Optimized Architectures, as proper tagging directly supports cost allocation, reporting, and optimization.

question: A solutions architect is designing the storage architecture for a new web application used for storing and viewing engineering drawings. All application components will be deployed on the AWS infrastructure. The application design must support caching to minimize the amount of time that users wait for the engineering drawings to load. The application must be able to store petabytes of data.Which combination of storage and caching should the solutions architect use?
options: Amazon S3 with Amazon CloudFront
Amazon S3 Glacier with Amazon ElastiCache
Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes with Amazon CloudFront
AWS Storage Gateway with Amazon ElastiCache
explanation: The correct Answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): Amazon S3 Glacier with Amazon ElastiCache Glacier is optimized for archival storage with retrieval times in minutes to hours, not for frequent, low-latency access. ElastiCache speeds up database queries or in-memory data stores, but Glacier cannot serve as a high-performance origin for serving engineering drawings. Does not meet the requirement for near-instantaneous retrieval of large engineering files. Option C (INCORRECT): Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes with Amazon CloudFront EBS volumes are limited to tens of terabytes per volume and require manual scaling; they are not suited for petabyte-scale storage. EBS is block storage attached to EC2, not an object store that CloudFront can directly use as a global content origin. Option D (INCORRECT): AWS Storage Gateway with Amazon ElastiCache Storage Gateway is designed for hybrid on-premises to cloud integration, not for pure cloud-native, petabyte-scale object storage. ElastiCache accelerates database or in-memory workloads—it does not cache large static objects for global distribution. Option A (CORRECT): Amazon S3 with Amazon CloudFront Amazon S3 natively scales to store petabytes (and beyond) of engineering drawings with high durability and availability. CloudFront caches objects at edge locations worldwide, minimizing latency and improving load times for end users. This combination is cost-effective, fully managed, and aligns with best practices for high-performing architectures. In summary, we’ve learned that the ideal solution for storing petabytes of engineering drawings and delivering them with minimal latency is to use Amazon S3 as the scalable object store and Amazon CloudFront for global caching. This question belongs to Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company has hired an external vendor to perform work in the company’s AWS account. The vendor uses an automated tool that is hosted in an AWS account that the vendor owns. The vendor does not have IAM access to the company’s AWS account. The company needs to grant the vendor access to the company’s AWS account.Which solution will meet these requirements MOST securely?
options: Create an IAM role in the company’s account to delegate access to the vendor’s IAM role. Attach the appropriate IAM policies to the role for the permissions that the vendor requires.

Create an IAM user in the company’s account with a password that meets the password complexity requirements. Attach the appropriate IAM policies to the user for the permissions that the vendor requires.

Create an IAM group in the company’s account. Add the automated tool’s IAM user from the vendor account to the group. Attach the appropriate IAM policies to the group for the permissions that the vendor requires.

Create an IAM user in the company’s account that has a permission boundary that allows the vendor’s account. Attach the appropriate IAM policies to the user for the permissions that the vendor requires.
explanation: The correct answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): “Create an IAM user in the company’s account with a password that meets the password complexity requirements. Attach the appropriate IAM policies to the user for the permissions that the vendor requires.” • Creating a long-lived IAM user in your account is less secure because you must manage credentials (passwords/keys) and handle rotation. • It does not leverage cross-account role assumptions, so you lose the ability to enforce IAM best practices like short-lived credentials and centralized access control. Option C (INCORRECT): “Create an IAM group in the company’s account. Add the automated tool’s IAM user from the vendor account to the group. Attach the appropriate IAM policies to the group for the permissions that the vendor requires.” • IAM groups cannot include principals from other AWS accounts. • You cannot add a user from an external (vendor) account into a group in your account. Cross-account access requires roles, not group membership. Option D (INCORRECT): “Create an IAM user in the company’s account that has a permission boundary that allows the vendor’s account. Attach the appropriate IAM policies to the user for the permissions that the vendor requires.” • Permission boundaries restrict what the principal can do, but they do not establish trust between accounts. • You cannot set a boundary to “allow” another AWS account to assume an IAM user’s credentials. Cross-account delegation still requires a role with a proper trust policy. Option A (CORRECT): “Create an IAM role in the company’s account to delegate access to the vendor’s IAM role. Attach the appropriate IAM policies to the role for the permissions that the vendor requires.” • You define a trust policy on the new IAM role, allowing the vendor’s AWS account (or specific role) to assume it. • The vendor never needs long-lived credentials in your account—they simply call AssumeRole to get short-lived, scoped-down permissions. • This follows AWS security best practices for cross-account access: least privilege, temporary credentials, and centralized policy management. Summary: We learned how to securely grant an external vendor cross-account access using IAM roles rather than creating permanent users or misusing groups or permission boundaries. This question belongs to Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company has a multi-tier payment processing application that is based on virtual machines (VMs). The communication between the tiers occurs asynchronously through a third-party middleware solution that guarantees exactly-once delivery. The company needs a solution that requires the least amount of infrastructure management. The solution must guarantee exactly-once delivery for application messaging. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
options: Use AWS Lambda for the compute layers in the architecture.
Use Amazon EC2 instances for the compute layers in the architecture.
Use Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) as the messaging component between the compute layers.
Use Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queues as the messaging component between the compute layers.
Use containers that are based on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) for the compute layers in the architecture.
explanation: The correct answer is A, D Option B (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon EC2 instances for the compute layers in the architecture.” • EC2 requires you to manage servers, patching, scaling, and high-availability yourself. • The requirement is to minimize infrastructure management, so EC2 is not the best fit. Option C (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) as the messaging component between the compute layers.” • SNS is “at‐least-once” delivery and does not guarantee exactly-once semantics. • To meet exactly-once delivery, you need FIFO ordering and deduplication provided by SQS FIFO. Option E (INCORRECT): “Use containers that are based on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) for the compute layers in the architecture.” • EKS reduces some undifferentiated heavy lifting but still requires cluster management, updates, and scaling. • AWS Lambda offers truly serverless compute with no EC2/EKS management overhead. Option A (CORRECT): “Use AWS Lambda for the compute layers in the architecture.” • Lambda is fully managed and auto-scales with demand, eliminating server management. • It integrates natively with SQS FIFO, enabling event-driven, exactly-once processing. Option D (CORRECT): “Use Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queues as the messaging component between the compute layers.” • SQS FIFO provides exactly-once processing with deduplication and ordered delivery. • It is a fully managed service, requiring minimal operational overhead compared to custom middleware. In summary, combining AWS Lambda (serverless compute) with Amazon SQS FIFO (exactly-once messaging) meets the requirement for minimal infrastructure management and guaranteed exactly-once delivery. This question falls under Domain 2 – Design Resilient Architectures, focusing on ensuring reliable, fault-tolerant communication between application tiers.

question: A hospital needs to store patient records in an Amazon S3 bucket. The hospital’s compliance team must ensure that all protected health information (PHI) is encrypted in transit and at rest. The compliance team must administer the encryption key for data at rest. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Create a public SSL/TLS certificate in AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Associate the certificate with Amazon S3. Configure default encryption for each S3 bucket to use server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS). Assign the compliance team to manage the KMS keys.

Use the aws:SecureTransport condition on S3 bucket policies to allow only encrypted connections over HTTPS (TLS). Configure default encryption for each S3 bucket to use server-side encryption with S3 managed encryption keys (SSE-S3). Assign the compliance team to manage the SSE-S3 keys.

Use the aws:SecureTransport condition on S3 bucket policies to allow only encrypted connections over HTTPS (TLS). Configure default encryption for each S3 bucket to use server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS). Assign the compliance team to manage the KMS keys.

Use the aws:SecureTransport condition on S3 bucket policies to allow only encrypted connections over HTTPS (TLS). Use Amazon Macie to protect the sensitive data that is stored in Amazon S3. Assign the compliance team to manage Macie.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): Creating a public ACM certificate and “associating” it with S3 is unnecessary because S3 already supports SSL/TLS by default; you don’t attach ACM certificates to S3 buckets in that way. You correctly configure SSE-KMS for at-rest encryption, but the invalid certificate association step makes this solution unworkable. Option B (INCORRECT): Using aws:SecureTransport in the bucket policy enforces HTTPS in transit (good), but SSE-S3 uses Amazon-managed keys that the compliance team cannot administer. The requirement specifies that the compliance team must manage the encryption key for data at rest, which SSE-S3 does not allow. Option D (INCORRECT): Enforcing HTTPS via aws:SecureTransport is correct, but Amazon Macie is for discovering, classifying, and protecting sensitive data—not for providing customer-managed encryption keys. Macie does not handle server-side encryption or key administration for S3 objects. Option C (CORRECT): Uses the aws:SecureTransport condition in an S3 bucket policy to require HTTPS, ensuring encryption in transit. Configures default S3 bucket encryption to use SSE-KMS with a customer-managed CMK. The compliance team can own and administer this KMS key, satisfying the at-rest encryption and key-management requirement. This meets both compliance requirements: enforced TLS for all connections and customer-managed keys for data at rest. In summary, we learned how to enforce encryption in transit using aws:SecureTransport and how to meet at-rest encryption and key-management requirements with SSE-KMS and a customer-managed CMK. This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company is running a custom application on Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances. The application has frontend nodes that need to run 24 hours a day, 7 days a week and backend nodes that need to run only for a short time based on workload. The number of backend nodes varies during the day. The company needs to scale out and scale in more instances based on workload. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Use Reserved Instances for the frontend nodes. Use AWS Fargate for the backend nodes.
Use Reserved Instances for the frontend nodes. Use Spot Instances for the backend nodes.
Use Spot Instances for the frontend nodes. Use Reserved Instances for the backend nodes.
Use Spot Instances for the frontend nodes. Use AWS Fargate for the backend nodes.
explanation: The correct answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): “Use Reserved Instances for the frontend nodes. Use AWS Fargate for the backend nodes.” While Reserved Instances are a great fit for the always-on frontend servers, AWS Fargate billing (per vCPU/sec + per GB memory/sec) tends to be more expensive than Spot Instances for highly variable workloads. Fargate has less flexibility on bidding or capacity-optimized pools compared to EC2 Spot, so it’s not the MOST cost-effective for backend bursts. Option C (INCORRECT): “Use Spot Instances for the frontend nodes. Use Reserved Instances for the backend nodes.” Frontend nodes require 24x7 availability, but Spot Instances can be reclaimed at any time—leading to potential downtime. Backend workloads are transient and variable, so locking them into Reserved Instances wastes money when capacity isn’t needed. Option D (INCORRECT): “Use Spot Instances for the frontend nodes. Use AWS Fargate for the backend nodes.” Again, Spot Instances are unsuitable for persistent 24x7 frontends due to interruptions. Fargate, while serverless, generally costs more per compute unit than Spot Instances for heavy or bursty backend jobs. Option B (CORRECT): “Use Reserved Instances for the frontend nodes. Use Spot Instances for the backend nodes.” Reserved Instances lock in the lowest hourly rate for always-on, predictable frontend servers, ensuring both capacity and cost savings. Spot Instances offer up to 90% discount for EC2, making them ideal for short-lived, variable backend processing. Auto Scaling can seamlessly scale Spot-backed groups out/in based on workload, delivering the MOST cost-effective solution. Summary: We learned that blending Reserved Instances for steady, 24x7 workloads with Spot Instances for variable, short-lived tasks achieves optimal cost savings. This question falls under Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company has released a new version of its production application. The company's workload uses Amazon EC2, AWS Lambda, AWS Fargate, and Amazon SageMaker. The company wants to cost optimize the workload now that usage is at a steady state. The company wants to cover the most services with the fewest savings plans. Which combination of savings plans will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
options: Purchase an EC2 Instance Savings Plan for Amazon EC2 and SageMaker.
Purchase a Compute Savings Plan for Amazon EC2, Lambda, and SageMaker.
Purchase a SageMaker Savings Plan.
Purchase a Compute Savings Plan for Lambda, Fargate, and Amazon EC2.
Purchase an EC2 Instance Savings Plan for Amazon EC2 and Fargate.
explanation: The correct answer is C, D. Option A (INCORRECT): “Purchase an EC2 Instance Savings Plan for Amazon EC2 and SageMaker.” EC2 Instance Savings Plans only apply to EC2 instance usage within a chosen instance family and region. They do not cover Amazon SageMaker compute charges—SageMaker requires its own Savings Plan. Option B (INCORRECT): “Purchase a Compute Savings Plan for Amazon EC2, Lambda, and SageMaker.” Compute Savings Plans cover EC2, AWS Lambda, and AWS Fargate usage. They do not apply to SageMaker; SageMaker usage isn’t included under Compute Plans. Option E (INCORRECT): “Purchase an EC2 Instance Savings Plan for Amazon EC2 and Fargate.” EC2 Instance Savings Plans only cover EC2 instance usage (per family/region). They do not include AWS Fargate tasks. Option D (CORRECT): “Purchase a Compute Savings Plan for Lambda, Fargate, and Amazon EC2.” Compute Savings Plans apply across EC2, Lambda, and Fargate, giving you maximum coverage and flexibility. One plan covers all three compute services with a single commitment. Option C (CORRECT): “Purchase a SageMaker Savings Plan.” SageMaker Savings Plans are specifically designed to reduce costs for SageMaker training and inference instance usage. This plan covers all SageMaker compute charges regardless of instance type or region. In summary, combining a Compute Savings Plan (for EC2, Lambda, Fargate) with a SageMaker Savings Plan (for SageMaker) covers all four services with just two commitments. This question falls under Domain 4 – Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: An entertainment company is using Amazon DynamoDB to store media metadata. The application is read intensive and experiencing delays. The company does not have staff to handle additional operational overhead and needs to improve the performance efficiency of DynamoDB without reconfiguring the application. What should a solutions architect recommend to meet this requirement?
options: Use Amazon ElastiCache for Redis.
Use Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX).
Replicate data by using DynamoDB global tables.
Use Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached with Auto Discovery enabled.
explanation: The correct answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): Use Amazon ElastiCache for Redis. While Redis can cache reads, it introduces operational overhead—you must manage cluster nodes, scaling, patching, and failover. The application would need to be reconfigured to check the cache first and fall back to DynamoDB on a miss. The requirement states there is no extra staff to handle new operational complexity. Option C (INCORRECT): Replicate data by using DynamoDB global tables. Global tables provide multi-region redundancy and high availability, not read-caching for performance. They increase write costs (replicating data across regions) and add latency for cross-region writes. This does not directly address read latency or remove operational overhead—still uses DynamoDB APIs without caching. Option D (INCORRECT): Use Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached with Auto Discovery enabled. Memcached also requires application logic changes to read from cache first and write through to DynamoDB on a miss. Managing a Memcached cluster (scale-out, failover, monitoring) adds operational overhead. The question specifies no extra operational staff and no application reconfiguration. Option B (CORRECT): Use Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX). DAX is a fully managed, in-memory cache for DynamoDB that delivers up to a 10x read performance improvement. It requires minimal code changes (just swap your DynamoDB client with a DAX client) and no ongoing cluster management. Because DAX sits within the DynamoDB API calls, the application logic remains essentially unchanged—meeting the requirement of no reconfiguration and no added operational overhead. In summary, we learned that to improve DynamoDB read performance with zero operational overhead and minimal application changes, Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is the appropriate choice. This scenario falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company has an application with a REST-based interface that allows data to be received in near-real time from a third-party vendor. Once received, the application processes and stores the data for further analysis. The application is running on Amazon EC2 instances. The third-party vendor has received many 503 Service Unavailable Errors when sending data to the application. When the data volume spikes, the compute capacity reaches its maximum limit and the application is unable to process all requests. Which design should a solutions architect recommend to provide a more scalable solution?
options: Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to ingest the data. Process the data using AWS Lambda functions.
Use Amazon API Gateway on top of the existing application. Create a usage plan with a quota limit for the third-party vendor.
Use Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) to ingest the data. Put the EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer.
Repackage the application as a container. Deploy the application using Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) using the EC2 launch type with an Auto Scaling group.
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): Use Amazon API Gateway on top of the existing application and create a usage plan with a quota limit for the third-party vendor. API Gateway rate‐limits or throttles requests but does not buffer or queue them; excess calls still receive 429/503 errors rather than being held for later processing. A usage plan simply caps the total requests, which may lead to dropped data rather than scalable ingestion during spiky loads. It does not decouple the vendor from the backend compute, so your EC2 fleet still faces burst‐induced overloads. Option C (INCORRECT): Use Amazon SNS to ingest the data and place EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. SNS is a push‐based notification service, not a durable queue; subscribers must keep up or messages may be retried/dropped. SNS + ALB + EC2 still couples ingestion directly to compute capacity without elastic buffering of high‐throughput streams. This design does not guarantee ordering or long‐term retention needed for near-real-time analytics at scale. Option D (INCORRECT): Repackage the application as a container and deploy on Amazon ECS (EC2 launch type) with an Auto Scaling group. Containerizing and using ECS with Auto Scaling helps manage compute, but it does not address burst buffering or decoupling. Spiky loads could still exceed scaled-out container capacity and result in throttled requests or 503 errors. A scalable ingestion layer (stream or queue) is needed to smooth traffic spikes before processing. Option A (CORRECT): Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to ingest the data and process it with AWS Lambda functions. Kinesis Data Streams provides a durable, fault-tolerant, and auto‐scaling ingestion layer that can absorb traffic spikes without dropping data. Lambda consumers can scale out in parallel to process shards at their own pace, decoupling ingestion from compute capacity. This design ensures near-real-time analytics, high throughput, and no 503 errors back to the vendor, as Kinesis buffers the incoming records. In this discussion we learned that properly decoupling data ingestion from processing is key to handling unpredictable traffic spikes. By using Amazon Kinesis Data Streams plus Lambda we achieve elastic scaling, durable buffering, and near-real-time processing. This question falls under Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A research laboratory needs to process approximately 8 TB of data. The laboratory requires sub-millisecond latencies and a minimum throughput of 6 GBps for the storage subsystem. Hundreds of Amazon EC2 instances that run Amazon Linux will distribute and process the data. Which solution will meet the performance requirements?
options: Create an Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP file system. Sat each volume’ tiering policy to ALL. Import the raw data into the file system. Mount the fila system on the EC2 instances.

Create an Amazon S3 bucket to store the raw data. Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system that uses persistent SSD storage. Select the option to import data from and export data to Amazon S3. Mount the file system on the EC2 instances.

Create an Amazon S3 bucket to store the raw data. Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system that uses persistent HDD storage. Select the option to import data from and export data to Amazon S3. Mount the file system on the EC2 instances.
Create an Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP file system. Set each volume’s tiering policy to NONE. Import the raw data into the file system. Mount the file system on the EC2 instances.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Let’s step through why A, C, and D are not correct, and why B is the correct choice: Option A (INCORRECT): Create an Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP file system with each volume’s tiering policy set to ALL. ONTAP is not optimized for sub-millisecond latencies and sustained 6 GBps throughput required by HPC-style workloads. Tiering policy “ALL” moves data to lower-cost storage tiers, which increases access latency and reduces throughput. Option C (INCORRECT): Create an Amazon S3 bucket and an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system that uses persistent HDD storage. HDD-backed storage cannot deliver the sub-millisecond latencies or multi-GBps throughput (6 GBps) required for this use case. Option D (INCORRECT): Create an Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP file system with each volume’s tiering policy set to NONE. Even without tiering, ONTAP cannot sustain the consistent high throughput and ultra-low latencies needed to process 8 TB at ≥6 GBps. Option B (CORRECT): Create an Amazon S3 bucket for raw data and an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system with persistent SSD storage, selecting the import/export integration with S3. FSx for Lustre is purpose-built for high-performance compute workloads, offering sub-millisecond file access. Persistent SSD storage delivers the high IOPS and consistently scalable throughput (well above 6 GBps) needed to feed hundreds of EC2 instances. Native S3 import/export simplifies data loading and archival without sacrificing performance. In summary, leveraging FSx for Lustre with SSD ensures the sub-millisecond latencies and multi-GBps throughput required by this research workload. This question belongs to Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A solutions architect runs a web application on multiple Amazon EC2 instances that are in individual target groups behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). Users can reach the application through a public website. The solutions architect wants to allow engineers to use a development version of the website to access one specific development EC2 instance to test new features for the application. The solutions architect wants to use an Amazon Route 53 hosted zone to give the engineers access to the development instance. The solution must automatically route to the development instance even if the development instance is replaced.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Create an A Record for the development website that has the value set to the ALB. Create a listener rule on the ALB that forwards requests for the development website to the target group that contains the development instance.
Recreate the development instance with a public IP address. Create an A Record for the development website that has the value set to the public IP address of the development instance.

Create an A Record for the development website that has the value set to the ALB. Create a listener rule on the ALB to redirect requests for the development website to the public IP address of the development instance.

Place all the instances in the same target group. Create an A Record for the development website. Set the value to the ALB. Create a listener rule on the ALB that forwards requests for the development website to the target group.
explanation: The correct Answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): This suggests assigning a public IP to the development instance and pointing a Route 53 A record directly to that IP. If the instance is replaced (e.g., due to scaling or maintenance), its IP will change, breaking the DNS entry. Does not leverage the existing ALB and target-group architecture for automatic routing or health checks. Option C (INCORRECT): Uses an ALB listener rule to redirect to the instance’s public IP. Redirects send an HTTP 3xx response, not a forward. Bypasses target‐group health checks and load‐balancer benefits, and IP can change when the instance is replaced. Not a best practice for internal routing within an ALB setup. Option D (INCORRECT): Places all instances—including production and development—in the same target group. You cannot isolate traffic for the development website; requests would be distributed across all instances. Fails to guarantee that dev requests always hit only the development instance. Option A (CORRECT): Create a Route 53 A record (e.g., dev.example.com) pointing to the ALB’s DNS name—no hard-coded IP. Add a host-based listener rule on the ALB: if Host header == dev.example.com, forward to the development target group. The target group contains only the dev instance; when it’s replaced, the new instance is registered automatically. This leverages ALB health checks, automatic scaling, and keeps DNS static. In summary, we learned how to use Route 53 together with ALB host-based routing rules and target groups to provide reliable, automatic access to a specific development instance—even if it is replaced. This solution belongs to Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company is building a cloud-based application on AWS that will handle sensitive customer data. The application uses Amazon RDS for the database, Amazon S3 for object storage, and S3 Event Notifications that invoke AWS Lambda for serverless processing. The company uses AWS IAM Identity Center to manage user credentials. The development, testing, and operations teams need secure access to Amazon RDS and Amazon S3 while ensuring the confidentiality of sensitive customer data. The solution must comply with the principle of least privilege. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Use IAM roles with least privilege to grant all the teams access. Assign IAM roles to each team with customized IAM policies defining specific permission for Amazon RDS and S3 object access based on team responsibilities.

Enable IAM Identity Center with an Identity Center directory. Create and configure permission sets with granular access to Amazon RDS and Amazon S3. Assign all the teams to groups that have specific access with the permission sets.

Create individual IAM users for each member in all the teams with role-based permissions. Assign the IAM roles with predefined policies for RDS and S3 access to each user based on user needs. Implement IAM Access Analyzer for periodic credential evaluation.

Use AWS Organizations to create separate accounts for each team. Implement cross-account IAM roles with least privilege. Grant specific permission for RDS and S3 access based on team roles and responsibilities.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): “Use IAM roles with least privilege to grant all the teams access. Assign IAM roles to each team with customized IAM policies defining specific permission for Amazon RDS and S3 object access based on team responsibilities.” This approach relies on native IAM roles and policies, but the company already uses AWS IAM Identity Center for single sign-on and centralized user management. Managing individual IAM roles and policies per team increases operational overhead and complexity when scaling permissions or rotating credentials. It does not leverage the built-in features of IAM Identity Center (permission sets, group assignments), so it’s not the least overhead solution. Option C (INCORRECT): “Create individual IAM users for each member in all the teams with role-based permissions. Assign the IAM roles with predefined policies for RDS and S3 access to each user based on user needs. Implement IAM Access Analyzer for periodic credential evaluation.” Individual IAM user management is labor-intensive and violates centralized credential management best practices. It increases the risk of credential sprawl and manual errors, contrary to least privilege and compliance. Periodic credential evaluation adds more operational overhead compared to using IAM Identity Center permission sets. Option D (INCORRECT): “Use AWS Organizations to create separate accounts for each team. Implement cross-account IAM roles with least privilege. Grant specific permission for RDS and S3 access based on team roles and responsibilities.” Creating separate AWS accounts per team and managing cross-account roles is a valid security boundary, but it adds significant operational overhead. Requires account provisioning, networking setup, consolidated billing, and cross-account role trust policies management. Overkill for simply granting scoped access to Amazon RDS and S3 within one organization’s environment. Option B (CORRECT): “Enable IAM Identity Center with an Identity Center directory. Create and configure permission sets with granular access to Amazon RDS and Amazon S3. Assign all the teams to groups that have specific access with the permission sets.” Leverages AWS IAM Identity Center for centralized user and group management, enabling SSO and consistent credential policies. Permission sets allow you to define least-privilege policies once and assign them to multiple groups or teams, reducing duplication. Least operational overhead: you don’t need to manage individual IAM users, credential rotations, or cross-account role trusts. Ensures compliance with least privilege and keeps sensitive data access tightly controlled. Summary: We learned that AWS IAM Identity Center permission sets provide a streamlined, least-privilege way to grant secure access to AWS resources with minimal operational overhead. This question belongs to Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company has more than 5 TB of file data on Windows file servers that run on premises. Users and applications interact with the data each day. The company is moving its Windows workloads to AWS. As the company continues this process, the company requires access to AWS and on-premises file storage with minimum latency. The company needs a solution that minimizes operational overhead and requires no significant changes to the existing file access patterns. The company uses an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection for connectivity to AWS.What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
options: Deploy and configure Amazon FSx for Windows File Server on AWS. Move the on-premises file data to FSx for Windows File Server. Reconfigure the workloads to use FSx for Windows File Server on AWS.
