Deploy and configure an Amazon S3 File Gateway on premises. Move the on-premises file data to the S3 File Gateway. Reconfigure the on-premises workloads and the cloud workloads to use the S3 File Gateway.

Deploy and configure an Amazon S3 File Gateway on premises. Move the on-premises file data to Amazon S3. Reconfigure the workloads to use either Amazon S3 directly or the S3 File Gateway. depending on each workload's location.

Deploy and configure Amazon FSx for Windows File Server on AWS. Deploy and configure an Amazon FSx File Gateway on premises. Move the on-premises file data to the FSx File Gateway. Configure the cloud workloads to use FSx for Windows File Server on AWS. Configure the on-premises workloads to use the FSx File Gateway.
explanation: The correct answer is D Option A (INCORRECT): Deploying only Amazon FSx for Windows File Server in AWS and moving all on-premises data into it forces all clients—both on-premises and in AWS—to access files over the VPN. This adds latency for local users, does not provide local caching, and does not satisfy the “minimum latency” requirement without operational overhead. Option B (INCORRECT): An Amazon S3 File Gateway presents an object store as a file share, but it is backed by Amazon S3, not a native Windows file system. You lose Windows ACLs, SMB compatibility nuances, and you introduce changes to file-access patterns for both on-prem and cloud workloads. Option C (INCORRECT): Similar to B, an S3 File Gateway backed by S3 is not a native Windows file solution. Applications expecting SMB-based semantics, NTFS permissions, and consistent file-share behavior will break or require code/config changes. This fails the requirement for no significant changes to existing access patterns. Option D (CORRECT): Amazon FSx for Windows File Server in AWS provides a fully managed, native SMB file system with Windows ACLs and high throughput. An FSx File Gateway deployed on-premises caches hot data locally and fronts the same FSx file system in AWS, giving users minimal latency access without data duplication management. No significant changes to existing SMB-based access patterns—on-prem clients use the local gateway endpoint; AWS workloads use the FSx endpoint directly. Operational overhead is minimal: AWS manages the file server, and the gateway handles caching and synchronization over the existing VPN. Summary: We learned that to provide hybrid SMB file access with minimum latency, native Windows file semantics, and minimal operational overhead, the combination of Amazon FSx for Windows File Server in AWS plus an on-premises FSx File Gateway is ideal. This ensures local caching for low latency and a single managed file system for both environments. This scenario falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company is migrating a Linux-based web server group to AWS. The web servers must access files in a shared file store for some content. The company must not make any changes to the application. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
options: Create an Amazon S3 Standard bucket with access to the web servers.
Configure an Amazon CloudFront distribution with an Amazon S3 bucket as the origin.
Create an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Mount the EFS file system on all web servers.
Configure a General Purpose SSD (gp3) Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. Mount the EBS volume to all web servers.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): Create an Amazon S3 Standard bucket with access to the web servers. S3 is object storage, not a shared POSIX file system. The application expects a traditional file system and cannot be modified to use S3 APIs or a FUSE adapter. Option B (INCORRECT): Configure an Amazon CloudFront distribution with an Amazon S3 bucket as the origin. CloudFront is a CDN designed for HTTP(s) delivery, not a network file share for EC2 instances. Using CloudFront would require changing the application to fetch files over HTTP rather than file I/O. Option D (INCORRECT): Configure a General Purpose SSD (gp3) Amazon EBS volume. Mount the EBS volume to all web servers. Standard EBS volumes can only be attached to a single instance at a time. Although EBS Multi-Attach exists, it requires cluster-aware file systems and additional configuration, which means changing the application. Option C (CORRECT): Create an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Mount the EFS file system on all web servers. EFS provides a fully managed, scalable, POSIX-compliant NFS file system accessible concurrently by multiple EC2 instances. No application changes are required because EFS behaves like a traditional file system. EFS scales storage and throughput automatically and offers high availability across Availability Zones. In summary, when you need a shared file system for Linux-based web servers without modifying the application, Amazon EFS is the correct choice. This question belongs to Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company wants to give a customer the ability to use on-premises Microsoft Active Directory to download files that are stored in Amazon S3. The customer’s application uses an SFTP client to download the files. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead and no changes to the customer’s application?
options: Set up AWS Transfer Family with SFTP for Amazon S3. Configure integrated Active Directory authentication.
Set up AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to synchronize the on-premises client with Amazon S3. Configure integrated Active Directory authentication.
Set up AWS DataSync to synchronize between the on-premises location and the S3 location by using AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS Single Sign-On).
Set up a Windows Amazon EC2 instance with SFTP to connect the on-premises client with Amazon S3. Integrate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM).
explanation: The correct answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) is specifically designed to migrate relational databases, data warehouses, NoSQL stores, and other types of databases—not to provide an SFTP interface for downloading files from S3. It cannot authenticate users via on-premises Active Directory over SFTP, and it adds unnecessary complexity when the goal is simple file transfer. Option C (INCORRECT): AWS DataSync is intended for automated, high-performance data transfer between storage systems—not for exposing an SFTP endpoint. AWS IAM Identity Center (SSO) does not directly integrate with on-premises Active Directory for SFTP authentication, so the customer would need to change their application or add extra components. Option D (INCORRECT): Running a Windows EC2 instance with SFTP software means you must manage the server OS, patching, scaling, and high availability yourself—high operational overhead. While you could integrate IAM roles or even AD via AD Connector on that instance, it still requires infrastructure management and doesn’t leverage a fully managed service. Option A (CORRECT): AWS Transfer Family for SFTP is a fully managed service that presents standard SFTP endpoints backed by S3 storage. It supports integrated Active Directory authentication—either via AD Connector to on-prem AD or using AWS Managed Microsoft AD—so users can continue using their existing AD credentials without changing their SFTP client. Minimal operational overhead: AWS handles the SFTP server, scaling, patching, logging, and security, while you manage only the access policies and directory integration. In summary, AWS Transfer Family with SFTP and integrated Active Directory authentication meets the requirements with the least operational overhead and zero changes to the customer’s SFTP application. This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures, as it focuses on secure access and authentication integration.

question: A company needs to create an AWS Lambda function that will run in a VPC in the company's primary AWS account. The Lambda function needs to access files that the company stores in an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. The EFS file system is located in a secondary AWS account. As the company adds files to the file system, the solution must scale to meet the demand.Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Create a new EFS file system in the primary account. Use AWS DataSync to copy the contents of the original EFS file system to the new EFS file system.
Create a VPC peering connection between the VPCs that are in the primary account and the secondary account.

Create a second Lambda function in the secondary account that has a mount that is configured for the file system. Use the primary account's Lambda function to invoke the secondary account's Lambda function.
Move the contents of the file system to a Lambda layer. Configure the Lambda layer's permissions to allow the company's secondary account to use the Lambda layer.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): Create a new EFS in the primary account and use AWS DataSync to copy data. Duplicates storage costs—pay for two EFS file systems. DataSync adds data transfer and task costs, and requires ongoing management to keep file systems in sync. More operational overhead and higher cost compared to direct access. Option C (INCORRECT): Deploy a second Lambda in the secondary account to mount the EFS and invoke it from the primary account. Introduces cross-account invocation latency and added complexity. Requires orchestrating two Lambdas and passing data between them. Unnecessary extra Lambda costs; less cost-effective than direct file access. Option D (INCORRECT): Move the file contents into a Lambda layer and share the layer. Lambda layers have a size limit (250 MB unzipped) — not suitable for growing file sets. Layers are for code/libraries, not for large or dynamic data storage. Not scalable or cost-effective for potentially large and changing files. Option B (CORRECT): Create a VPC peering connection between the primary and secondary account VPCs. Allows the Lambda in the primary account (within its VPC) to mount the EFS file system in the secondary account over NFS. No need to duplicate data or storage; you pay only for the existing EFS and Lambda usage. Scales seamlessly with EFS performance and capacity, and incurs minimal cross-account connectivity cost. Summary: By establishing VPC peering, you enable direct, secure, and cost-efficient access from the Lambda function in the primary account to the EFS file system in the secondary account without duplicating data or incurring extra storage and management costs. This question belongs to Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company runs an application that uses Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. The application receives traffic only on weekdays during business hours. The company wants to optimize costs and reduce operational overhead based on this usage.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Use the Instance Scheduler on AWS to configure start and stop schedules.
Turn off automatic backups. Create weekly manual snapshots of the database.
Create a custom AWS Lambda function to start and stop the database based on minimum CPU utilization.
Purchase All Upfront reserved DB instances.
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): “Turn off automatic backups. Create weekly manual snapshots of the database.” Disabling automatic backups removes point-in-time recovery and jeopardizes data durability. Manual snapshots are less frequent, add operational overhead, and do not optimize cost during off-hours effectively. Option C (INCORRECT): “Create a custom AWS Lambda function to start and stop the database based on minimum CPU utilization.” CPU utilization is not a reliable indicator of true workload requirements; low CPU may still require DB availability. Custom automation increases maintenance overhead compared to a managed scheduling solution. Option D (INCORRECT): “Purchase All Upfront reserved DB instances.” Reserved Instances lower hourly costs but still incur charges 24/7, even when the database is idle off-hours. Does not allow shutting down the DB to eliminate costs outside business hours. Option A (CORRECT): “Use the Instance Scheduler on AWS to configure start and stop schedules.” Automates starting and stopping Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL on a defined schedule (e.g., weekdays during business hours), directly reducing off-hours costs. A fully managed solution with minimal operational overhead—no need to build or maintain custom scripts. Allows automatic backups and maintenance tasks to run during working hours, satisfying both cost-optimization and data protection requirements. Summary: We learned that AWS Instance Scheduler is the simplest, managed way to align RDS runtime with business hours, cutting costs and reducing operational effort without sacrificing backups. This question falls under Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A gaming company is building an application with Voice over IP capabilities. The application will serve traffic to users across the world. The application needs to be highly available with an automated failover across AWS Regions. The company wants to minimize the latency of users without relying on IP address caching on user devices. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
options: Use AWS Global Accelerator with health checks.
Use Amazon Route 53 with a geolocation routing policy.
Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution that includes multiple origins.
Create an Application Load Balancer that uses path-based routing.
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): Use Amazon Route 53 with a geolocation routing policy. Route 53 relies on DNS lookups, which are subject to client and resolver caching (TTL). This delays failover in a global outage scenario. Geolocation routing directs traffic based on the user’s location, but it cannot guarantee the lowest network latency or the fastest path for VoIP traffic. It does not provide static anycast IPs or accelerated network paths like Global Accelerator does. Option C (INCORRECT): Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution that includes multiple origins. CloudFront is optimized for HTTP/HTTPS content caching and delivery, not real-time VoIP (UDP/TCP) traffic. It introduces caching layers which add latency variability, unsuitable for interactive voice applications. CloudFront cannot manage cross-Region failover for non-HTTP protocols or provide static entry points for real-time streaming. Option D (INCORRECT): Create an Application Load Balancer that uses path-based routing. An Application Load Balancer is Regional and cannot natively span or fail over across multiple AWS Regions. Path-based routing applies to URL paths on HTTP/HTTPS; it does not address global traffic acceleration or health-checked failover. ALB does not provide static anycast IP addresses or minimize client-perceived DNS caching delays. Option A (CORRECT): Use AWS Global Accelerator with health checks. Global Accelerator provides two static anycast IP addresses that serve as a single fixed entry point for your users worldwide. It continuously health-checks your application endpoints in multiple Regions and instantly directs traffic to the nearest healthy endpoint, without DNS caching delays. It optimizes performance over the AWS global network for TCP and UDP traffic, making it ideal for low-latency, real-time VoIP applications. In summary, AWS Global Accelerator meets the high-availability, low-latency, and cross-Region failover requirements for a global VoIP gaming application. We’ve learned how to choose the right global traffic management service for real-time workloads. This scenario belongs to Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company deploys an application on five Amazon EC2 instances. An Application Load Balancer (ALB) distributes traffic to the instances by using a target group. The average CPU usage on each of the instances is below 10% most of the time, with occasional surges to 65%. A solutions architect needs to implement a solution to automate the scalability of the application. The solution must optimize the cost of the architecture and must ensure that the application has enough CPU resources when surges occur. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm that enters the ALARM state when the CPUUtilization metric is less than 20%. Create an AWS Lambda function that the CloudWatch alarm invokes to terminate one of the EC2 instances in the ALB target group.

Create an EC2 Auto Scaling group. Select the existing ALB as the load balancer and the existing target group as the target group. Set a target tracking scaling policy that is based on the ASGAverageCPUUtilization metric. Set the minimum instances to 2, the desired capacity to 3, the maximum instances to 6, and the target value to 50%. Add the EC2 instances to the Auto Scaling group.

Create an EC2 Auto Scaling group. Select the existing ALB as the load balancer and the existing target group as the target group. Set the minimum instances to 2, the desired capacity to 3, and the maximum instances to 6. Add the EC2 instances to the Auto Scaling group.

Create two Amazon CloudWatch alarms. Configure the first CloudWatch alarm to enter the ALARM state when the average CPUUtilization metric is below 20%. Configure the second CloudWatch alarm to enter the ALARM state when the average CPUUtilization matric is above 50%. Configure the alarms to publish to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to send an email message. After receiving the message, log in to decrease or increase the number of EC2 instances that are running.
explanation: The correct answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): This only automates scale-in (terminates an instance when CPU < 20%). There is no mechanism to scale out when CPU surges, so the application could run out of capacity during spikes. Using a Lambda-driven termination is more complex than native Auto Scaling policies and does not meet the “ensure enough CPU resources” requirement. Option C (INCORRECT): An Auto Scaling group without any scaling policy will not adjust capacity automatically. You’d have a fixed desired capacity of 3 instances and no way to respond to CPU surges or drop instances when idle. This fails the requirement to automate scalability based on CPU load. Option D (INCORRECT): Relies on manual intervention (email → login → add/remove instances), which is neither fully automated nor instantaneous. Does not optimize cost since the team might over-provision or react too slowly to spikes. Fails the “automate scalability” and “cost-optimized” requirements. Option B (CORRECT): Creates an EC2 Auto Scaling group attached to the existing ALB and target group, satisfying integration requirements. Uses a target‐tracking scaling policy on ASGAverageCPUUtilization = 50%, which automatically scales out on traffic surges and scales in when idle. Specifies min=2, desired=3, max=6, ensuring enough capacity during peaks (up to 6 instances) and cost efficiency during low load. In summary, we have learned how to implement a fully automated, CPU-based scaling solution that attaches an Auto Scaling group to an Application Load Balancer, uses target-tracking policies for dynamic up/down scaling, and balances performance with cost efficiency. This question belongs to Domain 4 – Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: An online gaming company hosts its platform on Amazon EC2 instances behind Network Load Balancers (NLBs) across multiple AWS Regions. The NLBs can route requests to targets over the internet. The company wants to improve the customer playing experience by reducing end-to-end load time for its global customer base. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Create Application Load Balancers (ALBs) in each Region to replace the existing NLBs. Register the existing EC2 instances as targets for the ALBs in each Region.
Configure Amazon Route 53 to route equally weighted traffic to the NLBs in each Region.
Create additional NLBs and EC2 instances in other Regions where the company has large customer bases.
Create a standard accelerator in AWS Global Accelerator. Configure the existing NLBs as target endpoints.
explanation: The correct Answer is D Option A (INCORRECT): Replacing Network Load Balancers (NLBs) with Application Load Balancers (ALBs) does not address global latency. ALBs are regional and focus on HTTP/HTTPS-level routing, not optimized global traffic acceleration. This change would not reduce end-to-end latency for a worldwide user base. Option B (INCORRECT): Using Amazon Route 53 with equally weighted routing simply distributes traffic evenly across regions but does not select the lowest-latency endpoint for each user. Without latency-based or geoproximity policies, end-users may still be routed to distant regions, failing to improve performance. Option C (INCORRECT): Creating additional NLBs and EC2 instances in more regions can improve local presence, but it requires substantial operational overhead and does not automatically route users to the optimal edge. It also increases cost and complexity without providing the network-level acceleration that AWS Global Accelerator offers. Option D (CORRECT): AWS Global Accelerator provides a static anycast IP address front end and routes user traffic over the AWS global network to the optimal regional endpoint. By configuring the existing NLBs as Global Accelerator endpoints, you benefit from reduced jitter, improved throughput, and lower latency—directly addressing the requirement to speed up end-to-end load times for a global audience. In summary, we learned that for global performance optimization, AWS Global Accelerator is the best choice because it leverages the AWS backbone to route traffic to the closest healthy endpoint. This question falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company has a service that produces event data. The company wants to use AWS to process the event data as it is received. The data is written in a specific order that must be maintained throughout processing. The company wants to implement a solution that minimizes operational overhead.How should a solutions architect accomplish this?
options: Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue to hold messages. Set up an AWS Lambda function to process messages from the queue.
Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to deliver notifications containing payloads to process. Configure an AWS Lambda function as a subscriber.
Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) standard queue to hold messages. Set up an AWS Lambda function to process messages from the queue independently.
Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to deliver notifications containing payloads to process. Configure an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue as a subscriber.
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option A (CORRECT): “Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue to hold messages. Set up an AWS Lambda function to process messages from the queue.” SQS FIFO queues guarantee that messages are processed in the exact order they are received (per message group). Lambda integration with SQS FIFO minimizes operational overhead—you don’t manage servers or scaling. FIFO also provides exactly-once processing and deduplication, further supporting strict ordering requirements. Option B (INCORRECT): “Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to deliver notifications containing payloads to process. Configure an AWS Lambda function as a subscriber.” SNS does not guarantee the order in which subscribers receive messages. Multiple concurrent Lambda invocations could process messages out of sequence. SNS is optimized for fan-out, not ordered processing. Option C (INCORRECT): “Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) standard queue to hold messages. Set up an AWS Lambda function to process messages from the queue independently.” SQS standard queues provide at‐least‐once delivery but do not guarantee order. Messages might be delivered more than once and out of sequence. Does not meet the strict ordering requirement. Option D (INCORRECT): “Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to deliver notifications containing payloads to process. Configure an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue as a subscriber.” Although you could subscribe an SQS queue to SNS, SNS itself does not preserve message order. Even if the SQS queue is FIFO, SNS pub/sub does not maintain end-to-end ordering. Operational overhead is higher if you had to manage subscription filters or chaining services. Summary: We need guaranteed, ordered, serverless message processing with minimal operational overhead. Amazon SQS FIFO with Lambda polling is the optimal choice. This question belongs to Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures, because it focuses on achieving ordered, reliable, and scalable event processing.

question: A development team uses multiple AWS accounts for its development, staging, and production environments. Team members have been launching large Amazon EC2 instances that are underutilized. A solutions architect must prevent large instances from being launched in all accounts. How can the solutions architect meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Update the IAM policies to deny the launch of large EC2 instances. Apply the policies to all users.
Define a resource in AWS Resource Access Manager that prevents the launch of large EC2 instances.
Create an IAM role in each account that denies the launch of large EC2 instances. Grant the developers IAM group access to the role.

Create an organization in AWS Organizations in the management account with the default policy. Create a service control policy (SCP) that denies the launch of large EC2 instances, and apply it to the AWS accounts.
explanation: The correct answer is D Option A (INCORRECT): Update the IAM policies to deny the launch of large EC2 instances. You would need to write and maintain custom IAM policies with specific instance-type conditions in every account. This approach adds operational overhead each time you update users or accounts, and IAM alone isn’t centralized across multiple accounts. Option B (INCORRECT): Define a resource in AWS Resource Access Manager that prevents the launch of large EC2 instances. AWS Resource Access Manager is for sharing resources (e.g., VPC subnets, Route 53 Resolver rules), not for enforcing launch restrictions. It cannot restrict which EC2 instance types developers can provision. Option C (INCORRECT): Create an IAM role in each account that denies the launch of large EC2 instances and grant developers access. Still requires per-account role creation and ongoing management whenever policies or user assignments change. Higher operational overhead compared to a centralized policy mechanism. Option D (CORRECT): Use AWS Organizations in the management account, create a Service Control Policy (SCP) that denies the launch of large EC2 instances, and apply it to all member accounts. SCPs are inherited by all accounts in the organization, providing a single point of enforcement. Prevents users and roles—even with full EC2 permissions—from launching disallowed instance types. Minimizes operational overhead by centrally managing restrictions instead of updating each account individually. Summary: We reviewed why Options A, B, and C each introduce extra per-account management or use services unsuited for instance-type restrictions. Option D leverages AWS Organizations and SCPs to centrally and consistently enforce denial of large EC2 instances across all environments. This question belongs to Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures, as it focuses on controlling resource usage to reduce costs.

question: A company operates an ecommerce website on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in an Auto Scaling group. The site is experiencing performance issues related to a high request rate from illegitimate external systems with changing IP addresses. The security team is worried about potential DDoS attacks against the website. The company must block the illegitimate incoming requests in a way that has a minimal impact on legitimate users. What should a solutions architect recommend?
options: Deploy Amazon Inspector and associate it with the ALB.
Deploy AWS WAF, associate it with the ALB, and configure a rate-limiting rule.
Deploy rules to the network ACLs associated with the ALB to block the incomingtraffic.
Deploy Amazon GuardDuty and enable rate-limiting protection when configuring GuardDuty.
explanation: The correct answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): “Deploy Amazon Inspector and associate it with the ALB.” Amazon Inspector is a vulnerability assessment service for EC2 and container images—it does not provide request‐level filtering or rate‐limiting at the ALB. It cannot block or throttle malicious HTTP traffic in real time. Option C (INCORRECT): “Deploy rules to the network ACLs associated with the ALB to block the incoming traffic.” Network ACLs work at the subnet level and are stateless—they cannot track request rates or maintain state for dynamic IP addresses. Updating NACLs for every changing IP is operationally intensive and does not offer rate limiting. Option D (INCORRECT): “Deploy Amazon GuardDuty and enable rate-limiting protection when configuring GuardDuty.” Amazon GuardDuty is a threat detection service that identifies malicious activity, but it does not provide inline request filtering or rate-limiting. GuardDuty findings can alert you to attacks but cannot block or throttle traffic at the ALB. Option B (CORRECT): “Deploy AWS WAF, associate it with the ALB, and configure a rate-limiting rule.” AWS WAF integrates directly with ALB to inspect HTTP/S requests and apply custom rules. You can configure rate-based rules to block or count IPs that exceed a threshold, automatically handling changing IP addresses. This approach blocks excessive illegitimate requests with minimal impact on legitimate users. Summary: By using AWS WAF with rate-based rules, you gain inline protection against high-volume unwanted traffic and DDoS‐style attacks without impacting real customers. This question falls under Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures, as it focuses on implementing security controls to protect and secure an application’s traffic.

question: A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances in a private subnet. The application needs to store and retrieve data in Amazon S3 buckets. According to regulatory requirements, the data must not travel across the public internet. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Deploy a NAT gateway to access the S3 buckets.
Deploy AWS Storage Gateway to access the S3 buckets.
Deploy an S3 interface endpoint to access the S3 buckets.
Deploy an S3 gateway endpoint to access the S3 buckets.
explanation: The correct answer is D Option A (INCORRECT): “Deploy a NAT gateway to access the S3 buckets.” A NAT gateway sends traffic over the internet to reach S3, which violates the requirement that data must not traverse the public internet. Additionally, NAT gateways incur hourly charges and data processing fees, making this approach neither secure nor cost-effective. Option B (INCORRECT): “Deploy AWS Storage Gateway to access the S3 buckets.” Storage Gateway is designed for on-premises hybrid storage use cases (e.g., file, volume, or tape gateways), not for EC2-to-S3 access within a VPC. This approach introduces unnecessary infrastructure, complexity, and cost without meeting the simple VPC-native requirement. Option C (INCORRECT): “Deploy an S3 interface endpoint to access the S3 buckets.” An S3 interface endpoint (AWS PrivateLink) provisions elastic network interfaces in your subnet and charges per hour and per GB of data processed. This solution keeps traffic off the internet, but it is more expensive than a gateway endpoint and over-architected for S3 access. Option D (CORRECT): “Deploy an S3 gateway endpoint to access the S3 buckets.” S3 gateway endpoints are configured in your VPC route tables, sending S3 traffic directly over the AWS network—no public internet involved. Gateway endpoints for Amazon S3 are free to use and incur no additional data-processing charges, making them the most cost-effective option. This meets the regulatory requirement to avoid the public internet while minimizing cost and operational complexity. In summary, we learned that to ensure private, internet-free connectivity from EC2 to S3 while optimizing cost, an S3 gateway endpoint is the best solution. This scenario falls under Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures, as it focuses on secure, private access patterns.

question: A company has users all around the world accessing its HTTP-based application deployed on Amazon EC2 instances in multiple AWS Regions. The company wants to improve the availability and performance of the application. The company also wants to protect the application against common web exploits that may affect availability, compromise security, or consume excessive resources. Static IP addresses are required.What should a solutions architect recommend to accomplish this?
options: Put the EC2 instances behind Network Load Balancers (NLBs) in each Region. Deploy AWS WAF on the NLBs. Create an accelerator using AWS Global Accelerator and register the NLBs as endpoints.
Put the EC2 instances behind Application Load Balancers (ALBs) in each Region. Deploy AWS WAF on the ALBs. Create an accelerator using AWS Global Accelerator and register the ALBs as endpoints.

Put the EC2 instances behind Network Load Balancers (NLBs) in each Region. Deploy AWS WAF on the NLBs. Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with an origin that uses Amazon Route 53 latency-based routing to route requests to the NLBs.

Put the EC2 instances behind Application Load Balancers (ALBs) in each Region. Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with an origin that uses Amazon Route 53 latency-based routing to route requests to the ALBs. Deploy AWS WAF on the CloudFront distribution.
explanation: The correct answer is Option B Option A (INCORRECT): This suggests placing EC2 instances behind Network Load Balancers and deploying AWS WAF on the NLBs. However, AWS WAF does not support NLB endpoints; it only integrates with ALBs, CloudFront, and API Gateway. Without ALBs or CloudFront, you cannot apply WAF rules to block common web exploits. Option C (INCORRECT): Also uses NLBs with AWS WAF. As above, WAF is not supported on NLBs, so you cannot protect against web exploits at the load-balancer layer. Introducing CloudFront with Route 53 latency-based routing does improve performance, but you still lack static IP addresses and proper WAF integration. Option D (INCORRECT): CloudFront paired with Route 53 latency-based routing and WAF can protect the application globally, but CloudFront endpoints do not provide dedicated static IPs per customer—they use dynamic anycast IP ranges. There’s no guarantee on fixed IP addresses, which fails the static-IP requirement. Option B (CORRECT): Application Load Balancers (ALBs) support AWS WAF, letting you block SQL injection, XSS, and other OWASP-Top-10 exploits directly at the edge of each Region. AWS Global Accelerator provides two static anycast IP addresses that serve as fixed entry points into your multi-Region ALBs, improving performance via the AWS global network and offering health-based failover. Combining ALBs + WAF + Global Accelerator addresses high availability, low-latency performance, global static IPs, and security requirements in one architecture. Summary: We learned how to deliver a globally available, high-performance, and secure HTTP application using ALBs protected by AWS WAF and fronted by AWS Global Accelerator for static IPs and optimal routing. This scenario falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A social media company runs its application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The ALB is the origin for an Amazon CloudFront distribution. The application has more than a billion images stored in an Amazon S3 bucket and processes thousands of images each second. The company wants to resize the images dynamically and serve appropriate formats to clients. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Install an external image management library on an EC2 instance. Use the image management library to process the images.
Create a CloudFront origin request policy. Use the policy to automatically resize images and to serve the appropriate format based on the User-Agent HTTP header in the request.
Use a Lambda@Edge function with an external image management library. Associate the Lambda@Edge function with the CloudFront behaviors that serve the images.
Create a CloudFront response headers policy. Use the policy to automatically resize images and to serve the appropriate format based on the User-Agent HTTP header in the request.
explanation: The correct answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): Install an external image management library on an EC2 instance. Use the image management library to process the images. This adds significant operational overhead: you must manage, scale, patch, and monitor EC2 instances. It does not leverage CloudFront edge locations for low-latency processing and delivery. Scaling to thousands of image operations per second would require complex auto-scaling policies. Option B (INCORRECT): Create a CloudFront origin request policy. Use the policy to automatically resize images and to serve the appropriate format based on the User-Agent HTTP header in the request. CloudFront origin request policies only control which headers, cookies, and query strings are forwarded to the origin—they do not perform image transformations. There is no built-in CloudFront feature to resize or reformat images solely via origin request policies. Option D (INCORRECT): Create a CloudFront response headers policy. Use the policy to automatically resize images and to serve the appropriate format based on the User-Agent HTTP header in the request. Response headers policies only add HTTP headers to responses; they cannot transform image content. There is no capability in CloudFront to perform dynamic image resizing or reformatting purely via response headers. Option C (CORRECT): Use a Lambda@Edge function with an external image management library. Associate the Lambda@Edge function with the CloudFront behaviors that serve the images. Lambda@Edge runs your code at CloudFront edge locations, reducing latency and offloading processing from your origin. You can use libraries such as Sharp in Node.js to dynamically resize images and convert formats (WebP, JPEG, etc.) based on request headers. Operational overhead is minimal: AWS handles scaling, patching, and high availability of Lambda@Edge functions. In summary, we’ve learned that for dynamic image resizing and format negotiation at scale with low operational overhead, Lambda@Edge is the ideal solution. This question falls under Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: An ecommerce company uses Amazon Route 53 as its DNS provider. The company hosts its website on premises and in the AWS Cloud. The company's on-premises data center is near the us-west-1 Region. The company uses the eu-central-1 Region to host the website. The company wants to minimize load time for the website as much as possible. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Set up a geolocation routing policy. Send the traffic that is near us-west-1 to the on-premises data center. Send the traffic that is near eu-central-1 to eu-central-1.
Set up a simple routing policy that routes all traffic that is near eu-central-1 to eu-central-1 and routes all traffic that is near the on-premises datacenter to the on-premises data center.
Set up a latency routing policy. Associate the policy with us-west-1.
Set up a weighted routing policy. Split the traffic evenly between eu-central-1 and the on-premises data center.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): Using a Geolocation routing policy sends traffic based on the user’s geographic location, not on actual network latency. This does not guarantee the lowest latency path—users in regions without explicit geolocation rules may go to a suboptimal endpoint, and the policy is not designed to measure real-time network performance. Option B (INCORRECT): A Simple routing policy always returns the same endpoint for a given DNS name. There is no mechanism for deciding between on-premises and eu-central-1 based on proximity or latency, so it cannot minimize load time dynamically. Option D (INCORRECT): A Weighted routing policy splits traffic according to static weights. Distributing 50/50 does not account for which endpoint actually provides lower latency for each user, so it won’t optimize performance. Option C (CORRECT): A Latency routing policy directs each DNS query to the endpoint (on-premises near us-west-1 or the eu-central-1 Region) that provides the lowest network latency for the requester. This ensures that users are always sent to the fastest available site, minimizing load time. In summary, we learned that to optimize for performance across multiple endpoints, Amazon Route 53’s Latency routing policy is the right choice. This question falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company hosts a three-tier ecommerce application on a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances. The instances run in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). All ecommerce data is stored in an Amazon RDS for MariaDB Multi-AZ DB instance. The company wants to optimize customer session management during transactions. The application must store session data durably.Which solutions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
options: Turn on the sticky sessions feature (session affinity) on the ALB.
Use an Amazon DynamoDB table to store customer session information.
Deploy an Amazon Cognito user pool to manage user session information.
Deploy an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster to store customer session information.
Use AWS Systems Manager Application Manager in the application to manage user session information.
explanation: The correct answer is B, D. Option A (INCORRECT): Turn on the sticky-sessions feature (session affinity) on the ALB. Sticky sessions bind a client to a single instance but still store session state in-memory on that instance. If an instance fails or is replaced by Auto Scaling, all in-memory sessions are lost—so this is not a durable solution. Option C (INCORRECT): Deploy an Amazon Cognito user pool to manage user session information. Amazon Cognito handles user authentication, tokens, and basic identity management—it does not store arbitrary application session data (shopping carts, transaction state). It’s not intended as a general purpose session store. Option E (INCORRECT): Use AWS Systems Manager Application Manager in the application to manage user session information. Systems Manager Application Manager is used for application discovery, performance monitoring, and operational insights—not for storing or managing end-user session data. Option B (CORRECT): Use an Amazon DynamoDB table to store customer session information. DynamoDB is a fully managed, serverless NoSQL database that provides single-digit millisecond latency and built-in high availability across AZs. Session data stored here is durable, persistent, and can be read/written by all application instances. Scaling is automatic, so you maintain consistent performance without managing cache invalidation or node failovers. Option D (CORRECT): Deploy an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster to store customer session information. Redis is an in-memory data store that can be configured with Multi-AZ replication and snapshot backups for persistence. It delivers very low-latency performance for session reads and writes, and supports high availability. ElastiCache transparently handles failover and ensures that session data is not lost in the event of a primary node failure (when persistence is enabled). Summary: We have learned that durable, shared session storage across a fleet of EC2 instances can be achieved with either DynamoDB (a serverless NoSQL datastore) or ElastiCache for Redis (an in-memory store with persistence and replication). Sticky sessions and Cognito do not satisfy the durability requirement, and Systems Manager is not designed for session storage. This scenario falls under Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A development team is collaborating with another company to create an integrated product. The other company needs to access an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue that is contained in the development team's account. The other company wants to poll the queue without giving up its own account permissions to do so.How should a solutions architect provide access to the SQS queue?
options: Create an instance profile that provides the other company access to the SQS queue.
Create an IAM policy that provides the other company access to the SQS queue.
Create an SQS access policy that provides the other company access to the SQS queue.
Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) access policy that provides the other company access to the SQS queue.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): “Create an instance profile that provides the other company access to the SQS queue.” Instance profiles are used to attach IAM roles to EC2 instances, not to grant cross-account API permissions. They cannot be used by an external company to poll an SQS queue directly. Option B (INCORRECT): “Create an IAM policy that provides the other company access to the SQS queue.” An IAM policy attached to your IAM users or roles grants permissions within your own account’s identities. It does not allow an external AWS account’s users to assume those permissions unless you also set up cross-account IAM roles or resource-based policies. Option D (INCORRECT): “Create an Amazon SNS access policy that provides the other company access to the SQS queue.” SNS access policies control topics, not SQS queues. There is no direct link from an SNS policy to allow polling of an SQS queue by an external account. Option C (CORRECT): “Create an SQS access policy that provides the other company access to the SQS queue.” Amazon SQS supports resource-based policies (queue policies) that allow you to specify which AWS principals (including external accounts) can perform actions on the queue. You can grant the other AWS account’s root or a specific IAM user/role the permission to sqs:ReceiveMessage, sqs:DeleteMessage, and sqs:GetQueueAttributes. This approach lets the partner poll the queue using their own IAM credentials, without requiring you to share your account’s IAM users or roles. Summary: By using a resource-based policy on the SQS queue, you securely grant cross-account access and allow the partner to poll messages with their own credentials. This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company runs an application using Amazon ECS. The application creates resized versions of an original image and then makes Amazon S3 API calls to store the resized images in Amazon S3. How can a solutions architect ensure that the application has permission to access Amazon S3?
options: Update the S3 role in AWS IAM to allow read/write access from Amazon ECS, and then relaunch the container.
Create an IAM role with S3 permissions, and then specify that role as the taskRoleArn in the task definition.
Create a security group that allows access from Amazon ECS to Amazon S3, and update the launch configuration used by the ECS cluster.
Create an IAM user with S3 permissions, and then relaunch the Amazon EC2 instances for the ECS cluster while logged in as this account.
explanation: The correct answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): Updating “the S3 role” in IAM and relaunching the container won’t work because ECS tasks don’t automatically assume an S3-specific role. You must attach permissions via an IAM role that the task (or underlying instance) can assume, not by editing a standalone S3 role. Option C (INCORRECT): Security groups control network traffic (IP/port), but Amazon S3 is a public AWS service accessed over HTTPS—there’s no inbound SG rule to permit. You cannot use security groups to grant S3 API permissions. Option D (INCORRECT): Creating an IAM user and logging into EC2 instances is not recommended and does not integrate with ECS task-level permissions. Hard-coding long-term credentials is insecure and not how ECS tasks automatically obtain S3 access. Option B (CORRECT): Create an IAM role that has the required S3 read/write policies. In your ECS task definition, set taskRoleArn to this IAM role. When each container starts, ECS automatically assumes that role so your application can securely call the S3 API without embedded credentials. In this discussion, we learned how Amazon ECS tasks securely obtain permissions using IAM task roles rather than static credentials or security groups. Assigning an IAM role via taskRoleArn ensures least-privilege access to S3. This question belongs to Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company is designing an application where users upload small files into Amazon S3. After a user uploads a file, the file requires one-time simple processing to transform the data and save the data in JSON format for later analysis. Each file must be processed as quickly as possible after it is uploaded. Demand will vary. On some days, users will upload a high number of files. On other days, users will upload a few files or no files. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Configure Amazon EMR to read text files from Amazon S3. Run processing scripts to transform the data. Store the resulting JSON file in an Amazon Aurora DB cluster.

Configure Amazon S3 to send an event notification to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Use Amazon EC2 instances to read from the queue and process the data. Store the resulting JSON file in Amazon DynamoDB.

Configure Amazon S3 to send an event notification to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Use an AWS Lambda function to read from the queue and process the data. Store the resulting JSON file in Amazon DynamoDB.

Configure Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) to send an event to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams when a new file is uploaded. Use an AWS Lambda function to consume the event from the stream and process the data. Store the resulting JSON file in an Amazon Aurora DB cluster.
explanation: The correct answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): “Configure Amazon EMR to read text files from Amazon S3. Run processing scripts to transform the data. Store the resulting JSON file in an Amazon Aurora DB cluster.” Amazon EMR is designed for large-scale, distributed data processing (big data). It introduces significant startup latency and management overhead for small, one‐off file transforms. Maintaining EMR clusters and scaling them up/down based on variable demand increases operational complexity and cost. Using Aurora for simple JSON storage is overkill when a serverless NoSQL store or S3 itself could suffice. Option B (INCORRECT): “Configure Amazon S3 to send an event notification to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Use Amazon EC2 instances to read from the queue and process the data. Store the resulting JSON file in Amazon DynamoDB.” Managing EC2 instances (autoscaling, patching, capacity planning) adds operational overhead compared to a fully managed serverless solution. Even though DynamoDB is a good choice for JSON storage, the EC2 layer is unnecessary for simple, event-driven transforms. Option D (INCORRECT): “Configure Amazon EventBridge (CloudWatch Events) to send an event to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams when a new file is uploaded. Use an AWS Lambda function to consume the event from the stream and process the data. Store the resulting JSON file in an Amazon Aurora DB cluster.” Kinesis Data Streams requires shard management and provisioning, adding cost and operational burden. Routing S3 events through EventBridge and Kinesis before Lambda is overly complex for simple file transforms. Again, Aurora adds unnecessary operational and cost overhead for small JSON objects. Option C (CORRECT): “Configure Amazon S3 to send an event notification to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Use an AWS Lambda function to read from the queue and process the data. Store the resulting JSON file in Amazon DynamoDB.” Serverless components (S3, SQS, Lambda, DynamoDB) remove the need to manage servers or clusters. Lambda automatically scales with demand—processing each file as quickly as possible without provisioning EC2 capacity. SQS decouples S3 events from Lambda, providing reliability and at-least-once delivery for spikes in upload volume. DynamoDB is a fully managed NoSQL database that easily stores JSON documents with low latency. Summary: We need a solution that processes each uploaded file immediately, scales automatically with variable demand, and minimizes operational overhead. A fully serverless pipeline using S3 events → SQS → Lambda → DynamoDB meets these requirements most efficiently. This scenario falls under Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures, as it emphasizes minimal operational overhead and pay-as-you-go scalability.

question: A company runs an infrastructure monitoring service. The company is building a new feature that will enable the service to monitor data in customer AWS accounts. The new feature will call AWS APIs in customer accounts to describe Amazon EC2 instances and read Amazon CloudWatch metrics.What should the company do to obtain access to customer accounts in the MOST secure way?
options: Ensure that the customers create an IAM role in their account with read-only EC2 and CloudWatch permissions and a trust policy to the company’s account.
Create a serverless API that implements a token vending machine to provide temporary AWS credentials for a role with read-only EC2 and CloudWatch permissions.
Ensure that the customers create an IAM user in their account with read-only EC2 and CloudWatch permissions. Encrypt and store customer access and secret keys in a secrets management system.

Ensure that the customers create an Amazon Cognito user in their account to use an IAM role with read-only EC2 and CloudWatch permissions. Encrypt and store the Amazon Cognito user and password in a secrets management system.
explanation: The correct Answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): • A token vending machine pattern is used to grant temporary credentials to users of your application, not to grant cross-account access into customer AWS accounts. • You would still need long-lived credentials to authenticate to the token vending service, adding complexity and potential security risks. Option C (INCORRECT): • Creating an IAM user in each customer account requires storing and rotating long-term access keys, which is against security best practices. • If secrets are compromised or not rotated properly, attackers could gain persistent access to customer resources. Option D (INCORRECT): • Amazon Cognito is designed for authentication of application users, not for granting AWS API permissions to external services. • Managing Cognito user credentials and mapping them to IAM roles is overly complex and not intended for cross-account service integrations. Option A (CORRECT): • Customers create an IAM role in their account with read-only permissions for EC2 and CloudWatch. • The role’s trust policy allows only your company’s AWS account (or specific IAM principal) to assume it. • No long-term credentials are stored or shared; access is granted securely via AWS STS AssumeRole. In summary, using a cross-account IAM role (Option A) is the most secure way to monitor customer EC2 instances and CloudWatch metrics without sharing long-lived credentials. This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: What should a solutions architect do to ensure that all objects uploaded to an Amazon S3 bucket are encrypted?
options: Update the bucket policy to deny if the PutObject does not have an s3:x-amz-acl header set.
Update the bucket policy to deny if the PutObject does not have an s3:x-amz-acl header set to private.
Update the bucket policy to deny if the PutObject does not have an aws:SecureTransport header set to true.
Update the bucket policy to deny if the PutObject does not have an x-amz-server-side-encryption header set.
explanation: The correct answer is D. Option A (INCORRECT): “Update the bucket policy to deny if the PutObject does not have an s3:x-amz-acl header set.” This condition checks for an ACL header, not encryption headers. It does not enforce server-side encryption, so objects could be uploaded unencrypted. Option B (INCORRECT): “Update the bucket policy to deny if the PutObject does not have an s3:x-amz-acl header set to private.” Setting ACL to private controls access permissions but does not guarantee encryption at rest. This has no effect on server-side encryption of the object content. Option C (INCORRECT): “Update the bucket policy to deny if the PutObject does not have an aws:SecureTransport header set to true.” This enforces HTTPS (in-transit encryption), not server-side encryption at rest. While securing transport is best practice, it does not ensure objects in S3 are encrypted on storage. Option D (CORRECT): “Update the bucket policy to deny if the PutObject does not have an x-amz-server-side-encryption header set.” This bucket policy condition enforces that every PutObject request includes the x-amz-server-side-encryption header. If a client attempts to upload without specifying server-side encryption, the request is denied, ensuring all objects are encrypted at rest. In summary, we reviewed why A and B fail to enforce encryption, and C only enforces HTTPS. Only D guarantees that every S3 object is encrypted at rest by requiring the x-amz-server-side-encryption header. This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company is using AWS DataSync to migrate millions of files from an on-premises system to AWS. The files are 10 KB in size on average. The company wants to use Amazon S3 for file storage. For the first year after the migration, the files will be accessed once or twice and must be immediately available. After 1 year, the files must be archived for at least 7 years. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Use an archive tool to group the files into large objects. Use DataSync to migrate the objects. Store the objects in S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval for the first year. Use a lifecycle configuration to transition the files to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 1 year with a retention period of 7 years.

Use an archive tool to group the files into large objects. Use DataSync to copy the objects to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA). Use a lifecycle configuration to transition the files to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval after 1 year with a retention period of 7 years.

Configure the destination storage class for the files as S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval. Use a lifecycle policy to transition the files to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 1 year with a retention period of 7 years.

Configure a DataSync task to transfer the files to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA). Use a lifecycle configuration to transition the files to S3 Deep Archive after 1 year with a retention period of 7 years.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): “Use an archive tool to group the files into large objects. Use DataSync to migrate the objects. Store the objects in S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval for the first year. Use a lifecycle configuration to transition the files to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 1 year with a retention period of 7 years.” Introducing a grouping/archive tool adds operational complexity and makes individual files harder to retrieve on demand. S3 storage pricing is per-GB-month, not per-object; grouping won’t reduce storage costs significantly but will complicate retrieval of single files. DataSync can copy millions of small files natively to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval without pre-archiving. Option B (INCORRECT): “Use an archive tool to group the files into large objects. Use DataSync to copy the objects to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA). Use a lifecycle configuration to transition the files to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval after 1 year with a retention period of 7 years.” Standard-IA has a minimum object size charge of 128 KB — your 10 KB files incur extra costs unless grouped, which again adds complexity. S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval offers lower storage costs for infrequent access and immediate retrieval compared to Standard-IA. Grouping has the same drawbacks as in Option A. Option D (INCORRECT): “Configure a DataSync task to transfer the files to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA). Use a lifecycle configuration to transition the files to S3 Deep Archive after 1 year with a retention period of 7 years.” Standard-IA is more expensive ($0.0125 per GB-month) than Glacier Instant Retrieval ($0.004 per GB-month) for infrequent yet immediate access. Your small files (10 KB) still incur the 128 KB minimum charge in Standard-IA, which drives up costs. While Deep Archive is the lowest-cost tier long-term, the initial choice of Standard-IA is suboptimal vs Glacier Instant Retrieval. Option C (CORRECT): “Configure the destination storage class for the files as S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval. Use a lifecycle policy to transition the files to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 1 year with a retention period of 7 years.” S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval provides millisecond access at $0.004 per GB-month—ideal for the first year when files are accessed only once or twice. No minimum object size charge (unlike Standard-IA), so cost scales directly with your 10 KB files. After 1 year, lifecycle transitions to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval—an archival tier with low storage cost ($0.0036 per GB-month) and retention for 7+ years. Summary: We need immediate, infrequent access for the first year and ultra-low-cost archival for the next 7 years. S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval meets the “immediate access” requirement at a low price, and transitioning to Glacier Flexible Retrieval afterwards achieves long-term retention cost-effectively. This question falls under Domain 4 – Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company needs to store data in Amazon S3 and must prevent the data from being changed. The company wants new objects that are uploaded to Amazon S3 to remain unchangeable for a nonspecific amount of time until the company decides to modify the objects. Only specific users in the company's AWS account can have the ability 10 delete the objects. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
options: Create an S3 Glacier vault. Apply a write-once, read-many (WORM) vault lock policy to the objects.
Create an S3 bucket with S3 Object Lock enabled. Enable versioning. Set a retention period of 100 years. Use governance mode as the S3 bucket’s default retention mode for new objects.
Create an S3 bucket. Use AWS CloudTrail to track any S3 API events that modify the objects. Upon notification, restore the modified objects from any backup versions that the company has.

Create an S3 bucket with S3 Object Lock enabled. Enable versioning. Add a legal hold to the objects. Add the s3:PutObjectLegalHold permission to the IAM policies of users who need to delete the objects.
explanation: The correct answer is D Option A (INCORRECT): Creating an S3 Glacier vault with a WORM vault lock enforces immutability at the Glacier level, not in an S3 bucket. The requirement is to store objects in Amazon S3 and make them unchangeable there. Glacier vault locks do not apply to S3 object APIs, so this does not meet the requirement. Option B (INCORRECT): Enabling S3 Object Lock in governance mode with a 100-year retention period does enforce immutability, but: Governance mode can be bypassed by users with the s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permission, potentially allowing unintended deletions or modifications. Setting a fixed 100-year retention is arbitrary and not truly “nonspecific” — you cannot easily adjust it without administrative effort or risking data loss if retention is accidentally shortened. This option does not provide the flexible, indefinite lock-until-needed and tightly controlled deletion permissions the company wants. Option C (INCORRECT): Using AWS CloudTrail to detect modifications only provides audit and restoration capabilities—it does not prevent objects from being changed in the first place. The requirement is to make new objects unchangeable until the company explicitly decides to modify or delete them. Option D (CORRECT): Enable S3 Object Lock and versioning on the bucket to enforce immutability on all new objects. Apply a Legal Hold (instead of a fixed retention period) so objects remain unchangeable for an indefinite, nonspecific duration. Grant only specific IAM principals the s3:PutObjectLegalHold permission, allowing them alone to remove legal holds and then delete objects. This satisfies the requirement to keep objects WORM-protected indefinitely until the company chooses to remove the hold, and restricts deletion rights to authorized users only. In summary, we learned how to use S3 Object Lock with legal holds to achieve indefinite immutability and granular deletion permissions. This question falls under Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company needs to save the results from a medical trial to an Amazon S3 repository. The repository must allow a few scientists to add new files and must restrict all other users to read-only access. No users can have the ability to modify or delete any files in the repository. The company must keep every file in the repository for a minimum of 1 year after its creation date. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Use S3 Object Lock in governance mode with a legal hold of 1 year.
Use S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a retention period of 365 days.
Use an IAM role to restrict all users from deleting or changing objects in the S3 bucket. Use an S3 bucket policy to only allow the IAM role.

Configure the S3 bucket to invoke an AWS Lambda function every time an object is added. Configure the function to track the hash of the saved object so that modified objects can be marked accordingly.
explanation: Option A (INCORRECT): “Use S3 Object Lock in governance mode with a legal hold of 1 year.” Governance mode allows certain privileged users to override or shorten retention, which does not guarantee that no one can delete or modify objects. Legal holds are indefinite until explicitly removed; they’re not a fixed 1-year retention period and don’t enforce an automatic expiration. Option C (INCORRECT): “Use an IAM role to restrict all users from deleting or changing objects in the S3 bucket. Use an S3 bucket policy to only allow the IAM role.” This approach can block deletes or overwrites but cannot guarantee a minimum one-year retention. IAM policies can be changed or updated, and they don’t provide immutable retention. There’s no enforcement of keeping objects for at least 365 days—users with sufficient privileges (or future admins) could alter or remove the policy. Option D (INCORRECT): “Configure the S3 bucket to invoke an AWS Lambda function every time an object is added. Configure the function to track the hash of the saved object so that modified objects can be marked accordingly.” Hash tracking does not prevent deletion or modification; it only detects changes after the fact. This solution does not enforce a one-year retention, nor does it make objects immutable in S3. Option B (CORRECT): “Use S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a retention period of 365 days.” Compliance mode enforces a write-once-read-many (WORM) model: no user—even the root—can overwrite or delete the object until the retention period expires. The specified 365-day retention automatically prevents modifications or deletions for at least one year after object creation. This exactly meets the requirement for immutability and the one-year minimum retention. In summary, S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a 365-day retention period is the only solution that makes data immutable and enforces the one-year retention. This question belongs to Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures, as it focuses on enforcing data immutability and retention policies.

question: A company is developing an application that will run on a production Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) cluster. The EKS cluster has managed node groups that are provisioned with On-Demand Instances. The company needs a dedicated EKS cluster for development work. The company will use the development cluster infrequently to test the resiliency of the application. The EKS cluster must manage all the nodes. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Create a managed node group that contains only Spot Instances.
Create two managed node groups. Provision one node group with On-Demand Instances. Provision the second node group with Spot Instances.
Create an Auto Scaling group that has a launch configuration that uses Spot Instances. Configure the user data to add the nodes to the EKS cluster.
Create a managed node group that contains only On-Demand Instances.
explanation: The correct answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): Create two managed node groups, one with On-Demand Instances and one with Spot Instances. The requirement is for an infrequently used development cluster—On-Demand Instances in one of the groups will sit idle and incur full cost even when you’re not testing. This approach is not the most cost-effective because you pay for the On-Demand group continuously. Option C (INCORRECT): Create an Auto Scaling group with a launch configuration using Spot Instances and user data to join the EKS cluster. This uses a self-managed node group (Auto Scaling group), not an EKS managed node group. The requirement states “The EKS cluster must manage all the nodes.” A self-managed group does not satisfy this. Option D (INCORRECT): Create a managed node group that contains only On-Demand Instances. On-Demand Instances guarantee availability but are costly when left idle. For infrequent, development/résilience-testing usage, always-on On-Demand Instances are not cost-optimized. Option A (CORRECT): Create a managed node group that contains only Spot Instances. Spot Instances provide up to 90% cost savings compared to On-Demand, ideal for infrequent development/testing. A managed node group ensures EKS handles provisioning, scaling, and lifecycle of the nodes automatically. Spot interruptions are acceptable in a development cluster meant to test application resiliency. In summary, using a managed node group with only Spot Instances meets the requirement for an EKS-managed, cost-effective, infrequently used development cluster. This question tests your ability in Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company manages AWS accounts in AWS Organizations. AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS Single Sign-On) and AWS Control Tower are configured for the accounts. The company wants to manage multiple user permissions across all the accounts. The permissions will be used by multiple IAM users and must be split between the developer and administrator teams. Each team requires different permissions. The company wants a solution that includes new users that are hired on both teams. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Create individual users in IAM Identity Center for each account. Create separate developer and administrator groups in IAM Identity Center. Assign the users to the appropriate groups. Create a custom IAM policy for each group to set fine-grained permissions.

Create individual users in IAM Identity Center for each account. Create separate developer and administrator groups in IAM Identity Center. Assign the users to the appropriate groups. Attach AWS managed IAM policies to each user as needed for fine-grained permissions.

Create individual users in IAM Identity Center. Create new developer and administrator groups in IAM Identity Center. Create new permission sets that include the appropriate IAM policies for each group. Assign the new groups to the appropriate accounts. Assign the new permission sets to the new groups. When new users are hired, add them to the appropriate group.

Create individual users in IAM Identity Center. Create new permission sets that include the appropriate IAM policies for each user. Assign the users to the appropriate accounts. Grant additional IAM permissions to the users from within specific accounts. When new users are hired, add them to IAM Identity Center and assign them to the accounts.
explanation: Option A (INCORRECT): Creating individual users in IAM Identity Center for each account increases operational overhead compared to managing centrally. Custom IAM policies per group complicate management and updates as the number of accounts and users grows. Option B (INCORRECT): Attaching AWS managed IAM policies to each user in IAM Identity Center is not supported – permission sets are used instead of direct IAM user attachments. This option again manages permissions per user rather than via reusable permission sets, increasing operational overhead. Option D (INCORRECT): Defining permission sets per user and then granting additional rights inside each account negates the centralized management benefits of IAM Identity Center. Operational overhead remains high when onboarding or changing permissions for new hires. Option C (CORRECT): IAM Identity Center permission sets let you define reusable, fine-grained IAM policies once and assign them across multiple accounts. Grouping users (developers vs. administrators) and attaching the appropriate permission sets ensures least-privilege access with minimal repeated configuration. Onboarding new team members is as simple as adding them to the correct IAM Identity Center group—no per-account or per-user IAM changes required. In summary, by leveraging IAM Identity Center permission sets and groups, you achieve centralized, least-privilege access management across all accounts with minimal operational overhead. This question falls under Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company wants to migrate a Windows-based application from on premises to the AWS Cloud. The application has three tiers: an application tier, a business tier, and a database tier with Microsoft SQL Server. The company wants to use specific features of SQL Server such as native backups and Data Quality Services. The company also needs to share files for processing between the tiers. How should a solutions architect design the architecture to meet these requirements?
options: Host all three tiers on Amazon EC2 instances. Use Amazon FSx File Gateway for file sharing between the tiers.
Host all three tiers on Amazon EC2 instances. Use Amazon FSx for Windows File Server for file sharing between the tiers.
Host the application tier and the business tier on Amazon EC2 instances. Host the database tier on Amazon RDS. Use Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) for file sharing between the tiers.

Host the application tier and the business tier on Amazon EC2 instances. Host the database tier on Amazon RDS. Use a Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume for file sharing between the tiers.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): “Host all three tiers on Amazon EC2 instances. Use Amazon FSx File Gateway for file sharing between the tiers.” Amazon FSx File Gateway is a Storage Gateway integration that presents an NFS/SMB interface to on-premises applications—it is not a managed, highly available SMB file share within AWS. It adds unnecessary complexity and is not intended for intra-VPC file sharing between EC2 tiers. Option C (INCORRECT): “Host the application and business tiers on Amazon EC2 instances. Host the database tier on Amazon RDS. Use Amazon EFS for file sharing between the tiers.” Amazon RDS for SQL Server does not support Data Quality Services or native backup/restore to S3 the way you need for your custom workflows. Amazon EFS provides only NFS access—it is not suitable for Windows-based SMB file shares required by your application tiers. Option D (INCORRECT): “Host the application and business tiers on Amazon EC2 instances. Host the database tier on Amazon RDS. Use a Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) Amazon EBS volume for file sharing between the tiers.” EBS volumes cannot be attached to more than one Windows EC2 instance at a time for concurrent SMB file sharing. You would need a clustered file system or third-party solution to share an EBS volume across multiple instances, which adds complexity and risk. Option B (CORRECT): “Host all three tiers on Amazon EC2 instances. Use Amazon FSx for Windows File Server for file sharing between the tiers.” Running SQL Server on EC2 gives you full control—native backups, Data Quality Services, and any third-party extensions are fully supported. Amazon FSx for Windows File Server provides a fully managed, highly available SMB file share that can be mounted by all Windows-based EC2 instances across tiers. This design meets your application’s Windows requirements and simplifies file sharing while leveraging AWS managed services. In summary, we learned that to preserve advanced SQL Server features and enable native SMB file sharing between Windows tiers, you must host the database on EC2 and use Amazon FSx for Windows File Server. This question belongs to Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures, as it focuses on choosing the services that deliver full feature support and optimal performance for a Windows-based application.

question: A company has a static website that is hosted on Amazon CloudFront in front of Amazon S3. The static website uses a database backend. The company notices that the website does not reflect updates that have been made in the website’s Git repository. The company checks the continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipeline between the Git repository and Amazon S3. The company verifies that the webhooks are configured properly and that the CI/CD pipeline is sending messages that indicate successful deployments. A solutions architect needs to implement a solution that displays the updates on the website. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Add an Application Load Balancer.
Add Amazon ElastiCache for Redis or Memcached to the database layer of the web application.
Invalidate the CloudFront cache.
Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to validate the website’s SSL certificate.
