Create the required backup plan.” Governance mode allows certain privileged users (e.g., root) to alter or delete backups before the retention period ends, which violates the immutability requirement. It does not enforce a strict Write Once Read Many (WORM) policy required by the regulatory mandate. Option B (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager to create the required automated snapshot policy.” Data Lifecycle Manager manages EBS snapshots but does not enforce immutability or retention lock on S3 or on the snapshots themselves. It cannot guarantee that snapshots cannot be deleted or altered before the retention period lapses. Option C (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon S3 File Gateway to create the backup. Configure the appropriate S3 Lifecycle management.” S3 Lifecycle policies manage object transitions and expirations but do not provide WORM immutability by themselves. S3 Object Lock (which provides WORM) could be used, but File Gateway alone plus lifecycle rules does not meet the regulatory write-once requirement. Option D (CORRECT): “Use AWS Backup to create a backup vault that has a vault lock in compliance mode. Create the required backup plan.” Compliance mode on an AWS Backup vault lock enforces WORM—no one (including root) can delete or alter backups until the retention period expires. AWS Backup supports both EBS/EC2 and S3 backups in a unified plan, ensuring all data sources are covered. This meets the regulatory need for immutable backup retention over a defined period. In summary, we’ve learned how AWS Backup vault locks operate in governance vs. compliance modes, and why compliance mode is required to enforce true immutability. This question falls under Domain 2 - Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A financial services company wants to shut down two data centers and migrate more than 100 TB of data to AWS. The data has an intricate directory structure with millions of small files stored in deep hierarchies of subfolders. Most of the data is unstructured, and the company’s file storage consists of SMB-based storage types from multiple vendors. The company does not want to change its applications to access the data after migration. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Use AWS Direct Connect to migrate the data to Amazon S3.
Use AWS DataSync to migrate the data to Amazon FSx for Lustre.
Use AWS DataSync to migrate the data to Amazon FSx for Windows File Server.
Use AWS Direct Connect to migrate the data on-premises file storage to an AWS Storage Gateway volume gateway.
explanation: The correct answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): “Use AWS Direct Connect to migrate the data to Amazon S3.” • Direct Connect is a network link, not a migration tool. It only provides a private connection to AWS. • Migrating file‐based SMB shares directly into S3 breaks the existing directory structure and requires application changes to use S3 APIs or a gateway. • S3 is object storage, not a native SMB file system, so it won’t present the same file‐share interface to your applications. Option B (INCORRECT): “Use AWS DataSync to migrate the data to Amazon FSx for Lustre.” • FSx for Lustre is tailored for high‐performance computing and uses the Lustre protocol, not SMB. • Applications expecting a Windows‐style SMB share would need to be modified to mount Lustre file systems. • This does not meet the requirement of “no application changes” after migration. Option D (INCORRECT): “Use AWS Direct Connect to migrate the on‐premises file storage to an AWS Storage Gateway volume gateway.” • Volume Gateway exposes block storage (iSCSI), not SMB/CIFS file shares. • Applications expecting SMB endpoints cannot mount block volumes directly without additional file servers. • Operational overhead remains high to deploy and manage file servers on EC2 or elsewhere to present SMB shares. Option C (CORRECT): “Use AWS DataSync to migrate the data to Amazon FSx for Windows File Server.” • DataSync handles large-scale migrations of file data, preserving directory hierarchies and metadata. • Amazon FSx for Windows File Server provides a fully managed, native SMB file system that applications can mount without any changes. • This solution minimizes operational overhead—no need to stand up or manage file servers—and supports deep folder structures and millions of small files. In summary, Amazon DataSync combined with Amazon FSx for Windows File Server meets the requirements of migrating 100 TB of SMB‐based unstructured data with deep directory hierarchies, preserving the existing file‐share interface, and minimizing operational overhead. This question falls under Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company stores data in Amazon S3. According to regulations, the data must not contain personally identifiable information (PII). The company recently discovered that S3 buckets have some objects that contain PII. The company needs to automatically detect PII in S3 buckets and to notify the company’s security team.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Use Amazon Macie. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to filter the SensitiveData event type from Macie findings and to send an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) notification to the security team.

Use Amazon GuardDuty. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to filter the CRITICAL event type from GuardDuty findings and to send an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) notification to the security team.

Use Amazon Macie. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to filter the SensitiveData:S3Object/Personal event type from Macie findings and to send an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) notification to the security team.

Use Amazon GuardDuty. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to filter the CRITICAL event type from GuardDuty findings and to send an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) notification to the security team.
explanation: The correct Answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon GuardDuty. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to filter the CRITICAL event type from GuardDuty findings and to send an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) notification to the security team.” GuardDuty is focused on threat detection in your AWS account (e.g., malicious activity, compromised resources), not on scanning S3 objects for PII or sensitive data. The CRITICAL event type in GuardDuty refers to security threats, not to data classification or PII detection. Option C (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon Macie. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to filter the SensitiveData:S3Object/Personal event type from Macie findings and to send an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) notification to the security team.” Although Macie is the correct service to detect PII, sending notifications via SQS is not the most direct way to “notify” a security team. They would still need a polling mechanism to read the queue. The requirement is to notify the team automatically; SNS provides push notifications immediately, whereas SQS requires additional processing logic. Option D (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon GuardDuty. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to filter the CRITICAL event type from GuardDuty findings and to send an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) notification to the security team.” Mixes up GuardDuty (for threat detection) with PII scanning use case. Also uses SQS which is not optimal for direct notifications. Option A (CORRECT): “Use Amazon Macie. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to filter the SensitiveData event type from Macie findings and to send an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) notification to the security team.” Amazon Macie is designed to automatically discover, classify, and protect sensitive data such as PII in S3 buckets. Macie findings emit events (e.g., “SensitiveData:S3Object/Personal”) to Amazon EventBridge. You can filter on the broad SensitiveData event type to catch all relevant PII detections. Using Amazon SNS sends immediate notifications (email, SMS, HTTP endpoint) to the security team without additional polling logic. In this discussion, we learned that Amazon Macie is the appropriate service for automated PII detection in S3, and that Amazon EventBridge plus SNS provides a simple, real-time notification mechanism. This question falls under Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: An ecommerce company is experiencing an increase in user traffic. The company’s store is deployed on Amazon EC2 instances as a two-tier web application consisting of a web tier and a separate database tier. As traffic increases, the company notices that the architecture is causing significant delays in sending timely marketing and order confirmation email to users. The company wants to reduce the time it spends resolving complex email delivery issues and minimize operational overhead. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
options: Create a separate application tier using EC2 instances dedicated to email processing.
Configure the web instance to send email through Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES).
Configure the web instance to send email through Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS).
Create a separate application tier using EC2 instances dedicated to email processing. Place the instances in an Auto Scaling group.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): “Create a separate application tier using EC2 instances dedicated to email processing.” • This adds operational overhead of managing, patching, scaling EC2 instances. • It does not address deliverability challenges or provide built-in analytics, bounce handling, or complaint management. • Using SES is more efficient than rolling your own email servers. Option C (INCORRECT): “Configure the web instance to send email through Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS).” • SNS is designed for pub/sub notifications, not direct email delivery. • It supports only basic email-to-topic subscriptions and lacks SES’s deliverability features (DKIM, bounce/complaint handling). • You’d still need SES under the hood for high-volume, reliable email sends. Option D (INCORRECT): “Create a separate application tier using EC2 instances dedicated to email processing. Place the instances in an Auto Scaling group.” • Auto Scaling helps handle load but still incurs EC2-management overhead. • Fails to leverage a fully managed email delivery service that handles scaling, bounces, feedback, and reputation management. • Higher cost and complexity compared to SES. Option B (CORRECT): “Configure the web instance to send email through Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES).” • SES is a fully managed, highly scalable email service built for marketing and transactional email. • It automatically handles bounce and complaint tracking, DKIM signing, and deliverability optimizations. • Offloads all operational overhead—no EC2 email servers to manage—while reducing latencies and costs. In summary, leveraging Amazon SES simplifies email delivery, improves reliability, and minimizes operational overhead. This question falls under Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company uses a three-tier web application to provide training to new employees. The application is accessed for only 12 hours every day. The company is using an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance to store information and wants to minimize costs. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
options: Configure an IAM policy for AWS Systems Manager Session Manager. Create an IAM role for the policy. Update the trust relationship of the role. Set up automatic start and stop for the DB instance.

Create an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cache cluster that gives users the ability to access the data from the cache when the DB instance is stopped. Invalidate the cache after the DB instance is started.

Launch an Amazon EC2 instance. Create an IAM role that grants access to Amazon RDS. Attach the role to the EC2 instance. Configure a cron job to start and stop the EC2 instance on the desired schedule.

Create AWS Lambda functions to start and stop the DB instance. Create Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) scheduled rules to invoke the Lambda functions. Configure the Lambda functions as event targets for the rules.
explanation: The correct answer is D Option A (INCORRECT): “Configure an IAM policy for AWS Systems Manager Session Manager. Create an IAM role for the policy. Update the trust relationship of the role. Set up automatic start and stop for the DB instance.” The steps describe configuring Session Manager, which is unrelated to automating RDS start/stop. AWS Systems Manager Session Manager is used for secure shell access to EC2 instances, not for scheduling RDS operations. No mechanism is provided here to actually schedule the DB instance start/stop automatically. Option B (INCORRECT): “Create an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cache cluster that gives users the ability to access the data from the cache when the DB instance is stopped. Invalidate the cache after the DB instance is started.” You cannot keep ElastiCache in sync with RDS automatically when the database is stopped—data divergence is almost certain. Users still need the primary RDS for writes and consistent data; caching can’t replace the database when it’s unavailable. This does not address cost optimization by stopping the RDS instance itself. Option C (INCORRECT): “Launch an Amazon EC2 instance. Create an IAM role that grants access to Amazon RDS. Attach the role to the EC2 instance. Configure a cron job to start and stop the EC2 instance on the desired schedule.” This only automates start/stop of an EC2 instance, not the RDS DB instance. The requirement is to minimize RDS costs by stopping the DB instance, not an unrelated EC2 host. Also, cron on EC2 is a less serverless, more maintenance-heavy solution compared to Lambda + EventBridge. Option D (CORRECT): “Create AWS Lambda functions to start and stop the DB instance. Create Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) scheduled rules to invoke the Lambda functions. Configure the Lambda functions as event targets for the rules.” Lambda allows you to run code on a schedule without managing servers. EventBridge (CloudWatch Events) scheduled rules can trigger Lambda at the desired 12-hour on/off times. This approach directly automates RDS start/stop, minimizing database uptime and cost. In summary, we learned how to automate cost-saving operations on Amazon RDS for non-production or time-restricted workloads by using Lambda and EventBridge. This question belongs to Domain 4 – Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: An ecommerce company wants to use machine learning (ML) algorithms to build and train models. The company will use the models to visualize complex scenarios and to detect trends in customer data. The architecture team wants to integrate its ML models with a reporting platform to analyze the augmented data and use the data directly in its business intelligence dashboards.Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Use AWS Glue to create an ML transform to build and train models. Use Amazon OpenSearch Service to visualize the data.
Use Amazon SageMaker to build and train models. Use Amazon QuickSight to visualize the data.
Use a pre-built ML Amazon Machine Image (AMI) from the AWS Marketplace to build and train models. Use Amazon OpenSearch Service to visualize the data.
Use Amazon QuickSight to build and train models by using calculated fields. Use Amazon QuickSight to visualize the data.
explanation: The correct Answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): “Use AWS Glue to create an ML transform to build and train models. Use Amazon OpenSearch Service to visualize the data.” AWS Glue ML transforms are specialized for tasks like data deduplication or finding matching records, not for full-fledged model building and training at scale. Amazon OpenSearch Service is designed for search and log analytics, not for directly powering BI dashboards with ML‐augmented data. This approach would require additional glue jobs, cluster management, and custom integrations, increasing operational overhead. Option C (INCORRECT): “Use a pre-built ML Amazon Machine Image (AMI) from the AWS Marketplace to build and train models. Use Amazon OpenSearch Service to visualize the data.” Using a marketplace AMI means you must provision, patch, and scale your own EC2 instances—high operational overhead. OpenSearch Service again is focused on search and log analytics, not a native BI reporting tool for dashboards. Lacks the managed, end‐to‐end model lifecycle and built‐in integration with BI services that you get from SageMaker and QuickSight. Option D (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon QuickSight to build and train models by using calculated fields. Use Amazon QuickSight to visualize the data.” QuickSight’s ML-powered insights (e.g., anomaly detection, forecasting) are limited to built‐in algorithms and do not replace a full model training environment. You cannot train custom, complex ML models or tune hyperparameters within QuickSight’s calculated fields. This option fails the requirement to build, train, and deploy custom ML models for advanced scenario visualization. Option B (CORRECT): “Use Amazon SageMaker to build and train models. Use Amazon QuickSight to visualize the data.” Amazon SageMaker provides a fully managed, end‐to‐end ML platform: data labeling, model building, training, tuning, and deployment with minimal infrastructure management. Amazon QuickSight integrates seamlessly with SageMaker endpoints and AWS data sources to ingest augmented data, build dashboards, and deliver BI reports. This solution minimizes operational overhead by leveraging fully managed services for both ML and BI. In summary, we learned how to choose managed AWS services—SageMaker for ML model development and QuickSight for BI dashboards—to minimize operational overhead while fulfilling complex analysis requirements. This question aligns with Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company is developing a new mobile app. The company must implement proper traffic filtering to protect its Application Load Balancer (ALB) against common application-level attacks, such as cross-site scripting or SQL injection. The company has minimal infrastructure and operational staff. The company needs to reduce its share of the responsibility in managing, updating, and securing servers for its AWS environment.What should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?
options: Configure AWS WAF rules and associate them with the ALB.
Deploy the application using Amazon S3 with public hosting enabled.
Deploy AWS Shield Advanced and add the ALB as a protected resource.
Create a new ALB that directs traffic to an Amazon EC2 instance running a third-party firewall, which then passes the traffic to the current ALB.
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): “Deploy the application using Amazon S3 with public hosting enabled.” Amazon S3 static hosting only supports static content. It cannot run dynamic web applications that require server‐side logic or databases. Publicly exposing an S3 bucket does not provide application‐layer protection against XSS or SQL injection attacks. Option C (INCORRECT): “Deploy AWS Shield Advanced and add the ALB as a protected resource.” AWS Shield Advanced focuses on DDoS protection, not on mitigating application‐layer attacks like cross‐site scripting or SQL injection. It does not provide customizable rules for inspecting HTTP requests or blocking malicious payloads at the application level. Option D (INCORRECT): “Create a new ALB that directs traffic to an Amazon EC2 instance running a third‐party firewall, which then passes the traffic to the current ALB.” This approach introduces additional infrastructure to manage (EC2 servers, third‐party OS/patches, license overhead), increasing operational burden. It contradicts the requirement to minimize server management and offload security responsibility to a managed service. Option A (CORRECT): “Configure AWS WAF rules and associate them with the ALB.” AWS WAF is a fully managed, scalable web application firewall that protects against common exploits such as XSS and SQL injection. It integrates directly with Application Load Balancers, allowing you to define custom or managed rule sets without managing any servers. Being a managed service, AWS handles patching, scaling, and operational overhead, which aligns with reducing the company’s infrastructure responsibilities. In summary, using AWS WAF with your ALB delivers targeted, application‐level protection against common web attacks while minimizing operational effort. This question falls under Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A solutions architect is designing a security solution for a company that wants to provide developers with individual AWS accounts through AWS Organizations, while also maintaining standard security controls. Because the individual developers will have AWS account root user-level access to their own accounts, the solutions architect wants to ensure that the mandatory AWS CloudTrail configuration that is applied to new developer accounts is not modified.Which action meets these requirements?
options: Create an IAM policy that prohibits changes to CloudTrail. and attach it to the root user.
Create a new trail in CloudTrail from within the developer accounts with the organization trails option enabled.
Create a service control policy (SCP) that prohibits changes to CloudTrail, and attach it the developer accounts.
Create a service-linked role for CloudTrail with a policy condition that allows changes only from an Amazon Resource Name (ARN) in the management account.
explanation: The correct Answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): “Create an IAM policy that prohibits changes to CloudTrail and attach it to the root user.” An IAM policy cannot be attached to the root user. IAM policies are for IAM users, groups, or roles. The root user always has full access in the account, and you cannot limit its permissions via an IAM policy. Option B (INCORRECT): “Create a new trail in CloudTrail from within the developer accounts with the organization trails option enabled.” Organization trails must be created by the management (master) account, not by member accounts. This does not prevent a developer from deleting or modifying their own trail if they have root access. Option D (INCORRECT): “Create a service-linked role for CloudTrail with a policy condition that allows changes only from an ARN in the management account.” Service-linked roles delegate permissions to AWS services but do not enforce account-wide guardrails. They cannot prevent a root user from editing or deleting CloudTrail settings in their account. Option C (CORRECT): “Create a service control policy (SCP) that prohibits changes to CloudTrail, and attach it to the developer accounts.” SCPs are the proper mechanism in AWS Organizations to apply mandatory permissions guardrails across member accounts. Even the root user is subject to SCP restrictions, so developers cannot modify or delete the organizational CloudTrail trail. Attaching the SCP at the OU or account level enforces the policy automatically for any new or existing developer account. In summary, we learned that to enforce mandatory AWS service configurations—especially against even the account root user—you should use Service Control Policies within AWS Organizations. This question belongs to Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company recently launched Linux-based application instances on Amazon EC2 in a private subnet and launched a Linux-based bastion host on an Amazon EC2 instance in a public subnet of a VPC. A solutions architect needs to connect from the on-premises network, through the company's internet connection, to the bastion host, and to the application servers. The solutions architect must make sure that the security groups of all the EC2 instances will allow that access.Which combination of steps should the solutions architect take to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
options: Replace the current security group of the bastion host with one that only allows inbound access from the application instances.
Replace the current security group of the bastion host with one that only allows inbound access from the internal IP range for the company.
Replace the current security group of the bastion host with one that only allows inbound access from the external IP range for the company.
Replace the current security group of the application instances with one that allows inbound SSH access from only the private IP address of the bastion host.
Replace the current security group of the application instances with one that allows inbound SSH access from only the public IP address of the bastion host.
explanation: The correct answer is C, D Option A (INCORRECT): Replacing the bastion host’s security group to allow inbound only from the application instances doesn’t help you reach the bastion host from your on-premises network. You need to permit your corporate IP range to SSH into the bastion, not the private app servers. Option B (INCORRECT): Allowing inbound access to the bastion host only from your internal corporate IP range (i.e., your on-premises private addresses) won’t work over the internet. The bastion sees the public IP of your corporate gateway/NAT, not your private LAN space. Option E (INCORRECT): Granting the application servers SSH access only from the bastion’s public IP will fail because, inside the VPC, traffic originates from the bastion’s private IP address. The SG needs to reference that private address. Option C (CORRECT): Configure the bastion host’s security group to allow inbound SSH only from your company’s external (public) IP range. This ensures only your on-premises network can reach the bastion over the internet. It locks down SSH access to a known, fixed CIDR instead of 0.0.0.0/0. Option D (CORRECT): Configure the application instances’ security group to allow inbound SSH only from the bastion host’s private VPC IP. Within the VPC, the bastion’s outgoing SSH traffic carries its private IP as the source. Restricting SG rules to that single IP locks down access to just your hardened jump server. In summary, you must allow your on-premises public address range to SSH into the bastion (Option C), and then permit only the bastion’s private VPC IP to SSH into the application servers (Option D). This question tests your ability to Design Secure Architectures, which maps to Domain 1 of the AWS Solutions Architect – Associate exam.

question: A company has a business-critical application that runs on Amazon EC2 instances. The application stores data in an Amazon DynamoDB table. The company must be able to revert the table to any point within the last 24 hours.Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Configure point-in-time recovery for the table.
Use AWS Backup for the table.
Use an AWS Lambda function to make an on-demand backup of the table every hour.
Turn on streams on the table to capture a log of all changes to the table in the last 24 hours. Store a copy of the stream in an Amazon S3 bucket.
explanation: The correct answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): “Use AWS Backup for the table.” AWS Backup can orchestrate backups for DynamoDB, but it relies on scheduled or on‐demand snapshots rather than continuous, per‐second recovery points. To achieve point‐in‐time restores within 24 hours, you would need very frequent scheduled backups and retention management—adding operational overhead. Option C (INCORRECT): “Use an AWS Lambda function to make an on-demand backup of the table every hour.” Hourly backups only allow restoring to the nearest hourly snapshot—not to any arbitrary second within the last 24 hours. You must build, deploy, and monitor the Lambda schedule, handle failures, and manage snapshot retention—unnecessary operational complexity. Option D (INCORRECT): “Turn on streams on the table to capture a log of all changes to the table in the last 24 hours. Store a copy of the stream in an Amazon S3 bucket.” DynamoDB Streams retains data only for 24 hours and does not provide built-in point‐in‐time restore functionality—you’d have to manually replay changes to reconstruct state. This approach demands custom code to replay, maintain idempotency, and handle stream-to-S3 export—significant operational overhead. Option A (CORRECT): “Configure point-in-time recovery for the table.” Point-in-time recovery (PITR) is a built‐in DynamoDB feature that continuously backs up data changes, allowing restores to any second in the last 35 days (including the past 24 hours). No custom scripts, schedules, or additional AWS services are required—just a simple enable, and DynamoDB handles everything automatically. This solution meets the requirement with the least operational overhead. Summary: Enabling DynamoDB’s built-in point-in-time recovery is the simplest way to restore a table to any point within the last 24 hours, with virtually no operational overhead. This question falls under Domain 2 – Design Resilient Architectures, as it addresses data durability and recovery strategies.

question: A company wants to improve its ability to clone large amounts of production data into a test environment in the same AWS Region. The data is stored in Amazon EC2 instances on Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes. Modifications to the cloned data must not affect the production environment. The software that accesses this data requires consistently high I/O performance. A solutions architect needs to minimize the time that is required to clone the production data into the test environment. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Take EBS snapshots of the production EBS volumes. Restore the snapshots onto EC2 instance store volumes in the test environment.

Configure the production EBS volumes to use the EBS Multi-Attach feature. Take EBS snapshots of the production EBS volumes. Attach the production EBS volumes to the EC2 instances in the test environment.

Take EBS snapshots of the production EBS volumes. Create and initialize new EBS volumes. Attach the new EBS volumes to EC2 instances in the test environment before restoring the volumes from the production EBS snapshots.

Take EBS snapshots of the production EBS volumes. Turn on the EBS fast snapshot restore feature on the EBS snapshots. Restore the snapshots into new EBS volumes. Attach the new EBS volumes to EC2 instances in the test environment.
explanation: The correct answer is D. Option A (INCORRECT): • You cannot restore an EBS snapshot directly onto an instance store volume—snapshots can only create new EBS volumes. • Instance store volumes are ephemeral. They lose data on stop/termination, which breaks the requirement for a stable test clone. • Doesn’t address fast, high-I/O performance from first read. Option B (INCORRECT): • EBS Multi-Attach lets multiple EC2 instances share a single volume concurrently, but it is not a cloning mechanism. • Attaching production volumes directly to test instances means test writes could affect production data (even though Multi-Attach is read-only for some OS configurations, it isn’t designed as an immutable clone). • Does not speed up data copy. Option C (INCORRECT): • Restoring standard snapshots into new EBS volumes without Fast Snapshot Restore means lazy loading. The first read of each block can be very slow, and you must pre-warm volumes manually to get consistent performance. • The “initialize new EBS volumes” step incurs additional time and operational overhead. • Does not guarantee instant high I/O performance. Option D (CORRECT): • EBS Fast Snapshot Restore (FSR) fully initializes blocks ahead of time so volumes are instantly ready at maximum throughput and IOPS. • You still use snapshots (point‐in‐time, immutable), so test modifications never impact production volumes. • Minimizes clone time and guarantees consistently high I/O from first use without manual pre-warming. In summary, enabling EBS Fast Snapshot Restore on your production snapshots and then restoring those snapshots into new EBS volumes (Option D) delivers a rapid, high-performance clone for a test environment without risking production data integrity. This scenario falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company is using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) keys to encrypt AWS Lambda environment variables. A solutions architect needs to ensure that the required permissions are in place to decrypt and use the environment variables. Which steps must the solutions architect take to implement the correct permissions?(Choose two.)
options: Add AWS KMS permissions in the Lambda resource policy.
Add AWS KMS permissions in the Lambda execution role.
Add AWS KMS permissions in the Lambda function policy.
Allow the Lambda execution role in the AWS KMS key policy.
Allow the Lambda resource policy in the AWS KMS key policy.
explanation: The correct answer is B, D. Option A (INCORRECT): “Add AWS KMS permissions in the Lambda resource policy.” • AWS Lambda does not have a “resource policy” for KMS operations on environment variables. • Permissions for decrypting environment variables must be granted to the execution role (IAM policy) and allowed in the KMS key policy, not in a non-existent Lambda resource policy. Option C (INCORRECT): “Add AWS KMS permissions in the Lambda function policy.” • There is no separate “function policy” distinct from the Lambda execution role’s IAM policy. • You grant permissions by attaching an IAM policy to the role assumed by the function, not to a standalone “function policy.” Option E (INCORRECT): “Allow the Lambda resource policy in the AWS KMS key policy.” • Again, Lambda has no resource policy relating to KMS usage. • KMS key policies reference IAM principals (roles, users), not Lambda-specific “resource policies.” Option B (CORRECT): “Add AWS KMS permissions in the Lambda execution role.” • The Lambda execution role needs an IAM policy granting kms:Decrypt (and kms:Encrypt if writing) on the key. • This allows the function, when assuming its role, to call KMS APIs to decrypt the environment variables at runtime. Option D (CORRECT): “Allow the Lambda execution role in the AWS KMS key policy.” • A KMS key policy must explicitly permit the IAM role (the Lambda execution role) to use the key. • Without this, even if the role’s IAM policy allows kms:Decrypt, KMS will block usage if the key policy doesn’t include that principal. Summary: We’ve learned that to decrypt Lambda environment variables encrypted with a KMS key, you must grant the Lambda execution role permission in two places: its own IAM policy (Option B) and the key policy (Option D). This ensures both AWS IAM and KMS key policy trust the role. Domain: Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures

question: A retail company has several businesses. The IT team for each business manages its own AWS account. Each team account is part of an organization in AWS Organizations. Each team monitors its product inventory levels in an Amazon DynamoDB table in the team's own AWS account. The company is deploying a central inventory reporting application into a shared AWS account. The application must be able to read items from all the teams' DynamoDB tables. Which authentication option will meet these requirements MOST securely?
options: Integrate DynamoDB with AWS Secrets Manager in the inventory application account. Configure the application to use the correct secret from Secrets Manager to authenticate and read the DynamoDB table. Schedule secret rotation for every 30 days.

In every business account, create an IAM user that has programmatic access. Configure the application to use the correct IAM user access key ID and secret access key to authenticate and read the DynamoDB table. Manually rotate IAM access keys every 30 days.

In every business account, create an IAM role named BU_ROLE with a policy that gives the role access to the DynamoDB table and a trust policy to trust a specific role in the inventory application account. In the inventory account, create a role named APP_ROLE that allows access to the STS AssumeRole API operation. Configure the application to use APP_ROLE and assume the crossaccount role BU_ROLE to read the DynamoDB table.

Integrate DynamoDB with AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Generate identity certificates to authenticate DynamoDB. Configure the application to use the correct certificate to authenticate and read the DynamoDB table.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): “Integrate DynamoDB with AWS Secrets Manager in the inventory application account. Configure the application to use the correct secret from Secrets Manager to authenticate and read the DynamoDB table. Schedule secret rotation for every 30 days.” DynamoDB does not support direct authentication via ACM or Secrets Manager. Secrets Manager simply stores credentials; you still need an IAM principal or role to call DynamoDB APIs. This approach would require distributing long-lived credentials across accounts, which increases risk and administrative overhead. Option B (INCORRECT): “In every business account, create an IAM user that has programmatic access. Configure the application to use the correct IAM user access key ID and secret access key to authenticate and read the DynamoDB table. Manually rotate IAM access keys every 30 days.” Storing and managing IAM user access keys across multiple accounts is insecure and operationally burdensome. IAM users are not the recommended best practice for cross-account application authentication; roles are preferred for temporary credentials. Option D (INCORRECT): “Integrate DynamoDB with AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Generate identity certificates to authenticate DynamoDB. Configure the application to use the correct certificate to authenticate and read the DynamoDB table.” DynamoDB does not support mutual TLS or client certificates for authentication via ACM. No AWS service natively issues per-client certificates for DynamoDB API calls; IAM roles and policies are required. Option C (CORRECT): “In every business account, create an IAM role named BU_ROLE with a policy granting read access to the DynamoDB table and a trust policy that allows a specific role in the inventory application account to assume it. In the inventory account, create a role named APP_ROLE that can call sts:AssumeRole. Configure the application to use APP_ROLE, then call AssumeRole on each BU_ROLE to obtain temporary credentials and read the tables.” Uses IAM roles and AWS STS to provide short-term, scoped credentials—no long-lived keys to manage. Cross-account trust policies enforce least-privilege access per business team. Fully aligns with AWS best practices for secure, auditable cross-account access. In summary, the secure and scalable way to grant a central application cross-account read access to multiple DynamoDB tables is via IAM roles and STS AssumeRole. This solution avoids hard-coded credentials, enforces least privilege, and leverages temporary tokens. This question belongs to Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company regularly uploads confidential data to Amazon S3 buckets for analysis. The company's security policies mandate that the objects must be encrypted at rest. The company must automatically rotate the encryption key every year. The company must be able to track key rotation by using AWS CloudTrail. The company also must minimize costs for the encryption key. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Use server-side encryption with customer-provided keys (SSE-C)
Use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3)
Use server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS)
Use server-side encryption with customer managed AWS KMS keys
explanation: The correct answer is Option D Option A (INCORRECT): Use server-side encryption with customer-provided keys (SSE-C). You must manage and supply the encryption key on every request; there is no AWS-managed rotation. CloudTrail does not log SSE-C key usage or rotation since AWS never has access to your key material. This approach adds operational complexity and fails the automatic annual rotation requirement. Option B (INCORRECT): Use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3). SSE-S3 uses an AWS‐owned key that you cannot rotate or control. Automatic rotation is handled by AWS, but you cannot configure or track the schedule. CloudTrail does not expose S3‐managed key rotation events or details. Option C (INCORRECT): Use server-side encryption with AWS managed KMS keys (SSE-KMS). This uses an AWS-owned CMK that does not support customer‐defined rotation. You cannot enable or track annual key rotation on AWS-managed CMKs. CloudTrail will log encryption API calls but not any rotation you cannot configure. Option D (CORRECT): Use server-side encryption with customer managed AWS KMS keys. You create a customer‐managed CMK in AWS KMS and enable automatic key rotation every 365 days. CloudTrail logs all KMS key usage and rotation events, fulfilling the audit requirement. This solution incurs only the minimal KMS key charge and meets the company's cost and security policies. In summary, we evaluated all SSE options against the requirements for annual key rotation, CloudTrail auditing, and cost optimization. Only a customer-managed AWS KMS key (Option D) satisfies automatic yearly rotation and provides full auditability via CloudTrail while keeping costs minimal. This question belongs to Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A robotics company is designing a solution for medical surgery. The robots will use advanced sensors, cameras, and AI algorithms to perceive their environment and to complete surgeries. The company needs a public load balancer in the AWS Cloud that will ensure seamless communication with backend services. The load balancer must be capable of routing traffic based on the query strings to different target groups. The traffic must also be encrypted. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Use a Network Load Balancer with a certificate attached from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Use query parameter-based routing.
Use a Gateway Load Balancer. Import a generated certificate in AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). Attach the certificate to the load balancer. Use HTTP path-based routing.
Use an Application Load Balancer with a certificate attached from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Use query parameter-based routing.
Use a Network Load Balancer. Import a generated certificate in AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). Attach the certificate to the load balancer. Use query parameter-based routing.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Let’s step through why A, B, and D are not correct, and why C is the right choice: Option A (INCORRECT): Use a Network Load Balancer with a certificate attached from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) and query parameter–based routing. Network Load Balancer operates at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP) and does not inspect HTTP details like query strings. It cannot perform content-based routing on query parameters; only an Application Load Balancer can do that. Option B (INCORRECT): Use a Gateway Load Balancer, import a generated certificate in IAM, attach the certificate, and use HTTP path–based routing. Gateway Load Balancer is for transparently deploying virtual appliances (firewalls, IDS/IPS), not for TLS termination or HTTP routing. It forwards packets at Layers 3/4 and does not support HTTP path or query string inspection. Option D (INCORRECT): Use a Network Load Balancer, import a generated certificate in IAM, attach the certificate, and use query parameter–based routing. NLB can terminate TLS only with certificates managed in ACM; IAM-imported certs apply to Classic Load Balancer, not NLB. Even with TLS offload, NLB cannot perform Layer 7 routing on query strings. Option C (CORRECT): Use an Application Load Balancer with a certificate attached from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) and query parameter–based routing. ALB operates at Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) and natively supports routing rules based on host, path, headers, and query strings. It integrates with ACM for seamless TLS certificate management and encrypted traffic termination. Query parameter–based routing allows directing requests to different target groups based on the query string values, satisfying the requirement. Summary: Only the Application Load Balancer supports advanced content-based routing on query parameters and integrates with ACM for TLS encryption. This question falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company runs a web-based portal that provides users with global breaking news, local alerts, and weather updates. The portal delivers each user a personalized view by using mixture of static and dynamic content. Content is served over HTTPS through an API server running on an Amazon EC2 instance behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The company wants the portal to provide this content to its users across the world as quickly as possible. How should a solutions architect design the application to ensure the LEAST amount of latency for all users?
options: Deploy the application stack in a single AWS Region. Use Amazon CloudFront to serve all static and dynamic content by specifying the ALB as an origin.
Deploy the application stack in two AWS Regions. Use an Amazon Route 53 latency routing policy to serve all content from the ALB in the closest Region.
Deploy the application stack in a single AWS Region. Use Amazon CloudFront to serve the static content. Serve the dynamic content directly from the ALB.
Deploy the application stack in two AWS Regions. Use an Amazon Route 53 geolocation routing policy to serve all content from the ALB in the closest Region.
explanation: The correct answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): “Deploy the application stack in two AWS Regions. Use an Amazon Route 53 latency routing policy to serve all content from the ALB in the closest Region.” Having two Regions doubles operational complexity and cost without leveraging edge caching. Route 53 latency routing only directs users to the nearest Region, but users still fetch dynamic content directly from that Region’s ALB, which may introduce more latency for static objects and repeated dynamic requests. It doesn’t optimize delivery at the edge the way Amazon CloudFront does. Option C (INCORRECT): “Deploy the application stack in a single AWS Region. Use Amazon CloudFront to serve the static content. Serve the dynamic content directly from the ALB.” This improves static asset delivery but fails to accelerate dynamic API responses via edge locations. Dynamic content still incurs round-trip latency to the origin Region for every request. CloudFront can accelerate dynamic content too (by caching DNS lookups, TCP and TLS handshakes, and optionally using Lambda@Edge), so limiting it to static content is suboptimal. Option D (INCORRECT): “Deploy the application stack in two AWS Regions. Use an Amazon Route 53 geolocation routing policy to serve all content from the ALB in the closest Region.” Geolocation routing directs traffic based on user location but still pulls content directly from regional ALBs. Static and dynamic objects incur origin latency on every request. It doesn’t leverage a global CDN for caching or connection optimizations. Option A (CORRECT): “Deploy the application stack in a single AWS Region. Use Amazon CloudFront to serve all static and dynamic content by specifying the ALB as an origin.” CloudFront edge locations cache static objects near users worldwide, drastically reducing latency. For dynamic content, CloudFront still optimizes TCP/TLS handshakes, maintains persistent connections to the origin, and can even offload custom logic with Lambda@Edge. This design minimizes complexity (single Region), leverages a global CDN for both static and dynamic content acceleration, and provides the lowest possible latency. In summary, using Amazon CloudFront with an ALB origin in a single Region delivers both static and dynamic content with the least latency by caching at edge locations and optimizing network connections. This solution exemplifies Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company uses Amazon EC2 instances to host its internal systems. As part of a deployment operation, an administrator tries to use the AWS CLI to terminate an EC2 instance. However, the administrator receives a 403 (Access Denied) error message. The administrator is using an IAM role that has the following IAM policy attached: What is the cause of the unsuccessful request?
options: The EC2 instance has a resource-based policy with a Deny statement.
The principal has not been specified in the policy statement.
The "Action" field does not grant the actions that are required to terminate the EC2 instance.
The request to terminate the EC2 instance does not originate from the CIDR blocks 192.0.2.0/24 or 203.0.113.0/24.
explanation: The correct Answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): EC2 instances do not support resource-based policies in the same way S3 or Lambda do. You cannot attach a Deny statement directly on an EC2 instance—access control is managed via identity-based IAM policies (roles/users), not via a resource policy on the instance itself. Option B (INCORRECT): In an identity-based policy (one attached to an IAM role), you do not need to specify a Principal element. The policy inherently applies to the IAM entity to which it is attached, so omitting “Principal” does not cause an Access Denied. Option D (INCORRECT): Although you can add a Condition on aws:SourceIp to restrict by CIDR block, the question’s described policy does not include any IP‐address condition. Therefore, a source‐IP restriction is not the reason for the 403 error. Option C (CORRECT): The IAM policy’s Action list does not include ec2:TerminateInstances, so the role is not granted permission to terminate instances. Without explicitly allowing that API call, any attempt to terminate will be denied. Summary: We’ve learned that IAM identity-based policies must explicitly list every API action you intend to allow—omitting ec2:TerminateInstances results in a 403 error when trying to terminate an instance. This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures, as it tests your understanding of IAM policy permission boundaries and secure access control.

question: An application development team is designing a microservice that will convert large images to smaller, compressed images. When a user uploads an image through the web interface, the microservice should store the image in an Amazon S3 bucket, process and compress the image with an AWS Lambda function, and store the image in its compressed form in a different S3 bucket. A solutions architect needs to design a solution that uses durable, stateless components to process the images automatically.Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
options: Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Configure the S3 bucket to send a notification to the SQS queue when an image is uploaded to the S3 bucket.
Configure the Lambda function to use the Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue as the invocation source. When the SQS message is successfully processed, delete the message in the queue.

Configure the Lambda function to monitor the S3 bucket for new uploads. When an uploaded image is detected, write the file name to a text file in memory and use the text file to keep track of the images that were processed.

Launch an Amazon EC2 instance to monitor an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. When items are added to the queue, log the file name in a text file on the EC2 instance and invoke the Lambda function.

Configure an Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) event to monitor the S3 bucket. When an image is uploaded, send an alert to an Amazon ample Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic with the application owner's email address for further processing.
explanation: The correct answer is A, B. Option C (INCORRECT): “Configure the Lambda function to monitor the S3 bucket for new uploads. When an uploaded image is detected, write the file name to a text file in memory and use the text file to keep track of the images that were processed.” This approach relies on in-memory state, which is lost if the Lambda container is recycled. Lambda cannot “poll” S3 directly; you need an event source like SQS, SNS, or direct S3 notifications. Not durable or stateless—violates the requirement for durable, stateless components. Option D (INCORRECT): “Launch an Amazon EC2 instance to monitor an Amazon SQS queue. When items are added to the queue, log the file name in a text file on the EC2 instance and invoke the Lambda function.” Introducing EC2 makes the solution stateful (managing an instance) and increases operational overhead. Logging to a local file on EC2 is not durable or serverless. We can invoke Lambda directly from SQS without the extra EC2 layer. Option E (INCORRECT): “Configure an Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) event to monitor the S3 bucket. When an image is uploaded, send an alert to an Amazon SNS topic with the application owner's email address for further processing.” SNS email notifications only alert a human—they do not trigger the image-compression process. Does not provide automatic, durable invocation of the Lambda function to compress images. Option A (CORRECT): “Create an Amazon SQS queue. Configure the S3 bucket to send a notification to the SQS queue when an image is uploaded to the S3 bucket.” S3 Event Notifications can deliver messages to SQS, decoupling upload from processing. SQS provides durability, retry semantics, and a fully managed queue for stateless processing. Option B (CORRECT): “Configure the Lambda function to use the Amazon SQS queue as the invocation source. When the SQS message is successfully processed, delete the message in the queue.” Lambda integrates natively with SQS as an event source—no polling code required. Messages are deleted only after successful processing, ensuring at-least-once delivery. This pattern is fully serverless, durable, and stateless. In summary, we learned how to build a durable, serverless, and stateless pipeline using S3 Event Notifications → SQS → Lambda → compressed S3 output. This design leverages decoupling and managed services to ensure automatic, reliable processing. This question belongs to Domain 2 – Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company deploys its applications on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) behind an Application Load Balancer in an AWS Region. The application needs to store data in a PostgreSQL database engine. The company wants the data in the database to be highly available. The company also needs increased capacity for read workloads. Which solution will meet these requirements with the MOST operational efficiency?
options: Create an Amazon DynamoDB database table configured with global tables.
Create an Amazon RDS database with Multi-AZ deployments.
Create an Amazon RDS database with Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment.
Create an Amazon RDS database configured with cross-Region read replicas.
explanation: The correct answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): “Create an Amazon DynamoDB database table configured with global tables.” DynamoDB is a NoSQL key–value store, not a relational PostgreSQL database engine. Global tables provide multi-Region replication for DynamoDB, but they don’t satisfy the requirement for a PostgreSQL engine. This option would require rewriting the application to use a completely different data model. Option B (INCORRECT): “Create an Amazon RDS database with Multi-AZ deployments.” Multi-AZ RDS provides high availability by synchronously replicating to a standby in another AZ. However, the standby instance is not readable, so this does not increase read capacity. It meets HA but fails the requirement for increased read throughput. Option D (INCORRECT): “Create an Amazon RDS database configured with cross-Region read replicas.” Cross-Region read replicas let you offload reads to another Region, but they are asynchronous and can incur lag. This does not provide synchronous high-availability failover within the same Region. Operational complexity increases with cross-Region replication and multi-Region failover planning. Option C (CORRECT): “Create an Amazon RDS database with Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment.” An RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster (e.g., Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL) provides a primary writer and reader replicas in different AZs. Automatic synchronous replication ensures high availability and fast failover. Reader endpoints distribute read traffic across AZ-based replicas, delivering increased read capacity with minimal operational overhead. Aurora’s managed clustering reduces administrative tasks such as patching, backups, and failover management. In summary, for a highly available PostgreSQL solution with increased read capacity and maximum operational efficiency, Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment (Option C) is the best fit. This question falls under Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company is moving its on-premises Oracle database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL. The database has several applications that write to the same tables. The applications need to be migrated one by one with a month in between each migration. Management has expressed concerns that the database has a high number of reads and writes. The data must be kept in sync across both databases throughout the migration. What should a solutions architect recommend?
options: Use AWS DataSync for the initial migration. Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to create a change data capture (CDC) replication task and a table mapping to select all tables.

Use AWS DataSync for the initial migration. Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to create a full load plus change data capture (CDC) replication task and a table mapping to select all tables.

Use the AWS Schema Conversion Tool with AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) using a memory optimized replication instance. Create a full load plus change data capture (CDC) replication task and a table mapping to select all tables.

Use the AWS Schema Conversion Tool with AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) using a compute optimized replication instance. Create a full load plus change data capture (CDC) replication task and a table mapping to select the largest tables.
explanation: Let’s step through why options A, B, and D are INCORRECT, and why option C is the CORRECT choice: Option A (INCORRECT): “Use AWS DataSync for the initial migration. Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to create a change data capture (CDC) replication task and a table mapping to select all tables.” DataSync is designed for file and object data movement, not database schema conversion or ongoing transactional replication. Only using CDC without an initial full load means the target will be empty at cutover, causing data loss until the CDC task catches up. There is no schema conversion step, so Oracle‐specific constructs (PL/SQL, proprietary data types) won’t be translated to PostgreSQL. Option B (INCORRECT): “Use AWS DataSync for the initial migration. Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to create a full load plus change data capture (CDC) replication task and a table mapping to select all tables.” Again, DataSync is not suitable for structured database migration; use AWS SCT and DMS instead. While the full load + CDC in DMS is correct, skipping the AWS Schema Conversion Tool will leave Oracle-specific objects unconverted. Option D (INCORRECT): “Use the AWS Schema Conversion Tool with AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) using a compute optimized replication instance. Create a full load plus change data capture (CDC) replication task and a table mapping to select the largest tables.” Limiting the table mapping to only the largest tables leaves smaller (but critical) tables unsynchronized. A compute-optimized DMS instance may not provide the memory capacity needed for high-throughput CDC buffering, potentially causing replication lag. Option C (CORRECT): “Use the AWS Schema Conversion Tool with AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) using a memory optimized replication instance. Create a full load plus change data capture (CDC) replication task and a table mapping to select all tables.” AWS SCT handles Oracle-to-PostgreSQL schema conversion automatically, ensuring code and data types are translated correctly. DMS with a memory-optimized replication instance supports high read/write throughput and large transaction volumes during CDC. The full load plus CDC approach provides an initial snapshot of the entire dataset and then keeps it in sync in near-real time, allowing applications to be migrated one by one over time. Summary: We’ve learned that for migrating a high-transaction Oracle database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL while keeping two systems in sync, you need both AWS Schema Conversion Tool and DMS with a full load + CDC on a memory-optimized instance. This question falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A solutions architect is designing an application that helps users fill out and submit registration forms. The solutions architect plans to use a two-tier architecture that includes a web application server tier and a worker tier. The application needs to process submitted forms quickly. The application needs to process each form exactly once. The solution must ensure that no data is lost. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Use an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue between the web application server tier and the worker tier to store and forward form data.
Use an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API between the web application server tier and the worker tier to store and forward form data.
Use an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) standard queue between the web application server tier and the worker tier to store and forward form data.
Use an AWS Step Functions workflow. Create a synchronous workflow between the web application server tier and the worker tier that stores and forwards form data.
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): “Use an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API between the web application server tier and the worker tier to store and forward form data.” API Gateway is designed for exposing and securing HTTP endpoints, not for durable message buffering. It does not persist messages if the worker tier is unavailable, which risks data loss. There is no built-in exactly-once delivery guarantee or message replay protection. Option C (INCORRECT): “Use an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) standard queue between the web application server tier and the worker tier to store and forward form data.” SQS Standard guarantees at-least-once delivery, which can lead to duplicate processing. It does not enforce strict ordering or exactly-once semantics, so the worker might see the same form more than once. Option D (INCORRECT): “Use an AWS Step Functions workflow. Create a synchronous workflow between the web application server tier and the worker tier that stores and forwards form data.” Synchronous Step Functions will block the web tier while the worker processes, reducing scalability and increasing latency. It is not primarily a durable queuing mechanism and does not inherently prevent duplicates or guarantee exactly-once execution without custom idempotency logic. Option A (CORRECT): “Use an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue between the web application server tier and the worker tier to store and forward form data.” SQS FIFO provides exactly-once processing and preserves message order, ensuring each form is handled only once. Messages are durably stored until the worker successfully processes them, so no data is lost. Built-in deduplication and visibility timeouts help avoid duplicate deliveries and data loss. In summary, using an SQS FIFO queue guarantees durable, ordered, exactly-once message delivery between tiers, meeting the requirements of no data loss and single processing per form. This question falls under Domain 2 - Design Resilient Architectures, as it focuses on reliability and fault-tolerant message handling.

question: A company is building a data analysis platform on AWS by using AWS Lake Formation. The platform will ingest data from different sources such as Amazon S3 and Amazon RDS. The company needs a secure solution to prevent access to portions of the data that contain sensitive information.Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Create an IAM role that includes permissions to access Lake Formation tables.
Create data filters to implement row-level security and cell-level security.
Create an AWS Lambda function that removes sensitive information before Lake Formation ingests the data.
Create an AWS Lambda function that periodically queries and removes sensitive information from Lake Formation tables.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): Creating an IAM role grants broad access to Lake Formation tables but does not enforce fine-grained controls. It cannot restrict access to specific rows or cells containing sensitive information. Option C (INCORRECT): Using an AWS Lambda function to strip sensitive data before ingestion requires custom code, scheduling, monitoring, and error handling, which significantly increases operational overhead compared to native Lake Formation features. Option D (INCORRECT): Periodically running a Lambda to clean data after ingestion also imposes ongoing maintenance and may leave windows of exposure. It is less reliable and more complex than built-in security policies. Option B (CORRECT): Lake Formation’s data filters provide native row-level and cell-level security. By defining filter predicates in the data catalog, you can enforce fine-grained access controls without writing or managing ETL code, minimizing operational overhead while securing sensitive information. In summary, we’ve learned that AWS Lake Formation data filters are the simplest way to implement row- and cell-level security for sensitive data. This question belongs to Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company is creating a REST API. The company has strict requirements for the use of TLS. The company requires TLSv1.3 on the API endpoints. The company also requires a specific public third-party certificate authority (CA) to sign the TLS certificate.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Use a local machine to create a certificate that is signed by the third-party CImport the certificate into AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Create an HTTP API in Amazon API Gateway with a custom domain. Configure the custom domain to use the certificate.

Create a certificate in AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) that is signed by the third-party CA. Create an HTTP API in Amazon API Gateway with a custom domain. Configure the custom domain to use the certificate.

Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to create a certificate that is signed by the third-party CA. Import the certificate into AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Create an AWS Lambda function with a Lambda function URL. Configure the Lambda function URL to use the certificate.

Create a certificate in AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) that is signed by the third-party CA. Create an AWS Lambda function with a Lambda function URL. Configure the Lambda function URL to use the certificate.
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): AWS Certificate Manager cannot directly “create” a public TLS certificate signed by an arbitrary third-party CA—you can only issue certificates from Amazon’s own public CA or from ACM Private CA. There is no ACM-supported workflow to request a cert from an external CA via the console or API; you must import the externally-signed cert yourself. Option C (INCORRECT): Lambda function URLs don’t support attaching imported custom certificates or custom domains—you get an auto-generated AWS domain and certificate only. You cannot configure TLS versions or upload a third-party CA–signed cert to a function URL. Option D (INCORRECT): Same limitation as Option C: Lambda function URLs do not allow you to import or attach a third-party certificate. There’s no mechanism to enforce TLSv1.3 on a function URL with a custom cert—you cannot meet the strict TLS requirement here. Option A (CORRECT): Generate the TLS certificate locally or via your tooling, have it signed by the required third-party CA, then import that certificate (and private key) into ACM. Create an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API and configure a custom domain name that uses your imported ACM certificate. In the custom domain settings, set the minimum TLS policy to TLS₁.₃, fulfilling both the specific–CA and TLSv1.3 requirements. Summary: We’ve learned that when you require a certificate from a specific public CA and strict TLS policy (TLS 1.3), you must import your externally-signed cert into ACM and attach it to an API Gateway custom domain, where you can enforce the TLS version. This question belongs to Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A solutions architect needs to implement a solution to reduce a company's storage costs. All the company's data is in the Amazon S3 Standard storage class. The company must keep all data for at least 25 years. Data from the most recent 2 years must be highly available and immediately retrievable. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Set up an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive immediately.
Set up an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 2 years.
Use S3 Intelligent-Tiering. Activate the archiving option to ensure that data is archived in S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
Set up an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition objects to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) immediately and to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 2 years.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): “Set up an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive immediately.” • This moves all data into Glacier Deep Archive at once, making it non-immediately retrievable for the first two years. • Violates the requirement that the most recent 2 years of data be highly available and instantly accessible. Option C (INCORRECT): “Use S3 Intelligent-Tiering. Activate the archiving option to ensure that data is archived in S3 Glacier Deep Archive.” • Intelligent-Tiering adds small monthly monitoring and automation fees. • Data moved into the Glacier or Deep Archive tiers still requires a restore operation (minutes to hours), so it isn’t “immediately retrievable.” • Does not guarantee instant access for the latest 2 years at lowest cost. Option D (INCORRECT): “Set up an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition objects to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access immediately and to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 2 years.” • S3 One Zone-IA is cheaper, but it stores data in a single Availability Zone, risking data loss on AZ failure—violates high-availability requirement. • Doesn’t address long-term cost effectiveness beyond 2 years as optimally as Glacier Deep Archive. Option B (CORRECT): “Set up an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 2 years.” • Keeps the latest 2 years in S3 Standard for high availability and instant retrieval. • Moves older data (23 additional years) into the lowest‐cost storage class (Glacier Deep Archive), meeting the 25-year retention and minimizing storage costs. • Fully satisfies both the availability requirement for recent data and the cost-optimization for long-term retention. In summary, B is the best solution because it balances instant access for the recent two years with the lowest-cost archive for the remaining retention period. This question belongs to Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company has a highly dynamic batch processing job that uses many Amazon EC2 instances to complete it. The job is stateless in nature, can be started and stopped at any given time with no negative impact, and typically takes upwards of 60 minutes total to complete. The company has asked a solutions architect to design a scalable and cost-effective solution that meets the requirements of the job. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Implement EC2 Spot Instances.
Purchase EC2 Reserved Instances.
Implement EC2 On-Demand Instances.
Implement the processing on AWS Lambda.
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): Purchase EC2 Reserved Instances. Reserved Instances require a 1– or 3–year commitment and are best for steady-state usage. This batch workload is highly dynamic and stateless, with no guarantee of long-term steady usage. You cannot cancel Reserved Instances without financial penalty, so they are not cost-effective for unpredictable, short-lived jobs. Option C (INCORRECT): Implement EC2 On-Demand Instances. On-Demand Instances provide flexibility but at a higher hourly rate compared to Spot Instances. For a job that can tolerate interruptions and is stateless, Spot Instances offer significant cost savings (up to 90%). Using only On-Demand would not be the most cost-optimized approach for this batch process. Option D (INCORRECT): Implement the processing on AWS Lambda. AWS Lambda has a maximum execution duration of 15 minutes per invocation. This batch job typically runs for around 60 minutes total and may require more resources than Lambda’s limits. Lambda cold starts and concurrency limits make it less suitable for large, long-running, parallel compute loads. Option A (CORRECT): Implement EC2 Spot Instances. Spot Instances can be up to 90% cheaper than On-Demand, ideal for cost-sensitive, stateless, fault-tolerant workloads. The batch job is stateless and can be restarted without negative impact, tolerating Spot interruptions. You can use Auto Scaling groups or Spot Fleets to scale out compute capacity dynamically across Availability Zones. If a Spot Instance is reclaimed, the job can resume on another instance, keeping the total run time within tolerance. In summary, we learned that for highly dynamic, fault-tolerant batch workloads, EC2 Spot Instances provide the best balance of scalability and cost savings. This question falls under Domain 4 – Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A hospital recently deployed a RESTful API with Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda. The hospital uses API Gateway and Lambda to upload reports that are in PDF format and JPEG format. The hospital needs to modify the Lambda code to identify protected health information (PHI) in the reports. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Use existing Python libraries to extract the text from the reports and to identify the PHI from the extracted text.
Use Amazon Textract to extract the text from the reports. Use Amazon SageMaker to identify the PHI from the extracted text.
Use Amazon Textract to extract the text from the reports. Use Amazon Comprehend Medical to identify the PHI from the extracted text.
Use Amazon Rekognition to extract the text from the reports. Use Amazon Comprehend Medical to identify the PHI from the extracted text.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): “Use existing Python libraries to extract the text from the reports and to identify the PHI from the extracted text.” • This requires custom code for both PDF/JPEG parsing and PHI entity recognition. • High operational overhead: you must manage library updates, OCR accuracy, and maintain custom PHI detection logic (including handling HIPAA compliance). • Not a managed service approach. Option B (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon Textract to extract the text from the reports. Use Amazon SageMaker to identify the PHI from the extracted text.” • SageMaker would require you to build, train, deploy, and maintain a custom NLP model for PHI detection. • Operational overhead is significant: data labeling, model retraining, endpoint management, and scalability concerns. • Not the simplest managed solution for PHI identification. Option D (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon Rekognition to extract the text from the reports. Use Amazon Comprehend Medical to identify the PHI from the extracted text.” • Amazon Rekognition’s text‐detection is geared toward scenes and labels, not document‐grade OCR for complex PDF forms. • Document-oriented Textract provides far better accuracy and structure (forms, tables) versus Rekognition. • Although Comprehend Medical is correct for PHI, the OCR tool choice is suboptimal and risks extraction errors. Option C (CORRECT): “Use Amazon Textract to extract the text from the reports. Use Amazon Comprehend Medical to identify the PHI from the extracted text.” • Amazon Textract is designed for high-accuracy document OCR, supporting PDF and image formats with form/table extraction. • Amazon Comprehend Medical is a fully managed service that natively identifies PHI entities (e.g., names, dates, medical terms) with HIPAA eligibility. • Minimal operational overhead: you simply orchestrate two AWS services in your Lambda code without building or maintaining custom models. In summary, we learned that leveraging fully managed AWS services—Textract for document text extraction and Comprehend Medical for PHI detection—minimizes custom code and operational burden. This question falls under Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures, as it addresses secure handling and processing of protected health information (PHI).

question: A company wants to run its payment application on AWS. The application receives payment notifications from mobile devices. Payment notifications require a basic validation before they are sent for further processing. The backend processing application is long running and requires compute and memory to be adjusted. The company does not want to manage the infrastructure. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Integrate the queue with an Amazon EventBridge rule to receive payment notifications from mobile devices. Configure the rule to validate payment notifications and send the notifications to the backend application. Deploy the backend application on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) Anywhere. Create a standalone cluster.

Create an Amazon API Gateway API. Integrate the API with an AWS Step Functions state machine to receive payment notifications from mobile devices. Invoke the state machine to validate payment notifications and send the notifications to the backend application. Deploy the backend application on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). Configure an EKS cluster with self-managed nodes.

Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Integrate the queue with an Amazon EventBridge rule to receive payment notifications from mobile devices. Configure the rule to validate payment notifications and send the notifications to the backend application. Deploy the backend application on Amazon EC2 Spot Instances. Configure a Spot Fleet with a default allocation strategy.
