Launch another EC2 instance. Configure a crontab schedule to run shell scripts that will start and stop the existing EC2 instances and DB instances on a schedule.
Create an AWS Lambda function that will start and stop the EC2 instances and DB instances. Configure Amazon EventBridge to invoke the Lambda function on a schedule.
explanation: The correct answer is D Option A (INCORRECT): “Scale the EC2 instances by using elastic resize. Scale the DB instances to zero outside of business hours.” AWS does not support scaling EC2 instances “to zero”—you can only stop instances, not resize them away. RDS DB instances cannot be scaled down to zero capacity. You can only stop and start them (for up to 7 days), but there’s no “scale-to-zero” feature. This approach misuses the concept of resizing and fails the requirement to automatically start/stop without additional manual steps. Option B (INCORRECT): “Explore AWS Marketplace for partner solutions that will automatically start and stop the EC2 instances and DB instances on a schedule.” Bringing in a third-party tool adds extra licensing costs and operational overhead. AWS-native services (Lambda + EventBridge) already provide a simpler, serverless, no-maintenance solution. The requirement calls for minimizing cost and infrastructure maintenance—Marketplace solutions typically run against those goals. Option C (INCORRECT): “Launch another EC2 instance. Configure a crontab schedule to run shell scripts that will start and stop the existing EC2 instances and DB instances on a schedule.” Introduces an extra EC2 instance that you must patch, monitor, secure, and pay for even when idle. Cron-based scripts add operational complexity and a single point of failure. Does not meet the “minimize infrastructure maintenance” requirement as well as a serverless solution would. Option D (CORRECT): “Create an AWS Lambda function that will start and stop the EC2 instances and DB instances. Configure Amazon EventBridge to invoke the Lambda function on a schedule.” Fully serverless—no servers to provision, patch, or manage other than the function itself. EventBridge (formerly CloudWatch Events) can trigger the Lambda on any cron or rate schedule you define. You pay only for the brief execution time of the function and the minimal cost of scheduled events—perfect for cost optimization. Automatically starts and stops both EC2 and RDS instances outside business hours with no manual intervention. Summary: Using AWS Lambda together with Amazon EventBridge delivers a fully managed, serverless solution to schedule start/stop operations for EC2 and RDS instances. This approach minimizes both cost and infrastructure maintenance. Domain: Domain 4 – Design Cost-Optimized Architectures

question: A company uses Amazon EC2 instances and Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes to run an application. The company creates one snapshot of each EBS volume every day to meet compliance requirements. The company wants to implement an architecture that prevents the accidental deletion of EBS volume snapshots. The solution must not change the administrative rights of the storage administrator user. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST administrative effort?
options: Create an IAM role that has permission to delete snapshots. Attach the role to a new EC2 instance. Use the AWS CLI from the new EC2 instance to delete snapshots.
Create an IAM policy that denies snapshot deletion. Attach the policy to the storage administrator user.
Add tags to the snapshots. Create retention rules in Recycle Bin for EBS snapshots that have the tags.
Lock the EBS snapshots to prevent deletion.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): This proposal actually *enables* deletion from an EC2 instance rather than *preventing* deletion—so it runs counter to the requirement. It does not address accidental deletion or enforce a retention policy; it simply provides another pathway to delete snapshots via the AWS CLI. It also adds unnecessary operational overhead by requiring and managing a separate EC2 instance and IAM role. Option B (INCORRECT): Attaching a “deny snapshot deletion” policy directly to the storage administrator *does* prevent snapshot deletions, but it changes the administrator’s permissions—violating the requirement not to alter the storage admin’s rights. It also represents a manual IAM change that must be maintained over time, increasing administrative effort. Option D (INCORRECT): There is no native “snapshot lock” feature on EBS snapshots outside of AWS Backup’s immutable vault lock for backups, which is not directly applicable to daily EBS snapshots unless you redesign your backup workflow around AWS Backup. Implementing AWS Backup vault lock is heavier in administrative effort and may require reconfiguring existing snapshots under Backup plans. Option C (CORRECT): Amazon EC2 Recycle Bin supports retention rules for EBS snapshots based on resource type and tags. By tagging each snapshot and creating a Recycle Bin rule, you enforce a minimum retention period during which snapshots cannot be deleted—preventing accidental deletion. This solution does *not* require changes to the storage administrator’s IAM permissions and is quick to set up with minimal administrative overhead. Summary: We’ve learned that the AWS Recycle Bin for EBS snapshots is the simplest, least intrusive way to enforce snapshot retention and prevent accidental deletion without modifying user permissions. This question falls under Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company recently deployed a new auditing system to centralize information about operating system versions, patching, and installed software for Amazon EC2 instances. A solutions architect must ensure all instances provisioned through EC2 Auto Scaling groups successfully send reports to the auditing system as soon as they are launched and terminated. Which solution achieves these goals MOST efficiently?
options: Use a scheduled AWS Lambda function and run a script remotely on all EC2 instances to send data to the audit system.
Use EC2 Auto Scaling lifecycle hooks to run a custom script to send data to the audit system when instances are launched and terminated.
Use an EC2 Auto Scaling launch configuration to run a custom script through user data to send data to the audit system when instances are launched and terminated.
Run a custom script on the instance operating system to send data to the audit system. Configure the script to be invoked by the EC2 Auto Scaling group when the instance starts and is terminated.
explanation: The correct Answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): “Use a scheduled AWS Lambda function and run a script remotely on all EC2 instances to send data to the audit system.” • A polling or scheduled approach introduces delays—reports may not arrive immediately after launch or termination. • Remotely executing scripts against all instances at intervals is inefficient, error-prone, and harder to scale. Option C (INCORRECT): “Use an EC2 Auto Scaling launch configuration to run a custom script through user data to send data to the audit system when instances are launched and terminated.” • User data runs only at instance launch—not at termination—so you cannot capture the shutdown event. • There is no built-in mechanism in launch configurations to hook into instance termination. Option D (INCORRECT): “Run a custom script on the instance operating system to send data to the audit system. Configure the script to be invoked by the EC2 Auto Scaling group when the instance starts and is terminated.” • Auto Scaling groups don’t directly invoke OS-level scripts on termination—lifecycle hooks are required for that. • This answer is vague about how the ASG triggers the script and omits the use of lifecycle hooks. Option B (CORRECT): “Use EC2 Auto Scaling lifecycle hooks to run a custom script to send data to the audit system when instances are launched and terminated.” Lifecycle hooks pause the launch or termination process, giving you a window to run your custom script (for example, via AWS Lambda or Systems Manager Run Command) and submit the audit report immediately. This approach captures both the launch and termination events reliably and triggers at the right time without polling. Fully managed by Auto Scaling, it scales automatically with your fleet and ensures no instance state change is missed. In summary, lifecycle hooks provide a seamless, event-driven way to report instance metadata at both startup and shutdown. We’ve learned to choose AWS-native hooks over polling or one-way scripts for robust, real-time auditing. This question belongs to Domain 2 - Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A development team is creating an event-based application that uses AWS Lambda functions. Events will be generated when files are added to an Amazon S3 bucket. The development team currently has Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) configured as the event target from Amazon S3.What should a solutions architect do to process the events from Amazon S3 in a scalable way?
options: Create an SNS subscription that processes the event in Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) before the event runs in Lambda.
Create an SNS subscription that processes the event in Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) before the event runs in Lambda
Create an SNS subscription that sends the event to Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS). Configure the SOS queue to trigger a Lambda function.
Create an SNS subscription that sends the event to AWS Server Migration Service (AWS SMS). Configure the Lambda function to poll from the SMS event.
explanation: The correct Answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): “Create an SNS subscription that processes the event in Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) before the event runs in Lambda.” ECS adds unnecessary operational overhead for simple event handling. It does not provide native buffering or retry semantics for a flood of S3 events. Lambda can be triggered directly from SQS much more efficiently for scaling. Option B (INCORRECT): “Create an SNS subscription that processes the event in Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) before the event runs in Lambda.” EKS is heavier to manage and not optimized for simple message buffering. Operational complexity and cost are much higher than using a managed queue. Does not solve the decoupling and retry requirements as cleanly as SQS. Option D (INCORRECT): “Create an SNS subscription that sends the event to AWS Server Migration Service (AWS SMS). Configure the Lambda function to poll from the SMS event.” AWS SMS is designed for migrating on-premises servers, not for event processing. Lambda cannot poll SMS; there is no built-in integration for messaging or buffering. This choice does not provide scalable, reliable event delivery. Option C (CORRECT): “Create an SNS subscription that sends the event to Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS). Configure the SQS queue to trigger a Lambda function.” SQS acts as a fully managed buffer to absorb spikes in S3 events. Lambda integrations with SQS provide automatic scaling and retry capabilities. Decouples producers (SNS/S3) from consumers (Lambda) for better reliability and throughput. In summary, by routing S3 notifications through SNS into SQS and then triggering Lambda from SQS, we achieve a highly scalable, resilient, and decoupled event-driven architecture. This question belongs to Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A survey company has gathered data for several years from areas in the United States. The company hosts the data in an Amazon S3 bucket that is 3 TB in size and growing. The company has started to share the data with a European marketing firm that has S3 buckets. The company wants to ensure that its data transfer costs remain as low as possible. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Configure the Requester Pays feature on the company's S3 bucket.
Configure S3 Cross-Region Replication from the company's S3 bucket to one of the marketing firm's S3 buckets.
Configure cross-account access for the marketing firm so that the marketing firm has access to the company's S3 bucket.
Configure the company's S3 bucket to use S3 Intelligent-Tiering. Sync the S3 bucket to one of the marketing firm's S3 buckets.
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): “Configure S3 Cross-Region Replication from the company's S3 bucket to one of the marketing firm's S3 buckets.” Replication will copy all data to the destination bucket, incurring data transfer charges from the source region to the destination region for every object. Ongoing replication of a growing 3 TB+ dataset will steadily increase your cross-region data transfer costs. Option C (INCORRECT): “Configure cross-account access for the marketing firm so that the marketing firm has access to the company's S3 bucket.” Cross-account access still means the bucket owner pays for data egress out of the AWS region when the marketing firm downloads objects. It does not shift transfer costs to the requester; you remain responsible for data-transfer charges. Option D (INCORRECT): “Configure the company's S3 bucket to use S3 Intelligent-Tiering. Sync the S3 bucket to one of the marketing firm's S3 buckets.” Intelligent-Tiering optimizes storage cost tiers, but it does not affect data transfer costs. Syncing data via aws s3 sync or similar will incur egress charges for each object transferred. Option A (CORRECT): “Configure the Requester Pays feature on the company's S3 bucket.” With Requester Pays enabled, the requester (the European marketing firm) is responsible for both the GET request charges and the data transfer charges when they download objects. The bucket owner does not incur egress fees, keeping your data-transfer costs as low as possible. No extra storage replication or tiering changes are needed—just a permission update and Requester Pays configuration. In summary, enabling Requester Pays shifts all data retrieval and transfer costs to the requester, making it the most cost-efficient way to share large datasets with an external party. This question falls under Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company needs to store contract documents. A contract lasts for 5 years. During the 5-year period, the company must ensure that the documents cannot be overwritten or deleted. The company needs to encrypt the documents at rest and rotate the encryption keys automatically every year. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take to meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose two.)
options: Store the documents in Amazon S3. Use S3 Object Lock in governance mode.
Store the documents in Amazon S3. Use S3 Object Lock in compliance mode.
Use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed encryption keys (SSE-S3). Configure key rotation.
Use server-side encryption with AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed keys. Configure key rotation.
Use server-side encryption with AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer provided (imported) keys. Configure key rotation.
explanation: The correct answer is B, D. Option A (INCORRECT): “Store the documents in Amazon S3. Use S3 Object Lock in governance mode.” Governance mode still allows privileged users (with bypass permissions) to overwrite or delete objects, violating the immutable requirement. Compliance mode is required to enforce a write-once-read-many (WORM) retention that cannot be altered by any user. Option C (INCORRECT): “Use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed encryption keys (SSE-S3). Configure key rotation.” SSE-S3 encrypts objects at rest but does not provide customer control over key rotation timing; AWS rotates keys on its own schedule. You cannot configure annual rotation with SSE-S3; only SSE-KMS customer-managed CMKs support automatic rotation configuration. Option E (INCORRECT): “Use server-side encryption with AWS KMS customer provided (imported) keys. Configure key rotation.” Imported keys in KMS cannot be automatically rotated—you must manually re-import and update all objects. This adds significant operational overhead, which violates the requirement for least operational work. Option B (CORRECT): “Store the documents in Amazon S3. Use S3 Object Lock in compliance mode.” Compliance mode enforces a WORM retention period up to 5 years that cannot be overridden by any user or role. Meets the requirement to prevent overwrite or deletion for the entire contract duration. Option D (CORRECT): “Use server-side encryption with AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed keys. Configure key rotation.” CMKs in KMS support automatic yearly rotation, satisfying the annual key rotation requirement with no extra operational steps. Provides strong encryption at rest under your control, integrating seamlessly with S3 encryption settings. In summary, we learned that S3 Object Lock in compliance mode is required for an immutable 5-year retention, and that AWS KMS customer-managed keys support automatic annual rotation to meet encryption-at-rest requirements with minimal operational overhead. This question belongs to Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A research company uses on-premises devices to generate data for analysis. The company wants to use the AWS Cloud to analyze the data. The devices generate .csv files and support writing the data to an SMB file share. Company analysts must be able to use SQL commands to query the data. The analysts will run queries periodically throughout the day. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively? (Choose three.)
options: Deploy an AWS Storage Gateway on premises in Amazon S3 File Gateway mode.
Deploy an AWS Storage Gateway on premises in Amazon FSx File Gateway made.
Set up an AWS Glue crawler to create a table based on the data that is in Amazon S3.
Set up an Amazon EMR cluster with EMR File System (EMRFS) to query the data that is in Amazon S3. Provide access to analysts.
Set up an Amazon Redshift cluster to query the data that is in Amazon S3. Provide access to analysts.
Setup Amazon Athena to query the data that is in Amazon S3. Provide access to analysts.
explanation: The correct answer is A, C, F. Option B (INCORRECT): Deploying an AWS Storage Gateway in Amazon FSx File Gateway mode is unnecessary here. FSx File Gateway is intended for providing a cache for FSx file systems, not for writing data directly to S3 via SMB. It also incurs higher costs compared to the S3 File Gateway option. Option D (INCORRECT): Setting up an Amazon EMR cluster with EMRFS to query the data in Amazon S3 is overkill for simple CSV querying. EMR clusters require cluster management, long startup times, and higher operational costs. For periodic SQL queries on CSV data, a serverless approach is more cost-effective. Option E (INCORRECT): Launching an Amazon Redshift cluster just to query CSV files in S3 is not cost-optimal. Redshift requires provisioning and managing a dedicated cluster, which is more expensive and complex than using a serverless query service designed for in-place data in S3. Option A (CORRECT): Deploy an AWS Storage Gateway on premises in Amazon S3 File Gateway mode. Provides an SMB file share interface for your on-premises devices to write .csv files directly. Automatically uploads the files to an S3 bucket as objects—no need for manual syncs or extra infrastructure. Charges are based on gateway usage and S3 storage, keeping costs low. Option C (CORRECT): Set up an AWS Glue crawler to create a table based on the data that is in Amazon S3. Automatically discovers the schema of the CSV files in S3 and populates the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Keeps the table definitions up to date as new files arrive. Option F (CORRECT): Setup Amazon Athena to query the data that is in Amazon S3. A serverless, pay-per-query service—no clusters to manage or provision. Works directly with the AWS Glue Data Catalog tables created by the crawler. Ideal for ad-hoc or periodic queries on CSV data, ensuring cost efficiency. In summary, we learned that to ingest on-premises CSV files via SMB into AWS cost-effectively, an S3 File Gateway is ideal. AWS Glue crawlers automate schema discovery, and Amazon Athena provides serverless SQL querying without the overhead of clusters. This scenario falls under Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company is developing an ecommerce application that will consist of a load-balanced front end, a container-based application, and a relational database. A solutions architect needs to create a highly available solution that operates with as little manual intervention as possible. Which solutions meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
options: Create an Amazon RDS DB instance in Multi-AZ mode.
Create an Amazon RDS DB instance and one or more replicas in another Availability Zone.
Create an Amazon EC2 instance-based Docker cluster to handle the dynamic application load.
Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with a Fargate launch type to handle the dynamic application load.
Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with an Amazon EC2 launch type to handle the dynamic application load.
explanation: The correct answer is A, D. Option B (INCORRECT): • Using one or more Read Replicas across Availability Zones improves read scalability but does not provide automatic failover for the primary instance. You would need to manually promote a replica, which conflicts with the “as little manual intervention” requirement. Option C (INCORRECT): • Managing a Docker cluster on EC2 instances requires you to provision, patch, and scale the underlying servers yourself. This adds operational overhead and does not meet the “minimal manual intervention” criterion. Option E (INCORRECT): • ECS with EC2 launch type still requires you to manage the EC2 instances (patching, scaling, capacity management). This adds operational burden and is less “hands-off” than a serverless approach. Option A (CORRECT): • Amazon RDS Multi-AZ automatically provisions and maintains a synchronous standby replica in a different Availability Zone. • In case of planned maintenance or an AZ outage, RDS fails over automatically without manual intervention, ensuring high availability. Option D (CORRECT): • Amazon ECS with Fargate launch type is a serverless containers solution that eliminates the need to provision or manage EC2 instances. • Fargate automatically scales and distributes tasks across AZs, providing high availability with minimal operational overhead. In summary, by combining RDS Multi-AZ for automated database failover and ECS Fargate for a fully managed container platform, you achieve a highly available ecommerce architecture with minimal manual intervention. This question falls under Domain 2 - Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company is running a publicly accessible serverless application that uses Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda. The application’s traffic recently spiked due to fraudulent requests from botnets. Which steps should a solutions architect take to block requests from unauthorized users? (Choose two.)
options: Create a usage plan with an API key that is shared with genuine users only.
Integrate logic within the Lambda function to ignore the requests from fraudulent IP addresses.
Implement an AWS WAF rule to target malicious requests and trigger actions to filter them out.
Convert the existing public API to a private API. Update the DNS records to redirect users to the new API endpoint.
Create an IAM role for each user attempting to access the API. A user will assume the role when making the API call.
explanation: The correct answer is A, C Option B (INCORRECT): Integrating logic within the Lambda function to ignore requests from fraudulent IPs may work, but this pushes security into your business logic, increasing maintenance overhead and latency. AWS services like WAF handle IP filtering more efficiently at the edge before invoking your Lambda. Option D (INCORRECT): Converting the public API to a private API restricts access to within your VPC or via VPC endpoints. This breaks legitimate public use and requires network configuration changes—overkill for filtering out bot traffic. Option E (INCORRECT): Creating an IAM role per user is impractical for publicly accessible APIs. IAM is designed for AWS identity management, not for end-user authentication on a public API Gateway endpoint. Option A (CORRECT): A usage plan with an API key lets you throttle requests and ensure only clients with valid keys can access your API. While API keys are not a full authentication mechanism, they effectively block unauthorized or unregistered clients and help mitigate bot traffic. Option C (CORRECT): AWS WAF sits in front of API Gateway and lets you define rules to block, allow, or count requests based on IP addresses, geolocation, request patterns, and known malicious signatures. Deploying WAF rules is a best practice to protect serverless APIs from botnets and other common web threats. Summary: We determined that the best way to block unauthorized botnets is to enforce API keys via a usage plan (Option A) and leverage AWS WAF for advanced filtering (Option C). This question falls under Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company collects and processes data from a vendor. The vendor stores its data in an Amazon RDS for MySQL database in the vendor's own AWS account. The company’s VPC does not have an internet gateway, an AWS Direct Connect connection, or an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection. The company needs to access the data that is in the vendor database. Which solution will meet this requirement?
options: Instruct the vendor to sign up for the AWS Hosted Connection Direct Connect Program. Use VPC peering to connect the company's VPC and the vendor's VPC.
Configure a client VPN connection between the company's VPC and the vendor's VPC. Use VPC peering to connect the company's VPC and the vendor's VPC.
Instruct the vendor to create a Network Load Balancer (NLB). Place the NLB in front of the Amazon RDS for MySQL database. Use AWS PrivateLink to integrate the company's VPC and the vendor's VPC.
Use AWS Transit Gateway to integrate the company's VPC and the vendor's VPC. Use VPC peering to connect the company’s VPC and the vendor's VPC.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): Instructing the vendor to sign up for the AWS Hosted Connection Direct Connect Program does not create a private, cross-account link between two VPCs on its own. VPC Peering alone cannot traverse a Direct Connect hosted‐connection; it requires peered VPCs to have network reachability, which you don’t have without an Internet Gateway, DX, or VPN on the company side. Additionally, Direct Connect hosted connections are for on-premises to AWS traffic, not between two AWS accounts’ VPCs directly. Option B (INCORRECT): A Client VPN connection is used by clients (end users or devices) to access resources in a VPC, not to link two VPCs. You cannot use an AWS Client VPN endpoint plus VPC Peering to transparently bridge networks between two AWS accounts. Also, your VPC has no internet gateway, so you can’t establish a managed Client VPN endpoint there. Option D (INCORRECT): Transit Gateway is a hub that interconnects VPCs and on-premises networks, but you still need some network path (VPN, DX, IGW) on the company side to attach to the Transit Gateway. Using VPC Peering in addition to Transit Gateway is redundant—peering and TGW are mutually exclusive attachment methods. Your company’s VPC has no external connectivity (no IGW/VPN/DX), so it cannot attach to a Transit Gateway either. Option C (CORRECT): The vendor places a Network Load Balancer in front of the RDS for MySQL instance in their VPC. They create a PrivateLink service pointing at that NLB; your company then creates an Interface VPC Endpoint in your VPC. No Internet Gateway, VPN, or Direct Connect is required—traffic flows privately over the AWS network between your VPC endpoint and the vendor’s NLB. This solution is secure, cross-account, and fully managed by AWS. Summary: We’ve compared all options and determined that AWS PrivateLink (Option C) is the only solution that provides private, cross-account access to the vendor’s RDS without requiring internet, VPN, or Direct Connect. This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures, as it focuses on securely connecting VPCs and limiting exposure to the public Internet.

question: A company wants to run an in-memory database for a latency-sensitive application that runs on Amazon EC2 instances. The application processes more than 100,000 transactions each minute and requires high network throughput. A solutions architect needs to provide a cost-effective network design that minimizes data transfer charges.Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Launch all EC2 instances in the same Availability Zone within the same AWS Region. Specify a placement group with cluster strategy when launching EC2 instances.
Launch all EC2 instances in different Availability Zones within the same AWS Region. Specify a placement group with partition strategy when launching EC2 instances.
Deploy an Auto Scaling group to launch EC2 instances in different Availability Zones based on a network utilization target.
Deploy an Auto Scaling group with a step scaling policy to launch EC2 instances in different Availability Zones.
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): Launching EC2 instances in different Availability Zones with a partition placement group will reduce network performance between instances. Partition groups are designed to isolate faulty hardware but not to maximize low-latency, high-throughput communication. Also, cross-AZ data transfers incur additional charges. Option C (INCORRECT): An Auto Scaling group that scales based on network utilization does not guarantee low-latency, high-throughput within a single network fabric, nor does it minimize data transfer costs between instances. It simply adds or removes instances based on traffic metrics. Option D (INCORRECT): A step-scaling policy in an Auto Scaling group addresses dynamic workload demands but does nothing to optimize network topology for latency or throughput, and does not prevent inter-AZ data transfer fees. Option A (CORRECT): Launching all EC2 instances in the same Availability Zone using a cluster placement group: Ensures low-latency, high-bandwidth network communication between instances (ideal for in-memory databases handling 100,000+ transactions per minute). Keeps all traffic within a single AZ and placement group, avoiding cross-AZ data transfer fees. Is a cost-effective design that meets both performance and cost-optimization requirements. Summary: We learned that to achieve ultra-low latency and high throughput for a latency-sensitive, in-memory database—and to minimize data transfer charges—the best practice is to use a cluster placement group in a single Availability Zone. This question falls under Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company hosts an application on AWS. The application gives users the ability to upload photos and store the photos in an Amazon S3 bucket. The company wants to use Amazon CloudFront and a custom domain name to upload the photo files to the S3 bucket in the eu-west-1 Region. Which solution will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
options: Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to create a public certificate in the us-east-1 Region. Use the certificate in CloudFront.
Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to create a public certificate in eu-west-1. Use the certificate in CloudFront.
Configure Amazon S3 to allow uploads from CloudFront. Configure S3 Transfer Acceleration.
Configure Amazon S3 to allow uploads from CloudFront origin access control (OAC).
Configure Amazon S3 to allow uploads from CloudFront. Configure an Amazon S3 website endpoint.
explanation: The correct answers are A, D. Option B (INCORRECT): “Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to create a public certificate in eu-west-1. Use the certificate in CloudFront.” CloudFront distributions only accept ACM certificates that are issued in the us-east-1 (N. Virginia) Region. ACM certificates issued in other Regions (such as eu-west-1) cannot be attached to a CloudFront distribution. Option C (INCORRECT): “Configure Amazon S3 to allow uploads from CloudFront. Configure S3 Transfer Acceleration.” S3 Transfer Acceleration provides a specialized endpoint for faster uploads over long distances, not a CloudFront-backed custom domain upload path. It does not integrate with CloudFront’s distribution for PUT/POST requests via your custom domain. Option E (INCORRECT): “Configure Amazon S3 to allow uploads from CloudFront. Configure an Amazon S3 website endpoint.” S3 static website endpoints only support GET, HEAD, and some POST via HTML forms—they do not support authenticated PUT/POST via CloudFront. You cannot use an S3 website endpoint behind CloudFront for secure, authenticated uploads to a private bucket. Option A (CORRECT): “Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to create a public certificate in the us-east-1 Region. Use the certificate in CloudFront.” CloudFront requires that ACM certificates be created in the us-east-1 Region, regardless of where your origin (S3) resides. This allows you to attach your custom domain (CNAME) to the distribution and serve HTTPS traffic. Option D (CORRECT): “Configure Amazon S3 to allow uploads from CloudFront origin access control (OAC).” Origin Access Control (OAC) is the modern, recommended way to grant CloudFront secure, least-privilege access to your S3 bucket. It ensures that only CloudFront can PUT/GET objects in the bucket, and you can enforce TLS and signature version 4 for all requests. Summary: We learned that CloudFront distributions can only use ACM certificates from us-east-1 and that OAC (Origin Access Control) is the correct mechanism for secure uploads to a private S3 bucket. This question falls under Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company has applications that run in an organization in AWS Organizations. The company outsources operational support of the applications. The company needs to provide access for the external support engineers without compromising security. The external support engineers need access to the AWS Management Console. The external support engineers also need operating system access to the company’s fleet ofAmazon EC2 instances that run Amazon Linux in private subnets. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST securely?
options: Confirm that AWS Systems Manager Agent (SSM Agent) is installed on all instances. Assign an instance profile with the necessary policy to connect to Systems Manager. Use AWS IAM Identity Center to provide the external support engineers console access. Use Systems Manager Session Manager to assign the required permissions.

Confirm that AWS Systems Manager Agent (SSM Agent) is installed on all instances. Assign an instance profile with the necessary policy to connect to Systems Manager. Use Systems Manager Session Manager to provide local IAM user credentials in each AWS account to the external support engineers for console access.

Confirm that all instances have a security group that allows SSH access only from the external support engineers’ source IP address ranges. Provide local IAM user credentials in each AWS account to the external support engineers for console access. Provide each external support engineer an SSH key pair to log in to the application instances.

Create a bastion host in a public subnet. Set up the bastion host security group to allow access from only the external engineers’ IP address ranges. Ensure that all instances have a security group that allows SSH access from the bastion host. Provide each external support engineer an SSH key pair to log in to the application instances. Provide local account IAM user credentials to the engineers for console access.
explanation: The correct answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): • This suggests using Systems Manager Session Manager to distribute local IAM user credentials for console access—but Session Manager is for instance access, not for managing AWS Management Console credentials. • Distributing local IAM users per account increases administrative overhead and security risk (hard to rotate credentials and enforce least privilege centrally). Option C (INCORRECT): • Opening SSH directly from external IP ranges to private-subnet instances exposes your environment to IP-spoofing and requires managing and rotating SSH keys per engineer. • Giving local IAM user credentials in each account for console access similarly complicates credential management and lacks centralized control and auditing. Option D (INCORRECT): • Bastion hosts and SSH keys introduce another surface for patching, vulnerability, and key management. • Local IAM users per account still mean decentralized credential stores and harder auditing. • AWS best practice prefers Session Manager (no bastion, no open SSH ports, no keys) for secure, auditable access to Linux instances. Option A (CORRECT): • Use AWS IAM Identity Center (formerly AWS SSO) to grant developers external engineers time-bounded, centrally-managed AWS Management Console access—no local IAM users. • Leverage AWS Systems Manager Session Manager (with the SSM Agent and an appropriate instance profile) to connect securely to EC2 instances in private subnets—no bastion hosts or open SSH ports needed. • This approach meets the principle of least privilege, provides full audit logging of console and OS-level sessions, and eliminates key management and public-internet exposure. Summary: By centralizing console access via AWS IAM Identity Center and instance-level access via Systems Manager Session Manager, you minimize attack surface, simplify credential management, enforce least privilege, and maintain comprehensive audit trails. This scenario falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: An online learning company is migrating to the AWS Cloud. The company maintains its student records in a PostgreSQL database. The company needs a solution in which its data is available and online across multiple AWS Regions at all times.Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST amount of operational overhead?
options: Migrate the PostgreSQL database to a PostgreSQL cluster on Amazon EC2 instances.
Migrate the PostgreSQL database to an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance with the Multi-AZ feature turned on.
Migrate the PostgreSQL database to an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. Create a read replica in another Region.
Migrate the PostgreSQL database to an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. Set up DB snapshots to be copied to another Region.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): Migrate the PostgreSQL database to a PostgreSQL cluster on Amazon EC2 instances. Requires you to manage EC2 instances, OS patches, backups, replication, failover, and scaling manually. Does not natively provide cross-Region high availability without complex custom setup. Operational overhead is high compared to managed services. Option B (INCORRECT): Migrate the PostgreSQL database to an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance with the Multi-AZ feature turned on. Multi-AZ provides high availability within a single AWS Region only. It fails over to a standby in the same Region, not across Regions. Does not meet the requirement of “online across multiple AWS Regions.” Option D (INCORRECT): Migrate the PostgreSQL database to an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. Set up DB snapshots to be copied to another Region. Snapshots are point-in-time copies and are not continuously available as a live database. Requires manual or automated restore processes in the target Region, causing downtime and delay. Does not provide an “always online” solution across Regions. Option C (CORRECT): Migrate the PostgreSQL database to an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. Create a read replica in another Region. Amazon RDS managed cross-Region read replicas offer near-real-time replication to a standby in another Region. Data is continuously replicated, and the replica is available for read operations across Regions. Failover can be promoted with minimal downtime, and AWS handles replication, patching, and instance management. This solution provides the least operational overhead while ensuring multi-Region online availability. Summary: We learned that cross-Region high availability with minimal operational overhead is best achieved using Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with a cross-Region read replica. This question belongs to Domain 2 - Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company containerized a Windows job that runs on .NET 6 Framework under a Windows container. The company wants to run this job in the AWS Cloud. The job runs every 10 minutes. The job’s runtime varies between 1 minute and 3 minutes.Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Create an AWS Lambda function based on the container image of the job. Configure Amazon EventBridge to invoke the function every 10 minutes.
Use AWS Batch to create a job that uses AWS Fargate resources. Configure the job scheduling to run every 10 minutes.
Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate to run the job. Create a scheduled task based on the container image of the job to run every 10 minutes.

Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate to run the job. Create a standalone task based on the container image of the job. Use Windows task scheduler to run the job every 10 minutes.
explanation: The correct answer is C. Option A (INCORRECT): Create an AWS Lambda function based on the container image of the job and invoke it every 10 minutes. AWS Lambda supports container images but only on Amazon Linux (Linux containers), not Windows containers. Your job is packaged as a Windows container, so Lambda cannot execute it. Option B (INCORRECT): Use AWS Batch with AWS Fargate resources and schedule the job every 10 minutes. AWS Batch is designed for complex, large-scale batch workloads and adds orchestration overhead. Although Fargate pricing is the same, AWS Batch introduces extra complexity and configuration, making it less cost-effective for a simple periodic task. Option D (INCORRECT): Use Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate to run a standalone task and rely on Windows Task Scheduler inside the container. Windows Task Scheduler would require the container to run continuously, incurring cost 24/7. It defeats the pay-per-use benefit of Fargate, as you’d be billed whenever the container is up—even while idle. Option C (CORRECT): Use Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate to run the job as a scheduled task every 10 minutes. Fargate serverlessly provisions and bills compute only while the container runs (1–3 minutes per invocation). ECS Scheduled Tasks (via EventBridge) handle the 10-minute trigger natively—no always-on infrastructure. Supports Windows containers (as of recent updates) and .NET 6 workloads out of the box. Minimizes management overhead and delivers the most cost-optimized, scalable solution. In summary, we learned how to evaluate container orchestration options for a short-lived Windows/.NET 6 job on AWS. ECS on Fargate with Scheduled Tasks (Option C) meets the requirement of running every 10 minutes, supports Windows containers, and incurs costs only during actual execution. This question belongs to Domain 4 – Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company operates a two-tier application for image processing. The application uses two Availability Zones, each with one public subnet and one private subnet. An Application Load Balancer (ALB) for the web tier uses the public subnets. Amazon EC2 instances for the application tier use the private subnets. Users report that the application is running more slowly than expected. A security audit of the web server log files shows that the application is receiving millions of illegitimate requests from a small number of IP addresses. A solutions architect needs to resolve the immediate performance problem while the company investigates a more permanent solution. What should the solutions architect recommend to meet this requirement?
options: Modify the inbound security group for the web tier. Add a deny rule for the IP addresses that are consuming resources.
Modify the network ACL for the web tier subnets. Add an inbound deny rule for the IP addresses that are consuming resources.
Modify the inbound security group for the application tier. Add a deny rule for the IP addresses that are consuming resources.
Modify the network ACL for the application tier subnets. Add an inbound deny rule for the IP addresses that are consuming resources.
explanation: The correct answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): “Modify the inbound security group for the web tier. Add a deny rule for the IP addresses that are consuming resources.” Security groups are stateful and support only allow rules, not explicit deny rules. Even if you could deny, SGs apply at the instance or load-balancer level, but you cannot block traffic before it reaches the ALB’s network interface. Option C (INCORRECT): “Modify the inbound security group for the application tier. Add a deny rule for the IP addresses that are consuming resources.” Again, security groups do not support explicit deny rules. Blocking at the application tier means the ALB still processes the malicious requests and forwards them to the target group, consuming CPU and network on the ALB. Option D (INCORRECT): “Modify the network ACL for the application tier subnets. Add an inbound deny rule for the IP addresses that are consuming resources.” Although NACLs support deny rules, applying them on the private subnets only stops traffic just before the EC2 instances—but not before the ALB has already handled and forwarded the requests. This means the ALB still bears the load of illegitimate traffic, so performance issues on the web tier persist. Option B (CORRECT): “Modify the network ACL for the web tier subnets. Add an inbound deny rule for the IP addresses that are consuming resources.” Network ACLs are stateless and allow explicit deny entries, so you can block specific source IPs at the subnet boundary. Applying the deny rule on the public subnets stops malicious requests before they reach the ALB, immediately reducing load and improving performance. Changes to NACLs take effect quickly and provide an immediate mitigation while a more permanent solution (like AWS WAF) is investigated. Summary: By using a network ACL deny rule on the public subnets, we can immediately drop unwanted traffic before it consumes ALB resources. This question tests how to quickly improve performance under attack by leveraging stateless controls at the subnet level. This topic belongs to Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A digital image processing company wants to migrate its on-premises monolithic application to the AWS Cloud. The company processes thousands of images and generates large files as part of the processing workflow. The company needs a solution to manage the growing number of image processing jobs. The solution must also reduce the manual tasks in the image processing workflow. The company does not want to manage the underlying infrastructure of the solution.Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with Amazon EC2 Spot Instances to process the images. Configure Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) to orchestrate the workflow. Store the processed files in Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS).
Use AWS Batch jobs to process the images. Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate the workflow. Store the processed files in an Amazon S3 bucket.
Use AWS Lambda functions and Amazon EC2 Spot Instances to process the images. Store the processed files in Amazon FSx.
Deploy a group of Amazon EC2 instances to process the images. Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate the workflow. Store the processed files in an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume.
explanation: The correct Answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon ECS with Amazon EC2 Spot Instances, orchestrate with SQS, store in EFS.” Requires you to manage and patch EC2 instances in the ECS cluster—higher operational overhead. Amazon EFS adds cost and complexity; not ideal for massive batch output when S3 is simpler and more scalable. Option C (INCORRECT): “Use AWS Lambda functions and EC2 Spot Instances, store files in FSx.” Mixing Lambda and EC2 Spot Instances is inconsistent and complex to orchestrate. Amazon FSx is overkill for simple object storage; S3 provides better durability, scalability, and lower cost. You’d still manage EC2 Spot fleet complexities—higher operational overhead. Option D (INCORRECT): “Deploy a group of EC2 instances, orchestrate with Step Functions, store in EBS.” Managing a fleet of EC2 instances and EBS volumes is fully self-managed—fails the “least operational overhead” requirement. EBS is tied to a single instance and does not scale as easily as S3 for large batch outputs. Option B (CORRECT): “Use AWS Batch for processing, AWS Step Functions for orchestration, and store outputs in Amazon S3.” AWS Batch is a fully managed batch compute service that automatically provisions and scales compute resources—no EC2 management needed. AWS Step Functions provides serverless orchestration, reducing manual workflow steps. Amazon S3 offers virtually unlimited, durable, and cost-effective storage for processed images. Summary: We reviewed why Options A, C, and D introduce unnecessary infrastructure management or complexity, and why Option B meets the requirements with the least operational overhead by leveraging fully managed AWS Batch, Step Functions, and S3. This question falls under Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A solutions architect wants all new users to have specific complexity requirements and mandatory rotation periods for IAM user passwords.What should the solutions architect do to accomplish this?
options: Set an overall password policy for the entire AWS account.
Set a password policy for each IAM user in the AWS account.
Use third-party vendor software to set password requirements.
Attach an Amazon CloudWatch rule to the Create_newuser event to set the password with the appropriate requirements.
explanation: The correct Answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): AWS IAM does not support individual password policies per user. You can only configure a single account-wide password policy that applies to all users in the account. Option C (INCORRECT): No third-party software is required. AWS IAM provides native support for password complexity and rotation through the account password policy. Option D (INCORRECT): You cannot use a CloudWatch rule on user‐creation events to enforce password settings. Password complexity and rotation must be defined in the IAM account password policy. Option A (CORRECT): Defining an account-wide IAM password policy is the proper solution. This policy allows you to: Specify password complexity requirements (uppercase, lowercase, numbers, symbols). Enforce mandatory password rotation after a set number of days. Apply these rules to all new and existing IAM users in the AWS account. In summary, AWS IAM supports a single, account-level password policy to manage both complexity and rotation for all users. This question belongs to Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: As part of budget planning, management wants a report of AWS billed items listed by user. The data will be used to create department budgets. A solutions architect needs to determine the most efficient way to obtain this report information. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Run a query with Amazon Athena to generate the report.
Create a report in Cost Explorer and download the report.
Access the bill details from the billing dashboard and download the bill.
Modify a cost budget in AWS Budgets to alert with Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES).
explanation: The correct answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): “Run a query with Amazon Athena to generate the report.” Athena can query the AWS Cost and Usage Report stored in S3, but you must first enable and configure the CUR, set up partitions, and define a table in AWS Glue or Athena. This setup is more complex and time-consuming compared to using the built-in Cost Explorer functionality for on-demand reporting. Option C (INCORRECT): “Access the bill details from the billing dashboard and download the bill.” The billing dashboard provides high-level, aggregated costs and doesn’t allow you to group or filter costs by individual users. It’s not designed to deliver itemized, user-level breakout required for departmental budget planning. Option D (INCORRECT): “Modify a cost budget in AWS Budgets to alert with Amazon SES.” AWS Budgets and SES can notify you when spend thresholds are crossed, but they do not generate the detailed, user-level cost report. This option is for alerting, not for exporting or grouping cost data by user for budget allocation. Option B (CORRECT): “Create a report in Cost Explorer and download the report.” Cost Explorer supports filtering and grouping costs by tags (for example, a “User” tag) so you can see billed items per user. You can quickly configure the report in the console and export it as CSV for budget planning without extra setup. This is the most efficient, built-in way to obtain detailed, user-based billing data for departmental budgets. In this discussion we learned how to select the simplest AWS billing tool to produce a detailed, user-level cost report. This question falls under Domain 4 – Design Cost-Optimized Architectures, focusing on efficient cost reporting and budget planning.

question: A company is designing a cloud communications platform that is driven by APIs. The application is hosted on Amazon EC2 instances behind a Network Load Balancer (NLB). The company uses Amazon API Gateway to provide external users with access to the application through APIs. The company wants to protect the platform against web exploits like SQL injection and also wants to detect and mitigate large, sophisticated DDoS attacks. Which combination of solutions provides the MOST protection? (Choose two.)
options: Use AWS WAF to protect the NLB.
Use AWS Shield Advanced with the NLB.
Use AWS WAF to protect Amazon API Gateway.
Use Amazon GuardDuty with AWS Shield Standard
Use AWS Shield Standard with Amazon API Gateway.
explanation: The correct answer is B, C. Option A (INCORRECT): Use AWS WAF to protect the NLB. AWS WAF can only be associated with Application Load Balancers, API Gateway, CloudFront, or AppSync— it is not directly supported on a Network Load Balancer. Option D (INCORRECT): Use Amazon GuardDuty with AWS Shield Standard. GuardDuty is a threat-detection service—not a DDoS mitigation or web-application-firewall solution. AWS Shield Standard is automatically enabled and provides only network-layer DDoS protection with no cost, but cannot be escalated for advanced mitigation. Option E (INCORRECT): Use AWS Shield Standard with Amazon API Gateway. Shield Standard only covers network/infrastructure layer (Layer 3 and 4) for default AWS services, including API Gateway, but does not include application-layer protections. It won’t defend against complex Layer 7 attacks or SQL injection—WAF is required for that. Option B (CORRECT): Use AWS Shield Advanced with the NLB. Shield Advanced provides enhanced DDoS detection and mitigation for both Layers 3/4 and integrates with AWS WAF for Layer 7. You gain cost protection, 24/7 DDoS response team access, and detailed attack diagnostics for your Network Load Balancer. Option C (CORRECT): Use AWS WAF to protect Amazon API Gateway. AWS WAF allows you to write custom rules to block SQL injection, cross-site scripting, and other OWASP Top 10 threats. API Gateway integration with WAF safeguards your APIs at the application layer against web exploits. Summary: We learned that to defend against web exploits (SQL injection, XSS) you need AWS WAF on the API endpoint, and to mitigate large or sophisticated DDoS attacks you need AWS Shield Advanced on your Network Load Balancer. This question belongs to Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 Linux instances across multiple Availability Zones. The application needs a storage layer that is highly available and Portable Operating System Interface (POSIX)-compliant. The storage layer must provide maximum data durability and must be shareable across the EC2 instances. The data in the storage layer will be accessed frequently for the first 30 days and will be accessed infrequently after that time. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Use the Amazon S3 Standard storage class. Create an S3 Lifecycle policy to move infrequently accessed data to S3 Glacier.
Use the Amazon S3 Standard storage class. Create an S3 Lifecycle policy to move infrequently accessed data to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA).
Use the Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) Standard storage class. Create a lifecycle management policy to move infrequently accessed data to EFS Standard-Infrequent Access (EFS Standard-IA).
Use the Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) One Zone storage class. Create a lifecycle management policy to move infrequently accessed data to EFS One Zone-Infrequent Access (EFS One Zone-IA).
explanation: The correct answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): Use the Amazon S3 Standard storage class. Create an S3 Lifecycle policy to move infrequently accessed data to S3 Glacier. Amazon S3 is not POSIX-compliant—applications cannot mount S3 as a file system without additional software (e.g., S3FS), which adds complexity and latency. S3 Glacier is an archival tier with retrieval delays (minutes to hours), so it’s not suitable for data that might occasionally need faster access. Though durable and cost-effective for archives, this does not meet the POSIX and shared mounting requirements. Option B (INCORRECT): Use the Amazon S3 Standard storage class. Create an S3 Lifecycle policy to move infrequently accessed data to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA). Still not POSIX-compliant or directly mountable to EC2 without extra layers. S3 Standard-IA has a retrieval fee and is object storage—not a network file system—so it cannot be shared via NFS across Linux instances. Option D (INCORRECT): Use the Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) One Zone storage class. Create a lifecycle management policy to move infrequently accessed data to EFS One Zone-Infrequent Access (EFS One Zone-IA). One Zone storage class keeps data in a single AZ—risking data loss if that AZ fails (lower availability/durability). Requirement calls for highly available across multiple AZs, so One Zone does not satisfy the multi-AZ durability and availability need. Option C (CORRECT): Use the Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) Standard storage class. Create a lifecycle management policy to move infrequently accessed data to EFS Standard-Infrequent Access (EFS Standard-IA). EFS Standard is a POSIX-compliant, fully managed, elastic NFS file system that can be mounted concurrently across multiple AZs—meeting the high-availability and shareability requirements. Built for maximum durability and automatically replicates data across AZs. Lifecycle management can transition files not accessed for 30 days into the Standard-IA tier, reducing storage costs for infrequently accessed data. This combination delivers the required performance, durability, and POSIX compliance at the most cost-effective rate. In summary, we looked at various storage options and ruled out Amazon S3 (not POSIX-compliant) and EFS One Zone (single AZ risk). Amazon EFS Standard with lifecycle to EFS Standard-IA delivers a shared, POSIX-compliant file system across AZs with lifecycle-based cost optimization. This question belongs to Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A social media company wants to allow its users to upload images in an application that is hosted in the AWS Cloud. The company needs a solution that automatically resizes the images so that the images can be displayed on multiple device types. The application experiences unpredictable traffic patterns throughout the day. The company is seeking a highly available solution that maximizes scalability. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
options: Create a static website hosted in Amazon S3 that invokes AWS Lambda functions to resize the images and store the images in an Amazon S3 bucket.
Create a static website hosted in Amazon CloudFront that invokes AWS Step Functions to resize the images and store the images in an Amazon RDS database.

Create a dynamic website hosted on a web server that runs on an Amazon EC2 instance. Configure a process that runs on the EC2 instance to resize the images and store the images in an Amazon S3 bucket.

Create a dynamic website hosted on an automatically scaling Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster that creates a resize job in Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS). Set up an image-resizing program that runs on an Amazon EC2 instance to process the resize jobs.
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): • You cannot “host” a static website in CloudFront. CloudFront is a CDN distribution, not an origin for website content. • Invoking AWS Step Functions directly from a CDN request is not supported. • Storing images in an Amazon RDS database is inefficient and costly—object storage (Amazon S3) is the correct service for images. Option C (INCORRECT): • A single EC2-hosted web server lacks the automatic, unlimited scalability required for unpredictable traffic. • You’d need to manage OS patches, scaling policies, and server health yourself, which is not “highly available” by default. • Compared to serverless, this approach increases operational overhead and cost. Option D (INCORRECT): • Spinning up an ECS cluster plus EC2 workers and SQS adds unnecessary complexity. • You still manage container instances and EC2 resize programs, which reduces scalability and increases maintenance. • A pure serverless pipeline (S3 + Lambda) is simpler, more cost-effective, and scales automatically. Option A (CORRECT): Host a static website on Amazon S3 for the upload interface—no servers to manage. Use S3 Event Notifications to trigger AWS Lambda functions to resize images on upload. Store all resized variants back in S3, which offers virtually unlimited storage and high availability. This serverless design auto-scales with traffic, minimizes operational overhead, and maximizes cost efficiency. In summary, Option A meets all requirements with a fully serverless, scalable, and highly available design for image upload and resizing. This scenario falls under Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures, focusing on scalability and performance.

question: A company wants to deploy a new public web application on AWS. The application includes a web server tier that uses Amazon EC2 instances. The application also includes a database tier that uses an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance. The application must be secure and accessible for global customers that have dynamic IP addresses.How should a solutions architect configure the security groups to meet these requirements?
options: Configure the security group for the web servers to allow inbound traffic on port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. Configure the security group for the DB instance to allow inbound traffic on port 3306 from the security group of the web servers.

Configure the security group for the web servers to allow inbound traffic on port 443 from the IP addresses of the customers. Configure the security group for the DB instance to allow inbound traffic on port 3306 from the security group of the web servers.

Configure the security group for the web servers to allow inbound traffic on port 443 from the IP addresses of the customers. Configure the security group for the DB instance to allow inbound traffic on port 3306 from the IP addresses of the customers.

Configure the security group for the web servers to allow inbound traffic on port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. Configure the security group for the DB instance to allow inbound traffic on port 3306 from 0.0.0.0/0.
explanation: The correct answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): Configuring the web servers’ security group to allow inbound traffic on port 443 only from the IP addresses of the customers is not feasible because the customers have dynamic (changing) IPs. You cannot maintain an up-to-date list of all global customer IP addresses. Although the DB security group correctly references the web servers’ security group, the first part fails to meet the requirement of global accessibility. Option C (INCORRECT): Allowing inbound traffic on port 443 and port 3306 from the customers’ IP addresses exposes the database directly to the internet, which is insecure. It also ignores the best practice of restricting DB access to the application tier only. Option D (INCORRECT): Opening port 3306 on the DB instance to 0.0.0.0/0 makes the database publicly accessible. This violates the principle of least privilege and exposes sensitive data to the internet. Even though the web tier is correctly open on port 443, the DB tier must remain protected and only accept connections from the web servers. Option A (CORRECT): The web servers’ security group allows inbound HTTPS (port 443) from 0.0.0.0/0, so any global customer—regardless of IP address—can access the application securely. The RDS security group allows inbound MySQL (port 3306) only from the web servers’ security group, ensuring that only the application tier can connect to the database. This configuration follows AWS best practices by exposing only the web tier to the public internet and isolating the database tier behind security group rules. In summary, we learned how to configure security groups to allow global, secure access to a public web application while tightly controlling database access. This ensures a secure architecture by following the principle of least privilege. This question belongs to Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company uses high block storage capacity to runs its workloads on premises. The company's daily peak input and output transactions per second are not more than 15,000 IOPS. The company wants to migrate the workloads to Amazon EC2 and to provision disk performance independent of storage capacity. Which Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume type will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: GP2 volume type
io2 volume type
GP3 volume type
io1 volume type
explanation: The correct answer is C. GP3 volume type Option A (GP2) – INCORRECT: Performance (IOPS) scales linearly with volume size (3 IOPS per GB), so you must over‐provision capacity just to hit 15,000 IOPS, driving up cost. Burst credits can sustain higher IOPS only for short periods; they’re not a reliable way to guarantee sustained 15,000 IOPS daily. Does not allow decoupling performance from storage capacity. Option B (io2) – INCORRECT: Designed for very high durability and IOPS (up to 64,000), but at a premium price per IOPS. Overkill for a workload capped at 15,000 IOPS; significantly more expensive than needed. While you can provision IOPS independently, the cost‐per‐IOPS is far higher than GP3. Option D (io1) – INCORRECT: Also allows you to provision IOPS, but with lower durability than io2 and similar high cost per IOPS. Maximum of 50 IOPS per GB means you still need to allocate many GB to hit 15,000 IOPS if you don’t explicitly provision IOPS—but provisioning IOPS again raises cost. Not as cost‐effective as GP3 for moderate IOPS requirements. Option C (GP3) – CORRECT: Baseline performance of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s throughput, plus the ability to provision up to 16,000 IOPS and 1,000 MiB/s independently of capacity. Decouples storage size from performance, so you only pay for the capacity you need and the additional IOPS you provision. Most cost‐effective for a sustained workload requiring up to 15,000 IOPS without wasting GB of storage. Summary: We learned that GP3 is the optimal EBS volume type when you need to decouple performance from capacity and keep costs low for a workload up to 15,000 IOPS. This question belongs to Domain 4 – Design Cost‐Optimized Architectures.

question: A company hosts a website on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The website serves static content. Website traffic is increasing, and the company is concerned about a potential increase in cost.
options: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution to cache state files at edge locations
Create an Amazon ElastiCache cluster. Connect the ALB to the ElastiCache cluster to serve cached files
Create an AWS WAF web ACL and associate it with the ALB. Add a rule to the web ACL to cache static files
Create a second ALB in an alternative AWS Region. Route user traffic to the closest Region to minimize data transfer costs
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): Amazon ElastiCache is an in-memory key-value store (Redis/Memcached), not a CDN for serving static files. An Application Load Balancer cannot route HTTP requests directly to an ElastiCache cluster. Using ElastiCache would require custom application logic to fetch and serve files and wouldn’t yield the same cost savings or global caching benefits as a CDN. Option C (INCORRECT): AWS WAF is a web application firewall for filtering and protecting HTTP(S) traffic, not for caching content. You cannot configure WAF rules to cache or serve static files; it only inspects and blocks/allows requests. Option D (INCORRECT): Deploying a second ALB in another region adds infrastructure and cost—opposite of cost optimization. Routing users to the nearest region via Route 53 latency-based routing does not cache content or reduce origin request costs. Inter-region data transfer can actually incur additional charges. Option A (CORRECT): Amazon CloudFront is a CDN that caches static files at edge locations worldwide, reducing the load on your EC2 instances and ALB. By serving content from edge caches, you lower data transfer and request costs from the origin. CloudFront integrates seamlessly with ALB as an origin, improving both performance and cost efficiency as traffic grows. Summary: Using CloudFront to cache static content at edge locations offloads requests from the origin infrastructure, reduces data transfer costs, and improves user experience. This question falls under Domain 4 – Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A solutions architect has created a new AWS account and must secure AWS account root user access. Which combination of actions will accomplish this? (Choose two.)
options: Ensure the root user uses a strong password.
Enable multi-factor authentication to the root user.
Store root user access keys in an encrypted Amazon S3 bucket.
Add the root user to a group containing administrative permissions.
Apply the required permissions to the root user with an inline policy document.
explanation: The correct answer is A, B Option C (INCORRECT): “Store root user access keys in an encrypted Amazon S3 bucket.” Best practice is to not create access keys for the root user at all. Instead, delete any existing root access keys immediately. Storing sensitive long‐term credentials, even if encrypted, still poses an unnecessary security risk. Option D (INCORRECT): “Add the root user to a group containing administrative permissions.” The root user already has full administrative privileges by default. You cannot add the root user to an IAM group. IAM groups are solely for IAM users; the root user is not managed in that way. Option E (INCORRECT): “Apply the required permissions to the root user with an inline policy document.” The root user always has full access and cannot be restricted or modified via IAM policies. Inline policies apply only to IAM users, groups, and roles—not to the root account. Option A (CORRECT): “Ensure the root user uses a strong password.” Having a complex, unique password for the root account is the first defense against unauthorized access. It reduces the risk posed by brute‐force or dictionary attacks. Option B (CORRECT): “Enable multi-factor authentication to the root user.” MFA adds an extra layer of security beyond the password, requiring a physical or virtual token. Even if the password is compromised, an attacker cannot sign in without the second factor. In summary, securing the root account requires a strong password and MFA, and you should never create or store root access keys, nor attempt to manage the root user via IAM groups or policies. This question belongs to Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company runs an on-premises application on a Kubernetes cluster. The company recently added millions of new customers. The company's existing on-premises infrastructure is unable to handle the large number of new customers. The company needs to migrate the on-premises application to the AWS Cloud. The company will migrate to an Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) cluster. The company does not want to manage the underlying compute infrastructure for the new architecture on AWS. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Use a self-managed node to supply compute capacity. Deploy the application to the new EKS cluster.
Use managed node groups to supply compute capacity. Deploy the application to the new EKS cluster.
Use AWS Fargate to supply compute capacity. Create a Fargate profile. Use the Fargate profile to deploy the application.
Use managed node groups with Karpenter to supply compute capacity. Deploy the application to the new EKS cluster.
explanation: The correct Answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): • Self-managed nodes mean you must provision, patch, scale, and replace EC2 instances yourself. • This adds significant operational overhead, which contradicts the requirement to avoid managing compute infrastructure. Option B (INCORRECT): • Managed node groups simplify some lifecycle operations (AMI updates, scaling), but you still manage EC2 instances, networking, and scaling policies. • There is still non-negligible infrastructure management overhead. Option D (INCORRECT): • Karpenter automates node provisioning but still relies on EC2 instances under the hood. • You must configure scaling constraints, instance types, and IAM roles, which increases complexity and operational tasks compared to a fully serverless approach. Option C (CORRECT): AWS Fargate is a serverless compute engine for Amazon EKS: you deploy pods without managing any EC2 instances. Fargate automatically scales to meet demand, removing the need to manage, patch, or secure underlying servers. This delivers the LEAST operational overhead while providing seamless, on-demand capacity for your Kubernetes workloads. In summary, migrating your on-premises Kubernetes workloads to Amazon EKS on Fargate eliminates the need to manage EC2 instances, delivering the lowest operational overhead. This question falls under Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures, because it focuses on choosing a scalable, serverless compute option that automatically adjusts to millions of new customer workloads.

question: A company is building a three-tier application on AWS. The presentation tier will serve a static website The logic tier is a containerized application. This application will store data in a relational database. The company wants to simplify deployment and to reduce operational costs.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Use Amazon S3 to host static content. Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with AWS Fargate for compute power. Use a managed Amazon RDS cluster for the database.
Use Amazon CloudFront to host static content. Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with Amazon EC2 for compute power. Use a managed Amazon RDS cluster for the database.
Use Amazon S3 to host static content. Use Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) with AWS Fargate for compute power. Use a managed Amazon RDS cluster for the database.
Use Amazon EC2 Reserved Instances to host static content. Use Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) with Amazon EC2 for compute power. Use a managed Amazon RDS cluster for the database.
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon CloudFront to host static content. Use Amazon ECS with Amazon EC2 for compute power. Use a managed Amazon RDS cluster for the database.” CloudFront is a CDN, not a primary web hosting service—you still need an origin like S3 or EC2. Running ECS on EC2 instances adds operational overhead: you must manage and patch the EC2 fleet. This option does not minimize operational costs as effectively as a serverless compute option. Option C (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon S3 to host static content. Use Amazon EKS with AWS Fargate for compute power. Use a managed Amazon RDS cluster for the database.” EKS introduces Kubernetes control plane complexity—more operational overhead than ECS. Although Fargate removes node management, you still manage Kubernetes primitives (pods, namespaces, etc.). Not as simple as using ECS; higher learning curve and cost compared to ECS Fargate. Option D (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon EC2 Reserved Instances to host static content. Use Amazon EKS with Amazon EC2 for compute power. Use a managed Amazon RDS cluster for the database.” Hosting a static website on EC2 is unnecessary—S3 is fully managed, scalable, and cost-effective. EKS on EC2 Reserved Instances compounds management and operational burden. This architecture is the most complex and highest cost of all options. Option A (CORRECT): “Use Amazon S3 to host static content. Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with AWS Fargate for compute power. Use a managed Amazon RDS cluster for the database.” Amazon S3 is ideal for static websites—fully managed, highly available, and cost-efficient. ECS with Fargate removes the need to manage servers or clusters—simplifies deployment and lowers ops work. Amazon RDS provides a managed relational database with automated backups, patching, and scaling. This stack maximizes serverless and managed services to reduce operational overhead and cost. In summary, we learned that leveraging fully managed, serverless or serverless-style services (S3, ECS Fargate, RDS) delivers simplicity, cost optimization, and minimal operational overhead. This question belongs to Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A large company wants to provide its globally located developers separate, limited size, managed PostgreSQL databases for development purposes. The databases will be low volume. The developers need the databases only when they are actively working. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Give the developers the ability to launch separate Amazon Aurora instances. Set up a process to shut down Aurora instances at the end of the workday and to start Aurora instances at the beginning of the next workday.
