Associating AWS WAF with the CloudFront distribution inspects and filters all incoming HTTP(S) requests before they reach your origin. This design fully satisfies the requirement of storing a static website in S3, distributing it via CloudFront, and having all traffic inspected by AWS WAF. In summary, we learned how to secure a static S3–backed website by using a CloudFront Origin Access Identity to lock down bucket access, and by attaching AWS WAF directly to the CloudFront distribution so that every request is inspected. This question belongs to Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company needs to export its database once a day to Amazon S3 for other teams to access. The exported object size varies between 2 GB and 5 GB. The S3 access pattern for the data is variable and changes rapidly. The data must be immediately available and must remain accessible for up to 3 months. The company needs the most cost-effective solution that will not increase retrieval time. Which S3 storage class should the company use to meet these requirements?
options: S3 Intelligent-Tiering
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
S3 Standard
S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA)
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval • Although Glacier Instant Retrieval offers millisecond access, it is designed for long-term archive data with infrequent access patterns. • You incur retrieval fees on each access, making it expensive for workloads where access patterns are variable and unpredictable. • The question demands a solution that will not increase retrieval time and optimize cost; Glacier retrieval fees violate the cost requirement under variable access. Option C (INCORRECT): S3 Standard • S3 Standard provides immediate access and high throughput, but it also carries the highest storage cost per GB. • Since the data only needs to be retained for up to 3 months and access frequency is unpredictable, paying Standard rates is not the most cost-effective choice. Option D (INCORRECT): S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) • S3 Standard-IA offers lower storage costs but charges a retrieval fee per GB accessed. • With access patterns that “change rapidly,” retrieval costs could spike unpredictably. • There is also a 30-day minimum storage charge which, combined with retrieval fees, undermines overall cost efficiency for variable access. Option A (CORRECT): S3 Intelligent-Tiering • Automatically moves objects between a frequent-access tier and two infrequent-access tiers based on actual usage, without performance impact. • Provides immediate, millisecond retrieval with no retrieval fees, regardless of which tier your data resides in. • Ideal for unpredictable or rapidly changing access patterns—ensures you pay the lowest possible storage cost while keeping data instantly available. • Retention of up to 3 months (and beyond) fits the auto-tiering model, and the small monthly monitoring fee is offset by storage savings. Summary: We evaluated each S3 storage class against requirements of immediate availability, variable access patterns, 3-month retention, and cost-optimization. Only S3 Intelligent-Tiering adapts to unpredictable access without latency or retrieval fees, making it the best choice. This question belongs to Domain 4 – Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A global company runs its workloads on AWS. The company's application uses Amazon S3 buckets across AWS Regions for sensitive data storage and analysis. The company stores millions of objects in multiple S3 buckets daily. The company wants to identify all S3 buckets that are not versioning-enabled.Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Use Amazon S3 Storage Lens to identify all S3 buckets that are not versioning-enabled across Regions.
Enable IAM Access Analyzer for S3 to identify all S3 buckets that are not versioning-enabled across Regions.
Create an S3 Multi-Region Access Point to identify all S3 buckets that are not versioning-enabled across Regions.
explanation: The correct answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): “Enable IAM Access Analyzer for S3 to identify all S3 buckets that are not versioning-enabled across Regions.” IAM Access Analyzer for S3 is used to review bucket policies and detect public or cross-account access, not to report on bucket configuration details such as versioning. It does not provide aggregated metrics or dashboards for versioning status across multiple buckets or Regions. Option C (INCORRECT): “Create an S3 Multi-Region Access Point to identify all S3 buckets that are not versioning-enabled across Regions.” S3 Multi-Region Access Points simplify data access across buckets in different Regions but do not audit or report on bucket configuration states like versioning. They are purely for unified data access endpoints, not for compliance or configuration reporting. Option A (CORRECT): “Use Amazon S3 Storage Lens to identify all S3 buckets that are not versioning-enabled across Regions.” S3 Storage Lens provides organization-wide visibility into storage usage and activity metrics, including a configuration dashboard that shows which buckets have versioning disabled. It can aggregate metrics across all AWS Regions and S3 buckets, delivering insights through dashboards, actionable recommendations, and optional daily CSV/Parquet reports. This meets the requirement to identify at scale every bucket that is not versioning-enabled. In summary, we learned that Amazon S3 Storage Lens is the appropriate AWS service to gain cross-Region, aggregated insights into bucket configurations such as versioning status. This question falls under Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures, since versioning is a key feature to protect data from accidental deletion or overwrite.

question: A company is migrating from a monolithic architecture for a web application that is hosted on Amazon EC2 to a serverless microservices architecture. The company wants to use AWS services that support an event-driven, loosely coupled architecture. The company wants to use the publish/subscribe (pub/sub) pattern.Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Configure an Amazon API Gateway REST API to invoke an AWS Lambda function that publishes events to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Configure one or more subscribers to read events from the SQS queue.

Configure an Amazon API Gateway REST API to invoke an AWS Lambda function that publishes events to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic. Configure one or more subscribers to receive events from the SNS topic.
Configure an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API to write to a data stream in Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with enhanced fan-out. Configure one or more subscribers to receive events from the data stream.

Configure an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API to invoke an AWS Lambda function that publishes events to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic. Configure one or more subscribers to receive events from the topic.
explanation: The correct answer is D. Option A (INCORRECT): This design uses Amazon SQS, which is a polling-based queue, not a true pub/sub service. Subscribers must poll the queue and messages are delivered only once, making it tightly coupled to consumer polling logic. SQS also adds extra cost and complexity for long polling or visibility timeout management, which is not ideal for a lightweight, event-driven pub/sub architecture. Option B (INCORRECT): Although SNS is a correct pub/sub service, using the Amazon API Gateway REST API is more expensive compared to the newer HTTP API. REST APIs have higher per-million-request charges and added feature overhead that is not needed for simple event publishing scenarios. Option C (INCORRECT): Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with enhanced fan-out is designed for high-throughput streaming data, not lightweight event notifications. The enhanced fan-out feature incurs additional per-consumer throughput charges, driving cost up significantly for a basic pub/sub pattern. Option D (CORRECT): Amazon API Gateway HTTP API is the most cost-effective API offering for simple request-to-Lambda scenarios, with lower per-million-request pricing. AWS Lambda publishes events to an Amazon SNS topic, providing a fully managed, scalable pub/sub mechanism with multiple subscribers. This combination meets the requirements for an event-driven, loosely coupled microservices architecture at the lowest cost. In summary, Option D is the best fit because it leverages the lowest-cost HTTP API for request ingestion, Lambda for compute, and SNS for scalable pub/sub. This question belongs to Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company runs multiple Amazon EC2 Linux instances in a VPC across two Availability Zones. The instances host applications that use a hierarchical directory structure. The applications need to read and write rapidly and concurrently to shared storage.What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
options: Create an Amazon S3 bucket. Allow access from all the EC2 instances in the VPC.
Create an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Mount the EFS file system from each EC2 instance.
Create a file system on a Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. Attach the EBS volume to all the EC2 instances.
Create file systems on Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes that are attached to each EC2 instance. Synchronize the EBS volumes across the different EC2 instances.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): Create an Amazon S3 bucket. Allow access from all the EC2 instances in the VPC. S3 is object storage, not a POSIX-compliant file system. It does not support hierarchical directory structures or native file-level operations. Applications requiring rapid, concurrent read/write on a shared directory cannot use S3 as if it were a mounted file system. Option C (INCORRECT): Create a file system on a Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) EBS volume. Attach the EBS volume to all the EC2 instances. By default, EBS volumes can only be attached to a single instance at a time. Even with EBS Multi-Attach (io1/io2), all instances must be in the same Availability Zone and require special setup; it’s not a cross-AZ solution. Management overhead and risk of file system corruption make it unsuitable for standard multi-instance mounting. Option D (INCORRECT): Create file systems on EBS volumes that are attached to each EC2 instance. Synchronize the EBS volumes across the different EC2 instances. Maintaining synchronization (rsync, file-replication software) across instances is complex and error-prone. Data consistency and latency issues arise when changes occur concurrently in multiple AZs. This approach increases operational overhead and does not provide a true shared file system. Option B (CORRECT): Create an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Mount the EFS file system from each EC2 instance. EFS provides a fully managed, POSIX-compliant NFS file system with hierarchical directories. It supports highly concurrent, low-latency read/write access from multiple EC2 instances across Availability Zones. Automatically scales throughput and storage as demand grows, with built-in redundancy for high availability. In summary, Amazon EFS is the ideal solution for rapid, concurrent, shared filesystem access across multiple EC2 instances in different Availability Zones. We have learned to distinguish object storage (S3), block storage (EBS), and network file systems (EFS) when designing shared storage. This question belongs to Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: An application runs on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets. The application needs to access an Amazon DynamoDB table. What is the MOST secure way to access the table while ensuring that the traffic does not leave the AWS network?
options: Use a VPC endpoint for DynamoDB.
Use a NAT gateway in a public subnet.
Use a NAT instance in a private subnet.
Use the internet gateway attached to the VPC.
explanation: The correct answer is A Option B (INCORRECT): Use a NAT gateway in a public subnet. Although a NAT gateway enables EC2 instances in private subnets to reach AWS services using the internet gateway, it still routes traffic through public endpoints. This means traffic to DynamoDB would traverse the internet, which is less secure and does not guarantee that it remains entirely within the AWS network. Option C (INCORRECT): Use a NAT instance in a private subnet. A NAT instance functions similarly to a NAT gateway by routing traffic through the internet gateway. It also relies on public endpoints of DynamoDB and can become a single point of failure or performance bottleneck. Option D (INCORRECT): Use the internet gateway attached to the VPC. Attaching an internet gateway allows direct outbound internet access, but it exposes traffic to the public internet. This does not meet the requirement of keeping traffic within the AWS network. Option A (CORRECT): Use a VPC endpoint for DynamoDB. A VPC endpoint for DynamoDB provides a private connection between your VPC and DynamoDB without requiring an internet gateway, NAT device, VPN connection, or AWS Direct Connect. All traffic between your VPC and DynamoDB stays within the AWS network, ensuring maximum security and eliminating exposure to the public internet. This solution is fully managed, highly available, and scalable without the need to manage any NAT instances or gateways. From this discussion, we learned that using a VPC endpoint is the most secure way to connect private EC2 instances to DynamoDB while ensuring traffic never leaves the AWS network. This question aligns with Domain 1 - Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company runs a production database on Amazon RDS for MySQL. The company wants to upgrade the database version for security compliance reasons. Because the database contains critical data, the company wants a quick solution to upgrade and test functionality without losing any data. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Create an RDS manual snapshot. Upgrade to the new version of Amazon RDS for MySQL.
Use native backup and restore. Restore the data to the upgraded new version of Amazon RDS for MySQL.
Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to replicate the data to the upgraded new version of Amazon RDS for MySQL.
Use Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployments to deploy and test production changes.
explanation: The correct answer is D. Option A (INCORRECT): “Create an RDS manual snapshot. Upgrade to the new version of Amazon RDS for MySQL.” In-place upgrades using a snapshot still incur downtime during the upgrade process. Testing functionality before switching over is not possible without impacting production. Rollback requires a new restore from snapshot, increasing operational overhead. Option B (INCORRECT): “Use native backup and restore. Restore the data to the upgraded new version of Amazon RDS for MySQL.” Requires manual backup, S3 import/export or mysqldump, which is time-consuming for large datasets. Operational overhead is high due to custom scripting and manual steps. Longer downtime and complex rollback procedures. Option C (INCORRECT): “Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to replicate the data to the upgraded new version of Amazon RDS for MySQL.” DMS setup and ongoing replication tasks add operational complexity. Requires schema conversion and data validation steps. Although near-zero downtime is possible, it is overkill for a simple version upgrade. Option D (CORRECT): “Use Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployments to deploy and test production changes.” Creates a cloned “green” environment on the new MySQL version while the “blue” (production) remains live. Allows full functional testing on green before cutover, with minimal downtime. Rollback is as simple as switching endpoints back to blue, minimizing operational overhead. In summary, Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployments provides the quickest, safest way to upgrade a production database version with minimal downtime and operational effort. This scenario aligns with Domain 2 - Design Resilient Architectures, as it focuses on seamless version upgrades and high availability during migrations.

question: An ecommerce company has an order-processing application that uses Amazon API Gateway and an AWS Lambda function. The application stores data in an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL database. During a recent sales event, a sudden surge in customer orders occurred. Some customers experienced timeouts, and the application did not process the orders of those customers. A solutions architect determined that the CPU utilization and memory utilization were high on the database because of a large number of open connections. The solutions architect needs to prevent the timeout errors while making the least possible changes to the application. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Configure provisioned concurrency for the Lambda function. Modify the database to be a global database in multiple AWS Regions.
Use Amazon RDS Proxy to create a proxy for the database. Modify the Lambda function to use the RDS Proxy endpoint instead of the database endpoint.
Create a read replica for the database in a different AWS Region. Use query string parameters in API Gateway to route traffic to the read replica.
Migrate the data from Aurora PostgreSQL to Amazon DynamoDB by using AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS). Modify the Lambda function to use the DynamoDB table.
explanation: The correct Answer is B Option A (INCORRECT): Configure provisioned concurrency for the Lambda function and convert the database into an Aurora global database. Provisioned concurrency only stabilizes cold-start latency for Lambda—it does not reduce database connection count or CPU/memory pressure. Aurora Global Database is for cross-region replication and disaster recovery, not for connection pooling or reducing load in a single region. Option C (INCORRECT): Create a read replica in another region and route read traffic via API Gateway query strings. Read replicas only offload read queries; writes still hit the primary and cause high connection counts. Routing based on query strings adds complexity and does not solve the spike of write connections on the primary DB. Option D (INCORRECT): Migrate from Aurora PostgreSQL to DynamoDB using AWS DMS. Moving to DynamoDB is a major architectural change and not the “least possible change.” It requires rewriting data models, Lambda code, and potentially business logic—far more effort than necessary to solve connection pooling issues. Option B (CORRECT): Use Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the Aurora PostgreSQL database and point the Lambda function to the proxy endpoint. RDS Proxy maintains a pool of established connections and reuses them for incoming Lambda invocations, drastically reducing new connection overhead. It improves database efficiency under high concurrency by limiting the number of active connections, lowering CPU/memory usage, and preventing timeouts. Implementation requires minimal code change—just switch the database endpoint to the RDS Proxy endpoint. In summary, using Amazon RDS Proxy addresses the surge of connections with minimal application changes, resolves timeout errors, and optimizes database performance. This question belongs to Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company deploys Amazon EC2 instances that run in a VPC. The EC2 instances load source data into Amazon S3 buckets so that the data can be processed in the future. According to compliance laws, the data must not be transmitted over the public internet. Servers in the company's on-premises data center will consume the output from an application that runs on the EC2 instances. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Deploy an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon EC2. Create an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection between the company and the VPC.
Deploy a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3. Set up an AWS Direct Connect connection between the on-premises network and the VPC.
Set up an AWS Transit Gateway connection from the VPC to the S3 buckets. Create an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection between the company and the VPC.
Set up proxy EC2 instances that have routes to NAT gateways. Configure the proxy EC2 instances to fetch S3 data and feed the application instances.
explanation: The correct Answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): “Deploy an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon EC2. Create an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection between the company and the VPC.” An interface endpoint for EC2 only provides private access to EC2 API operations—it does not allow EC2 instances to route traffic to S3 privately. Although a Site-to-Site VPN gives private connectivity for on-prem to VPC, EC2-to-S3 traffic would still traverse the public internet because there is no S3 gateway endpoint in this design. Option C (INCORRECT): “Set up an AWS Transit Gateway connection from the VPC to the S3 buckets. Create an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection between the company and the VPC.” AWS Transit Gateway cannot be used as a direct endpoint for S3; you need a gateway VPC endpoint to access S3 over the AWS private network. Even with Transit Gateway, without a gateway endpoint for S3 the EC2-to-S3 path would fall back to the public internet. Option D (INCORRECT): “Set up proxy EC2 instances that have routes to NAT gateways. Configure the proxy EC2 instances to fetch S3 data and feed the application instances.” Using NAT gateways forces outbound traffic through the public internet, violating the compliance requirement that data must not traverse the internet. Managing custom proxy instances adds operational overhead and does not guarantee a fully private path to S3. Option B (CORRECT): “Deploy a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3. Set up an AWS Direct Connect connection between the on-premises network and the VPC.” A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 ensures that EC2-to-S3 traffic stays within the AWS global network and never traverses the public internet. AWS Direct Connect provides a dedicated, private network link between the on-premises data center and the VPC, so the output consumed by on-prem servers also never uses the public internet. This architecture fully meets the compliance requirement for private data transfer in both directions. In summary, we learned that combining a gateway VPC endpoint for S3 with AWS Direct Connect ensures end-to-end private connectivity—no traffic ever uses the public internet. This question belongs to Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures, as it focuses on securing data in transit and meeting compliance requirements.

question: A company previously migrated its data warehouse solution to AWS. The company also has an AWS Direct Connect connection. Corporate office users query the data warehouse using a visualization tool. The average size of a query returned by the data warehouse is 50 MB and each webpage sent by the visualization tool is approximately 500 KB. Result sets returned by the data warehouse are not cached. Which solution provides the LOWEST data transfer egress cost for the company?
options: Host the visualization tool on premises and query the data warehouse directly over the internet.
Host the visualization tool in the same AWS Region as the data warehouse. Access it over the internet.
Host the visualization tool on premises and query the data warehouse directly over a Direct Connect connection at a location in the same AWS Region.
Host the visualization tool in the same AWS Region as the data warehouse and access it over a Direct Connect connection at a location in the same Region.
explanation: Option A (INCORRECT): Host the visualization tool on premises and query the data warehouse directly over the internet. Every query returns 50 MB over the public internet, incurring high egress fees (≈0.05 GB × $0.09/GB = $0.0045 per query). Not cost-optimal compared to Direct Connect alternatives. Option B (INCORRECT): Host the visualization tool in the same AWS Region as the data warehouse and access it over the internet. Data warehouse → visualization is internal (no charge), but each webpage (≈0.5 MB) is delivered over the internet at $0.09/GB ≈ $0.000044 per query. Better than A, but still more expensive than using Direct Connect for that 0.5 MB. Option C (INCORRECT): Host the visualization tool on premises and query the data warehouse directly over a Direct Connect connection. 50 MB per query over Direct Connect at $0.02/GB ≈ $0.001 per query. Although cheaper than internet, you’re still transferring the full 50 MB back on-premises each time. Option D (CORRECT): Host the visualization tool in the same AWS Region as the data warehouse and access it over the existing Direct Connect connection. Data warehouse to visualization traffic is internal—no egress charges for the 50 MB result sets. Only the rendered webpage (~0.5 MB) traverses Direct Connect at $0.02/GB ≈ $0.00001 per query, the lowest possible egress cost. Summary: By colocating the visualization tool alongside the data warehouse and leveraging Direct Connect, you avoid egress on the large 50 MB result sets and only pay a minimal fee for the 0.5 MB webpage. This question tests your ability to minimize data transfer costs—Domain 4 – Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company wants to use an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB cluster to simplify time-consuming database administrative tasks for production database workloads. The company wants to ensure that its database is highly available and will provide automatic failover support in most scenarios in less than 40 seconds. The company wants to offload reads off of the primary instance and keep costs as low as possible. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Use an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment. Create one read replica and point the read workload to the read replica.
Use an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB duster deployment Create two read replicas and point the read workload to the read replicas.
Use an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment. Point the read workload to the secondary instances in the Multi-AZ pair.
Use an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment Point the read workload to the reader endpoint.
explanation: The correct answer is D Option A (INCORRECT): “Use an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment. Create one read replica and point the read workload to the read replica.” Standard RDS Multi-AZ failover can take 60–120 seconds (not within the required 40s). The standby in a Multi-AZ pair is not open for reads—you must provision a separate read replica, adding cost and complexity. Option B (INCORRECT): “Use an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment. Create two read replicas and point the read workload to the read replicas.” Provisioning two read replicas when one suffices increases costs unnecessarily. An Aurora DB cluster already provides a built-in reader endpoint; you don’t need to create extra replicas manually. Option C (INCORRECT): “Use an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment. Point the read workload to the secondary instance in the Multi-AZ pair.” Multi-AZ standbys are for failover only and cannot serve read traffic. There is no mechanism to route reads to the standby in a standard RDS Multi-AZ setup. Option D (CORRECT): “Use an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment. Point the read workload to the reader endpoint.” Aurora PostgreSQL (an RDS DB cluster) provides automated failover in under 30 seconds, satisfying the The cluster’s reader endpoint automatically load-balances and offloads read traffic to replicas. You only need one writer and one reader instance—minimizing cost while ensuring high availability. In summary, an Aurora PostgreSQL Multi-AZ DB cluster with its reader endpoint meets the company’s goals for sub-40 second failover, read scaling, and cost efficiency. This question belongs to Domain 2 – Design Resilient Architectures.

question: A company has a large data workload that runs for 6 hours each day. The company cannot lose any data while the process is running. A solutions architect is designing an Amazon EMR cluster configuration to support this critical data workload. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Configure a long-running cluster that runs the primary node and core nodes on On-Demand Instances and the task nodes on Spot Instances.
Configure a transient cluster that runs the primary node and core nodes on On-Demand Instances and the task nodes on Spot Instances.
Configure a transient cluster that runs the primary node on an On-Demand Instance and the core nodes and task nodes on Spot Instances.
Configure a long-running cluster that runs the primary node on an On-Demand Instance, the core nodes on Spot Instances, and the task nodes on Spot Instances.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): Configure a long-running cluster that runs the primary node and core nodes on On-Demand Instances and the task nodes on Spot Instances. This uses On-Demand core nodes (safe for data) but keeps the cluster alive 24/7, causing unnecessary idle costs outside the 6-hour window. The requirement is to be MOST cost-effective, which rules out paying for idle compute. Option C (INCORRECT): Configure a transient cluster that runs the primary node on an On-Demand Instance and the core nodes and task nodes on Spot Instances. Putting core nodes on Spot Instances risks losing HDFS data if a Spot interruption occurs during the 6-hour run. Since core nodes store and replicate data, they must be On-Demand to prevent any data loss. Option D (INCORRECT): Configure a long-running cluster that runs the primary node on an On-Demand Instance, the core nodes on Spot Instances, and the task nodes on Spot Instances. Core nodes on Spot Instances are vulnerable to interruptions, risking data loss in a critical workload. Additionally, a long-running cluster incurs idle costs outside the daily 6-hour processing window. Option B (CORRECT): Configure a transient cluster that runs the primary node and core nodes on On-Demand Instances and the task nodes on Spot Instances. Primary and core nodes on On-Demand ensure data is safely stored and replicated throughout the job. Task nodes are stateless, so using Spot Instances for them reduces cost without risking data loss. A transient cluster only runs during the 6-hour workload and terminates afterward, eliminating idle compute charges. In summary, we learned that for critical EMR workloads where no data can be lost, core nodes must be On-Demand, task nodes can be Spot, and using a transient cluster minimizes cost by avoiding idle runtime. This question belongs to Domain 4 - Design Cost-Optimized Architectures.

question: A company is developing a marketing communications service that targets mobile app users. The company needs to send confirmation messages with Short Message Service (SMS) to its users. The users must be able to reply to the SMS messages. The company must store the responses for a year for analysis. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
options: Create an Amazon Connect contact flow to send the SMS messages. Use AWS Lambda to process the responses.
Build an Amazon Pinpoint journey. Configure Amazon Pinpoint to send events to an Amazon Kinesis data stream for analysis and archiving.
Use Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) to distribute the SMS messages. Use AWS Lambda to process the responses.
Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) FIFO topic. Subscribe an Amazon Kinesis data stream to the SNS topic for analysis and archiving.
explanation: The correct answer is B. Option A (INCORRECT): Create an Amazon Connect contact flow to send the SMS messages. Use AWS Lambda to process the responses. Amazon Connect is a contact-center solution optimized for voice and chat, not bulk marketing SMS. While Connect can send SMS, it isn’t designed for customer journeys or large‐scale two‐way messaging for marketing use cases. You’d have to build and manage custom logic to capture replies and store them; there’s no native analytic or archiving pipeline for SMS responses. Option C (INCORRECT): Use Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) to distribute the SMS messages. Use AWS Lambda to process the responses. SQS is a message queue—it cannot natively send SMS. You would need a custom poller or Lambda to dequeue requests and then call SNS or Pinpoint for SMS delivery, adding complexity. Inbound replies have no direct path into SQS; you’d need to stitch together SNS, Lambda, and storage yourself. Option D (INCORRECT): Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) FIFO topic. Subscribe an Amazon Kinesis data stream to the SNS topic for analysis and archiving. SNS can send SMS, but it does not support two-way SMS; replies are not captured by SNS. FIFO topics are for ordered message delivery between AWS services, not for SMS ordering or receipt. There is no native mechanism for inbound SMS replies to flow into SNS or Kinesis without custom integrations. Option B (CORRECT): Build an Amazon Pinpoint journey. Configure Amazon Pinpoint to send events to an Amazon Kinesis data stream for analysis and archiving. Amazon Pinpoint is the AWS service built for marketing campaigns, multi-channel messaging, and two-way SMS conversations. It natively supports inbound SMS replies when you configure a dedicated long code or short code and set up event streaming. By enabling Pinpoint Event Stream to Kinesis Data Streams (or Firehose), all delivery events and user replies can be captured, analyzed, and stored (e.g., in S3) for a full year. This approach minimizes custom code, leverages managed services, and meets both the two-way messaging and long-term retention requirements. Summary: We learned that for large-scale, two-way SMS marketing you should use Amazon Pinpoint, which is designed for customer journeys and event streaming. Inbound replies can flow directly into Kinesis for downstream analysis and archival. This question falls under Domain 3 - Design High-Performing Architectures.

question: A company stores its application logs in an Amazon CloudWatch Logs log group. A new policy requires the company to store all application logs in Amazon OpenSearch Service (Amazon Elasticsearch Service) in near-real time. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Configure a CloudWatch Logs subscription to stream the logs to Amazon OpenSearch Service (Amazon Elasticsearch Service).
Create an AWS Lambda function. Use the log group to invoke the function to write the logs to Amazon OpenSearch Service (Amazon Elasticsearch Service).

Create an Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream. Configure the log group as the delivery streams sources. Configure Amazon OpenSearch Service (Amazon Elasticsearch Service) as the delivery stream's destination.

Install and configure Amazon Kinesis Agent on each application server to deliver the logs to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Configure Kinesis Data Streams to deliver the logs to Amazon OpenSearch Service (Amazon Elasticsearch Service).
explanation: The correct Answer is A. Option B (INCORRECT): “Create an AWS Lambda function. Use the log group to invoke the function to write the logs to Amazon OpenSearch Service.” This adds custom code you must maintain, monitor, and scale. Lambda concurrency and error handling introduce operational overhead. Not the lowest-touch, fully managed path for near-real-time streaming. Option C (INCORRECT): “Create an Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream. Configure the log group as the delivery stream’s source. Configure Amazon OpenSearch Service as the destination.” Firehose does give you automatic buffering and delivery to OpenSearch, but you still manage a Firehose stream and its IAM roles, encryption, and retry settings. You introduce another service to configure, monitor, and possibly transform data. While fully managed, it’s more moving parts than a direct subscription filter. Option D (INCORRECT): “Install and configure Amazon Kinesis Agent on each application server to deliver the logs to Kinesis Data Streams, then deliver to OpenSearch.” You must install and manage agents on every server. Kinesis Data Streams requires shard management, scaling, and throughput provisioning. This adds the most operational overhead of all options. Option A (CORRECT): “Configure a CloudWatch Logs subscription to stream the logs to Amazon OpenSearch Service.” CloudWatch Logs subscription filters can natively stream directly into Amazon OpenSearch Service. No additional servers, agents, or custom code to manage—fully managed by AWS. Provides near-real-time delivery with minimal configuration and ongoing operational overhead. In summary, we learned that the simplest, lowest-maintenance way to get CloudWatch Logs into OpenSearch in near real time is to use a built-in subscription filter. This question falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures, since it focuses on choosing the most efficient, low-latency streaming solution with minimal operational burden.

question: A company is deploying a two-tier web application in a VPC. The web tier is using an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group with public subnets that span multiple Availability Zones. The database tier consists of an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance in separate private subnets. The web tier requires access to the database to retrieve product information. The web application is not working as intended. The web application reports that it cannot connect to the database. The database is confirmed to be up and running. All configurations for the network ACLs, security groups, and route tables are still in their default states. What should a solutions architect recommend to fix the application?
options: Add an explicit rule to the private subnet’s network ACL to allow traffic from the web tier’s EC2 instances.
Add a route in the VPC route table to allow traffic between the web tier’s EC2 instances and the database tier.
Deploy the web tier's EC2 instances and the database tier’s RDS instance into two separate VPCs, and configure VPC peering.
Add an inbound rule to the security group of the database tier’s RDS instance to allow traffic from the web tiers security group.
explanation: The correct answer is Option D. Option A (INCORRECT): “Add an explicit rule to the private subnet’s network ACL to allow traffic from the web tier’s EC2 instances.” By default, the network ACL on a new VPC allows all inbound and outbound traffic. There is no need to modify it for intra-VPC communication unless it was explicitly changed. Changing the NACL is unnecessary when the default settings already permit the traffic. Option B (INCORRECT): “Add a route in the VPC route table to allow traffic between the web tier’s EC2 instances and the database tier.” The main route table for a VPC already contains a local route (Destination: 10.0.0.0/16 or your VPC CIDR) that enables traffic between all subnets in the VPC by default. No additional route is required for instances in public subnets to reach resources in private subnets within the same VPC. Option C (INCORRECT): “Deploy the web tier's EC2 instances and the database tier’s RDS instance into two separate VPCs, and configure VPC peering.” This adds unnecessary complexity and cost when both tiers can reside in the same VPC. VPC peering is intended for communication across different VPCs or accounts, which isn’t required here. Option D (CORRECT): “Add an inbound rule to the security group of the database tier’s RDS instance to allow traffic from the web tier’s security group.” By default, a newly created security group denies all inbound traffic. You must explicitly allow port 3306 (MySQL) or your chosen DB port. Referencing the web tier’s security group as the inbound source ensures that only the EC2 instances in that group can connect to the RDS instance. This is the standard, secure method to permit intra-VPC communication between tiers. In summary, the default network ACLs and route tables already allow intra-VPC traffic, but security groups are stateful and deny inbound traffic by default. To enable the web tier to communicate with the database, you must add an inbound rule to the RDS security group. This question belongs to Domain 1 – Design Secure Architectures.

question: A company runs an ecommerce application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The instances run in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. The Auto Scaling group scales based on CPU utilization metrics. The ecommerce application stores the transaction data in a MySQL 8.0 database that is hosted on a large EC2 instance. The database's performance degrades quickly as application load increases. The application handles more read requests than write transactions. The company wants a solution that will automatically scale the database to meet the demand of unpredictable read workloads while maintaining high availability. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Use Amazon Redshift with a single node for leader and compute functionality.
Use Amazon RDS with a Single-AZ deployment Configure Amazon RDS to add reader instances in a different Availability Zone.
Use Amazon Aurora with a Multi-AZ deployment. Configure Aurora Auto Scaling with Aurora Replicas.
Use Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached with EC2 Spot Instances.
explanation: The correct answer is C Option A (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon Redshift with a single node for leader and compute functionality.” Amazon Redshift is a data warehouse service optimized for complex analytical queries, not for high-throughput transactional workloads. A single-node Redshift cluster doesn’t provide the high availability or the automatic read-scaling needed for unpredictable ecommerce traffic. It’s not designed to serve as the primary OLTP database for an application that performs frequent small reads and writes. Option B (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon RDS with a Single-AZ deployment. Configure Amazon RDS to add reader instances in a different Availability Zone.” A Single-AZ primary still represents a single point of failure for writes; if the instance fails, downtime occurs until failover or manual recovery. Although you can add Read Replicas to RDS MySQL, they don’t automatically scale up or down based on load—you must manage the count and instance size manually or via custom scripts. This option lacks built-in high availability for the primary and automatic read-capacity scaling. Option D (INCORRECT): “Use Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached with EC2 Spot Instances.” ElastiCache is an in-memory data store used for caching frequently accessed data, not a primary transactional database. Spot Instances can be reclaimed at any time, making them unsuitable for critical data persistence layers. Caching may reduce read latency, but it doesn’t solve database write-throughput limitations or provide an auto-scaling, highly available database service. Option C (CORRECT): “Use Amazon Aurora with a Multi-AZ deployment. Configure Aurora Auto Scaling with Aurora Replicas.” Amazon Aurora MySQL-compatible automatically spreads storage across multiple Availability Zones and provides a highly available primary instance. Aurora Replicas share the same underlying storage and can scale out to handle unpredictable read workloads with low replication lag. Aurora Auto Scaling can add or remove replicas based on predefined CPU or connections metrics, ensuring reads scale automatically without manual intervention. This solution meets requirements for automatic read-scaling, high availability, and performance under variable load. Summary: We learned that Aurora’s built-in Multi-AZ storage, fast replicas, and Auto Scaling capabilities make it the ideal choice for unpredictable, read-heavy transaction workloads requiring high availability. This question falls under Domain 3 – Design High-Performing Architectures.
